title: Flip a Condition
story:
The staging firewall has an allowlist: one IP address per line in a file called
allowlist.txt. Priya's rule is the inverse of what you would think. She does not
care who is on the list; she cares who is not, because those get blocked and
those are the ones that wake her up. Write the check from her point of view.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: an IP address. The file
`allowlist.txt` (in the current directory) lists the allowed addresses, one
per line.
If the address is NOT listed, print
  BLOCK <ip>
If it is listed, print
  allow <ip>
The address must match a whole line exactly, and the dots are ordinary
characters (10.0.0.1 is not 10.0.0.15, and not 10x0x0x1).
Build the decision around `!` (not).
concepts: ! negates a condition
if ! command; then

required_patterns.message: Use ! to negate the test, e.g. if ! grep ...; then (or [[ ! ... ]]).

title: Does It Exist?
story:
Ollie wrote a cleanup script last week and pointed it at a path that did not
exist. It deleted nothing and printed nothing, and Ollie declared it a success.
Mara's lesson: a script should look before it leaps. Write the little
inspector every cleanup job should call first.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a path. Print exactly one line,
in the format `<path>: <kind>`, where kind is:
  regular file     if the path is a regular file
  directory        if the path is a directory
  something else   if it exists but is neither (a device, for example)
  not found        if nothing exists at that path
Use the file tests -f, -d and -e, and quote the path (it may contain spaces).
concepts: -e exists
-f regular file
-d directory

required_patterns.message: Use [[ -f ... ]] to recognise a regular file.
Use [[ -d ... ]] to recognise a directory.
Use [[ -e ... ]] to detect that something exists.

title: Permission Checks
story:
A deploy failed at midnight because someone copied a script to the server and
forgot to make it executable. Priya wants a pre-flight tool that tells you
what YOU, the user running it, can do with a file, in the same compact style
as `ls -l` does: three characters, one per right.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a path.
If nothing exists at the path, print to stderr
  no such file: <path>
and exit with status 1.
Otherwise print `<path>: ` followed by three characters describing what the
current user can do:
  r or -   (can read?)     w or -   (can write?)     x or -   (can execute?)
For example `deploy.sh: rwx` or `notes.txt: rw-` or `locked.key: ---`.
Test with -r, -w and -x (not by parsing ls).
concepts: -r readable
-w writable
-x executable

required_patterns.message: Use [[ -r ... ]] to test readability.
Use [[ -w ... ]] to test writability.
Use [[ -x ... ]] to test executability.

forbidden_patterns.message: Test the rights with -r -w -x instead of parsing ls.

title: Empty File?
story:
Gus gets a revenue CSV mailed to him at 6 a.m. every day. On Monday the mail
arrived on time with a perfectly polite attachment of zero bytes. Nobody
noticed until Gus tried to read it in a meeting. Insert a checkpoint before the
mail is sent: an empty report must stop the pipeline.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: the path of a report file.
If the file exists and has any content (size greater than zero), print
  ok: <file>, lines: <n>
where <n> is the number of lines in the file.
If the file is empty or does not exist, print to stderr
  empty or missing: <file>

Lanternfish's in-house service wrapper, `lanternctl`, is mostly a menu: say
"start", "stop", "restart" or "status" and it does the right thing. So far it

title: One-Line Decisions
story:
Theo shows off his favourite one-liner: `[[ $sev == critical ]] && notify
page-oncall || echo "logged"`. It looks lovely. Last Friday the pager service
was down, `notify` failed, and the script cheerfully logged the incident as
if nobody needed to know. Theo calls this "an unfortunate edge case". Mara
calls it a lesson. Write the one-liner properly.

  (on success it prints `paged on-call`).

  with exit status 0 and prints NOTHING to stdout in that case.
- For any other severity, print `logged: <severity>`.

Half of Lanternfish runs on Linux servers and the other half, including the
whole office, runs on Macs. The runbook tells people to "count the CPU cores
first", and Ollie tripped on the fact that the command for that is different
on each side. One script, two platforms: let it pick the right command for

title: The Deploy Gate
story:
After the pager-and-freeze incident, Mara and Priya sit down and write the
Lanternfish deploy policy on a napkin: nothing ships with red tests; staging
ships as soon as tests are green; production also needs two approvals and must
not be in a change freeze. Gus asks that it be turned into code before anyone
spills coffee on the napkin. This is the final test of the module: decisions
inside decisions.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes three arguments: ENV (`staging` or `prod`),
TESTS (`pass` or `fail`) and APPROVALS (a whole number).

  to stderr and exit 2.
- ENV other than `staging` or `prod`: print `unknown environment: <env>` to
  stderr and exit 2.
- Otherwise print exactly one line, using this policy:
    1. TESTS is not `pass`           -> BLOCKED: tests are not passing
    2. ENV is `staging`              -> DEPLOY: staging
    3. ENV is `prod` and the file `freeze.flag` exists
                                     -> BLOCKED: change freeze is active
    4. ENV is `prod` and APPROVALS < 2
                                     -> BLOCKED: prod needs 2 approvals, has <n>
    5. ENV is `prod` otherwise       -> DEPLOY: prod

the production rules.

Theo wrote a quick status script and swears it works: it reads the fleet
file, counts the machines that are down, and prints the number. It always
prints 0, even on the morning when half the harbour was offline. He has
stared at it for an hour. The starter below is his script. The loop is

title: Doubling Delays
story:
When the payment gateway hiccups, Theo's retry code hammers it every second
and makes the hiccup worse. Priya has a rule for that: each retry waits
twice as long as the one before, up to a ceiling. Before anyone changes the
real code, she wants to see the schedule on paper: how long would we wait,
attempt by attempt, and how much time does it add up to?

before the first retry), ATTEMPTS (how many retries) and CAP (the longest
single wait). The wait for attempt 1 is BASE; every later wait is double the
previous one, but never more than CAP. Print one line per attempt:
  attempt <k>: wait <seconds>s
and finally:
  total wait: <sum>s

arguments are given, print "usage: solution.sh BASE ATTEMPTS CAP" to stderr
and exit with status 2. Only compute and print the schedule: do not call sleep.

title: Loop over Command Output

Fifty servers, and Mara wants to know which disk will fill up first. The
company already has a command for that, fleet-disk, which prints one line
per server: its name and the percentage of disk used. Reading it by eye is
how people miss things at 3 a.m. She wants a script that loops over those
lines, remembers the fullest server, and counts how many are in the danger
zone. And, after the lesson of the last few levels, it must not lose its
variables.

output looks like "<host> <percent>", with the percent as a whole number
without a % sign. Using a loop over that output, find the server with the

servers with MORE than 80 percent. Print two lines:
  fullest: <host> (<percent>%)
  over 80%: <count>

The nightly backups all start at 02:00, and every night the storage array
groans under fifty simultaneous uploads. Noor suggests staggering them: the
first server starts at 02:00, the next a few minutes later, and so on. The

more) and STEP (minutes between starts, at least 1). Server number n

title: Stop at the First Match
story:
Priya is hunting for a single thing: an SSH config on the fleet that still
allows root to log in with a password. There are dozens of config files
collected from the servers, and she only needs to know whether at least one
is guilty, and which. Reading the rest after the first hit would be a waste,
and some of the files, she warns, were never copied over at all.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes config file paths as arguments and searches them
in the given order for a line that starts with "PermitRootLogin" followed by
whitespace and "yes" (a line starting with # is a comment and does not
count). Stop at the first file that matches.
- Found: print "first insecure config: <path>" and exit with status 0.
- Not found in any file: print "no insecure config found" and exit 1.
Files that do not exist are skipped quietly. With no arguments print
"usage: solution.sh FILE..." to stderr and exit with status 2.

as you have a match. Remember what you found in a variable.

grep -q as a yes/no test in if
a flag variable tells what happened after the loop

title: Background Jobs and wait
story:
The health sweep takes one second per server, which is fine for one server
and a coffee break for fifty. Mara looks at the clock on the wall. "The
servers do not depend on each other. Ask all of them at the same moment,
then collect the answers." The probe tool, probe-host, answers after one
second. Your script must not take longer than the slowest single probe.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes server names as arguments and checks them all
at the same time with `probe-host NAME` (it prints "up" or "down" after one
second). Start every probe in the background with `&`, then `wait` for all
of them. When all have finished, print one line per server IN THE ORDER OF
THE ARGUMENTS, whatever order the probes finished in:
  <name>: <up or down>
and finally:
  checked <N> hosts
The tests give you five seconds in total, so six probes one after another
would be too slow. Keep each probe's answer in a file inside a directory
made with mktemp -d, and remove that directory at the end.
With no arguments print "usage: solution.sh HOST..." to stderr and exit 2.

wait blocks until all background jobs are done
collect results in files, print in a fixed order

title: Return a Status
story:
Priya is building a cron job that watches disk usage and wants its answer as a
status code, the way every Unix tool reports back: 0 means "fine", anything else
means "look at me", and different numbers can say different things. You are
writing the checker she will plug in.

number). Define a function named check_disk that takes that percentage and uses
the return command to give back a status:

  80 to 94        return 1
  95 or more      return 2

variable and prints:
  disk <PCT>% -> status <N>
and then exits with that same status number (exit "$code").

$? holds the status of the last command, including a function

title: Local Variables
story:
Gus wants a tiny invoice calculator for hosting add-ons: quantity times unit
price, plus a flat 10 percent harbour tax. Ollie wrote the first version, and
Theo noticed it leaves its scratch variables lying around where later code can
trip over them. "Housekeeping," says Mara. "A function should clean up after
itself."

variables without local are global

Noor's support desk sets disk quotas by hand and last month someone typed

story:
Every five minutes the monitoring box dumps one line per server into a file:
the server name and its CPU load in percent. Gus wants it as a tidy status board
on the lobby screen, with a colour-free OK, WARN or CRIT label at the end of
each row. The formatting code is the same for every server, so it should be written

host and a percentage and prints one row with
  printf '%-10s %3d%%  %s\n' HOST PERCENT LABEL
where LABEL is  CRIT  for 90 and above,  WARN  for 70 to 89, otherwise  OK.
Call print_row from inside a while read -r loop, once per input line. Skip
blank lines. After the loop print
  rows: <number of rows printed>
Example input line "dory 45" gives:  dory        45%  OK
concepts: call a function once per loop iteration
while read -r a b; do fn "$a" "$b"; done

required_patterns.message: Define a function called print_row.
Read the lines with  while read -r host pct; do ... done.
Use the format '%-10s %3d%%  %s\n' inside print_row.

test_cases.name: three servers
test_cases.expected_stdout:
dory        45%  OK
marlin      72%  WARN
grouper     95%  CRIT
rows: 3

test_cases.name: thresholds
test_cases.expected_stdout:
a           69%  OK
b           70%  WARN
c           89%  WARN
d           90%  CRIT
rows: 4

title: Redefining a Function
story:
The platform team ships a shared script called defaults.sh with sensible
behaviour for every Lanternfish site: backups are kept for 30 days and
notifications are printed plainly. The Eel Street site is special: its
customers pay for 90-day retention, and its notices have to carry the ops desk
tag so they land in the right inbox. Nobody may edit the shared file. You
customise by overriding.
objective:
The shared library is fixtures/defaults.sh. It defines three functions:
notify, retention_days and report. report SITE calls the other two.
Write solution.sh that:
  1. loads the library with source,
  2. AFTER loading it, redefines  retention_days  so it prints 90, and
     redefines  notify  so it prints  [ops-desk] <all its arguments>,
  3. calls  report "$1"  (the library's own function, do not redefine it).
Expected output for the argument eel-street:
  [ops-desk] eel-street keeps backups for 90 days
If no argument is given, print "usage: solution.sh SITE" to stderr and exit 2.
Do not edit or copy the library; the point is that a later definition replaces
an earlier one.
concepts: defining a function again replaces the earlier definition
override after sourcing, and report keeps working with the new versions

required_patterns.message: Redefine retention_days AFTER sourcing fixtures/defaults.sh.
Redefine notify AFTER sourcing fixtures/defaults.sh.

forbidden_patterns.message: Leave report alone: it must pick up your new versions of the two helpers.

test_cases.name: site name with spaces
test_cases.expected_stdout: [ops-desk] north pier keeps backups for 90 days

title: A die() Helper
story:
Theo's scripts fail in forty different ways and with forty different messages:
"oops", "ERROR!!", a bare exit 1, once even a joke about Mondays. Priya wants
one convention. Every fatal problem goes through a single helper that prints an
"error:" line on stderr and ends the script with a meaningful status. Perl
programmers call it die; Bash programmers copy the name.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one argument: a file name. Define a function named
die that takes an exit CODE followed by a MESSAGE (which may be several
words). It prints  error: <message>  to stderr and then exits the whole script
with CODE.
Use die for every failure in the script:
  no argument given:      error: usage: solution.sh FILE      (exit 2)
  file does not exist:    error: no such file: <FILE>          (exit 3)
  file exists but empty:  error: file is empty: <FILE>         (exit 4)
Otherwise print  <FILE>: <N> lines  (N = number of lines in the file).
Use set -euo pipefail at the top.
concepts: die() { echo "error: $*" >&2; exit "$code"; }
exit inside a function ends the whole script

required_patterns.message: Define a function called die.
die should call exit, and the main script should call it like: die 3 "message".
Send the error message to stderr with >&2.

title: A log() Helper
story:
Marlin's disk-watch script is noisy: when everything is fine it still prints
twelve lines, and when something is wrong the important line is lost among them.
Priya wants levels. Debug chatter appears only when asked, warnings and errors
are tagged clearly, and the verbosity is chosen with an environment variable so
the cron job can stay quiet while a human can turn the noise up.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one argument PCT (disk usage, a whole number).
Define a function named log that takes a LEVEL word and a message:
    log INFO "checking disk usage"
It prints  [LEVEL] message  to stderr, but only when LEVEL is at least as
important as the threshold in the environment variable LOG_LEVEL
(default INFO). Importance order, lowest first: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR.
The main script runs, in this order:
    log DEBUG "raw argument: <PCT>"
    log INFO  "checking disk usage"
    PCT >= 90:  log ERROR "disk almost full: <PCT>%"
    PCT >= 75:  log WARN  "disk filling up: <PCT>%"     (when not >= 90)
    and finally prints to stdout:   checked: <PCT>%
Example: PCT=80 with the default threshold prints to stderr
    [INFO] checking disk usage
    [WARN] disk filling up: 80%
Use ${LOG_LEVEL:-INFO} for the default. The script exits 0 in every case.
concepts: a log helper with a threshold
level names mapped to numbers with case
defaults from the environment: ${LOG_LEVEL:-INFO}

required_patterns.message: Define a function called log.
Read the threshold with ${LOG_LEVEL:-INFO}.
Log lines go to stderr (>&2).

test_cases.expected_stderr:
[INFO] checking disk usage
[WARN] disk filling up: 80%

test_cases.name: error
test_cases.expected_stderr:
[INFO] checking disk usage
[ERROR] disk almost full: 95%

title: Name References
story:
Noor pastes hostnames from customer tickets into a file, one per line, and the
same host shows up three times because three customers complained. Ollie needs the
list without repeats, in order of first appearance. He also wants the dedupe rule
in a helper that can fill any list you name, because the invoice script needs
the same thing for customer codes. A helper that modifies the caller's list needs
a way to be told which list.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It reads one word per line from stdin. Blank lines are ignored.
An array is a variable holding a list: seen=() makes an empty one, seen+=("x")
appends, ${#seen[@]} is its length and "${seen[@]}" expands to every element.
Define a function named add_unique that takes the NAME of an array variable and a
VALUE. Inside, use a name reference  local -n  to work on that array, and append
VALUE only if it is not already in the array (exact, case-sensitive match).
Then the main script does:
    seen=()
    for each non-blank line: add_unique seen "$line"
    print   unique: <number of elements>
    print   one line per element, in order:   - <element>
Remember: pass the NAME (seen), not its value ($seen).
concepts: local -n ref=$1 makes ref an alias for the variable whose name is in $1
a function can fill the caller's array

required_patterns.message: Define a function called add_unique.
Use a name reference: local -n list=$1

test_cases.name: case matters and blanks are skipped

title: Return Several Values
story:
Gus wants a one-line summary of the response times (in milliseconds) from the
latest health-check run: fastest, slowest and total. Ollie's first version
walked through the numbers three times, once per answer. Mara shows him a neater
way: compute everything in one pass and let the function hand back all three
answers together, so the caller can unpack them in one go.
objective:
Write solution.sh. The arguments are whole numbers (they may be negative). Define a
function named stats that goes through all its arguments once and prints a single
line with three values separated by spaces:   <min> <max> <sum>
Use printf for that line. The main script captures the line and splits it into
three variables with  read -r min max sum <<< "$(stats "$@")"  and prints:
  min=<min> max=<max> sum=<sum>
With no arguments print "no numbers given" to stderr and exit 1 (before calling
stats).
concepts: a function prints several values on one line
read -r a b c <<< "$(fn)" splits them into variables

required_patterns.message: Define a function called stats.
Unpack the three values with  read -r min max sum <<< "$(stats "$@")".
Print the three values with printf.

title: Your Function Toolkit
story:
Friday afternoon, and Mara hands you the last job of the month: the new-customer
provisioning script. It has to take a business name and a disk quota, refuse nonsense,
explain what it is doing, and print the customer's home directory. "Five small
functions," she says, "each doing one thing. If any of them is longer than ten
lines, you are doing it wrong." This is where everything from the module comes together.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as  ./solution.sh NAME GB  (NAME may contain spaces if
quoted). Build it from these five functions, with exactly these names:
  die CODE MESSAGE...   prints "error: <message>" to stderr, exits with CODE
  log LEVEL MESSAGE...  prints "[LEVEL] message" to stderr
  slugify TEXT          prints TEXT lowercased, with every run of characters other
                        than a-z and 0-9 replaced by one hyphen, and no hyphen at
                        either end (use tr -cs and sed -E)
  valid_quota VALUE     succeeds (status 0) only if VALUE is a whole number from 1 to 500
  tier_for GB           prints small (up to 50), medium (up to 200) or large
The script then:
  1. fewer than 2 arguments:        die 2 "usage: solution.sh NAME GB"
  2. slug = $(slugify "$1"); empty:  die 3 "name has no usable characters"
  3. if ! valid_quota "$2":          die 4 "invalid quota: <GB>"
  4. log INFO "provisioning <slug>"
     log INFO "quota <GB>GB, tier <tier>"        (tier from $(tier_for ...))
  5. print to stdout:  home=/srv/customers/<slug>
Use set -euo pipefail. Check validity with valid_quota directly in an if.
concepts: small single-purpose functions combined into one script
status, stdout and stderr each used for what they are best at

required_patterns.message: Define die.
Define log.
Define slugify.
Define valid_quota.
Define tier_for.
Use the function directly as a condition: if ! valid_quota "$2"; then
Capture the slug with $(slugify "$1").
Capture the tier with $(tier_for "$2").

test_cases.name: name with nothing usable
test_cases.expected_stderr: error: name has no usable characters

title: How Long Is It?
story:
Theo is adding a signup form to the Lanternfish customer portal. The database
column for usernames holds at most 12 characters, and he is tired of the
cryptic "value too long" crash on the server. He asks for a tiny pre-check
that counts characters in a username and says whether it will fit.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a proposed username (it may be
empty and it may contain spaces). Print exactly two lines:

  length=<number of characters>
  status=<ok|too-short|too-long>

A username is "too-short" with fewer than 3 characters, "too-long" with more
than 12, and "ok" otherwise (3 to 12 inclusive). Count the characters with
Bash's own length expansion, not with an external command.
concepts: ${#var} is the length of the value
the length of an empty string is 0

required_patterns.message: Use the length expansion ${#name} to count the characters.

forbidden_patterns.message: Bash can count its own strings: use ${#name} instead of wc, awk or expr.

title: Substrings by Offset
story:
The backup robot at Lanternfish stamps every snapshot with a compact
timestamp like 20241107T093015, and Gus cannot read them at a glance. He
wants a friendly version for the monthly report. Because the stamp is
fixed-width, every piece sits at the same position, which is exactly what
offsets are for.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a timestamp in the exact form
YYYYMMDDThhmmss (15 characters, for example 20241107T093015). Print:

  date=YYYY-MM-DD
  time=hh:mm:ss

Cut the pieces out with substring expansion (offset and length). Do not use
cut, awk, sed, or date.
concepts: ${var:offset:length} extracts part of a value
offsets start counting at 0

required_patterns.message: Cut each piece with ${name:offset:length}, for example ${stamp:4:2}.

forbidden_patterns.message: The stamp is fixed-width: slice it with ${name:offset:length} instead of an external tool.

title: Counting from the End
story:
Priya found API keys pasted in full into a support ticket and has declared war
on it. From now on, anything that echoes a key must show only the last four
characters, enough for a human to recognise which key it was and nothing a
thief could use. Keys come in different lengths, so counting from the front
will not work.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, an API key. Print one line:

  masked=****<last 4 characters of the key>

If the key has fewer than 4 characters it is not a real key: print
"key too short" to stderr and exit with status 1 (print nothing to stdout).
Take the tail with a negative offset in a substring expansion.
concepts: ${var: -N} takes the last N characters
the space before the minus sign matters

required_patterns.message: Take the tail with a negative offset such as ${key: -4} (note the space before the minus).

forbidden_patterns.message: Use a negative offset in the substring expansion instead of an external tool.

test_cases.name: key with a dash at the end

title: Strip a Prefix
story:
Noor pastes customer links into tickets, and the link checker only wants the
part after the scheme: no "https://", no "ftp://". Some of the links are
sign-in redirects that carry a second full address in their query, and Noor
warns that those must keep that second address intact. Only the very first
scheme marker should go.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a URL, and prints it without its
scheme: everything up to and including the FIRST "://" is removed, and nothing
else.

  ./solution.sh https://shop.example/menu      prints  shop.example/menu

A URL with a second "://" later on (in a redirect) must keep it. A string with
no "://" at all is printed unchanged. Use the remove-shortest-prefix
expansion with a pattern; do not use sed, cut or awk.
concepts: ${var#pattern} removes the shortest matching prefix
* in a pattern matches any run of characters

required_patterns.message: Remove the prefix with ${name#pattern}, for example ${url#*://}.

forbidden_patterns.message: This level is about the # expansion: strip the prefix in Bash itself.
Use a single # here: it stops at the first match, so a second :// later in the URL survives.

title: Strip the Longest Prefix
story:
Ollie is building a dashboard of the largest log files and has a column of
full paths such as /var/log/nginx/error.log. The dashboard only has room for
the file name. He tried a quick one-liner but it kept trimming just the first
slash. Mara says it is time he met the greedy version of the trick.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes any number of paths as arguments. For each one,
print a line in this exact form:

  <path> -> <file name>

where the file name is everything after the LAST "/" (the whole path when it
has no slash, and an empty name when the path ends with a slash). Use the
remove-longest-prefix expansion; do not call basename, sed or awk.
concepts: ${var##pattern} removes the longest matching prefix
${var##*/} leaves the last path component

required_patterns.message: Strip the longest prefix with ${name##pattern}, for example ${path##*/}.

forbidden_patterns.message: The point of this level is ${name##*/}: no basename, sed, awk, cut or rev.

title: Strip a Suffix
story:
The nightly job leaves compressed dumps with names like db-2024.sql.gz, and
Gus wants a restore log that names the file you get after decompressing. That
is the same name minus the last extension and nothing more: "archive.tar.gz"
must become "archive.tar", because the tar part is still there to unpack.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a file name, and prints the name
with its LAST extension removed (the last "." and everything after it):

  ./solution.sh db-2024.sql.gz      prints  db-2024.sql

A name with no dot is printed unchanged. Remove the suffix with the
remove-shortest-suffix expansion, not with sed, cut, awk or basename.
concepts: ${var%pattern} removes the shortest matching suffix
${var%.*} drops the last extension

required_patterns.message: Remove the suffix with ${name%pattern}, for example ${file%.*}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Strip the extension with the % expansion instead of an external command.
Use a single %: the double form would eat every extension, not just the last one.

test_cases.name: dot inside the name with a space

title: Strip the Longest Suffix
story:
Lanternfish servers have long fully qualified names such as
web-03.eu-west.prod.lanternfish.example, but the paging tool only has room for
the short name, "web-03". Priya's on-call rota is full of these, and some
entries are already short (a bare "localhost"). One expansion can cut a name
down to its first label whatever its length.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads host names from standard input, one per line, and
prints for each line:

  <full name>  =>  <short name>

(two spaces on each side of the arrow). The short name is the part before the
FIRST dot, or the whole line if there is no dot. Use the remove-longest-suffix
expansion. Do not use cut, sed, awk or tr.
concepts: ${var%%pattern} removes the longest matching suffix
${fqdn%%.*} is the first label of a dotted name

required_patterns.message: Cut from the first dot with the greedy suffix remover ${name%%.*}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use ${name%%.*} instead of an external command.

test_cases.name: three full names
test_cases.expected_stdout:
web-03.eu-west.prod.lanternfish.example  =>  web-03
db-01.prod.lanternfish.example  =>  db-01
cache.lanternfish.example  =>  cache

title: Replace the First Match
story:
Marlin is replacing the old database host "eel". The connection list in a
customer's config is a comma-separated string of host:port entries, and the
first entry is the primary. Theo wants to move only the primary to the new
machine and leave the read replicas pointing where they are, even though they
may share the old name.
objective:
Write solution.sh taking three arguments: LIST, OLD and NEW. LIST is a
comma-separated string such as "eel:5432,eel:5433". Print LIST with the FIRST
occurrence of OLD replaced by NEW and every later occurrence untouched.
If OLD does not occur, print LIST as it was. OLD is plain text, not a pattern
(it may contain characters like [ or *), so quote it inside the expansion.
Use ${var/pattern/replacement}; no sed, awk or tr.
concepts: ${var/old/new} replaces the first match only
quoting "$old" makes the search text literal

required_patterns.message: Replace the first match with ${name/old/new} (a single slash).

forbidden_patterns.message: Do the replacement with ${name/old/new} instead of an external tool.
A double slash would replace every match; this level wants only the first.

test_cases.name: search text is literal, not a pattern
star is not a wildcard here

title: Replace Every Match
story:
Customers upload documents with names like "Tidewater Books / Q3 report.pdf".
The storage service rejects spaces and slashes, and Noor is tired of renaming
files by hand. The rule agreed with Priya: every space becomes an underscore
and every slash becomes a dash, so nothing can sneak into a different folder.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, an uploaded file name, and prints a
safe version of it:
  - every space becomes "_"
  - every "/" becomes "-"
All other characters stay as they are. The whole name may be empty. Use
${var//old/new} replacements; do not use tr, sed or awk.
concepts: ${var//old/new} replaces every match
a slash inside the pattern needs a backslash

required_patterns.message: Replace every occurrence with a double slash: ${name//old/new}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use ${name//old/new} instead of an external tool.

title: Anchored Replacements
story:
Lanternfish is moving its logs from /var/log/legacy to /var/log/lanternfish and
switching the rotated files from ".log" to ".log.gz". The migration list is
full of tricky paths: some mention "legacy" twice, some live elsewhere and only
look similar. Mara insists that only the true start of a path and the true
end of a name be touched.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads paths from standard input, one per line, and
prints each one after two anchored changes:
  1. if the path BEGINS with "/var/log/legacy/", replace that beginning with
     "/var/log/lanternfish/"
  2. if the path ENDS with ".log", replace that ending with ".log.gz"
Matches in the middle of a path must not change. Use the anchored forms
${var/#old/new} (start) and ${var/%old/new} (end). No sed or awk.
concepts: ${var/#old/new} replaces only at the start
${var/%old/new} replaces only at the end

required_patterns.message: Replace the beginning with ${name/#old/new}.
Replace the ending with ${name/%old/new}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use the anchored expansions ${name/#old/new} and ${name/%old/new}.

test_cases.name: legacy in the middle is left alone
log in the middle is left alone

title: UPPER and lower
story:
Two systems at Lanternfish disagree about MAC addresses. The DHCP server wants
them in capitals, like AA:BB:0C:1D:2E:3F, while the inventory database stores
them in lowercase and compares strings exactly. Ollie pastes addresses in
whatever mix of cases the network card vendor used, and the two tools keep
rejecting them.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a MAC address in any mix of upper and
lower case. Print two lines:

  dhcp=<the address in UPPERCASE>
  inventory=<the address in lowercase>

Digits and colons stay as they are. Use the case-changing parameter expansions;
do not use tr, awk or sed. (The tests use plain ASCII letters.)
concepts: ${var^^} converts every letter to uppercase
${var,,} converts every letter to lowercase

required_patterns.message: Make the DHCP form with ${name^^}.
Make the inventory form with ${name,,}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Bash can change case itself: ${name^^} and ${name,,}.

title: Capitalize Words
story:
Gus is printing invoices and the customer names coming out of the signup form
are a mess: "harbour bakery", "NORTH PIER DENTAL", "gull  &  anchor pub". He
wants Title Case on every invoice, whatever the customer typed. Capitalising
the whole string is easy; doing it word by word, and lowering the rest of each
word, takes a small loop.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a customer name, and prints it in
Title Case: every word starts with a capital letter and the rest of the word
is lowercase. Words are separated by one or more spaces; in the output they
are separated by exactly one space (and there are no spaces at the start or
end). An empty name prints an empty line.
  ./solution.sh "NORTH PIER dental"   prints  North Pier Dental
Process the words one at a time. Use ${word,,} and ${word^}; no tr, sed or awk.
concepts: ${word^} capitalizes the first letter only
${word,,} lowers the rest first
for word in $name splits on whitespace

required_patterns.message: Capitalise the first letter of each word with ${word^}.
Lower the rest of the word first with ${word,,}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use the ${word^} and ${word,,} expansions instead of an external tool.

title: Trim Whitespace
story:
Noor exports the contact list from the old ticketing system, and every field
is padded with spaces and the odd tab: "   Tidewater Books  ". Those blanks
break joins in the billing database. The spaces inside a name are real, though,
and "Harbour  Bakery" must stay as typed. You need a trim that only touches the
two ends.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads lines from standard input and prints each one
between square brackets after removing ALL leading and trailing whitespace
(spaces and tabs). Whitespace inside the line is kept exactly.

  "  Tidewater  Books \t"   prints   [Tidewater  Books]

A line that is empty or only whitespace prints []. Do the trimming with
parameter expansion and an extended glob pattern (shopt -s extglob). Do not
use sed, awk, tr or xargs.
concepts: shopt -s extglob enables +( ) patterns
${var##+([[:space:]])} trims the front, ${var%%+([[:space:]])} the back

required_patterns.message: Turn on extended patterns first: shopt -s extglob.
Match a run of blanks with +([[:space:]]) inside ${var##...} and ${var%%...}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Trim with ${var##+([[:space:]])} and ${var%%+([[:space:]])} instead.

test_cases.name: only blanks and an empty line

title: Pad and Truncate
story:
Gus prints the monthly plan summary on a line printer that dislikes surprises:
the customer column must be exactly 14 characters wide and the plan column
exactly 8, however long the names are. "Gull & Anchor Pub" must be cut, "Dory
Bikes" must be padded. A report whose columns wobble gets sent back.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads lines of the form  NAME,PLAN  from standard input
(one comma, no quotes) and prints one row per line:

  |<NAME padded or cut to 14, left-aligned>|<PLAN padded or cut to 8, right-aligned>|

A shorter NAME is padded with spaces on the right, a longer one is cut at 14
characters. PLAN is right-aligned in 8 characters and cut at 8 if longer.
Use a single printf format with width and precision (for example %-10.10s); do
not use cut, awk or column.
concepts: printf %-14.14s pads and truncates
%-N left-aligns, %N right-aligns, .N cuts at N characters

required_patterns.message: Use a width and precision together, for example %-14.14s.

forbidden_patterns.message: Let printf do the padding and cutting with a format like %-14.14s.

test_cases.name: plan longer than eight is cut
empty fields still fill the width

title: Split on a Delimiter
story:
Priya is auditing accounts on the servers. The classic account file, /etc/passwd,
stores each user as one colon-separated line: name, password marker, user id,
group id, comment, home directory, shell. She pastes lines into a ticket and
wants them turned into a readable summary. Some lines have empty fields, and
the home and shell must still come out right.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a passwd-style line with exactly 7
colon-separated fields, and prints:

  user=<field 1>
  uid=<field 3>
  home=<field 6>
  shell=<field 7>

Split the line into an array with  IFS=: read -ra  and pick the fields by
index (the first array element has index 0). Do not use cut, awk or sed.
concepts: IFS=: read -ra fields <<< "$line" splits into an array
${fields[2]} is the third element: indexes start at 0

required_patterns.message: Split with IFS=: read -ra fields <<< "$line" (a puts the pieces in an array).
Pick a field with ${fields[N]}, counting from 0.

forbidden_patterns.message: Split with IFS and read -a, not with an external tool.

test_cases.name: empty comment field keeps the positions

title: Join with a Separator
story:
Theo's web app reads its list of allowed hosts from one environment line, but
different deployment tools want different separators: commas for one, " | "
for another, a plain colon for a third. He needs a small helper that takes a
separator and a list of hosts and returns a single joined line, with no extra
separator at either end.
objective:
Write solution.sh. Its first argument is the separator (it can be several
characters long, or even empty); all remaining arguments are host names.
Print the host names joined by the separator, with the separator only BETWEEN
items:

  ./solution.sh ", " anchovy barracuda dory     prints  anchovy, barracuda, dory

One host prints just that host. No hosts prints an empty line. Collect the
hosts into an array and build the result by looping over it (the loop must
work for separators longer than one character).
concepts: hosts=("$@") copies the arguments into an array
"${hosts[@]}" expands to every element
${joined:+$sep} adds the separator only when something is already there

required_patterns.message: Loop over the array with "${hosts[@]}".

title: Reverse a String

The old support tool stored customer access tokens backwards as a cheap kind of
obfuscation, and Priya is retiring it. Before the migration she has to decode a
few thousand of them, with no extra tools installed on the isolated migration
host. A token is just a short string, so a loop that walks from its last
character to its first will do. It will also be a nice exercise in indexing.

prints the decoded token: the same characters in the opposite order. Spaces
and punctuation are characters like any other, and an empty argument prints

^ and $ anchor the regex to both ends

story:
Theo left a script behind before going on holiday, and half of it uses a
strange command called "let" while the other half uses double parentheses.
Mara wants you to understand both before touching it. "They do the same
job," she says, "but they behave a little differently when something
evaluates to zero. Let's see if you catch it."

called. Mara has decided that every disk gets a traffic light: green, amber or
red, based on how full it is. "Keep it simple," she says. "Two thresholds,

  OK         otherwise

Every customer's nightly backup used to start at exactly 02:00, and at

title: Rounding Division

The harbour cluster costs the same amount every month, and Gus has to split
it between the customers who share it. Amounts are in cents, so no one can
pay half a cent. "Do I charge them 3 cents, or 4?" he asks about a bill that

  floor=<AMOUNT / PARTS rounded down>
  nearest=<AMOUNT / PARTS rounded to the nearest whole number; exactly .5 rounds UP>
  ceiling=<AMOUNT / PARTS rounded up>

Examples: 7 / 2 = 3.5 gives floor 3, nearest 4, ceiling 4.
10 / 3 = 3.33 gives floor 3, nearest 3, ceiling 4. 8 / 4 = 2 gives 2, 2, 2.

If PARTS is 0, print "parts must be at least 1" to stderr and exit with
status 2. Use integer arithmetic only: no awk, no bc, no printf %.0f.

ceiling division: (a + b - 1) / b

title: Create an Array
story:
Lanternfish keeps a night-watch rota: three servers that get a human looking
at them while the harbour sleeps. Until now Mara kept it in a sticky note
on her monitor. She wants it in a script, as one variable that holds the
whole list, so later tools can loop over it, count it and slice it.

tonight's rota. Put them into one Bash array named `rota`, then print the

one element. If the number of arguments is not exactly 3, print
"usage: solution.sh SERVER1 SERVER2 SERVER3" to stderr and exit with status 2.

each element has a numbered index starting at 0

title: Remove an Item
story:
Five servers are racked in the east room, and this week some of them are
being retired. Priya wants the retire script to remove them from the live
inventory array, but she has seen scripts where removing the second machine
made the old third machine "become" the second one and a whole wrong box
got decommissioned. She wants to see exactly what the array looks like after
each removal, indexes included.

Write solution.sh. It starts with this array:
  fleet=(anchovy barracuda cuttlefish dory eel)

the original positions, so removing index 1 and then 3 must remove
barracuda and dory, never anything else. Arguments are valid and
distinct.

  left: <number of elements remaining>
and then the output of `declare -p fleet`.

  left: 3
  declare -a fleet=([0]="anchovy" [2]="cuttlefish" [4]="eel")

the other indexes do not shift - the array gets a gap

Nightly patching at Lanternfish is done in waves so the harbour never loses
every server at once. Mara keeps the machine list in a fixed order and wants
a tiny tool: give it a starting position and a wave size, and it names the
machines in that wave. Next week she wants "the last two" as well, without
anyone counting the list by hand.

every argument after them is a machine name (there may be none). Put the

ones that exist. OFFSET may be negative, which counts from the end of the
list (-2 means "the last two start here").

print "usage: solution.sh OFFSET SIZE [MACHINE...]" to stderr and exit
with status 2. Use an array slice, ${name[@]:offset:size}.

a negative offset counts from the end
a slice is a copy; the array is unchanged

meeting: the total billed, and how many invoices were "large" (100 dollars or

title: mapfile from a File
story:
Marlin is Lanternfish's busiest web box, and its host list lives in a plain
text file, one hostname per line, edited by three different people. Theo has
been loading it with `for h in $(cat hosts.txt)`, which falls over the day
someone writes "old dory" on a line, and quietly drops the blank line that
marks a section break. He asks you to load the file the proper way.

Write solution.sh. Its one argument is the path of a text file with one entry
per line. Load every line into an array with `mapfile -t`, reading the file
directly (`< "$file"`). Then print exactly:

  first: <first line>
  last: <last line>
Every line counts, including blank ones, and spaces inside a line are kept.

with status 2. If the file is not readable print "no such file: <path>" to
stderr and exit with status 1.

-t strips the trailing newline from each element

title: mapfile from a Command
story:
Each customer site at Lanternfish gets a config file ending in .conf, kept in
one directory per environment. Priya is auditing them and wants the list of
configs in a stable, sorted order, with a count on top, so that two audits can
be compared line for line. The directory listing has to come from a command,
because there is no ready-made list file for her to read.

Write solution.sh. Its one argument is a directory. Collect the paths of the
`*.conf` files directly inside it (not in subdirectories), in sorted order,
into an array with `mapfile -t`, fed from a command with process
substitution: `mapfile -t confs < <(find ... | sort)`.

  found: <number of files>
followed by one line per file with just its file name (no directory part).

with status 2; if it is not a directory print "not a directory: <arg>" to
stderr and exit with status 1.

process substitution keeps the array in the current shell

title: Search an Array
story:
Maintenance windows at Lanternfish are guarded by Priya's allow-list: only
people and machines on the list may touch production. A previous guard script
used a substring match, and the day "eel" was on the list, a user called
"wheelbarrow" walked straight in. Priya would like the guard rewritten so
that a name is allowed only if it matches an entry exactly.

Write solution.sh. The first argument is the NAME to check; every other
argument is an entry of the allow-list. Store the entries in an array and
look for a whole-element exact match (case-sensitive, spaces included).

and exit with status 0. If not found print
  <name>: denied
and exit with status 1. An empty list denies everyone. An empty NAME matches

exact match versus substring match
return/exit status carries the answer

title: Sort an Array

Theo has two lists to tidy before they go in the weekly status mail: the
hostnames that threw alerts, and the public ports they listen on. The
hostnames should be alphabetical and the ports should be in numeric order
(22 before 443, not after it). Both lists arrive in random order from the

title: Remove Duplicates
story:
Noor's desk gets a ticket every time a customer's monitor trips, and a flapping
server can generate a dozen identical tickets in an hour. She wants a daily
digest that mentions each server once, listed in the order it first
misbehaved, because that order tells her which fire started first. Sorting
would shuffle that story, so sort -u is out.

a search loop inside a loop

title: Associative Arrays

Every server at Lanternfish has an owner who gets paged when it misbehaves:
Theo owns the web boxes, Priya the vault, the dental practice's IT contact
owns their VM. The mapping is in a text file, "server owner" per line, and

title: Does the Key Exist?
story:
Theo's deployment tool reads a settings file full of key=value lines. His
script treated "I got an empty string" as "the setting is missing" and
happily applied a default timeout over the top of a setting someone had
deliberately left blank to mean "no timeout at all". Priya wants a checker
that tells the three situations apart: a setting with a value, a setting
that is set but blank, and a setting that is not there at all.

Write solution.sh. The first argument is a settings file with lines of the

  <key>: (not set)      when the key does not appear in the file

stderr and exit with status 2.

title: Arrays into Functions

Lanternfish runs two pools, the web servers and the database servers, and
Mara wants a one-glance health summary for each in the morning mail. She
has written the argument parsing, but the summary function is a stub: it
needs to look at an array, and a function cannot simply be handed one. Passing
"${web[@]}" to it would flatten both pools into one soup of words. The
function must receive the array's name and work on the real thing.
objective:
Write solution.sh. The arguments are the web servers, then the word "--",
then the database servers (the "--" and the database part may be missing;
then the db pool is empty). The starter already splits them into two arrays,
`web` and `db`.

title: Two Lists into One Map
story:
The network team handed over two files that were meant to travel together:
hosts.txt with server names and ips.txt with their addresses, line 1 matched
to line 1, line 2 to line 2. Nobody ever merged them, so DNS has been guessing.
Ollie volunteers to build the lookup table, and Mara asks you to make sure the
script refuses to guess when the two files do not have the same number of
lines, because a table that is shifted by one line is worse than no table.
objective:
Write solution.sh with two arguments, HOSTFILE and IPFILE. Load each file's
lines into its own array with mapfile -t. If the arrays have different
lengths print
  lists differ in length: <hosts> hosts, <ips> addresses
to stderr and exit with status 1. Otherwise zip them: build an associative
array that maps each host (line N of the first file) to the address on line N
of the second. If a host appears twice, the later line wins.
Print one line per distinct host as
  <host>=<ip>
sorted by host name in byte order (sort the keys, not the finished lines).
Two empty files print nothing. With fewer than two arguments print
"usage: solution.sh HOSTFILE IPFILE" to stderr and exit with status 2.
concepts: walk two arrays with one shared index
map[${keys[i]}]=${values[i]}
check the lengths before you zip

Load each file with mapfile -t.

title: A Grid in a Map
story:
Ollie has sketched the east machine room as a grid: one text line per rack
row, each cell the name of the machine in that rack, or "." for an empty
position. The cabling technician, though, walks the room column by column,
and the sketch is the wrong way round for her. Bash has no two-dimensional
arrays, but one associative array whose keys look like "2,3" can hold a whole
grid. Flip the sketch so she can read it down the columns.
objective:
Write solution.sh. Read the grid from standard input: one row per line,
cells separated by whitespace, no cell contains spaces. Skip empty lines.
Every row has the same number of cells. Store each cell in ONE associative
array under the key "<row>,<col>" (both counted from 0), for example
grid[$r,$c]. Then print the TRANSPOSED grid: one output line per original
column, containing that column's cells from the top row down, separated by
single spaces (no trailing space). Empty input prints nothing.
Example: the input
  anchovy dory .
  barracuda eel flounder
prints
  anchovy barracuda
  dory eel
  . flounder

one map as a 2D table
read -a splits a row into cells

Use a composite key such as grid[$r,$c].

title: Write to a File
story:
Gus keeps asking for "the morning numbers" and Mara is tired of pasting
terminal output into chat. Her new rule: every health check leaves a file
behind. The tool `tide-report` already exists, but it only talks to the
screen. Your first job on the logging team is to catch what it says.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a HOST name, and runs
`tide-report HOST`. Everything the tool prints must end up in the file
`report.txt` (in the current directory) and nothing may appear on the
screen.

If report.txt already exists, its old content must be replaced, not kept:
the file should only ever hold the latest report.

> truncates an existing file

title: Append to a File
story:
Priya wants an audit trail: every time someone touches a production box, one
line goes into `audit.log`. Yesterday Theo's script "logged" by overwriting
the file, so the whole week of history vanished and nobody noticed until the
audit. This time the log has to grow.

Write solution.sh that takes any number of arguments, each one an event
description (for example "restarted nginx on eel").

For every argument, add one line to `audit.log` in the current directory:

  [audit] <event>

Lines that are already in audit.log must stay, and the new lines must come
after them, in argument order. If audit.log does not exist yet it must be
created. With no arguments, do nothing and leave the file alone.
Print nothing on the screen.
concepts: >> appends to a file
creating a file on first append

required_patterns.message: Append to audit.log with >> so older lines survive.

forbidden_patterns.message: A single > would wipe the history. Use >>.

story:
The nightly backup of the Harbour Bakery site "works", says Theo, right up
until the morning someone notices a folder is missing. The tool did print a
warning at 3 a.m., into a terminal nobody was watching. Noor wants the
progress messages to stay visible in the cron mail, but the warnings must

into the file `backup-errors.log` instead. The file is created even when
there are no warnings (it is then empty).

stdout and stderr are separate streams

title: Both Streams, One File
story:
Priya's certificate watcher prints "checking..." on one channel and "expires
in 6 days!" on the other. When she reads the history she wants the story in
the order it happened, not two files she has to interleave by hand. One
file, everything in it, in order.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a DOMAIN, and runs
`cert-check DOMAIN`.

Put everything the tool prints, both stdout and stderr, into the single
file `cert.log`, in the order the lines were produced. Replace any old
content. Nothing should reach the screen from the tool.

After the tool has finished, print one line to stdout:

  saved N lines

where N is the number of lines in cert.log.

title: Merge stderr into stdout
story:
Ollie wrote `sync-tool "$1" 2>&1 > sync.log` and was baffled: the log had
the progress, but the error showed up on screen and was lost from the file.
"Same characters, wrong order," Mara says, and slides the keyboard over.
"Redirections are read left to right. Let's find out why that matters."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a TARGET, and runs
`sync-tool TARGET`.

Both of the tool's streams (stdout and stderr) must end up in the file
`sync.log`, and nothing from the tool may reach the screen. Write it the
portable way: send stdout to the file first, then point stderr at wherever
stdout now goes. Do not use `&>`.

Afterwards print one line to stdout: `sync exit status: N`, where N is the
exit status of sync-tool. The script itself must exit 0.
concepts: 2>&1 copies where stdout points
redirections are processed left to right

forbidden_patterns.message: Spell it out with > file 2>&1 instead of the &> shortcut.

title: Silence Is Golden
story:
The status board only needs a verdict per machine: up or down. But
`probe-host` is chatty: packet counts, timings, rate-limit notes, and
then, when a host is dead, a long complaint. Noor pasted the output of
twelve hosts into a ticket and nobody could find the answer in it. The tool
has a perfectly good exit status. Ask the question, throw away the
chatter.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a HOST, and prints exactly one
line:

  <host> is up       if `probe-host HOST` exits with status 0
  <host> is down     otherwise

Nothing else may appear on stdout or stderr: all output of probe-host
(both streams) must be discarded, and the script's own exit status is 0.
If no argument is given, print `usage: solution.sh HOST` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: /dev/null discards output
>/dev/null 2>&1 to silence both streams

required_patterns.message: Send the tool's output to /dev/null.
Silence both streams: > /dev/null 2>&1 (or &> /dev/null).

title: Input from a File
story:
Noor drafts customer notices in plain text files. The in-house mailer,
`lantern-mail`, was written by Theo on a Friday: it takes the recipient
as an argument and then waits for the message body to be typed on its
standard input. Nobody wants to type a notice twice. The file is already
right there.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: a RECIPIENT ($1) and a path to
a message FILE ($2).

If FILE does not exist or is not readable, print
`message file not found: <FILE>` to stderr and exit with status 1.

Otherwise run `lantern-mail RECIPIENT` and feed it the contents of FILE as
its standard input. Let the tool's own output appear on stdout.
Feed the file with the `<` redirection (not cat, not a pipe).
concepts: < connects a file to stdin (fd 0)

required_patterns.message: Connect the file to the command's stdin with <.

forbidden_patterns.message: No cat: let the shell open the file with <.
No pipe needed: redirect the file into the command.

title: Here-Docs with Variables
story:
Every maintenance window, someone at Lanternfish writes the same
customer notice by hand and changes three words. Last month it went to
the Gull & Anchor Pub with the Harbour Bakery's name in it. Gus is not
amused. The notice should live in the script as a template, with the
blanks filled in by the script's own variables.

Write solution.sh that takes three arguments: CUSTOMER ($1), HOST ($2) and
START ($3, a time such as 02:00). Print exactly this notice, with the
values filled in:

  Dear <CUSTOMER>,

  We will update <HOST IN CAPITALS> starting at <START> UTC.
  Please expect a restart of about 10 minutes.

  Signed: <your login name from $USER>, Lanternfish Hosting

The line "We will update ..." must show the host name in capitals (use
a parameter expansion inside the here-document, e.g. ${host^^}).
The signature uses the USER environment variable.
Write the notice as a single here-document, not as several echo lines.

variables and ${...} expand inside an unquoted here-doc

Do not quote the delimiter here: you WANT the variables expanded.

title: Quoted Here-Docs
story:
Theo wants a "scaffold" command that drops a ready-to-edit cron wrapper into a
folder: a little script full of `$BACKUP_DIR` and `$(date +%F)` that will
run LATER, on the server, with its own environment. His first attempt wrote
the file with the variables already replaced by the values from his laptop,
and every wrapper in the fleet backed up to /Users/theo. Priya has opinions.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a JOB name. If it is missing,
print `usage: solution.sh JOB` to stderr and exit 2.

Create the file `cron-<JOB>.sh` containing exactly these four lines, with
every `$` and backtick kept as literal text (nothing in them may be
expanded by your script):

  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  LOG_DIR="$BACKUP_DIR/logs"
  stamp=$(date +%F)
  echo "run at $stamp" >> "$LOG_DIR/run-$stamp.log"

Then print `wrote cron-<JOB>.sh` to stdout.
Write the four lines with ONE here-document whose delimiter is quoted.
concepts: <<'EOF' disables all expansion in the body
here-document redirected into a file

required_patterns.message: Quote the delimiter: <<'EOF' so nothing in the body is expanded.
Send cat's output into the cron-<JOB>.sh file with >.

title: Here-Strings
story:
Ollie is triaging the support queue and keeps pasting a customer's one-line
complaint into a little script that counts its words (long tickets go to
Mara) and shows it in capitals for the wallboard. His script does
`echo "$text" | wc -w`, and Priya points out that an `echo` just to feed a
command is one process too many. "The shell can hand a string to stdin
directly," she says.

Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a ticket TEXT (possibly empty).
Print two lines:

  words=<N>
  LOUD: <the text in capitals>

N is the number of words in the text (0 for an empty text). Use `wc -w`
and `tr` to do the work, and feed each of them the text with the
here-string operator `<<<`.
Do not use a pipe to supply the text. (`wc -w` pads its
result on macOS: wrap it in $(( ... )).)

forbidden_patterns.message: No pipes: <<< replaces echo | command.

title: Build a Pipeline
story:
Someone is hammering the Tidewater Books storefront with requests for pages
that do not exist: hundreds of 404s an hour, and Priya smells a scanner. She
does not need a dashboard, she needs a short list: which three addresses
are asking for missing pages the most? The web log is a plain text file
with one request per line. Five small tools, each doing one thing, will
answer the question in one line of shell.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: the path of an access log.
Each line looks like this:

  203.0.113.9 - - [10/Nov/2026:09:14:02 +0000] "GET /missing HTTP/1.1" 404 512

(client address first, then the quoted request, then the status code and
the size.)

Print the (up to) three client addresses with the most requests whose
status is 404, most active first, one per line as `<address>: <count>`.
Counts will never tie in the tests.
If the log has no 404 lines, print `no 404 responses`.
If the file does not exist, print `log not found: <path>` to stderr and
exit with status 1.
Build it as one pipeline of at least four commands (grep, cut, sort,
uniq -c, sort -rn, head ... and a final tool to reformat uniq's output).
concepts: a | b | c: stdout of one command becomes stdin of the next
sort | uniq -c | sort -rn counting idiom

required_patterns.message: Chain at least four commands with three or more pipes.
Count repeats with uniq -c (after sorting).

title: Who Failed in the Pipe?
story:
Priya's nightly log shipment is a three-stage pipeline: fetch the logs,
scrub personal data, ship the result. Last Tuesday the job reported success
and the archive was empty, because the fetch had failed and the later
stages happily processed nothing. A pipeline's exit status is only the
LAST command's. Mara wants the script to say exactly which stage broke.
objective:
Write solution.sh (no arguments) that runs this pipeline:

  fetch-logs | scrub-pii | ship-lines

and then reports each stage's own exit status, using the PIPESTATUS array
(do not use `set -o pipefail`).

After the pipeline, print one line to stdout:

  fetch=<A> scrub=<B> ship=<C>

If all three are 0, exit 0. Otherwise print
`pipeline failed at stage <K> (<name>)` to stderr, where K is the number
(1, 2 or 3) of the FIRST stage with a non-zero status and <name> is
fetch-logs, scrub-pii or ship-lines, and exit with status 1.
PIPESTATUS is overwritten by the very next command, so copy it right away.
concepts: ${PIPESTATUS[@]} holds one exit status per pipeline stage
copy PIPESTATUS immediately

required_patterns.message: Read the per-stage exit codes from the PIPESTATUS array.

forbidden_patterns.message: pipefail only tells you that SOMETHING failed; use PIPESTATUS.

title: Compare Two Outputs
story:
After a failed deploy, Theo swears the staging box and the production box
have "exactly the same packages". Mara does not. `pkg-list` prints the
installed packages of a host, but in whatever order the host feels like, and

wrong. There is a way to hand `diff` two command outputs as if they were files.

Write solution.sh that takes two host names: HOST_A ($1) and HOST_B ($2).

Compare the packages of the two hosts. `pkg-list HOST` prints one package

lists and let its normal output appear on stdout. If the sorted lists are
identical, print `hosts match` instead.

Do not create temporary files; use process substitution (`<( ... )`) for
both sides of the diff. The script exits 0 either way.

diff <(a) <(b)

forbidden_patterns.message: No temporary files: process substitution replaces them.

morning. Currently he does one or the other, never both, because `> log`

title: Open a File Descriptor
story:
Gus wants a one-page status sheet every morning, but the script that
checks services also prints chatty progress for the person running it. Mixing
the two in one stream gave him a sheet full of "checking..." lines. Mara
suggests giving the script a private channel: open the report file once as
a numbered descriptor of your own, and write to it from anywhere, while
stdout stays free for the operator.

title: Read Two Files at Once
story:
Noor has two lists from two systems: customer names in one file, their
server addresses in another, in the same order. She needs them side by
side for a handover document, and `paste` is not installed on the
jump host she must use (a policy thing, don't ask). A `while read` loop reads
one file easily. Reading two files in lockstep needs a second open door.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two file names: NAMES ($1) and ADDRESSES ($2).

If either file cannot be read, print `cannot read: <file>` to stderr (name
the first unreadable one, checking NAMES first) and exit 1.

Otherwise print one line per line of NAMES:

  <name> -> <address>

where <address> is the line at the same position in ADDRESSES. If
ADDRESSES has run out of lines, print `(none)` as the address. Extra lines
in ADDRESSES beyond the end of NAMES are ignored.
Read NAMES with the loop's own stdin (`done < "$1"`) and ADDRESSES through
your own descriptor 3: `exec 3< ...` and `read -u 3`.
concepts: exec 3<file opens a file for reading
read -u 3 reads one line from descriptor 3

required_patterns.message: Open the second file for reading with exec 3< file.
Read a line from the second file with read -u 3.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do it with a read loop and a second descriptor, not paste.

title: Close and Restore
story:
The site builder prints a screenful for every build, and Theo's wrapper
script scrolls it all past the on-call phone. The wrapper itself has just
two things to say: "started" and "finished". Mara's idea: point the script's
own stdout at a log file for the noisy part, then put it back. "Just
remember where the screen was," she says, "or you'll never see anything again."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a SITE name.

1. Print `build started: SITE` to the screen (stdout).
2. Redirect the script's own standard output to the file `build.log` for
   the rest of the noisy part: first write the line `site=SITE` into the
   log with `echo`, then run `compile-site SITE`. Neither of them may
   reach the screen. Do NOT put a `>` on those two commands: change stdout
   for the whole script with `exec`.
3. Restore stdout to the screen (save it before you redirect, restore it
   afterwards, and close your saved copy).
4. Print `build finished: <N> lines in build.log` to the screen, where N
   is the number of lines in build.log.
concepts: exec 4>&1 saves where stdout points
exec >file redirects the script's stdout; exec 1>&4 4>&- restores it

required_patterns.message: Save the screen first: exec 4>&1.
Redirect the script's stdout with exec > build.log.
Restore stdout from your saved copy: exec 1>&4.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not redirect the command itself; change stdout with exec.

title: Redirect a Whole Block
story:
Gus gets a daily capacity report by email, and the script that makes it
has grown to a header, a loop over hosts and a footer. Each piece has its own
`>> report.txt`, one forgotten `>>` wiped the middle last Friday, and the
warnings are mixed into the numbers Gus pastes into spreadsheets. Mara
has one last trick for this module: group the commands in braces and
redirect the group once.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes a DAY ($1, e.g. 2026-11-11) followed by one or
more HOST names.

Produce two files, report-<DAY>.txt and report-<DAY>.err, by running a
single brace group `{ ...; }` whose stdout is redirected to the report and
whose stderr is redirected to the .err file (both redirections on the
closing brace). Inside the group, in this order:

  1. print `== Capacity report for <DAY> ==`
  2. for each HOST, run `disk-usage HOST` (it prints one line to stdout and
     sometimes a warning to stderr)
  3. print `== end ==`

Nothing from the group may reach the screen. After the group, print
`wrote report-<DAY>.txt` to stdout.
If fewer than two arguments are given, print
`usage: solution.sh DAY HOST...` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: { commands; } > file redirects a group once
both stdout and stderr redirections on one block

required_patterns.message: Redirect the whole brace group once, on its closing brace: } > file.
Send the group's stderr to the .err file with 2> on the same closing brace.

forbidden_patterns.message: One redirection on the closing brace; no >> per command.

title: Check the Status
story:
Theo's deploy script deleted the wrong folder last night, and Mara has called a
meeting titled "Never again." Her first rule: before a script does anything
risky, it must know what the previous command really did. Today's warm-up is
small. Noor wants to know whether Harbour Bakery's site is in maintenance mode,
and "the script ran" is not an answer. Every command leaves a number behind
saying how it went. Learn to read it.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a status file. Look for a line that
is exactly
  maintenance=on
using `grep -qx` (quiet, whole-line match), then read the exit status of grep
with `$?`. Print, depending on that status:
  status 0 (line found):      maintenance: ON            (stdout, exit 0)
  status 1 (line not found):  maintenance: off           (stdout, exit 0)
  anything else (grep could not read the file, usually status 2):
      cannot read FILE (grep status N)                   (stderr, exit 2)
where FILE is the argument and N is grep's real status.
Hide grep's own error message with `2>/dev/null`. Save `$?` into a variable
on the very next line after grep, because the next command overwrites it.
Do not use `set -e` in this one: grep's status 1 is an answer here, not a crash.
concepts: $? holds the exit status of the last command
0 means success, anything else means something happened
grep tells 'not found' (1) apart from 'error' (2)

required_patterns.message: Read the status of grep with $?.
Use grep -q so grep prints nothing and only reports through its status.

forbidden_patterns.message: Leave set -e out: here grep's status 1 means 'not found' and you want to handle it yourself.

title: Or Else Exit
story:
Here is what really happened to Theo. His script ran `cd "$RELEASE_DIR"`, the
folder did not exist, `cd` complained and the script carried on anyway, now
standing in the wrong directory, and cheerfully ran `rm -f *.old` there. Mara
has a name for the missing piece: "an or-else". If this step fails, stop right
here. Add one to the cleanup script before anyone runs it again.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument: a release directory. It must
  1. enter that directory with `cd`,
  2. delete every file ending in .old inside it (`rm -f -- ./*.old`),
  3. print "cleaned DIR" (DIR is the argument) and finish with status 0.
If `cd` fails, print
  deploy: cannot enter DIR
to stderr and exit with status 1 immediately, before anything is deleted.
Hide the shell's own cd complaint with `2>/dev/null` so only your message shows.
Guard the `cd` with `||` followed by a group `{ ...; }` that prints the message
and exits. Never run the delete after a failed `cd`.
concepts: cmd || exit 1
a { ...; } group after || runs several commands
a failed cd leaves you in the wrong directory

required_patterns.message: Guard the cd directly: cd "$1" 2>/dev/null || { ...; exit 1; }

title: What set -e Does
story:
Ollie has read that `set -e` makes scripts safe and wants it everywhere. Gus
needs the nightly log archiver to stop the moment a copy fails, but he also wants
its summary to say whether the log contains FATAL lines, and a plain grep with
no match "fails" with status 1. Ollie is about to learn that set -e is a
tripwire with some very specific exceptions.
objective:
solution.sh takes one argument, a log file, and must run these steps in order:
  1. print "start"
  2. print "fatal lines present" if the log contains the text FATAL,
     otherwise print "no fatal lines"
  3. copy the log to archive/log.copy with `cp`
  4. print "done"
Turn on `set -e` at the top so the script stops at the first command that
fails: if the copy fails (for example the archive folder does not exist) the
script must exit with cp's status and never print "done".
Careful with step 2: a log without FATAL makes grep exit with 1, and that
must NOT stop the script. Put grep where set -e does not trigger on its
failure: as the condition of an `if`.
concepts: set -e exits when a command fails
exception: a command used as an if condition may fail
exception: failures in && and || lists (except the last command)

required_patterns.message: Turn on errexit with set -e.
Test the log with if grep ...; then ...; else ...; fi so grep's status 1 does not trip set -e.

title: set -u Catches Typos
story:
Priya found the second half of Theo's accident. His script said
`rm -rf "$BUILD_DIR/"*`, but earlier he had typed the variable as BUILD_DRI.
Bash saw an unset name, quietly turned it into an empty string, and the command
became `rm -rf "/"*`. Priya wants every Lanternfish script to refuse to run
on a variable that does not exist. Here is the "clear old releases" planner,
typo included. Make it safe, then make it honest.
objective:
solution.sh is a dry-run planner. It reads two environment variables:
  DEPLOY_ROOT   required: the folder holding the releases
  RELEASE_TAG   optional: defaults to "latest" when it is not set
and prints one line (it only prints, it deletes nothing):
  would clear DEPLOY_ROOT/releases/TAG
Turn on `set -u` so that using an unset variable aborts the script. The
starter has a typo in a variable name: find it and fix it. Give RELEASE_TAG its
default with `${RELEASE_TAG:-latest}`, because `set -u` would otherwise stop
the script when it is missing.
If DEPLOY_ROOT is unset, bash's own error must appear on stderr (it names the
variable, "DEPLOY_ROOT: unbound variable"), nothing is printed on stdout,
and the exit status is 1.
concepts: set -u (nounset)
an unset variable is silently empty without it
${var:-default} for variables that may legitimately be unset

required_patterns.message: Turn on nounset with set -u.
Give the optional RELEASE_TAG a default with ${RELEASE_TAG:-latest}.

test_cases.name: root missing is a hard stop

title: Failures Inside Pipes
story:
Priya's weekly traffic summary has been reporting "success" for days, yet
the numbers are strangely small. The cause: the log download from the
server drops its connection half-way, but the pipeline that sorts and saves
the result ends with a command that is perfectly happy, and a pipeline only
reports the status of its last command. The failure is swallowed by the pipe.
objective:
solution.sh takes a site name and builds a summary of its distinct request lines:
  fetchlog SITE | sort -u > summary.txt
After the pipeline, if it succeeded print
  summary ready: N distinct lines
where N is the number of lines in summary.txt. If the pipeline failed anywhere,
print
  fetch failed for SITE
to stderr and exit with status 3.
The starter already contains the pipeline and the check, and today it reports
success even when fetchlog fails. Make the pipeline's status reflect the
failure of ANY stage, using `set -o pipefail`. Do not use `set -e`.
concepts: a pipeline's status is its last command's by default
set -o pipefail: first failing stage decides

required_patterns.message: Turn on set -o pipefail so a failure anywhere in the pipe counts.

forbidden_patterns.message: Keep set -e out of this level: the script checks the pipeline itself.

test_cases.name: dropped connection on a quiet site

title: Strict Mode
story:
Mara pins a sticky note to your monitor: "set -euo pipefail. First line after
the shebang. Always." Today's script archives a customer site's stats and its
config into a backup folder, three steps that can each go wrong in a different
way: a variable nobody set, a command that fails, and a pipe whose first stage
dies. One line of strict mode covers all three.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one site name and uses the environment variable
BACKUP_DIR (the backup root; it is required). It must start with the
strict-mode line `set -euo pipefail` and then do, in order:
  1. mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR/SITE"
  2. pullstats SITE | sort > "$BACKUP_DIR/SITE/stats.txt"
  3. cp "sites/SITE.conf" "$BACKUP_DIR/SITE/site.conf"
  4. print "archived SITE: N lines" where N is the number of lines in stats.txt
Any failure must stop the script right there with a non-zero status (exit 1 in
these tests), so step 4 never runs after a failed step. In particular:
an unset BACKUP_DIR must produce bash's "unbound variable" error, and a
crash inside the pullstats pipe must not be hidden by sort.
concepts: set -e + set -u + pipefail as one habit
each flag covers a different kind of silent failure

required_patterns.message: Start with the strict-mode line: set -euo pipefail

test_cases.name: crash inside the pipe is not hidden
missing config stops before the summary

title: Cleanup on Exit
story:
Last Tuesday Theo's deploy crashed half-way and left a deploy.lock file
behind. Every deploy after that politely refused to start ("someone else is
deploying"), and nobody was. Mara's fix is a promise the script keeps no matter
how it ends: the lock is released at the very end, whether the deploy
succeeded, failed, or was killed by its own set -e.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a deploy wrapper with no arguments:
  1. start with `set -e` so a failing command stops the script
  2. create the lock file with `touch deploy.lock`
  3. register cleanup with `trap`, on the EXIT pseudo-signal: a function (or
     command) that removes deploy.lock and prints "lock released"
  4. run `lanternbuild` (it prints a line and may fail)
  5. print "deploy finished"
Set the trap right after creating the lock, before running the build.
"lock released" must be printed exactly once, always as the very last line, and
deploy.lock must be gone afterwards, even when lanternbuild fails (the script
then exits with lanternbuild's status and never prints "deploy finished").
concepts: trap 'commands' EXIT runs when the script ends, however it ends
cleanup registered once, close to what it cleans

required_patterns.message: Register the cleanup with trap ... EXIT.
Start with set -e.

test_cases.name: successful deploy
