building (lock: held)
deploy finished
lock released

title: Report the Failing Line
story:
Ollie ran the release packager at 02:00 and found only "exit status 1" in the
morning log. Which of the three steps died? Ollie has no idea, and is too polite
to say so. A script that stops without saying where is almost as bad as one
that does not stop. Bash can tell you the line number and the exact command at
the moment of failure; you only need to ask it to.
objective:
solution.sh packages a release. It has no arguments and runs these three
commands, in this order and spelled exactly like this:
  mkdir -p out
  cp release/app.tar out/
  grep -q ^version= release/app.version
followed by `echo "packaged"`.
Start with `set -e`, then register an ERR trap whose handler writes ONE line to
stderr in exactly this shape:
  error: line N: COMMAND
where N is the line number of the failing command in solution.sh (`$LINENO`)
and COMMAND is the text of that command (`$BASH_COMMAND`), for example
  error: line 9: cp release/app.tar out/
Register the trap before the first command. If all steps succeed, print
"packaged" and exit 0; on failure the script exits with the failing command's
status and prints nothing on stdout.
concepts: trap '...' ERR runs when a command fails
$LINENO and $BASH_COMMAND describe the failing command
single quotes keep $LINENO from expanding too early

required_patterns.message: Register the handler with trap ... ERR.
Report the line with $LINENO.
Report the command text with $BASH_COMMAND.
Use set -e so the script stops after the trap reports.

title: Handle Ctrl-C
story:
Gus loves the nightly customer import, and hates it when someone presses Ctrl-C
on it at batch 37 of 40. The next run starts again from batch 1 and re-bills
everyone. The import loop already works. What it lacks is manners: when it is
interrupted it should remember how far it got, say so, and leave with the
traditional "interrupted" status of 130.
objective:
solution.sh runs five import batches. The loop is already in the starter, along
with a line that simulates the operator pressing Ctrl-C after batch N
(`kill -INT $$`, only when the environment variable INTERRUPT_AFTER equals the
batch number). Add an INT trap with a handler that:
  - prints "interrupted after batch N" (N is the last finished batch)
  - writes N to the file import.state
  - exits with status 130
The loop prints "batch N done" after each batch, and
"import complete" at the end when it was never interrupted. A finished import
must not create import.state. Keep the variable `last` that the loop updates:
it is what your handler reports. Register the trap before the loop.
concepts: trap 'handler' INT catches Ctrl-C (SIGINT)
the handler decides: save state, say something, exit 130
130 = 128 + signal number 2

required_patterns.message: Catch Ctrl-C with trap ... INT.
Leave the handler with exit 130, the conventional status for Ctrl-C.

title: Graceful Shutdown
story:
When the harbour-side server `halibut` is rebooted for patching, the system sends
every process a polite TERM and, a few seconds later, an impolite KILL. The
night-queue worker used to die in the middle of a job and leave a half-written
invoice. Mara wants the worker to do the decent thing: finish the job it is
doing, refuse to start another, and hand back whatever is still waiting.
objective:
solution.sh is a queue worker. It reads job names from queue.txt (one per
line) and runs them one at a time. The loop is in the starter, together with a
line that makes the script send itself SIGTERM in the middle of one job (when
the environment variable TERM_DURING equals that job's name).
Add a TERM trap whose handler ONLY sets a flag, `stopping=1`: it must not
exit, the running job has to finish. Then:
  - at the top of every iteration, if stopping is set, leave the loop
  - after the loop, if stopping is set: print
      shutdown: N done, M left
    write the names of the jobs that never started, one per line, to the
    file queue.left (create it even if nothing is left), and exit 0
  - otherwise print
      drained: N done
N is the number of finished jobs, M the number of waiting ones.
concepts: trap 'stopping=1' TERM: handler sets a flag
finish the current unit of work, then stop at a safe point
the flag is checked between jobs, not during

required_patterns.message: Catch the shutdown request with trap ... TERM.
The handler should set stopping=1 and let the current job finish.

title: Temp Files That Vanish
story:
Priya ran `df` on the backup server and found 11 GB of files named
`/tmp/upload.tmp`, `/tmp/upload.tmp2`, `/tmp/upload.tmp.old`... all left over
from crashed uploads. Worse, two jobs once wrote to the same fixed name at the
same time and swapped each other's data. Scratch files need two things: a name
nobody else can pick, and a funeral that always happens.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one argument, a customer's list file, and
  1. starts with `set -e`
  2. creates a scratch file with `mktemp` and stores its path in a variable:
       tmp=$(mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/list.XXXXXX")
     (the XXXXXX are replaced by random characters; naming TMPDIR keeps the
     file in the right folder on both macOS and Linux)
  3. registers `trap ... EXIT` immediately, removing that scratch file with `rm -f`
  4. writes the sorted, de-duplicated list into the scratch file: `sort -u "$1" > "$tmp"`
  5. runs `lanternupload "$tmp"` (it prints what it received)
  6. prints "sent clean copy of FILE" where FILE is the argument
Whatever happens, success, a failed upload (the script then exits with
lanternupload's status) or an unreadable list file, the scratch file must not
exist afterwards. The tests check that the temporary folder is empty at the
end, and that the upload was given a path inside it.
concepts: mktemp creates a unique file and returns its path
trap ... EXIT removes it on every way out
register the trap right after creating the file

required_patterns.message: Create the scratch file with mktemp.
Remove it with a trap ... EXIT handler.
Start with set -e.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not invent a fixed /tmp name; mktemp chooses a unique one.

test_cases.expected_stdout:
received 3 lines
sent clean copy of customers.txt

title: Meaningful Exit Codes
story:
Noor's monitoring dashboard has one red light per script, and "exit 1" is the
only thing it ever sees. At 03:00 the pager goes off and nobody knows whether
the config was deleted, the config was broken, or the service itself fell over.
Each of those needs a different person. Noor asks for an agreed code per
failure so the dashboard can route the alert to the right one.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a health check that takes one argument, a config file.
It must look for a line `port=NUMBER` (digits only) and probe that port with
`probe NUMBER`. Exit codes and stderr messages:
  no argument given         usage: solution.sh CONFIG                 exit 2
  config file not readable  config not found: CONFIG                  exit 3
  no valid port=NUMBER line config has no valid port: CONFIG          exit 4
  probe fails               service on port NUMBER is down            exit 5
  all good                  stdout: healthy: port NUMBER              exit 0
CONFIG is the argument as given and NUMBER the port. If the file has several
port= lines use the first one. Messages go to stderr, the success line to
stdout. Silence the probe tool's own complaint with `2>/dev/null` so only
your message appears. Check the problems in the order listed above.
concepts: a distinct exit code for each kind of failure
codes are a contract with whoever calls the script
name the codes in variables, not magic numbers

required_patterns.message: Leave through exit with a specific code for each failure.

title: Validate Before Acting
story:
Theo's "retire old reports" script takes a list of files and moves each one into
the archive. On Friday the third file in the list had a typo. The first two were
already moved, the script died, and nobody could tell which half of the reports
was where. Mara's rule for anything that changes the world: look at everything
first, touch nothing until every input checks out.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one or more file names. With no arguments print
  usage: solution.sh FILE...
to stderr and exit 2.
Phase 1, validate: go through ALL the arguments before changing anything. Every
argument that is not an existing regular file (`[[ -f ... ]]`) gets one line on
stderr, in argument order:
  missing: NAME
If at least one argument was bad, exit 1 after reporting all of them. Nothing may
have been moved, and the archive folder must not even have been created.
Phase 2, act (only when every argument is fine): create the folder `archive`
and move each file into it, renamed with an .old suffix (report.txt becomes
archive/report.txt.old). Then print
  archived N files
where N is the number of files (use "1 files" style as is, no pluralising).
Names may contain spaces.
concepts: validate every input first, act second
collect all problems, then report them together
a failure halfway leaves a half-changed world

required_patterns.message: Test each argument with [[ -f "$f" ]].

test_cases.name: one bad name in the middle moves nothing
every bad name is reported, a folder counts as bad
test_cases.expected_stderr:
missing: nope.txt
missing: reports
missing: gone.txt

title: Retry a Flaky Command
story:
The CDN upload at Lanternfish fails about one time in ten with "connection
reset", and succeeds if you simply try again a moment later. Right now a
person does the trying again, usually at 4 a.m. Ollie suggests an infinite loop
that retries until it works, and Mara asks what happens on the night the CDN is
really down. Right: your script would never stop. Retries need a ceiling.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, MAX, the maximum number of attempts
(a whole number of at least 1). If MAX is missing, not made of digits, or zero,
print
  usage: solution.sh MAX
to stderr and exit 2.
Run `lanternpush` (silence it with `> /dev/null 2>&1`) up to MAX times:
  - after each attempt that fails print "attempt K failed" (K = 1, 2, ...)
    and, when there are attempts left, `sleep 0.1` before the next one
  - on the first success print "pushed on attempt K" and exit 0
  - when all MAX attempts have failed print
      giving up after MAX attempts
    to stderr and exit 1. No sleep after the last failure.
The command must never be run more than MAX times.
concepts: bounded retry loop
a counter plus a ceiling
pause between attempts, and stop after the last

required_patterns.message: Pause briefly between attempts with sleep 0.1.
Use a loop for the attempts.

test_cases.expected_stdout:
attempt 1 failed
attempt 2 failed
pushed on attempt 3

test_cases.name: gives up after the limit
test_cases.expected_stdout:
attempt 1 failed
attempt 2 failed
attempt 3 failed

test_cases.name: a single attempt is a single attempt

title: A Time Limit by Hand
story:
The nightly malware scan on `grouper` normally takes a minute. Once a month it
hangs forever, holds the backup lock, and Priya finds out at breakfast. A
`timeout` command exists on some systems, but not on the Mac you are developing
on, and not on the minimal image the server runs. Mara shrugs: "Then build it. A
time limit is just a background job, a sleep, and a kill."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, LIMIT: the number of seconds
(may be fractional, like 0.5) the scan may run. Do not use the `timeout`
command.
  1. Start `lanternscan` in the background with `&` and keep its PID (`$!`).
  2. `sleep` for LIMIT seconds.
  3. If the scan is still running (test with `kill -0 PID 2>/dev/null`), stop it
     with `kill PID`, collect it with `wait PID` (ignore its status) and
     print
       scan timed out after LIMIT seconds
     to stderr, then exit 124 (the status `timeout` itself uses).
  4. Otherwise the scan already ended: `wait PID` to get its exit status.
     Status 0: exit 0 (the scan prints "scan complete" itself).
     Any other status N: print "scan failed with status N" to stderr and exit N.
Every case must end within a second or so.
concepts: command & runs in the background; $! is its PID
kill -0 PID asks 'is it still alive?'
kill PID sends TERM; wait PID collects the status

title: Dependency Check
story:
Ollie's first solo deploy failed at step 4 with "tidepool: command not found".
Ollie installed it and tried again. It failed at step 9: "lanternctl: command
not found". Three more rounds of this and it was lunchtime. Mara sighs: "A
script should know what it needs before it starts, and when something is
missing it should name everything that is missing in one go." That is the job.
objective:
Write solution.sh. Its arguments are the names of the programs the deploy needs.
With no arguments print
  usage: solution.sh TOOL...
to stderr and exit 2.
Otherwise check every tool with `command -v` (hide its output with
`> /dev/null 2>&1`). Do NOT stop at the first missing one. At the end:
  - if every tool exists, print "all N tools found" (N = number of arguments)
    on stdout and exit 0
  - otherwise print on stderr one line
      missing: A B C
    listing the missing tools, space-separated, in the order they were given,
    and exit 1
Do not use `which`; `command -v` is the portable built-in check.
concepts: command -v NAME: is this tool available?
collect every problem in an array, report once
check dependencies at the top, before any work starts

required_patterns.message: Test for a tool with command -v.

forbidden_patterns.message: `which` is not portable; use command -v.

test_cases.name: only the last one is missing

title: Error Messages That Help
story:
Noor forwards a screenshot from North Pier Dental: their site config check says
only "error: bad config". Which file? Which line? What should they change? The
support desk spent forty minutes finding out. Mara's three-question test for any
error message: What went wrong? Where? What should the reader do about it?
The checker below already catches every problem; its messages are what need work.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a validator for site config files, taking one argument.
Config lines look like `name=value`; empty lines and lines starting with # are
ignored. Every failure is two lines on stderr (the second one starts with
two spaces) and exit status 1. Check in this order, report only the first
problem found:
  no argument:     usage: solution.sh CONFIG                (one line, exit 2)
  file not readable:
    error: config file not found: CONFIG
      fix: create it with: lanternctl init CONFIG
  a line that is not blank, not a comment and has no "=" (first such line):
    error: CONFIG:LINE: not a key=value line: "TEXT"
      fix: write it as name=value, or start the line with # to comment it out
  no line starting with domain=:
    error: CONFIG: required key "domain" is missing
      fix: add a line such as domain=example.com
LINE is the line number in the file (first line is 1) and TEXT the line as it
is written. Both lines go to stderr. When the file is valid print
  config ok: N keys
on stdout (N counts the name=value lines) and exit 0.
concepts: an error says what, where and how to fix it
errors go to stderr, results to stdout
line numbers from a read loop

required_patterns.message: Error messages belong on stderr: end the echo with >&2.

port=8443
tls=on

title: Exit Codes Through Layers
story:
The deploy pipeline is three stages: build, test, ship. Theo wrapped each stage
in a function that also saves its output to a log with `tee`. Since then the
pipeline has "succeeded" every night, including the night the tests failed and
the broken release was shipped anyway. The failure was real; it just got lost
on the way up through the function, the pipe and the main script. Today you make
the number arrive at the top, exactly as it left the bottom. It is the last
mission of the module: everything so far is in play.
objective:
Write solution.sh with a function `run_stage NAME` and a main part.
run_stage NAME must:
  - print "[NAME] start" on stdout
  - run `lanternci NAME 2>&1 | tee NAME.log` (so the stage's output appears
    on stdout and is saved in NAME.log)
  - if lanternci's exit status is not 0, print
      [NAME] failed with status N
    to stderr and `return N` with that same status.
The status that matters is lanternci's, not tee's: either `set -o pipefail`
or `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` gets it.
The main part runs run_stage for build, then test, then ship, in this order,
stops at the first stage that fails and exits with that stage's status (later
stages must not run, and must not leave a log). If all three succeed it prints
"deployed" and exits 0.
concepts: exit status travels: command -> pipe -> function -> script
return N in a function, exit $? in the caller
PIPESTATUS / pipefail so tee does not mask the status

required_patterns.message: tee would hide lanternci's status: use set -o pipefail or ${PIPESTATUS[0]}.
Pass the status up from the function with return.

deployed

title: Your First =~
story:
Priya has a theory: somebody is guessing passwords on the bastion host, and
the evidence is buried in thousands of sshd lines. She does not want a
clever tool yet. She wants a first filter she can read in ten seconds, one
that picks out the lines mentioning a failed password and leaves everything
else alone.

Write solution.sh that reads lines from standard input. For every line that
contains the text "Failed password" anywhere in it, print

  ALERT: <the whole line>

so "failed password" in lowercase does not count. Test each line with the
regex operator inside double brackets: [[ $line =~ regex ]]. Do not use
grep, case or the == operator.
concepts: [[ string =~ regex ]] tests a string against a regular expression
an unanchored regex matches anywhere inside the string

title: Anchors
story:
Before every audit Priya skims sshd_config for risky switches. The trouble is
that a commented-out "#PermitRootLogin yes" looks just as scary to a
careless script as the real one, and "PermitRootLogin yesterday" (a typo
someone once committed) is not a setting at all. She wants each line
sorted into a bucket, and the position of the text is what decides the bucket.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads config lines from standard input and prints one
word per line, in the same order, describing each line:

  blank     the line is empty
  comment   the line starts with #
  risky     the line ends with " yes" (a space, then yes, and nothing after)
  other     everything else

Check the rules in that order, so "#PermitRootLogin yes" is a comment, not
risky. Use [[ =~ ]] with ^ and $ anchors. No grep, case or sed.
concepts: ^ anchors a pattern to the start of the string
$ anchors a pattern to the end of the string
^$ matches the empty string

required_patterns.message: Use a ^ anchor in a regex, for example [[ $line =~ ^# ]].
Use a $ anchor at the end of a regex, for example [[ $line =~ yes$ ]].

forbidden_patterns.message: Use anchored regexes with =~ for this level.

title: Character Classes
story:
Ollie spent the afternoon labelling hardware, and now the inventory sheet is a
mix of proper tags and creative spelling. Every server rack tag at Lanternfish
follows one rule: the word "rack", a dash, one lowercase letter for the aisle,
and two digits for the slot, like rack-b07. Priya wants the bad ones listed
before the next audit walk-through.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads tags from standard input, one per line. For each
line print

  <tag>: ok       if the whole line is a valid tag
  <tag>: bad      otherwise

A valid tag is "rack-", then ONE lowercase letter a-z, then EXACTLY TWO
digits, and nothing else before or after. Build the regex from character
classes: [a-z] for the letter and [[:digit:]] for each digit. Anchor both
ends. Do not use \d, which is not portable.
concepts: [a-z] matches one character from a range
[[:digit:]] and other POSIX classes
a class matches exactly one character

Use the POSIX class [[:digit:]] for the digits.

title: Quantifiers
story:
Priya's security tickets all carry a reference: the team prefix in capitals,
a dash, and a number, like OPS-4410 or SEC-123. Urgent ones add "-P1" to
"-P3" at the end. The ticket importer refuses anything that does not
fit, and people keep pasting references with a stray trailing space or with
four-digit prefixes. Priya wants a checker that says which ones the importer
will accept.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads ticket references from standard input, one per
line, and prints for each line

  <line>: valid     or     <line>: invalid

A valid reference is, in this order:
  - one or more capital letters (the team prefix),
  - a dash,
  - between 3 and 5 digits,
  - optionally "-P" followed by one digit,
  - optionally trailing spaces (any number of them, including none),
and nothing else. Anchor both ends. Use the quantifiers + , {m,n} , ? and *
in a single [[ =~ ]] test. The output repeats the line exactly as read.
concepts: + one or more, * zero or more, ? zero or one
{n}, {n,} and {n,m} bounded repetition
a quantifier applies to the item just before it

required_patterns.message: Use a {min,max} quantifier for the 3 to 5 digits.
Use + after a class for the one-or-more capital letters.
Wrap the optional -P part in a group and put ? after it.

title: Alternation
story:
The firewall on barracuda writes a line for every packet decision, and the
action is spelled three different ways depending on which rule fired. Priya
does not need the lines, she needs the totals: how many packets were turned
away, how many were let in, and how many lines say something else entirely.
She plans to paste the numbers into a slide, so the format matters.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads firewall lines from standard input. Each
line contains a field "ACTION=<word>", for example
  barracuda kernel: ACTION=DROP SRC=203.0.113.9 DPT=22
Classify every line by its action:
  blocked   ACTION=DROP, ACTION=REJECT or ACTION=DENY
  allowed   ACTION=ACCEPT or ACTION=ALLOW
  other     anything else, including lines without an ACTION field
The action word must be complete: "ACTION=DROPPED" is "other". The field is
always followed by a space or the end of the line. After reading all input
print one line:
  blocked=<n> allowed=<n> other=<n>
Use alternation with | inside a group in [[ =~ ]]. Do not use grep or case.
concepts: a|b matches either alternative
( ) limits where the alternation starts and ends
bound the alternatives so DROP does not match DROPPED

title: Capture One Group
story:
Priya now knows that somebody is hammering the bastion. What she wants next
is a list of the accounts they are trying, so she can check whether any of
them really exist. Finding the failed-login lines is not enough: she needs the
username out of each one, on a line of its own, ready to paste into the
account audit.

Write solution.sh that reads auth-log lines from standard input. A line counts
only when it contains "Failed password for ", then ONE word (the username),
then " from ". For example:
  Nov  7 09:30:15 anchovy sshd[2211]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4022 ssh2
For every counting line print just the username, one per line, in input order.
Print nothing for the other lines. (A line such as "Failed password for
invalid user admin from ..." has more than one word before " from " and does
not count.)

${BASH_REMATCH[1]}. No grep, sed, awk or cut.

${BASH_REMATCH[1]} holds the first group
read BASH_REMATCH only after a successful match

Read the captured username from ${BASH_REMATCH[1]}.

title: Capture Several Groups
story:
Theo tags every release with a version like v2.14.3, and the deployment tracker
wants the three numbers in separate columns so Gus can see how far behind
each customer site is. Some tags in the repository are garbage, such as "latest" or

title: Validate an Email Address
story:
Noor runs the newsletter sign-up for Lanternfish customers, and the mailing
tool bounces every address it cannot parse, which costs real money per
bounce. The import file is full of typing slips: a missing domain extension,
two @ signs, a space inside. She asks for a gatekeeper that separates the
plausible addresses from the obvious junk before the import runs.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads one address per line from standard input and
prints

  OK <address>      if it looks valid
  BAD <address>     otherwise

An address looks valid when the whole line is:
  - a local part of one or more of: letters, digits, and the characters . _ % + -
  - one @
  - a domain of one or more of: letters, digits, dots and dashes
  - a dot
  - a final extension (TLD) of at least two letters

You are not asked to catch every rule of the real email standard, only the
rules above.

escape the dot you mean literally; place - last in a class
validate the whole string with ^ and $

The regex needs a literal @.
Escape the dot before the extension: \. means a real dot.
The extension needs at least two letters: {2,}.

title: Validate an IPv4 Address
story:
Priya maintains the blocklist that the edge firewall loads every hour. Last
week somebody pasted "256.300.1.1" into it and the firewall refused to
load the whole list; for three minutes nothing was blocked. She wants every
address checked before it goes in, and the check has to understand that
an address is four numbers that each stop at 255, not just four groups of
digits.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads one candidate per line from standard input and
prints

  <candidate> valid      or      <candidate> invalid

A candidate is valid when it consists of exactly four decimal numbers
separated by single dots, each number is 1 to 3 digits long, and each number
is between 0 and 255. Leading zeros are allowed ("192.168.01.1" is valid;
read 01 as 1). Anything else, including spaces, is invalid.
First use [[ =~ ]] with four capture groups to check the shape. Then compare
each captured number with 255 using arithmetic. Careful: a number that starts
with 0 is octal in Bash arithmetic, so force base 10 with 10#.
concepts: a regex checks the shape, arithmetic checks the range
capture the four octets with groups
10# forces base 10 so 08 and 09 are not invalid octal

required_patterns.message: Check the shape with [[ $ip =~ regex ]].
Read the four octets from BASH_REMATCH.
Use 10#$octet in arithmetic so leading zeros stay decimal.

forbidden_patterns.message: Capture the octets with =~ and compare them with arithmetic.

title: Validate a Date
story:
Gus is closing the books for the year and the invoice export has a column of
due dates typed by hand. The accounting system reads them as YYYY-MM-DD and
falls over on anything else: "2024-02-30", "2024-13-01", "2024-4-5". He
would like to know which rows to fix, and why, before he uploads the file.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads one date per line from standard input and prints

  <date>: ok            if it is a real calendar date
  <date>: bad format    if it is not exactly YYYY-MM-DD (4+2+2 digits)
  <date>: bad month     if the format is right but the month is not 01 to 12
  <date>: bad day       if the month is right but the day does not exist
                        in that month (day 00 never exists)

Days per month: 31 for 01 03 05 07 08 10 12; 30 for 04 06 09 11; February
has 28, or 29 in a leap year. A leap year is divisible by 4, except for
years divisible by 100, unless they are also divisible by 400 (2000 is a leap
year, 1900 is not). Check the format with a three-group regex in [[ =~ ]],
then check month and day with arithmetic (use 10# so 08 and 09 stay decimal).
concepts: capture year, month and day with groups
regex checks the shape, arithmetic checks the calendar
10# prevents octal surprises with 08 and 09

required_patterns.message: Check the format with [[ $date =~ regex ]].
Capture year, month and day: BASH_REMATCH[1], [2], [3].
Use 10# when you do arithmetic on month and day.

title: Regex in a Variable
story:
Priya's team keeps asking for one more variant of the same log filter, so she
wants a small reusable tool: you hand it the pattern, it filters lines.
Ollie wrote a first version and it behaves strangely: patterns with
anchors and classes never match, but they work fine in the terminal with
grep. The starter below is his script. Something about the way the pattern
reaches =~ is wrong.
objective:
Fix solution.sh. It takes two arguments: a MODE (regex or literal) and a
PATTERN. It reads lines from standard input and prints every line that
matches, unchanged:

  regex     the PATTERN is a POSIX extended regex
  literal   the PATTERN is plain text, every character stands for itself
            (a dot is a dot, a bracket is a bracket)

Any other mode: print "usage: solution.sh regex|literal PATTERN" to stderr
and exit 2. Missing arguments: the same message and exit status.
Use [[ =~ ]] for both modes. In regex mode the pattern must reach =~
UNQUOTED, through a variable ([[ $line =~ $pattern ]]). Quoted, it would be
taken literally. In literal mode that quoting is exactly what you want.
concepts: an unquoted right-hand side is a regex
a quoted right-hand side is literal text
keep the regex in a variable and use it unquoted

required_patterns.message: In regex mode, use the variable unquoted: [[ $line =~ $pattern ]].
In literal mode, quote the variable on purpose: [[ $line =~ "$pattern" ]].

title: grep -E Filters
story:
The reverse proxy in front of the customer sites logs a status code on every
request. Priya cares about the ones that look like someone knocking on
locked doors: 401 unauthorised, 403 forbidden and 429 too many requests.
Looping through the file in Bash would work, but the file has 400,000 lines
and grep was invented for exactly this. She wants a tiny script that filters
the file she points it at.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, the path of an access-log file,
and prints every line whose status field is 401, 403 or 429. In these logs
the status is the number between spaces right after the quoted request, like

  203.0.113.7 - [07/Nov/2024:09:30:15] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 403 512

so look for a space, one of the three codes, and another space. Numbers
that merely contain such digits elsewhere (a size of 4011, a path like
/v429/) must not count. Print the matching lines unchanged and in their
original order.
When nothing matches, print nothing and exit with status 0 (plain grep exits
with 1, which would be a failure under set -e). If no argument is given, print
"usage: solution.sh LOGFILE" to stderr and exit with status 2.
Use grep -E with alternation.
concepts: grep -E uses extended regex: ( ) | + ? { }
grep exits 1 when nothing matches
alternation inside grep

required_patterns.message: Use grep -E for extended regular expressions.
Use a group with alternation, for example (401|403|429).

forbidden_patterns.message: Use grep -E; no egrep, grep -P, awk or sed here.

title: Extract with grep -o
story:
The bastion's auth log is a mess of sentences, and somewhere in them are the
IP addresses Priya wants to put on the blocklist. The lines have different
shapes, some have two addresses (the client and a forwarded one), and she does
not care about the rest of the sentence. She wants the bare addresses, each
one listed once, in a tidy order, and she needs them ten minutes ago.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a log file, and prints every
IPv4-looking address found in it: four groups of 1 to 3 digits separated by
dots. Print each distinct address once, sorted in plain text order (what
sort gives you under LC_ALL=C). A line may contain several addresses, and an
address may repeat across lines. If the file contains no address, print
nothing and exit with status 0. If no argument is given, print
"usage: solution.sh LOGFILE" to stderr and exit with status 2.
Do not check the ranges; "999.1.1.1" counts as address-looking.
Use grep -o -E so that grep prints only the matching part of each line.
concepts: grep -o prints only the matched text, one match per line
extended regex with a repeated group
pipeline: grep -o | sort -u

required_patterns.message: Use grep -o -E (or -oE) to print only the matching text.
Pipe the matches into sort to order them and remove repeats.

forbidden_patterns.message: grep -o -E and sort are enough here.

title: Count and Invert
story:
The nightly sshd report is supposed to go to Gus as a two-number summary, not
a wall of text: how many real entries the log has, and how many of those are
failed passwords. The log files that Ollie rotates also contain comment lines
starting with "#" and empty lines, which are not entries at all and must not be
counted. Priya says the number of failures divided by the number of entries is
what she looks at first.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a log file, and prints exactly two
lines:

  entries: <number of lines that are neither empty nor start with #>
  failed: <number of lines containing "Failed password">

Count lines with grep -c, and skip comments and empty lines with an inverted
match (grep -v). A comment line or empty line is never an entry, even if it
contains "Failed password" (a "# Failed password" note is just a comment, so it
does not count in "failed" either). The counts must also print as 0 when there is no
match, and the script must exit with status 0. If no argument is given, print
"usage: solution.sh LOGFILE" to stderr and exit with status 2.
concepts: grep -c counts matching lines
grep -v selects the lines that do NOT match
grep -c prints 0 but exits 1 when nothing matches

required_patterns.message: Count with grep -c instead of piping into wc.
Skip comments and empty lines with grep -v.

title: sed Substitution
story:
A vendor needs the last week of application logs to debug a crash, and Priya
will not hand over the real internal names. Every occurrence of the internal
domain and of the internal install path has to be swapped for something
harmless before the file leaves the building. The original log stays
untouched; the sanitised copy goes to standard output so she can redirect it
wherever she likes.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a log file, and prints the file
to standard output with two substitutions applied to every line, every
time they occur (not only the first):

  lanternfish.internal   becomes   example.test
  /srv/lanternfish       becomes   /srv/app

The dots in the domain are literal dots: "lanternfishXinternal" must NOT be
changed. The file itself must not be modified. If no argument is given, print
"usage: solution.sh LOGFILE" to stderr and exit with status 2.
Use sed with s/old/new/g. For the path, pick a delimiter other than / so you
do not have to escape the slashes.

the g flag replaces every match on the line
any character can be the delimiter: s|old|new|
escape a regex dot with \.

title: sed Back-References
story:
Gus gets payment confirmations from the bank's European partner and the
dates are written the continental way: day, month, year, with slashes. His
accounting import wants ISO dates, year first, with dashes. The lines
around the dates are free text ("paid 07/11/2024 by BACS") and must be kept
exactly as they are. Retyping 3,000 of them by hand is not how Gus wants to
spend Friday.
objective:
Write solution.sh that copies standard input to standard output, rewriting every
date of the form DD/MM/YYYY (two digits, slash, two digits, slash, four digits)
into YYYY-MM-DD. Every such date on a line must be converted (a line may hold
two). All other text, including things that merely look similar such as
"7/11/2024" or "07/11/24", stays exactly as it is.
Use sed -E with one substitution that captures the three numbers in ( ) and
puts them back in a new order with \1, \2 and \3. Do not validate the numbers;
"99/99/2024" is converted like any other.

sed -E uses extended regex, like grep -E
reordering text with back-references

Use the back-references in the new order: \3-\2-\1.

title: Negated Classes
story:
The new application logger writes key="value" pairs, and most lines carry two
or three quoted fields: msg="...", user="...", host="...". Theo asks you for
a script that pulls out just the message text. Priya warns that his first try
with ".*" returned half the line, because it ran on to the last quote in the
line. You will need a different way to say "stop at the next quote".
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads log lines from standard input. Each line may
contain a field of the form msg="<text>", where the text has no double quote
inside it and may be empty or contain spaces and other fields' characters. For every line print

  msg: <text>          when the line has a msg="..." field
  no msg               when it does not

Lines can hold other quoted fields before or after msg, for example
  level=warn user="ollie" msg="disk is 91% full" host="halibut" code="D91"
and the text must stop at the quote that closes msg, not at the last quote on
the line. Use [[ =~ ]] with a capture group and a negated character class
[^"]* (any characters except a quote) instead of a greedy ".*".
No grep, sed, awk or cut.
concepts: [^"]* matches anything except a quote
a negated class stops at the next delimiter; ERE has no lazy .*?
the pattern as a variable keeps quotes readable

required_patterns.message: Use the negated class [^"] to stop at the next double quote.
Read the text from ${BASH_REMATCH[1]}.

forbidden_patterns.message: ERE has no lazy ".*?"; use [^"]* and a capture group, without external tools.

title: Log Line Parser
story:
The bastion log from last night is 40,000 lines long, and Priya has one
question: who was brute-forcing us, and did any of them get in? She does not
want a graph. She wants a short list she can paste straight into the blocklist
ticket, with the worst offenders first spelled out and a loud line for any
address that got a successful login after hammering the door. This is the
moment all the regex pieces have to work together.
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads sshd log lines from standard input. Two kinds of
line matter; everything else (cron, other services, malformed lines) is ignored.

  Nov  7 09:30:15 anchovy sshd[2211]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 port 4022 ssh2
  Nov  7 09:30:19 anchovy sshd[2212]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.9 port 4023 ssh2
  Nov  7 09:31:02 anchovy sshd[2214]: Accepted publickey for mara from 198.51.100.4 port 52114 ssh2

The format is: month name, day (padded with spaces, one or more), HH:MM:SS,
hostname, "sshd[pid]:", then either "Failed password for [invalid user ]USER
from IP port N ssh2" or "Accepted (password|publickey) for USER from IP
port N ssh2". The whole line must fit (anchored). USER is one word and IP
is digits and dots.
Track, per IP address, the number of failed attempts, the user and time of its
most recent failure. A "Failed password for invalid user admin" attempt counts
with the user "admin".
After reading all input, for every IP with 3 or more failures, in plain
sort order of the IP text, print

  BLOCK <ip> failures=<n> last-user=<user> last-seen=<HH:MM:SS>

and, directly below it, if that IP had an Accepted login at a moment when it
already had 3 or more failures:

  ALERT <ip> logged in as <user> after 3+ failures

(use the user of the last such login). If nothing qualifies, print nothing.
Exit status 0. Use [[ =~ ]] with capture groups (an optional group is allowed)
and an associative array. No grep, sed, awk or cut.
concepts: anchored regex with several groups, including an optional one
group numbering when a group is optional
associative arrays keyed by an extracted field
regex as parser: one pattern per line type

required_patterns.message: Parse each line with [[ $line =~ regex ]].
Read all four groups (time, optional 'invalid user ', user, ip) from BASH_REMATCH.
Keep the per-IP counters in an associative array (declare -A).

forbidden_patterns.message: Parse with =~ and BASH_REMATCH; no external text tools.

The shared file server at Lanternfish has one folder per customer website,
and every one of them was created by hand, slightly differently. Noor has
just signed a new customer and Mara has had enough. "Three folders, two log

the site folder `sites/CUSTOMER`:

  sites/CUSTOMER/logs/error.log
  sites/CUSTOMER/public/index.html

The customer name can contain spaces.

title: Don't Clobber
story:
Last Friday Theo ran his "save release notes" script twice and the second
run quietly replaced two hours of hand-written notes with a single line.
The shell did exactly what it was told. Priya would like the shell to be
told something different: "Overwriting should be something you do on
purpose, never by accident."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes a FILE, a TEXT and an optional third word
`--force`, and saves TEXT plus a newline into FILE with `>`.

Turn on the shell's overwrite protection at the top of the script with
`set -o noclobber`. Then:

- FILE does not exist yet: it is created. Print `wrote FILE`.
- FILE already exists and no `--force` was given: leave it untouched, print
  `refusing to overwrite FILE` to stderr and exit 1. The shell's own error
  message must not be shown.
- FILE already exists and the third argument is `--force`: overwrite it
  anyway using the redirection that bypasses noclobber, `>|`.
  Print `wrote FILE`.

With fewer than two arguments, print `usage: solution.sh FILE TEXT [--force]`
to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: set -o noclobber makes > refuse to replace files
>| overrides noclobber on purpose

required_patterns.message: Turn the protection on with set -o noclobber (or set -C).
For --force use the override redirection >| so the overwrite is deliberate.

story:

company to see. Her new rule: tokens live in a file and tickets only ever
show a masked version. Noor needs a tiny helper for the support desk that
reads a token file and prints just enough to recognise it.

Write solution.sh that takes one argument, the path of a token FILE which
holds a single token on its first line.

  masked=XXXX****

shorter than four characters is shown whole, still followed by `****`.

exit 1. With no argument, print `usage: solution.sh FILE` to stderr and
exit 2.

Gus wants a "how much writing do we actually keep on the file server"
number for his board slide, and he wants it by this afternoon. The support
team's notes are scattered over dozens of text files. Mara hands you a
warning along with the task: "wc is easy. wc on a Mac and wc on Linux

title: Copy with Checks
story:
Theo's backup line was `cp db.dump /backups/` and he reported "done". On
Monday the dump on the backup disk was 4 KB of a 900 MB file, because the
disk had filled up halfway. cp had complained, but nobody was reading.
Mara: "A copy that was not checked is a hope, not a backup."

Write solution.sh that takes a SOURCE file and a destination FOLDER and
copies the file into the folder under the same name, carefully:

1. SOURCE must be a readable regular file, otherwise print
   `cannot read SOURCE` to stderr and exit 1.
2. FOLDER must be an existing directory, otherwise print
   `no such folder: FOLDER` to stderr and exit 1.
3. If FOLDER already contains a file of that name, do not touch it: print
   `refusing to overwrite DEST` to stderr and exit 1 (DEST is the full
   path FOLDER/name).
4. Copy with `cp`, then verify that the copy is byte-for-byte identical

   `copy of SOURCE is corrupt, removed DEST` to stderr and exit 3.
5. On success print `copied SOURCE -> DEST`.

With the wrong number of arguments print `usage: solution.sh SOURCE FOLDER`
to stderr and exit 2.

cmp -s verifies a copy

The Tidewater Books upload folder is a zoo: half the photos end in .jpeg,
half in .jpg, and their shop software only accepts one of them. Renaming
four hundred files by hand is how interns become ex-interns. Ollie asks,

extension (both without the dot), for example:

looping over a glob and renaming with mv

title: Delete Carefully
story:
Priya keeps a framed printout above her desk. It is a postmortem from
another company: a cleanup script ran `rm -rf "$BUILD_DIR/"*` while
BUILD_DIR was empty, the shell saw `rm -rf /*`, and the rest is history.
Now Theo wants a "delete this customer's scratch folder" helper for the
file server, and Priya will review it with a very sharp pencil.
objective:
Write solution.sh that deletes one folder, but only if it is safely inside
the folder `shared` of the current directory. The argument is DIR, the
folder to delete. Apply these checks in this order and stop at the first
one that fails (all messages go to stderr):

1. No argument at all: `usage: solution.sh DIR`, exit 2.
2. DIR is an empty string: `refusing: empty path`, exit 2.
3. DIR is `/`: `refusing: that is the root folder`, exit 1.
4. DIR is not an existing directory: `refusing: DIR is not a folder`, exit 1.
5. Work out the real location of DIR with `cd` and `pwd -P` (this resolves
   `..` and symlinks). If it is the `shared` folder itself:
   `refusing: that is the shared folder itself`, exit 1.
6. If it is not somewhere below `shared`: `refusing: DIR is outside shared`,
   exit 1.

Only if every check passes, delete the folder and everything in it with
`rm -rf`, using the resolved path, and print `deleted: DIR` (DIR exactly
as the user typed it). Do not use a `*` wildcard after a variable in the
`rm` command.
concepts: guarding rm: empty values, root, and a base folder
pwd -P resolves .. and symlinks before checking

required_patterns.message: Resolve the real path with (cd "$dir" && pwd -P) before deciding.
Delete with rm -rf (after all checks) using the resolved path.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not write rm ... "$var"/* : with an empty $var that becomes /*. Delete the folder itself.

Noor's newsletter list has grown by copy and paste: the same customer
appears as Anna@Harbour.example and anna@harbour.example, there are blank
lines, and some people have been sent every mailing twice. She wants the
list cleaned in place, and Mara has one condition: "You cannot sort a
file straight into itself. The shell empties it before sort even starts.

never read and write the same file in one pipeline

title: Temporary Directories
story:
Every Friday a customer's website is packed into a tarball for the CDN.
Until now, Theo did it by copying files into `/tmp/stage`, tarring that,
and forgetting to clean up. Last week two people packed two different
customers at the same moment, and Tidewater Books shipped Harbour
Bakery's menu. The staging area needs to be private, new every time, and
gone when the job ends.

Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a SITE folder, and builds
`release.tar` in the current folder from the site's pages.

1. Create a private staging folder with `mktemp -d` and make sure it is

2. Copy every `*.html` file directly inside SITE into the staging folder,
   except those whose name starts with `draft-`.
3. Write a file named `MANIFEST` into the staging folder: one page name

   from inside the staging folder.
5. Print `packed N pages into release.tar` (N does not count MANIFEST),
   then the archive's file names, sorted, one per line (`tar -tf` piped
   through `sort`).

If it holds no pages to pack print `no pages to pack in SITE` to stderr,
exit 1 and create no archive. With no argument print
`usage: solution.sh SITE` to stderr and exit 2.

trap cleanup of a whole folder

title: Find by Name
story:
Priya is auditing the file server for forgotten keys and stray config
files, and she does not trust `ls` to look into forty nested folders.
"Give me a command that takes a folder and a name pattern and tells me
every place that name turns up. Same command for `*.conf`, for `id_rsa*`,
for anything I think of at midnight."

Write solution.sh that takes a FOLDER and a name PATTERN (a shell-style
wildcard such as `*.conf` or `id_*`, passed to your script as plain text)
and lists everything below FOLDER, at any depth, whose name matches the
pattern. Use `find` with `-name`.

Print the matching paths, one per line, sorted (pipe through `sort`, since
`find` does not promise any order), and finish with a line `found: N`.
With no match print only `found: 0`.

The pattern is matched against the file name, not the whole path, and
capital letters count (`*.conf` does not match `X.CONF`). If FOLDER is not
a directory print `no such folder: FOLDER` to stderr and exit 1. With

stderr and exit 2.

quote the pattern so find, not the shell, expands it

title: Find by Type and Size
story:
The file server's disk is 94% full and Gus has noticed, which is worse
than the disk being full. Before anyone buys more storage, Mara wants two
lists: the files that are suspiciously big, and the zero-byte leftovers
that crashed uploads left behind. "And mind the folders," she adds. "A
folder is not a file, however large `ls` makes it look."

Write solution.sh that takes a FOLDER and a size limit in BYTES (a whole
number, 0 or more) and reports on everything below FOLDER, at any depth,
using `find` with `-type` and `-size`.

Print, in this order:

1. `big: PATH` for every regular file larger than BYTES bytes, sorted.
2. `empty: PATH` for every regular file of size zero, sorted.
3. `folders: N`, the number of sub-folders below FOLDER (FOLDER itself is
   not counted).

Use the portable byte form of the size test (`-size +Nc`, with the `c`
suffix). Folders must never appear in the `big:` or `empty:` lines.
If FOLDER is not a directory print `no such folder: FOLDER` to stderr and
exit 1. If BYTES is not a whole number, or there are not exactly two
arguments, print `usage: solution.sh FOLDER BYTES` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: find -type f / -type d
find -size +Nc (bytes)

Count sub-folders with find ... -type d.
Test sizes in bytes with -size +${bytes}c (the c suffix keeps it portable).

title: Find by Age
story:
Two different questions keep landing on the support desk. Noor asks, "Which
of these customer uploads are older than a month, so we can ask whether
they still need them?" And Mara asks, "Which files changed since the last
backup ran?" The backup job leaves an empty marker file called
`.last-backup` in the folder, and its timestamp is the moment it finished.
Both questions are about time, and `find` can answer both.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes a FOLDER and a number of DAYS (a whole number
of 1 or more). FOLDER contains a marker file `.last-backup` (the marker
itself is never listed).

Using `find` on all regular files below FOLDER (`-type f`), print:

1. `old: PATH` for every file last modified more than DAYS days ago
   (`-mtime +DAYS`), sorted;
2. `changed: PATH` for every file modified after the marker was written
   (`-newer` the marker), sorted;
3. a final line `summary: A old, B changed`.

A file can be in both lists. If the marker does not exist print
`no marker: FOLDER/.last-backup` to stderr and exit 1. If DAYS is not a
whole number of at least 1 or the number of arguments is not two, print
`usage: solution.sh FOLDER DAYS` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: find -mtime +N (older than N days)
find -newer FILE (modified after FILE)

Find files changed after the marker with -newer "$folder/.last-backup".

title: Lock with mkdir
story:
The nightly sync is scheduled every hour, and last Tuesday one run took
ninety minutes. For half an hour two copies were syncing the same
customer folders, and each one "fixed" what the other was busy writing.
Theo wants "a lock", but this server has no `flock`. Mara grins: "The
oldest lock in Unix is a folder. `mkdir` either makes it or it doesn't,
and there is no 'both of you'."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes a JOB name and makes sure only one copy of
that job runs at a time, using a lock *directory* `run/JOB.lock`.

1. With no argument print `usage: solution.sh JOB` to stderr and exit 2.
2. Make sure the folder `run` exists (`mkdir -p run`).
3. Take the lock by creating `run/JOB.lock` with a plain `mkdir` (no `-p`).
   Do not test with `-d` or `-e` first: creating the folder is the test.
   If `mkdir` fails, another copy holds the lock: print
   `JOB is already running (lock: run/JOB.lock)` to stderr and exit 1,
   leaving that lock exactly as it was.
4. Once you hold the lock, remove it again when the script ends, however
   it ends (use `trap ... EXIT` with `rmdir`).
5. Append the line `JOB started` to `run/jobs.log`, run the command
   `run-job JOB`, and then append `JOB finished`. If `run-job` fails, the
   script must stop with the same exit status, without writing the
   `finished` line, and the lock must still be released.
concepts: mkdir is atomic: only one caller can create the directory
release the lock from a trap

required_patterns.message: Take the lock with mkdir on the lock path (no -p): it either creates the folder or fails.
Use trap ... EXIT so the lock is released on every exit path.
Release the lock with rmdir.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not check first and create second: two copies can both pass the check. Let mkdir itself be the test.

rotate-logs started
rotate-logs finished

title: Atomic Writes
story:
The web server re-reads `config/app.conf` every few seconds. On Monday
Theo's deploy script was halfway through writing a new one when the server
looked: it saw a file with half a line in it, tried to start on port
"80" instead of "8080", and took Harbour Bakery's shop offline for four
minutes. Mara's rule: "A reader must see the old file or the complete new
file. Never anything in between."
objective:
Write solution.sh, which reads a complete new configuration from standard
input and installs it as `config/app.conf` in an atomic way:

1. Create the folder `config` if it does not exist.
2. Make a temporary file *inside* `config` with `mktemp` (use the template
   `config/.app.conf.XXXXXX`, so it is on the same disk as the target) and
   write all of standard input into it.
3. The new configuration is valid only if it contains a line that is
   exactly `port=` followed by digits (for example `port=8080`). If it is
   not valid, delete the temporary file, print
   `invalid config: no port= line, keeping the old file` to stderr and
   exit 1. The existing `config/app.conf` must not be touched.
4. If it is valid: `chmod 644` the temporary file (`mktemp` files start
   private) and move it over `config/app.conf` with `mv`.
5. Print `installed config/app.conf (N lines)` with N the number of lines
   of the new file.

Never write to `config/app.conf` directly with `>`. When the script ends
there must be no temporary file left in `config`.
concepts: write to a temporary file, then rename it into place
mv within one file system is atomic

Finish with mv: renaming within one disk is atomic.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not write to the live file directly; write the temp file and mv it into place.

title: Rotate Backups
story:
The customer database dump is copied to `customers.sql.bak` every night,
and every night the copy replaces yesterday's. Last week a bad import
corrupted the dump on Tuesday afternoon; by Wednesday morning the only
backup was a copy of the corruption. Gus, who now carries the memory of
that morning, has one request: "Keep three. Always three nights back."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes a FILE and rotates its numbered backups, then
makes a fresh backup of it. FILE.1 is the newest backup, FILE.3 the
oldest. Keep at most three:

- the old FILE.3 is deleted,
- FILE.2 becomes FILE.3,
- FILE.1 becomes FILE.2,
- FILE is copied to FILE.1.

Backups that do not exist yet are simply skipped (do not fail and do not
create empty files for them). FILE itself stays in place. Do the shifting
oldest first, so nothing is overwritten before it has been moved.

At the end print `rotated FILE: N backups kept`, where N counts how many
of FILE.1, FILE.2, FILE.3 exist now. If FILE is not a regular file print
`cannot read FILE` to stderr and exit 1 (and touch nothing). With the
wrong number of arguments print `usage: solution.sh FILE` to stderr and
exit 2.

optional steps guarded with [[ -e ]]

Make the new FILE.1 with cp.

title: Directory Summary
story:
Gus finally gets to ask the question he has been saving: "What is
actually *on* the shared drive?" Not sizes this time, but kinds. How many
spreadsheets, how many photos, how many things with no type at all. The
cleanup of the file server is nearly done, and the last job is a report
that tells the story of what is left, built from everything you have
learned this module.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a FOLDER, and counts the regular
files below it, at any depth, grouped by file extension. Use `find` to
list the files.

The extension of a file is the text after the last dot of its **name**
(not of its path), in lowercase, provided the dot is not the first
character of the name and something follows it:

  photo.JPG -> jpg      backup.tar.gz -> gz      .gitignore -> (none)
  Makefile  -> (none)   notes.         -> (none)

Print one line per extension: `EXT: COUNT`, with the biggest counts first;
extensions with the same count are in alphabetical order (plain byte
order, so `(none)` comes before letters). Finish with `total: N files`
(always the word `files`, even for 1).

If FOLDER is not a directory print `no such folder: FOLDER` to stderr and
exit 1. With any other number of arguments than one print

title: Sort Lines

Ollie has been asked to print shelf labels for the server room, one per rack
position, and the label printer wants them in alphabetical order. He has the
list, in whatever order people typed it, and he has found out the hard way
that the labels for rack 10 end up in front of rack 2. Time to find out why.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It reads lines from standard input (no arguments) and
prints the same lines in ascending order, using the plain character order
that `sort` gives under `LC_ALL=C`: digits first, then capital letters, then
lowercase letters, comparing character by character. So `rack10-dory` comes
before `rack2-eel`, and `Eel` comes before `anchovy`.
Do not remove duplicates: a line that appears twice must be printed twice.
Empty input prints nothing. Use the sort command.

default order is by characters, not by numeric value

the fullest disks at the top of her screen when she arrives. The first draft
of the report put a 95 GB volume above a 120 GB one, which made her
eyebrow do the thing. The report needs to understand that used space is a
number and that the host name is only a tie-breaker.

Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a file of comma-separated lines:
  host,mount,used_gb
for example `dory,/data,430` (used_gb may have decimals, e.g. 7.5). There
is no header line. Print the same lines, sorted by used_gb from the largest
to the smallest. When two volumes have the same used_gb, the one whose host
name comes first alphabetically goes first (plain character order).
Print the lines unchanged. Use `sort` with -t to set the separator, -k to
choose the key fields, and the n flag for numeric comparison.
concepts: sort -t sets the field separator
sort -k picks the key field(s)
n and r flags on a key: numeric and reversed

title: Collapse Repeats

moments when the state changed, in the order they happened.

consecutive lines collapsed into a single line, keeping the original order:

A state that comes back later is printed again; only neighbours are merged.

uniq does not need or want sorting when order matters

title: Frequency Table
story:
Noor has a theory that customers only ever visit three pages of the Lanternfish
website and that the rest of the site is decoration. Nobody has proof. The web
server log has every request, so a quick tally of the most requested pages
would settle the argument over lunch.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, an access log. Each line has four
space-separated fields:
  <ip> <method> <path> <status>
for example `10.0.0.5 GET /menu 200`. Print one line per distinct path, in
the format
  <count> <path>
with a single space between them and no leading spaces, ordered by count from
the largest to the smallest. Paths with the same count are ordered
alphabetically (plain character order). An empty log prints nothing.
Build it as a pipeline: extract the path, group equal lines with sort,
count them with uniq -c, and order the result by count.
concepts: sort | uniq -c turns repeated lines into counts
sort -rn orders the counts, biggest first
uniq -c pads its counts; normalise before comparing

title: Translate Characters
story:
Theo is wiring every Lanternfish service into the new config system, and it
only accepts environment variable names in shouting capitals with
underscores: no dots, no dashes, no lowercase. The service list uses names like
`tidewater-books.api`. He has forty of them and is not going to retype them.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It reads service names from standard input, one per
line, and prints for each one an environment variable name:
  - every lowercase letter becomes the uppercase letter
  - every `.` becomes `_`
  - every `-` becomes `_`
Everything else (digits, capitals, other characters) stays as it is.
  tidewater-books.api  ->  TIDEWATER_BOOKS_API
Empty input prints nothing. Do it with a single tr command: no sed, no awk, no
${var^^}.
concepts: tr SET1 SET2 maps characters one-to-one
ranges like a-z and A-Z

required_patterns.message: Use tr to translate the characters.
Map the lowercase range a-z to the uppercase range A-Z.

forbidden_patterns.message: This level is about tr; leave sed, awk and ${var^^} for other jobs.

title: Delete and Squeeze

office, and every line arrives with an invisible carriage return at the end and
a random number of spaces between the words. Noor's import script rejects
the lot. Nothing is wrong with the content; it just needs a wash.

Write solution.sh. It reads text from standard input and prints it cleaned:
  1. delete every carriage return (the character \r, usually the last
     one on each line)
  2. squeeze every run of spaces into a single space
Newlines, tabs and all other characters stay exactly as they are. A line
such as `T-77   printer    jams\r` becomes `T-77 printer jams`.
Use tr for both steps, in one pipeline: tr -d for the first and tr -s for
the second. Empty input prints nothing.
concepts: tr -d deletes characters
tr -s squeezes repeats into one

required_patterns.message: Delete the carriage returns with tr -d.
Squeeze the repeated spaces with tr -s.

title: awk Sums and Averages

Gus keeps the harbour-office petty cash in a text file, one expense per line,
and every month he adds it up on the back of an envelope and gets a
different answer. He would like the machine to do it: how many entries,
the total, and the average. He would also like it not to divide by zero
in March, when nobody bought anything.

  count=<lines> total=<sum> avg=<average>

the result in an END block.

printf with %.2f

OFS is the output field separator used by print a, b

actually eating the pipe. The traffic export has one row per customer per
day, and the same customers appear dozens of times. She needs one line
per customer with the number of days they showed up and their total.

title: Align a Table
story:
Mara sends the weekly CPU report to the whole team by pasting it into chat,
where a monospaced block is the only thing standing between "readable" and
"a wall of commas". The data is a CSV; what she wants is a table whose
columns line up, with a header on top, so that the busy servers are obvious
at a glance.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a CSV file with three fields per
line and no header:
  <host>,<role>,<cpu_percent>
Print a header line and then one formatted line per input line, using awk's
printf with the format "%-12s %-10s %5s\n":
  HOST         ROLE        CPU%
  anchovy      web           42
That is: host left-aligned in 12 columns, a space, role left-aligned in
10, a space, and the cpu value right-aligned in 5. The header uses the same
format with the words HOST, ROLE and CPU%. Print the header even when the
file is empty. Values are never longer than their column.
concepts: printf %-12s pads text on the right (left-aligned)
printf %5s pads on the left (right-aligned)
printf does not add a newline by itself

required_patterns.message: Format the columns with printf.
Left-align text columns with a width like %-12s.
Right-align the number column with a width like %5s.

title: Parse key=value Files
story:
Every Lanternfish service keeps its settings in a plain `key=value` file, and
half the deploy scripts grep for them with patterns that break the moment a
value contains an equals sign. Theo's database URL did exactly that last
week. Mara wants one small, correct lookup tool that the other scripts can
call instead of reinventing it.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: a settings FILE and a KEY. Each
line of the file is `key=value`; the value is everything after the FIRST
equals sign and may itself contain equals signs (`url=https://x.example/?a=1`)
or be empty (`debug=`). Lines such as `# port=1234` are comments: their key
is `# port`, which never equals a real key. Blank lines are ignored.
If KEY appears several times, the last assignment wins. Print the value
(just the value) and exit 0. If KEY is not in the file, print
  key not found: KEY
to standard error and exit with status 1.
The last line of the file may have no trailing newline: still read it.
Parse with a Bash while loop and IFS='=' read -r, not with grep, sed, awk
or cut.
concepts: IFS='=' read -r key value splits a line at the first =
the last variable of read keeps the rest of the line, = signs included
while read ... done < file, and the last line without a newline

required_patterns.message: Split each line with IFS='=' read -r key value.
Loop over the file with while ... done < "$1".

forbidden_patterns.message: Use read with IFS for this one; no external tools.

test_cases.name: key on the last line without newline
empty value is still a value

title: Top-N Report
story:
The DNS resolver on eel logs every query, and Priya has noticed that people
keep asking for names that do not exist: typos, retired hosts, one very
stubborn printer. She wants a weekly leaderboard of the worst offenders so she
can fix the typos at the source. This is the module's final exam: no new
tool, but you must wire the old ones together.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: a resolver log and a number N.
Each log line has four space-separated fields:
  <time> <client_ip> <name> <rcode>
for example `10:01:02 10.0.0.5 wwww.harbourbakery.example NXDOMAIN`. Only
lines whose rcode is exactly NXDOMAIN count. Print a title line and then the
N most-queried names among them:
  Top N NXDOMAIN names
  1. <name> (<count>)
  2. <name> (<count>)
Rank 1 is the name with the most queries; names with equal counts are ordered
alphabetically (plain character order). If there are fewer than N
names, print all of them. If there are no NXDOMAIN lines, print just the title.
Build one pipeline: filter and pick the name column, group and count, order,
take the first N, and number the lines with awk. uniq -c pads its count
differently on macOS and Linux, so normalise it.
concepts: combining filters: awk | sort | uniq -c | sort | head | awk
normalising uniq -c output
numbering lines with NR

required_patterns.message: Count the repeats with sort | uniq -c.
Take the first N lines with head -n.
Use awk's NR to number the ranked lines.
Use awk to select the NXDOMAIN lines and to number the result.

title: A Proper Header
story:
Theo has left for a week of kayaking and his line counter, count-lines.sh, is
still in cron. Mara opened it and found no description, a shebang that points at
a path that does not exist on half the servers, and no safety switches: when
the report file is missing it quietly says "0 lines" and carries on. Your first
job in the craft module is to give the script a proper front door.
objective:
Edit solution.sh so that its first lines are a proper header, then keep the
behaviour below.

Header rules (checked):
  - line 1 is exactly: #!/usr/bin/env bash
  - within the next few lines, a comment starting with "# Description:"
    that says in one sentence what the script does
  - strict mode: the line  set -euo pipefail  before any other command

Behaviour: solution.sh takes one argument, a file. It prints
  lines: <N>
  done
where N is the number of lines in the file (no padding spaces). The count
must be taken from a pipeline that starts with cat, as it does now. With
strict mode on, a missing file stops the script before it prints anything
and exits with status 1, and so does a missing argument.
concepts: #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
a Description comment

required_patterns.message: Add the line set -euo pipefail near the top (after the header comment).

title: Usage and --help
story:
Noor keeps pasting the same instructions into chat: "ticket.sh wants a customer
and a subject, in that order". Ollie ran it with three words last week and got a
ticket for a customer called "Harbour". A script that can explain itself saves
everyone a message, so ticket.sh is getting a usage() function and a --help.
objective:
Write solution.sh as a ticket stub tool with a function named usage.

usage prints exactly these two lines:
  Usage: ticket.sh CUSTOMER SUBJECT
  Prints a one-line ticket stub.

Behaviour:
  - With -h or --help as the first argument: print usage to stdout, exit 0.
  - With any other number of arguments than two: print usage to stderr and
    exit 2.
  - With exactly two arguments: print  ticket for <CUSTOMER>: <SUBJECT>
    and exit 0.
Both the help and the error path must call the same usage function.
concepts: usage() function
usage to stdout for --help, to stderr for errors
exit 2 for bad invocation

required_patterns.message: Define a function: usage() { ... }
On a wrong argument count call usage >&2 so the text goes to stderr.

title: The main() Pattern
story:
Gus asked for a quick tally of how many lines each uploaded invoice file has, and
Theo delivered: forty lines of loose commands, with a helper function squeezed in
halfway down. It works, but nobody can tell where the program starts, and last
week someone appended a line after the final command and broke the exit status.
Mara asks you to give the script a spine.
objective:
Restructure solution.sh so that all the logic lives in functions and the only
top-level command after the function definitions is the last line:
  main "$@"
Behaviour (must not change):
  - arguments are files. For each readable file print  <file>: <N> lines
  - for an unreadable (missing) file print  skip: <file>  on stderr, keep
    going, and remember it
  - after the loop print  total: <sum of the lines of the readable files>
  - exit 0 if every file was readable, exit 1 if any were skipped
  - with no arguments print  usage: solution.sh FILE...  to stderr, exit 2
Define a function called main and put the usage check inside it.
concepts: main() function
main "$@" as the last line
helpers defined before they are called

required_patterns.message: Define a function named main: main() { ... }
The last line of the script should be exactly: main "$@"

title: Constants Block
story:
Priya found something in backup-path.sh that made her put her coffee down: the
backup root is read from the environment, so anybody who exports BACKUP_ROOT
before calling it can point Lanternfish's backups wherever they like. The same
numbers (14 days, tar.gz) also appear three times in the file, and Theo changed
only two of them last month. Configuration belongs in one block, and constants
should be unchangeable.
objective:
solution.sh takes two arguments, a host name and a date (for example
halibut 2026-03-01), and prints two lines:
  path=<BACKUP_ROOT>/<host>/<date>.<SUFFIX>
  keep=<KEEP_DAYS> days
Put a constants block at the top of the script that declares, with the
readonly builtin, exactly these three names:
  BACKUP_ROOT=/srv/backups
  KEEP_DAYS=14
  SUFFIX=tar.gz
Use those names in the rest of the script; no literal /srv/backups, 14 or
tar.gz outside the block. The environment must not be able to override them:
running with BACKUP_ROOT=/tmp/evil in the environment still prints
/srv/backups. Fewer than two arguments: print
"usage: solution.sh HOST DATE" to stderr, exit 2.
concepts: readonly NAME=value
one block of configuration at the top
constants ignore the inherited environment

required_patterns.message: Declare readonly BACKUP_ROOT=/srv/backups in a constants block.
Declare readonly KEEP_DAYS=14.
Declare readonly SUFFIX=tar.gz.

forbidden_patterns.message: A constant must not fall back to the environment. Assign it with readonly and no ${...:-...} default.

title: Filenames with Spaces
story:
Customers do not name files the way engineers do. Tidewater Books uploads
"Q3 sales.txt", the Gull & Anchor Pub sends "Pub *final*.txt", and the archiver
script Theo wrote handles exactly none of them. Noor has a ticket open: three
reports "disappeared" last night, and the script that was supposed to archive
them printed errors about files called "Q3" and "sales.txt".
objective:
solution.sh takes one argument, a directory. It must create the folder
archive/ in the current directory (if it does not exist), copy every file
ending in .txt from the given directory into archive/ under the same name,
and print one line per file:
  archived: <file name without the directory>
in the order the shell's glob lists them. If the directory contains no .txt
files, print "no reports" and copy nothing. The directory argument and the
file names may contain spaces and glob characters such as * and ?; quote
every expansion so each stays one word.
concepts: quote every expansion
unquoted variables are split and globbed
a glob in the pattern, a quoted variable around it

required_patterns.message: Glob inside the directory like this: "$1"/*.txt (quote the variable, leave the * outside the quotes).

test_cases.expected_stdout:

archived: Q3 sales.txt

title: Commands in Arrays
story:
Ollie wrote a little file finder for the support desk: give it a folder and some
name patterns and it lists the matches. It builds the find command in a string,
which works until Noor searches for "Q3 *", at which point find receives broken
fragments and the shell helpfully expands the star against whatever folder it
happens to be in. Mara says: never build commands in strings. Build them in
arrays.
objective:
solution.sh takes a directory, followed by zero or more name patterns. It
runs find on that directory for regular files (-type f) whose name matches
ANY of the patterns, and prints the paths sorted with sort. With no
patterns, every regular file matches.

Build the find arguments in an array, one element per word, and run the
command with "${array[@]}". The patterns are plain arguments and may contain
spaces; they must reach find unexpanded, exactly as typed.
Example: solution.sh logs '*.log' 'Q3 *' lists logs/a.log, logs/c.log
and logs/Q3 sales.txt. Without any argument print
"usage: solution.sh DIR [PATTERN...]" to stderr and exit 2.
Do not use eval and do not build the command in a plain string variable.
concepts: arrays hold arguments: cmd=(find ...) then "${cmd[@]}"
append with cmd+=( ... )
no eval, no command strings

required_patterns.message: Append to an array with name+=( ... ) as you collect the find arguments.
Expand the array with "${name[@]}" (quotes included) to keep each element a word.

forbidden_patterns.message: No eval here: an array carries the arguments safely without re-parsing them.

test_cases.name: pattern with a space and two patterns
the star must not be expanded by the shell

files.zzz.txt: this is in the current directory, not in logs

title: printf Over echo
story:
Gus wants a label printer script for the server-room shelf tags. Whatever
words people give it must appear on separate lines, exactly as typed. The first
version used echo, and the tag for the spare machine named "-n" came out blank.
Another tag said "50%d" and printed "50" followed by an error. Priya points out
that data should never be allowed to pose as options or as a format.
objective:
solution.sh takes any number of arguments. It prints each argument on its own
line, exactly as given (backslashes, percent signs and leading dashes
included), and then a final line
  count: <number of arguments>
With no arguments print only "count: 0".
Use printf with a fixed format string such as '%s\n'. Do not use echo at all.
concepts: printf '%s\n' "$data"
echo treats -n and -e as options
never put data in the format string

required_patterns.message: Print data with a fixed format: printf '%s\n' "$arg".

forbidden_patterns.message: Leave echo out; arguments such as -n or -e would be eaten as options.

test_cases.name: arguments that look like echo options
backslashes and percent signs are data

title: Don't Parse ls
story:
The disk-usage report Theo wrote for Gus loops over the output of ls. It was
fine until North Pier Dental dropped a file called "x-ray scan 1.txt" in the
upload folder: the report listed "x-ray", "scan" and "1.txt" as three items,
and two of them did not exist. Mara's rule is short: ls is for humans, globs are
for scripts.
objective:
solution.sh takes one argument, a directory. For every regular file directly
inside it (not directories, not hidden files) print
  <name>: <bytes> bytes
where <name> is the file name without the directory part and <bytes> its size
in bytes, listed in the order the shell's glob gives. Subdirectories are
skipped. If there are no such files print "empty".
Loop over a glob like "$1"/* and test each entry with [ -f ]. The word ls
must not appear in your script, and do not use find or stat.
concepts: for f in "$dir"/* instead of $(ls)
[ -f ] to keep regular files only
${f##*/} to strip the directory

required_patterns.message: Loop over a glob such as "$1"/* instead of the output of a command.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not use ls in a script; let the shell expand a glob.
Use a plain glob loop and a file test, not find or stat.

test_cases.name: directories and hidden files are skipped
directory name with a space, brackets in a file name

title: Local by Default
story:
The stock-check script that feeds Gus's weekly sheet prints each fish tank's
stock in a tidy aligned row. Last Friday somebody added a log line after each
row, and suddenly the log showed ANCHOVY in capitals and the wrong counts. A
helper function had been quietly reusing the caller's variable names. In bash,
every variable is global unless you say otherwise, so say otherwise.
objective:
solution.sh reads lines from stdin, each  NAME COUNT  (two words). For every
line it must print two lines:
  <NAME in upper case padded to 10 characters> <COUNT>
  logged <name exactly as read>
for example  "ANCHOVY    12"  followed by  "logged anchovy". After the last
line print  rows: <number of lines processed>  and  total: <sum of counts>.
The helper function format_row must declare every variable it uses with
local, so it cannot change the variables of its caller. Use these two
functions, which the starter already defines: format_row (prints the padded
row) and main (the loop). Blank lines are skipped and not counted. Empty
input prints  rows: 0  and  total: 0.
concepts: local var inside functions
functions share the caller's variables by default
local name=$(command) pitfalls are avoided by declaring first

required_patterns.message: Declare the helper's own variables with local inside format_row.
