title: Small Functions
story:
Priya audits the endpoint list that the load balancer is built from. The script
that cleans it up is one thirty-line loop that lowercases, strips a trailing dot,
validates the port, and formats the result all in the same breath. Nobody dares
to change the port rule because nobody can find it. She wants each rule in a
function you could read in one glance, and test on its own.
objective:
solution.sh reads lines from stdin. Each line should look like  host:port.
For every non-blank line print one of:
  endpoint=<host>:<port>          if the line is valid
  invalid: <the line as read>     if not (to stdout as well)
Rules: the host is the part before the colon, lower-cased, with a single
trailing dot removed. The port is the part after the colon, which must be
1 to 5 digits with a value between 1 and 65535. A line without a colon, with
an empty host, or with a bad port is invalid. Blank lines are skipped.

Structure (checked): define these four functions and call main on the
last line:
  normalise_host    prints the cleaned host given as $1
  is_port           returns 0 if $1 is a valid port, 1 otherwise
  format_endpoint   prints the endpoint=... line for a host and port
  main              reads stdin and ties the pieces together
Each function does one job.
concepts: one function, one job
functions that return status vs functions that print
main only orchestrates

required_patterns.message: Define normalise_host() { ... }
Define is_port() { ... }
Define format_endpoint() { ... }
End the script with: main "$@"

title: Flags, Positionals and --
story:
Gus wants a little tool for the price labels on the harbour-office wall. Words go
in, labels come out: optionally upper-cased, optionally with a prefix. Ollie's first
version read $1 and $2 by position, so "label.sh -u Cod" worked and "label.sh Cod -u"
printed a label that said "-u". Real tools take flags in any order, understand --,
and complain clearly. Time to write a proper parsing loop.
objective:
solution.sh accepts options first, then words:
  -u or --upper         print each word in UPPER CASE
  -p VALUE or --prefix VALUE   put VALUE directly before every word
  --                    end of options; everything after it is a word
and then one or more WORDS. Options can be combined in any order but must
come before the words. Print one word per line.
Errors (exit status 2, message on stderr, nothing on stdout):
  unknown option   -> "solution.sh: unknown option: <opt>"
  -p without value -> "solution.sh: option -p needs a value"
  no words at all  -> "usage: solution.sh [-u] [-p PREFIX] [--] WORD..."
Use a while loop with case and shift. The first argument that does not start
with - ends option parsing; so does --.
concepts: while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do case ... shift; done
-- ends the options
options with values: shift 2

required_patterns.message: Parse with a loop on the remaining argument count: while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do ...
Consume each parsed argument with shift.
Add a case branch for -- (end of options).

double dash lets a word start with a dash

title: Subcommands
story:
The night shift keeps a running list of chores on a sticky note that nobody can
find at 3 a.m. Mara wants a tiny tool instead, in the style of git: one program,
several verbs. "notes add", "notes list", "notes remove". Ollie has volunteered to
write the first version of the verbs; you are asked to build the frame that
dispatches to them so that adding a fourth verb later is a ten-line change.
objective:
solution.sh keeps its notes in the file notes.txt in the current directory,
one note per line. The first argument is a subcommand:
  add TEXT...   join the remaining words with single spaces, append them as a
                new line, print  added: <text>.  With no TEXT: usage error.
  list          print each note as  <n>) <text>  starting at 1. If the file is
                missing or empty print  no notes
  remove N      delete note number N, print  removed: <text>. N must be a
                positive whole number no larger than the number of notes,
                otherwise print  solution.sh: no such note: <N>  to stderr and
                exit 1.
No subcommand: print  usage: solution.sh add TEXT... | list | remove N  to
stderr and exit 2. An unknown subcommand: print
solution.sh: unknown command: <word>  to stderr and exit 2.
Write one function per verb named cmd_add, cmd_list and cmd_remove, and
dispatch to them with a case on the first argument.
concepts: case on $1 to dispatch
shift the subcommand away, pass the rest on
one function per subcommand

required_patterns.message: Dispatch with case "$1" in ... esac (or "${1:-}").
Define cmd_add() for the add verb.
Define cmd_list() for the list verb.
Define cmd_remove() for the remove verb.

title: Settings from the Environment
story:
The health poller on barracuda is configured by exporting variables before it
starts, which is nice and flexible and also how Theo once set the interval to
"fast" and took down the monitoring for a weekend. Priya's rule for anything read
from the environment: it has a default if it can, a check always, and an error
message that says exactly which variable is wrong.
objective:
solution.sh reads three environment variables and prints one summary line:
  host=<POLL_HOST> every=<POLL_SECONDS>s mode=<POLL_MODE>
Rules:
  POLL_HOST     required, must not be empty
  POLL_SECONDS  optional, default 30; a whole number from 1 to 3600
  POLL_MODE     optional, default normal; must be exactly fast or normal
A variable that is unset or set to the empty string counts as "not given"
and gets its default. Report the first problem found, checking in the order
host, seconds, mode, with exit status 2 and a message on stderr, nothing on stdout:
  solution.sh: POLL_HOST is required
  solution.sh: POLL_SECONDS must be a whole number from 1 to 3600
  solution.sh: POLL_MODE must be fast or normal
Use ${NAME:-default} for the defaults.
concepts: ${VAR:-default}
validate before use
empty and unset treated the same with :-

Whenever a customer's site setup fails halfway, support re-runs the provisioning
script, and every time Mara holds her breath. The current version crashes if the
folder already exists, overwrites the page the customer spent an hour editing,

title: Library or Program?
story:
Ollie wants to reuse Theo's slugify function, the one that turns "Harbour Bakery"
into "harbour-bakery" for URLs, in his own script. He wrote `source slugify.sh`
and his shell printed a usage message and closed. The file runs its program the
moment it is read. Mara asks you to make one file that behaves well both ways:
run it and it is a command, source it and it is a library.
objective:
Write solution.sh with a function slugify that takes one string and prints its
slug: lower case, every run of characters other than a-z and 0-9 replaced by a
single dash, and no dash at the start or the end.
  "Harbour Bakery"      -> harbour-bakery
  "  C++ & Go!  "       -> c-go
When EXECUTED, solution.sh prints the slug of every argument, one per line.
With no arguments it prints "usage: solution.sh TEXT..." to stderr and exits 2.
When SOURCED from another script it must only define slugify: print nothing,
not exit, not run main, and not leave shell options such as errexit switched
on in the caller. Turn strict mode on only when running as a program.
Decide between the two cases by comparing ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} with $0.
(Run `bash fixtures/use-lib.sh` in the workspace to see the library side.)
concepts: ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == $0 means executed, not sourced
libraries define, programs run
do not change the caller's shell options

required_patterns.message: Compare ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} with $0 to detect whether the file is being run or sourced.

title: Version Guard
story:
The new deploy helper uses associative arrays, which arrived in bash 4. Last week
it landed on an old appliance whose bash is 3.2, and instead of a clear message it
failed with a cryptic syntax error in the middle of a deployment. Mara wants a
guard at the very top: if the running bash is older than the script needs, say so
in plain words and stop before anything is touched.
objective:
solution.sh takes one argument, the minimum bash version the script needs,
written MAJOR or MAJOR.MINOR (for example 4.4, or just 5, which means 5.0).
Compare it with the bash that is running this script using the BASH_VERSINFO
array, and compare the parts as numbers, not as text (10.0 is newer than 9.0).
  - if the running bash is at least that version, print  ok: bash >= <argument>
    exactly as given, exit 0
  - otherwise print  solution.sh: requires bash <argument> or newer (running <A>.<B>)
    to stderr, where A and B are the running bash's major and minor numbers,
    and exit 1
  - if the argument is missing or is not MAJOR or MAJOR.MINOR with digits only,
    print  usage: solution.sh MINVERSION  to stderr and exit 2
Do not parse the text in $BASH_VERSION.
concepts: BASH_VERSINFO[0] and BASH_VERSINFO[1]
compare versions numerically
fail early with a clear message

required_patterns.message: Read the running major version from ${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}.
Read the running minor version from ${BASH_VERSINFO[1]}.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use the numeric BASH_VERSINFO array rather than the BASH_VERSION string.

title: POSIX-Friendly Code
story:
The recovery stick that Lanternfish keeps in the office safe boots a tiny Linux
whose only shell is dash, and the installer scripts on it start with #!/bin/sh.
The file classifier Theo wrote is full of bashisms, so on the stick it dies on
line 7. Priya wants a version that runs under any POSIX shell, without giving up
what it does.
objective:
Rewrite solution.sh in portable POSIX shell. Line 1 must be #!/bin/sh.
The script takes one or more paths and prints, for each, one line
  <path>: <kind>
where kind is the first of these that applies:
  missing     the path does not exist
  directory   it is a directory
  image       the name ends in .png .jpg .jpeg or .gif, in any letter case
  archive     the name ends in .tar.gz .tgz or .zip, in any letter case
  log         the name ends in .log, in any letter case
  other       anything else
After the paths print  items: <number of paths>.  With no arguments print
"usage: solution.sh PATH..." to stderr and exit 2.
It must also run correctly under plain sh. Use [ ] and case, and avoid
bash-only features: no [[ ]], no (( )), no ${var,,}, no ==, no function
keyword, no local, no arrays, no here-strings, no source.
concepts: [ ] and case instead of [[ ]]
$(( )) arithmetic is POSIX, (( )) is not
tr for case conversion, printf instead of echo -e

required_patterns.message: Classify by file name with a case statement and glob patterns.

forbidden_patterns.message: [[ ]] is a bashism; use [ ] or case.
(( )) is a bashism; use $(( )) for arithmetic or [ ... -lt ... ].
${var,,} and ${var^^} are bash 4 only; use tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'.
Use a single = inside [ ]; == is not POSIX.
Stay with POSIX: no function keyword, local, declare, source or mapfile.
Here-strings, =~ and &> are bash features.

title: Self-Documenting Help
story:
Every script at Lanternfish has a documentation comment at the top, and every
script has a --help that prints a hand-copied version of it, which is out of date
after the first edit. Mara's final lesson for the craft module: keep one copy. The
header comment is the help. Make the script read its own first lines and show them.
If you edit the header tomorrow, the help changes with it.
objective:
solution.sh is tidy-tmp.sh, a small cleanup tool. It already has a header
comment block (the comment lines that follow the shebang, up to the first
line that is not a comment). Keep that block exactly as it is.

  --help or -h as the only argument: print the header block to stdout,
    with the leading "# " (or a bare "#") removed from each line, and exit 0.
    The shebang line is not part of the help. The text must be read from
    the script file itself (through $0), not copied into the code.
  no arguments: print the same help text to stderr, exit 2.
  DIR: delete the files named *.tmp directly inside DIR, then print
    removed <N>. If DIR is not a directory print
    tidy-tmp.sh: no such directory: <DIR>  to stderr and exit 1.
A checker will insert an extra line into your header and run --help again;
the new line must appear.

awk or sed reading the leading comment block
one source of truth for documentation

title: Trace with set -x
story:
At 03:12 the pager goes off: Harbour Bakery's backup folder is nowhere to be
found, yet Theo's setup script printed "ready". Mara, in a dressing gown and
very calm, says: "Don't guess. Make the script show its work." The easiest way

these three commands, in this order:

(`ready: backups/NAME` on stdout), while the trace of the three commands goes
to stderr, each line starting with `+ `.

trace lines start with + (the PS4 prefix)
the trace shows the quoting Bash would need

the set +x command is itself traced

title: PS4 with Line Numbers
story:
Theo's 200-line deploy script failed overnight and the trace says
`+ [[ -e /srv/app ]]`. Which of the nine `[[ -e` tests in the file is that?
Nobody knows. Priya suggests the cheapest fix in the world: teach the trace to
print the line number in front of every command.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes any number of arguments (file names) and, for
each one, prints `found: NAME` to stdout if a file or directory with that
name exists, or `missing: NAME` if not. Write the loop with the check and the
two echos each on their own lines, for example:
  for f in "$@"; do
    if [[ -e $f ]]; then
      echo "found: $f"
    else
      echo "missing: $f"
    fi
  done
Turn on tracing with `set -x` above the loop and set the trace prefix
variable PS4 before that so every trace line looks like
  + L12: [[ -e notes.txt ]]
that is: `+ L`, the line number of that command in solution.sh, then `: `.
Single-quote the PS4 value so Bash fills in the line number at every trace
line, not once when PS4 is assigned.

PS4 is expanded for each trace line, so quote it
$LINENO inside PS4 gives the line number

title: Trace to a File
story:
Noor's inbox is filling up: the cron job that counts customer pages mails its
stderr to the support desk, and since Ollie turned on `set -x` every morning
brings forty lines of trace to people who just want to know if anything is
wrong. "Keep the trace," Mara says, "but give it its own room."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments, a SITE name and a PAGES number,
and does the following:
  1. Open file descriptor 3 onto the file trace.log (`exec 3>trace.log`) and
     point `BASH_XTRACEFD` at it, so that tracing goes to the file instead
     of stderr.
  2. Turn on `set -x`, then run exactly these two commands:
       count=$(( $2 + 1 ))
       echo "site $1 has $count pages"
     and turn tracing off with `set +x`.
  3. Afterwards print `warning: SITE is slow` to stderr (a normal message,
     not part of the trace).
Result: stdout is the `site ...` line, stderr holds only the warning, and
trace.log holds three lines: the trace of the two commands and of `set +x`.
concepts: BASH_XTRACEFD names the file descriptor that receives the trace
exec N>file opens a descriptor for the whole script
stderr stays free for real messages

ports per site, starting at 8000. Use `set -euo pipefail`. Steps:

`debug "last=$last"` after it. Stdout is the one `... uses ports ...` line
in every case; the debug lines appear on stderr only in debug mode.

if instead of && keeps the function's status 0 under set -e

title: LINENO in Messages
story:
Ollie's error message at 03:40 was "something is wrong with the config".
Which check said so? The script has four of them. Noor asks for a promise: from
now on every error says where in the script it was raised, so whoever reads the
log can open the file and go straight to it.
objective:
Write solution.sh that checks a config file given as its only argument. Use
`set -u`. Perform these two checks, each on its own lines, in this order:
  1. If the file does not exist, print
       error (line N): file not found: NAME
     to stderr and exit with status 1.
  2. If the file exists but is empty (size 0), print
       error (line N): file is empty: NAME
     to stderr and exit with status 2.

take it from `$LINENO` inside that very command, do not type a number. If
both checks pass, print `config ok: NAME` to stdout and exit 0.

messages that name their own origin

title: The Call Stack
story:
The log rotation script died deep inside `compress`, and the error says only
"disk full". Ollie stares at a file with eleven functions that call each
other like a game of pass-the-parcel. "Who called whom?" Ollie asks. Bash
actually keeps that list; you only have to read it.

`nightly` (each calls the next, see the starter), plus a mode argument.

running ABOVE itself (so `stack` itself is not listed), innermost first:
  "  at FUNCTION, called from line N"

called: use the arrays FUNCNAME and BASH_LINENO. The bottom pseudo-entry
"main" that Bash adds for the top level must not be printed.

title: Where Was This Defined?
story:
Theo copied `host_label` into three scripts, then into a shared library, and
now the nightly report prints labels with a different format than the
dashboard. Which copy is running? Mara's answer is a script that can be
both things at once: a library other scripts can `source`, and a command you
can run, and that knows the name of the file it was defined in.
objective:
Write solution.sh that works both when run and when sourced. Use `set -u`.
Define:
  host_label()  prints:  host: NAME (defined in FILE)
    where NAME is its first argument and FILE is the base name (no
    directories) of the file the function was defined in, taken from
    `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`.
  main()  takes the script's arguments; with no arguments it prints
    `usage: solution.sh HOSTNAME` to stderr and exits 2, otherwise it calls
    `host_label "$1"`.
Call `main "$@"` only when the file is being run directly
(`${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` equals `$0`). When another script sources
solution.sh, nothing may run or print, and afterwards `host_label eel`
must work and say `defined in solution.sh`.

$0 is the script that was started; they differ when sourced
the main guard: run only when executed, not when sourced

title: ERR Trap with Context
story:
The 03:00 restart job for the customer sites exited with status 7 and left
one word in the log: "failed". Seven what? Which command? Priya wants the
next failure to leave a full statement: what ran, what it returned and where
in the script it happened, written by the script itself, in the moment.
objective:
solution.sh takes a SITE name and runs the function `publish`, given in the
starter (it calls the commands `healthcheck "$1"` and `restart-site "$1"`,
and prints a line after each). Make the script explain a failure:
  - start with `set -eE` (the E makes the trap also work inside functions)
  - register an ERR trap, before `publish` is called, whose handler writes ONE
    line to stderr in this exact shape:
      failed: COMMAND (status S) at line N
    COMMAND is `$BASH_COMMAND`, S is the exit status of the failing command
    and N is `$LINENO`; for example
      failed: healthcheck "$1" (status 3) at line 8

trap fires. The script must still stop with the failing command's status.
When nothing fails there is no stderr output.

$BASH_COMMAND, $LINENO and $? describe the failure
set -E lets functions inherit the ERR trap

title: Dry-Run Mode
story:
Priya will not let Theo's new site-provisioning script near production until
it can answer one question without touching anything: "What are you about to
do?" The company ethos, since the day somebody deleted the wrong bucket, is
look first, then act. Give the script a `--dry-run` flag.

  chmod 750 "sites/$SITE"

command. In dry-run mode it executes nothing and instead prints one line to

After the commands, print `provisioned SITE` (real mode) or `dry run only,
nothing changed` (dry-run mode). If SITE is missing, print
`usage: solution.sh [--dry-run] SITE` to stderr and exit 2.

printf ' %q' quotes words so they can be pasted back
dry-run changes nothing

title: Assertions
story:
Gus checks the quarterly price list by eye and has twice missed a typo that cost
real money. Theo's answer: let the script check itself. A tiny helper that
compares what you got with what you expected and complains loudly when they
differ turns "looks fine to me" into a sentence the computer can verify.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh EXPECTED ACTUAL LABEL`. It defines
a function `assert_eq` that takes the same three values and compares them as
strings:
  - equal: print `PASS: LABEL` to stdout and return 0
  - different: print
      FAIL: LABEL: expected 'EXPECTED' but got 'ACTUAL'
    to stderr (the values wrapped in single quotes) and return 1
The script then calls `assert_eq "$1" "$2" "$3"` as its last command, so its
exit status is the function's: 0 when the values match, 1 when they do not.
Use `set -euo pipefail`, and compare inside `[[ ]]` with both sides quoted so
values with spaces or glob characters are compared literally.

return status of a function becomes the script's status
quoted right-hand side in [[ == ]] is a literal match

title: A Mini Test Harness
story:
Theo has written eleven little check functions for the billing helpers, all
named `test_something`, and runs them by pasting their names into the
terminal one at a time. Mara has seen enough. "A test harness is just a loop
that finds the tests, runs each one safely, and counts. Build us a small one
and we will never paste names again."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh TESTFILE`. TESTFILE is a Bash file
that defines functions; some are tests (names starting with `test_`), others
are helpers. Your script must:
  1. `source` the file.
  2. Find every function whose name starts with `test_` (`compgen -A function
     test_`), sorted alphabetically.
  3. Run each test in a subshell `( ... )`, so an `exit` or a crash inside one
     cannot stop the harness, and throw away the test's own output. A test
     passes when its status is 0.
  4. Print one line per test to stdout: `PASS name` or `FAIL name`.
  5. Finally print `N passed, M failed` (counts) and exit with status 1 if any
     test failed, otherwise 0.
With no test functions it prints `0 passed, 0 failed` and exits 0.
concepts: compgen -A function lists function names

the owner needs it. The retention script is supposed to keep the newest three
backups. Somebody counted, and it keeps only two. Theo swears he "just
tidied the loop". Mara hands you his version: "Don't rewrite it. Find the one
character that is wrong."

`solution.sh KEEP` and reads backup names from stdin, one per line, oldest

(oldest first), then `kept: N` where N is how many backups are left.

The release plan has twenty steps and, since last night's change, it fails
somewhere. Each full rehearsal takes ten minutes on the scratch machine, and

doing a linear search," Mara sighs. "Whatever breaks is in the first K steps

`try-steps` calls must be at most 1 + ceil(log2 N).

title: Run in the Background
story:
The nightly snapshots at Lanternfish run one server after another, and every
`snapshot` takes a while. Mara looked at the clock last night and counted
five servers sitting in a queue while the machine did almost nothing. "They
do not depend on each other," she says. "Start them all at once, but keep a
note of which process is which."
objective:
Write solution.sh. Every argument is a server name; with no arguments print
`usage: solution.sh SERVER...` to stderr and exit with status 2.

For each SERVER, in the order given:
  1. start `snapshot SERVER` in the background with `&`, so the loop moves
     on at once (no waiting between servers);
  2. append the new process's ID (the special variable `$!`) to the file
     `pids.txt`, one ID per line.

When every snapshot has been started, print exactly
  started N snapshots
where N is the number of servers, then wait for all of them to finish
(a plain `wait` is enough) and exit with status 0.

The `snapshot` command prints nothing; it takes about half a second.
concepts: cmd & starts a command in the background
$! is the PID of the most recent background job

Read the new job's process ID from $! right after starting it.

story:
Priya's `integrity-check` scans one server's disks for rot. It prints
nothing at all; the only answer it gives is how it exits: 0 when the disks
are clean, something else when they are not. Priya wants the check running
in the background so the script can keep talking to the console, and she
wants the verdict at the end.

wait returns the job's exit status in $?

title: Wait for Them All
story:
Gus wants one line in the morning email: "the weekend backups went fine" or
the names of the servers where they did not. Backing up the VMs one by one
takes most of the night, so Theo started them all together. The problem is
that the first backup to finish is rarely the first one you started, and a
plain `wait` forgets who failed.

Write solution.sh. Every argument is a server name; with no arguments it
does nothing but print the summary below.

Start `vmbackup SERVER` in the background for every server (all running at
the same time) and remember each PID. Then wait for the jobs one by one,
in the order the servers were given, using `wait "$pid"` for each, and
keep each exit status.

After the last wait, print one line per server, in the order given:
  SERVER ok            (status 0)
  SERVER failed (N)    (any other status N)
then a summary line
  A ok, B failed
Exit with status 0 if everything succeeded, otherwise 1.

The jobs finish in an unpredictable order, but your output must not. Print
only after all waits are done. Do not use a bare `wait`.

collect one status per job
report in submission order, not completion order

title: Still Running?
story:
The search index at Lanternfish is rebuilt by `reindex`, which takes anywhere
from a few seconds to a few minutes. Noor has a dashboard that should say
"reindex finished" as soon as it ends, and "still running" if it drags on,
without freezing the dashboard script while it waits. Theo mutters that you
can ask the system whether a process is alive without disturbing it.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, CHECKS (a positive whole number).
Without it, print `usage: solution.sh CHECKS` to stderr and exit with
status 2.

1. Start `reindex` in the background and keep its PID.
2. Look at the job up to CHECKS times. Each look is `kill -0 "$pid"`: it
   sends no signal at all, it only succeeds while the process still exists.
   (Silence its error message with `2>/dev/null`.)
3. If the process is gone at a look, print `reindex finished` and exit 0.
4. Otherwise sleep 0.1 seconds and look again.
5. If it is still there after CHECKS looks, print
   `reindex still running after CHECKS checks` and exit with status 1.
   Leave the job alone; do not wait for it and do not kill it.

Do not use `wait` or `jobs` for the looks; the point is `kill -0`.
concepts: kill -0 PID tests whether a process exists
polling a background job without blocking

Keep the background job's PID from $!.

title: Stop a Job
story:
Last Friday somebody started `soaktest` on a staging box and went home. It
is meant to run for a minute; this one ran until Monday and ate the disk.
Mara wants a launcher that starts the soak test, gives it a fixed amount of
time, and then stops it politely if it is still going. She also wants to know
how it ended, because "stopped by us" and "crashed" are not the same story.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, GRACE: the number of seconds to
let the test run (it may be a decimal such as 0.3). Without it print
`usage: solution.sh GRACE` to stderr and exit with status 2.

1. Start `soaktest` in the background and keep its PID.
2. `sleep "$GRACE"`.
3. Try to stop it with a plain `kill "$pid"` (silence errors with
   `2>/dev/null`).
   - If the kill worked, the job was still running: `wait "$pid"` to collect
     it and print `soaktest stopped (status N)`.
   - If the kill failed, the job had already ended by itself: `wait "$pid"`
     to collect its status and print `soaktest finished by itself (status N)`.
N is the status that `wait` returned. A job ended by the default signal
of `kill` reports 143 (128 + 15).

Always exit with status 0 once the message is printed. By default
`soaktest` runs for 30 seconds, far longer than your GRACE.
concepts: kill PID sends SIGTERM
wait PID reaps the job and shows 128+signal
kill fails when the process is already gone

Collect the job with wait "$pid" to get its status.

title: A Worker Limit
story:
Harbour Bakery uploaded four hundred product photos and Theo's shell loop
started `resize` on all of them at once. The little server `cuttlefish`
swapped itself to a standstill. Starting jobs one by one is too slow and
starting everything at once is too much; Mara wants "at most three at a
time, and start the next one the moment a slot frees up".
objective:
Write solution.sh. The first argument is MAX, the largest number of
`resize` jobs allowed to run at the same moment; the remaining arguments
are the image names. With no arguments at all print
`usage: solution.sh MAX NAME...` to stderr and exit with status 2.

Run `resize NAME` in the background for every NAME. Never have more than
MAX running together, and keep MAX of them busy whenever there is work
left: as soon as one job ends, start the next. Use `wait -n`, which waits
for whichever job finishes first and returns that job's status.

After the last job has ended, print
  done: A ok, B failed
and exit with status 1 if B is above zero, otherwise 0. With no names,
print `done: 0 ok, 0 failed`.

a running-jobs counter keeps the pool at MAX

title: Subshell Isolation
story:
Ollie asks a good question over lunch: "When my script sets `LOG_LEVEL=debug`
for one command, why is every later command suddenly chatty?" Mara slides
a napkin across the table. It says: "A child process can never change its
parent. Use that on purpose." Time to build a wrapper that gives one probe a
noisy, labelled environment and leaves the rest of the script untouched.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, LABEL (it may contain spaces).
Without it, print `usage: solution.sh LABEL` to stderr and exit 2.

At the top, set `LOG_LEVEL=info` and export it. Then:
  1. Open a subshell with `( ... )`. Inside it: set and export
     `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, export `PROBE_LABEL` with the value of LABEL, run
     `probe`, and finish with `exit 7`.
  2. Right after the closing `)`, capture the subshell's status and print
       subshell exited with N
     Use `|| status=$?` (set status=0 before it), so a non-zero status does
     not stop a script that uses `set -e`.
  3. Run `probe` again, outside the subshell.
  4. Print `main LOG_LEVEL=` followed by the current value of LOG_LEVEL.

`probe` prints a line like `probe level=... label=...` from the environment
it sees (`label=none` when PROBE_LABEL is not set). Nothing done inside the
subshell may leak out.
concepts: ( ... ) runs commands in a child shell
variable changes and exit inside a subshell stay inside
the subshell's exit status arrives in $?

required_patterns.message: Open the subshell with ( at the start of a line and close it with ).
Capture the status right after the ): ( ... ) || status=$?

title: cd Without Consequences
story:
Theo's `build-all.sh` walks through the customer sites and runs the site
builder in each one. It works for the first site and then mysteriously
builds the second one inside the first one's folder, because nobody went back
after the `cd`. Priya's comment in the review is one word: "Isolate." The
fix is to let each site have its own little shell.

Write solution.sh. Every argument is a folder that holds one customer
site; with no arguments print `usage: solution.sh SITE_DIR...` to stderr and
exit with status 2.

SITE_DIR, in order:
  - run `sitebuild` inside that folder, using a subshell so that your own
    working directory never changes: `( cd "$dir" && sitebuild )`;
  - if that succeeded print `built SITE_DIR`, otherwise print
    `failed SITE_DIR` (a missing folder counts as a failure) and carry on
    with the next one.
After the last one print `built A of N sites`, where A is the number that
succeeded and N the number of arguments. Then print
`still in the starting folder` if `$PWD` equals `start`, or
`moved away from the starting folder` if not.

Exit with status 1 if any site failed, otherwise 0. `sitebuild` needs a
`site.conf` in the folder it runs in, and it writes its result to
`build.log` there.

a failing subshell as an if condition

title: Command Groups
story:
Gus wants a one-page fleet report he can print: a title, the list of servers
in alphabetical order, and a total at the bottom. Theo's first draft has
three separate `>>` redirections and twice it left half a report behind when
a step failed. Mara suggests grouping the commands so the whole page is
written through a single door, and using a second group to bail out neatly.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, LIST, a file with one server
name per line (it may contain blank lines and repeated names).

- With no argument print `usage: solution.sh LIST` to stderr, exit 2.
- If LIST is not a readable file, print `cannot read LIST` to stderr and
  exit with status 1, without creating report.txt. Do this with a command
  group after `||`: `[[ -r $list ]] || { ...; exit 1; }`.
- Otherwise create `report.txt` with a single redirection on a command
  group: `{ command1; command2; command3; } > report.txt`. Its content is
    == fleet report ==
    <every server once, blank lines skipped, sorted alphabetically>
    total: N
  where N is the number of distinct servers.
- Finally print `wrote report.txt (N servers)` to stdout.

Use awk 'NF' to drop blank lines and sort -u for sorting and de-duplicating.
concepts: { cmd1; cmd2; } groups commands in the current shell
one redirection for the whole group
exit inside a group ends the script (unlike a subshell)

required_patterns.message: Close the group with } > report.txt so one redirect covers all of it.
Use a command group after || for the error exit: [[ -r $list ]] || { ...; exit 1; }

title: Collect Job Results
story:
Ollie wrote a neat latency probe: `result=$(latency "$host") &` inside a loop,
then he printed `$result` and got nothing. Five times. He is close to tears.
Mara explains that every background job is a separate process with its own
copy of the variables, so a variable assigned in it never comes back. The
way out is old and humble: let every job write to its own file.
objective:
Write solution.sh. Every argument is a host name; with no arguments print
`usage: solution.sh HOST...` to stderr and exit with status 2.

1. Make a private scratch folder with `mktemp -d` and remember its name.
2. Start `latency HOST` in the background for every host, all at once. Each
   job writes both its output and its error messages to its own file in the
   scratch folder: `> "$tmp/N" 2>&1`, with N the position of the host
   (1, 2, 3, ...).
3. `wait` for all the jobs.
4. Print the contents of the files in the order the hosts were given, so
   that the report does not depend on which job finished first.
5. Remove the scratch folder completely.
6. Print `checked N hosts`.

`latency HOST` prints `HOST NNms`; for a host that does not answer it prints
`HOST: unreachable` on stderr and exits with status 1. Both kinds of line
belong in the report. Exit with status 0.
concepts: variables set in a background job are lost
one temp file per job, read back in submission order
mktemp -d and cleaning up

required_patterns.message: Create the scratch folder with mktemp -d.
Send each job's output to its own file inside the scratch folder: > "$tmp/$n" 2>&1.
Wait for the jobs before reading the files.

title: Named Pipes
story:
`tailfeed` streams a server's log line by line, slowly, the way a real log
grows. Noor wants every ERROR line shouted out the moment it arrives, without
storing a huge copy of the log and without waiting for the stream to end.
A normal `|` pipe would do, but `tailfeed` insists on being given a pipe by
name, so you are going to build one in the file system.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, SRC, the log for `tailfeed` to
stream. With no argument print `usage: solution.sh SRC` to stderr and
exit with status 2.

1. Create a named pipe called `feed.pipe` in the current folder with `mkfifo`.
2. Start `tailfeed SRC feed.pipe` in the background (it writes the log lines
   into the pipe) and keep its PID.
3. In the foreground, read the pipe line by line with a `while read` loop
   whose input is `feed.pipe`. For every line that contains `ERROR`, print
   `!! ` followed by the line, and count it.
4. When the stream ends, print `errors=N`.
5. Collect `tailfeed` with `wait`, delete `feed.pipe` with `rm`, and exit
   with tailfeed's own exit status.

Read with `IFS= read -r` so lines are kept exactly. Do the counting in the
`while` loop itself (not behind another pipe) so the count survives.

a writer in the background, a reader in the foreground
opening a FIFO blocks until the other end is open

title: Signal Yourself
story:
Theo is building `lanternd`, a little daemon that people poke with signals
instead of restarting it: one signal flips verbose logging, another prints
a status line. Before it touches production he wants a harness that can poke
the program from the inside, using a scripted list of actions, so the
handlers can be tested without a second terminal and without `ps`.
objective:
Write solution.sh. Each argument is an action word; with no arguments print
`usage: solution.sh ACTION...` to stderr and exit with status 2.

Keep two variables: `verbose` (starts as `off`) and `steps` (starts at 0).
Install two handlers with `trap`:
  - on `USR1`: toggle `verbose` between off and on, then print
      verbose is now on        (or: verbose is now off)
  - on `USR2`: print
      status: N steps, verbose=on|off

Then handle the actions in order:
  go        add 1 to `steps`; if verbose is on, also print `step N`
  verbose   send USR1 to yourself with `kill -USR1 $$`
  status    send USR2 to yourself with `kill -USR2 $$`
  anything else   print `unknown command: WORD` to stderr and exit 2

The handlers must be reached only through the signals, never called
directly.
concepts: kill -SIGNAL $$ sends a signal to the script itself
trap handler USR1 USR2 runs a function when the signal arrives
a trap handler runs in the main shell and can change its variables

Install a handler for USR2: trap handler_name USR2
Signal yourself with kill -USR1 $$ (the PID of this script is $$).

title: Reload on HUP
story:
Every time Priya changes the welcome banner, somebody restarts the greeter
service, and every restart drops a few customers' connections. The grown-up
way is the one nginx and sshd use: leave the process running and send it
SIGHUP, the traditional "please re-read your configuration". Priya's deploy
tool `confpush` already does its half: it overwrites the config file and then
sends HUP. You write the half that listens.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, CONF, the path of a config file
containing a line `greeting=SOMETHING` (the text may contain spaces or more
`=` signs). Without it print `usage: solution.sh CONF` to stderr, exit 2.

1. Define a function that reads the greeting from CONF (everything after the
   first `=` on the `greeting=` line) into the variable `greeting`.
2. Load it once and print `loaded greeting=<value>`.
3. Install a handler for `HUP` with `trap`. On HUP it must load the config
   again, set `reloaded=1`, and print `reloaded greeting=<new value>`.
4. Only then start the pusher: `confpush "$$" "$CONF" &`. It rewrites CONF
   about 0.3 seconds later and then sends HUP to PID `$$`.
5. Poll up to 20 times: `sleep 0.1`, then stop looking as soon as
   `reloaded` is 1.
6. If the reload happened, print `reload handled` and exit 0. If it did not
   arrive after 20 polls, print `no reload received` to stderr and exit 1.

Install the trap before starting `confpush`: the default action of HUP is to
terminate the process.
concepts: SIGHUP as the conventional 'reload your config' signal
a handler that re-reads state and sets a flag
the trap must be in place before the signal can arrive

Start confpush in the background: confpush "$$" "$conf" &

title: Ignore and Restore Signals
story:
The nightly database migration has one fragile stretch in the middle where
an impatient SIGTERM, from a deploy tool that "just wants to restart
everything", would leave the schema half changed. Mara wants that stretch
shielded, and then the shield removed again. She also asks you to prove a
surprising rule: a signal you ignore is ignored by every program you start
while the shield is up.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, NAME (it may contain spaces).
Without it print `usage: solution.sh NAME` to stderr and exit 2.

Use the helper `worker`. It sends SIGTERM to itself, and if it is still
alive afterwards prints `worker: still alive after TERM`.

1. Ignore TERM with `trap '' TERM`.
2. Send TERM to yourself with `kill -TERM $$` and print `shielded NAME`.
   The script must survive.
3. Run `worker`, capture its exit status without letting a non-zero status
   stop the script, and print `phase 1 (NAME): status N`.
4. Restore the default behaviour with `trap - TERM`.
5. Run `worker` again, capture its status the same way, and print
   `phase 2 (NAME): status N`.

title: A FIFO Semaphore
story:
Mara closes the module with a trick from the old guard. "Counting running jobs
by hand is fine until the day you forget one decrement. Let the operating
system count for you." Her idea: a pipe holding a few tokens, one per free
seat. To start a job you take a token out of the pipe, and if there is none you
simply wait until one appears. When the job ends it puts the token back. The pipe
is the counter, and `read` is the bouncer.
objective:
Write solution.sh. The first argument is SLOTS, the most `render` jobs that
may run at once; the other arguments are scene names. With no arguments
print `usage: solution.sh SLOTS NAME...` to stderr and exit 2.

Build a semaphore from a named pipe:
  1. Create the FIFO `slots.fifo` with `mkfifo` and open it for reading and
     writing on file descriptor 3 with `exec 3<> slots.fifo` (opening it
     read-write means the open does not block). Then delete the name with
     `rm slots.fifo`: the open descriptor keeps working.
  2. Put SLOTS tokens into it: SLOTS times `echo >&3` (a token is one newline).
  3. Empty `failed.log` at the start (`: > failed.log`).
  4. For every NAME: take a token with `read -r -u 3` (this waits while all
     tokens are in use), then start in the background a group that runs
     `render NAME`, appends NAME to `failed.log` if render failed, and always
     puts the token back with `echo >&3`.
  5. `wait` for all jobs.

Print `rendered N, failed F`: N is the number of names, F the number of
lines in failed.log. Exit with status 1 if F is above zero, otherwise 0.
Do not use `wait -n` or `xargs`; the pipe is the limit.
concepts: a FIFO filled with tokens is a counting semaphore
read -u 3 blocks until a token is available
exec 3<> opens a pipe for both reading and writing

required_patterns.message: Create the semaphore with mkfifo slots.fifo.
Open the FIFO read-write on a descriptor: exec 3<> slots.fifo.
Take a token with read -r -u 3 (it blocks while none are left).

forbidden_patterns.message: The FIFO is the limiter in this level: no wait -n and no xargs.

title: An Iterator over Lines
story:
The sales team keeps new customers in a "queue file" that is not a table.
Each customer takes three lines in a row: the name, the plan, the monthly
price. Gus wants a clean one-line-per-customer list for the invoice
run. "A `while read` loop gives you one line per turn," Mara says, "and you
need three. Build something you can ask for the next line from anywhere in
the loop."

line of QUEUE_FILE in the variable `LINE` and returns 0; when there are no
lines left it returns 1 and leaves `LINE` alone. Keep the position in a
variable named `cursor`.

complete record print:
  NAME: PLAN plan, PRICE EUR/month

"incomplete record starting at line N" to stderr (N counts from 1 and is the
line of that record's name) and exit 1; records before it have already
been printed.

stderr and exit 1. An empty file prints nothing.

title: Event Handlers
story:
When something happens at Lanternfish, several people want to know:
a deploy should go to the log and to #ops, a full disk should page whoever
is on call. Today each alert script calls the others by name, and adding a
listener means editing the sender. Mara wants it the other way round. "The
sender shouts the event. Whoever signed up for it hears it."
objective:
Write solution.sh. It reads commands from standard input, one per line:
  on EVENT HANDLER        register the function HANDLER for EVENT
  emit EVENT WORD...      call every handler registered for EVENT, in
                          registration order, passing the WORDs as arguments
The script defines three handler functions:
  h_log    prints "log: " followed by its arguments joined with spaces
  h_mail   prints "mail to ops: " followed by its arguments
  h_page   prints "paging on-call: " followed by its arguments
Keep the registrations in an associative array keyed by event name.
Problems are reported on stderr, the run continues, and the exit status is 1
at the end if any problem happened:
  on with a HANDLER that is not a function:  "on: no such handler 'HANDLER'"
  emit for an event nobody registered for:   "emit: nobody listens to 'EVENT'"
  any other command word:                    "unknown command 'WORD'"
Blank lines are ignored.

appending to a map entry: handlers[$event]+=" $fn"
emit loops over the registered names and forwards the arguments

title: Builder Pattern
story:
Customers order virtual machines with a form that has fifteen optional
fields, and the provisioning script takes them as fifteen positional
arguments. Last week someone swapped RAM and disk, and a dental practice
got a 4 GB disk. "Name your arguments," Mara says. "Collect them one
option at a time, check each as it arrives, and only build the thing when
you have all of it."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh NAME [KEY=VALUE ...]`.
The spec of a machine lives in an associative array. Write these functions:
  vm_new NAME      reset the spec to the defaults: cpus=1 ram_gb=2 disk_gb=20 region=eu-north
  with_cpus N      1 to 16 (whole number)
  with_ram_gb N    1 to 64
  with_disk_gb N   10 to 500
  with_region R    one of eu-north, eu-south, us-east
  build            check the combination, then print the spec
A setter that gets a bad value prints "with_cpus: invalid value 'X'" (with
its own name) to stderr and returns 1; otherwise it stores the value.
`build` fails with "build: N cpus need at least M GB of RAM" (M = 2 times N)
when ram_gb is too small, otherwise it prints exactly five lines:
  vm=NAME
  cpus=...
  ram_gb=...
  disk_gb=...
  region=...
The script calls vm_new, then one setter per KEY=VALUE argument (keys:
cpus, ram_gb, disk_gb, region), then build. Any setter or build failure
ends the script with exit 2 and nothing on stdout. An unknown key prints
"unknown option: KEY" to stderr and exits 2. With no NAME print
"usage: solution.sh NAME [KEY=VALUE ...]" to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: state in an associative array, one setter function per option
validate each value when it is set, validate the combination at build
fail before producing output

required_patterns.message: Define with_cpus() and the other setters (with_ram_gb, with_disk_gb, with_region).
Define a build() function that checks and prints the spec.
Keep the spec in an associative array.

title: Strategy Pattern
story:
Gus's invoice run turns amounts in cents into whole euros, and every
customer contract seems to round differently. Harbour Bakery pays the
nearest euro, Tidewater Books always rounds up ("it is in the contract,
page nine"), and the Gull & Anchor Pub negotiated rounding down. Theo's
script has the same `if` copied into four places. Mara pulls out a marker:
"One loop. One variable that says how to round. Change the variable, change
the behaviour."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh STRATEGY`. STRATEGY is one of
nearest, up, down. Standard input has one amount in cents per line (a
whole number); blank lines are ignored.
Write three functions taking the amount as `$1` and printing whole euros:
  round_nearest   half rounds up:     1249 -> 12,  1250 -> 13
  round_up        any fraction up:    1201 -> 13,  1200 -> 12
  round_down      fraction dropped:   1299 -> 12
Choose the function ONCE, before reading any input, and store its name in a
variable called `strategy`. The loop that processes lines must call
`"$strategy" "$cents"` and must not mention the three names.
For each amount print:  AMOUNTc -> EUROS EUR   (for example "1250c -> 13 EUR").
A line that is not a whole number prints "skip: 'LINE' is not an amount"
to stderr, the run continues, and the exit status is 1 at the end.
An unknown STRATEGY prints "unknown strategy: NAME" to stderr and exits 2;
with no argument print "usage: solution.sh nearest|up|down" to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: a variable holding a function name: strategy=round_up
choose the algorithm once, call it everywhere
same interface (cents in, euros out), different behaviour

required_patterns.message: Store the chosen function name in a variable called strategy.
Call the chosen function as "$strategy" "$cents".

title: Middleware Chain
story:
Noor's support desk copies customer messages into the archive, and every
message needs tidying first: some need their padding trimmed, some should be
lowercased, the ones that mention card numbers need the digits hidden.
Different mailboxes need different combinations. "Make each tidy-up its own
small function," Mara says, "and let the caller choose which ones, and in
what order, like pipes with names."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh STEP...` (zero or more steps).
Standard input holds messages, one per line. Read each line exactly as it
is, keeping leading and trailing spaces. Pass each line through every STEP,
in the order given: the output of one step is the input of the next.
Print the final text of each line between square brackets: [text]
Each step NAME is implemented by a function `mw_NAME` that takes the text as
`$1` and prints the changed text. Write these five:
  mw_trim      remove leading and trailing spaces
  mw_lower     lowercase everything
  mw_squeeze   collapse each run of spaces into one space
  mw_mask      replace every digit with #
  mw_clip      keep only the first 12 characters
Before reading any input, check that every STEP names an existing function
(use `declare -F`); if not, print "unknown middleware: NAME" to stderr and
exit 2 without printing anything else. With no steps, lines are printed
unchanged (still in brackets).
concepts: an array of function names as a pipeline
value=$("mw_$step" "$value"): each output feeds the next input
the order of the chain changes the result
IFS= read -r keeps the line exactly as is

title: Retry Wrapper
story:
The nightly sync to the offsite store fails about once a week because of a
network blip, and so do a handful of other nightly commands. Everybody has
written their own little retry loop, and each one is slightly wrong: one
always exits 1, one retries forever, one drops the arguments with
spaces. Mara wants one `retry` that wraps *any* command, and gets it right
once.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh ATTEMPTS COMMAND [ARG...]`.
Define a function `retry ATTEMPTS COMMAND [ARG...]` that runs the command
with its arguments, unchanged, up to ATTEMPTS times:
  - on success it stops at once and returns 0; the command's own output
    goes to stdout as usual;
  - after each failed attempt it prints
      retry: attempt K/N failed (status S)
    to stderr (K is the attempt number, N is ATTEMPTS, S the command's
    exit status);
  - after the last failed attempt it also prints "retry: giving up" to
    stderr and returns the exit status of the LAST attempt;
  - between attempts it sleeps for ${RETRY_DELAY:-0} seconds (not after the
    last one).
The script calls `retry "$@"` and its own exit status is retry's.
ATTEMPTS must be a whole number of at least 1 and a COMMAND must be given;
otherwise print "usage: solution.sh ATTEMPTS COMMAND [ARG...]" to stderr and
exit 2. The `flaky` stub fails with status 7 for its first FLAKY_FAILS calls,
then succeeds.
concepts: a generic wrapper: shift the count, run "$@"
capturing a failing status without set -e exiting: cmd || rc=$?
return the last status, not a generic 1

Run the wrapped command as "$@" so its arguments stay intact.

title: Timing Wrapper
story:
The nightly report got slower and nobody can say which command is to blame.
Gus has a theory about the database; Theo has a theory about the network;
Ollie suggests, shyly, that someone could simply measure. "Good idea," Mara
says. "And do it without editing any of the commands. Wrap them, and let the
wrapper tell us how long each one took."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh COMMAND [ARG...]`.
Define a function `timed COMMAND [ARG...]` that runs the command with its
arguments, then prints one line to stderr:
  timed: COMMAND ARG... took S.mmms
where the words of the command are joined by single spaces and the duration is
in seconds with exactly three decimals (milliseconds), for example
"timed: sleep 1 took 1.002s" or "timed: echo hi took 0.000s".
The command's stdout passes through untouched, and `timed` returns the
command's own exit status (the line is printed even when the command fails).
Measure with Bash's `EPOCHREALTIME` (seconds since 1970 with microseconds);
do not use `date` or `time`.
The script calls `timed "$@"` and exits with its status. With no COMMAND
print "usage: solution.sh COMMAND [ARG...]" to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: EPOCHREALTIME: seconds.microseconds; strip the dot and use integer math
SECONDS counts whole seconds: too coarse for this
printf '%d.%03d' to format milliseconds

Run the wrapped command as "$@".

title: Audit Wrapper
story:
After the incident with the missing customer folder, Priya asks one
question and nobody can answer it: who ran what, and did it work? The
maintenance bot runs a list of commands every night, and none of them
leave a trace. "I will not ask you to rewrite the bot," Priya says. "I will
ask you to put one function between the bot and every command it runs, and
I will ask to read the log tomorrow."
objective:
Write solution.sh. It reads commands from standard input, one per line,
split into words on spaces (no quote handling needed; blank lines are
ignored), and runs each one through a function `audited COMMAND [ARG...]`.
`audited` runs the command (stdout and stderr untouched), then appends one
line to the audit log:
  USER: WORDS status=N
where USER is the value of $USER, WORDS are the command and its arguments
written with `printf '%q'` and separated by single spaces (so odd characters
are visible: `a;b` is logged as `a\;b`), and N is the command's exit status.
A failing command must not stop the run, and must be logged too, including a
command that does not exist (status 127).
The log is the file named by $AUDIT_LOG, or `audit.log` in the current
directory if that variable is empty or unset. Do not create the file if no
command was run.
The script's own exit status is 1 if any command failed, otherwise 0.
concepts: a wrapper that logs after running: "$@" || rc=$?
printf -v line '%q ' "$@" shows words exactly (escapes spaces and metacharacters)
${VAR:-default} for a configurable log path, appending with >>
read -ra splits a line into an array without globbing

Log the words with printf '%q' so odd characters stay visible.
Append to the log with >>.

title: Load a .env File Safely
story:
Theo's new storefront reads its settings from a `.env` file, and his deploy
script loads it with `source .env`. Priya spotted it during the review and
went very quiet. "That file is edited by customers through the control panel,"
she says. "Anything they type after the equals sign runs on our server with
our permissions. Read it as data. Never run it."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh ENV_FILE`. Read the file line by
line and export each setting into the environment, then print three lines:
  name=<value of SITE_NAME>
  port=<value of SITE_PORT>
  motd=<value of SITE_MOTD>
A variable that was never set prints `(unset)` as its value.
Parsing rules:
  - blank lines and lines whose first non-blank character is `#` are ignored
  - a setting is `KEY=VALUE`; KEY is letters, digits and underscores and does
    not start with a digit; blanks around KEY, around `=` and at the end of
    the value are dropped
  - the value is everything after the first `=` (it may contain more `=`)
  - if the value is wrapped in a matching pair of "double" or 'single'
    quotes, remove that pair
  - nothing in the file is ever expanded or executed: `$(...)`, backticks and
    `$VAR` stay literal text
  - any other line is skipped with `skipped line N` on stderr (N counts from 1)
  - if two lines set the same key, the last one wins; a setting in the file
    replaces a variable already in the environment
If ENV_FILE cannot be read, print `cannot read ENV_FILE` to stderr and exit 1.
Do not use `source`, `.` or `eval`.
concepts: parse a config file as data, never execute it
regex capture groups with BASH_REMATCH
export "$key=$value" stores text without evaluating it

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not source, dot or eval the file: read it line by line and export the parsed values.

title: Layered Defaults
story:
Three customers use the shared mail relay and each wants it slightly
different: the pub needs port 2525 because their router blocks 25, the
bookshop sends over TLS, and everyone else just wants it to work. Noor is
tired of three copies of the same script. "One script," says Mara, "three
layers: what we ship, what the customer's file says, and what the
environment says on the day. Higher layers win."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh [CONFIG_FILE]`. It decides three
settings and prints them in this format:
  host=<RELAY_HOST>
  port=<RELAY_PORT>
  tls=<RELAY_TLS>
Each setting is taken from the first layer that provides it, highest first:
  1. an environment variable with that name (RELAY_HOST, RELAY_PORT, RELAY_TLS)
  2. a `NAME=VALUE` line in CONFIG_FILE
  3. the built-in default: host `localhost`, port `25`, tls `off`
An empty value (in the environment or in the file) counts as "not provided".
CONFIG_FILE is optional and may not exist; then the file layer is simply
empty. In the file, ignore comment lines (starting with `#`), blank lines,
unknown names, and blanks around the name and the value. A value may itself
contain `=`. Use `${VAR:-default}` for the environment layer.

${VAR:-fallback} treats unset and empty alike
IFS='=' read -r key value splits at the first =

title: Flags Beat Everything
story:
Ollie ran the nightly backup by hand for North Pier Dental and typed
`--retention 3` because the disk was almost full. Next morning the cron job
still used 30 days: the config file said so, and the file had won. "A flag you
type on the command line is the most deliberate thing anyone can say to a
program," Mara explains. "It has to beat the environment, the file and the
defaults, every time."
objective:
Write solution.sh, a mini front end for `tide-backup`. It accepts these
options, in any order:
  --retention DAYS      (or --retention=DAYS)
  --dest DIR            (or --dest=DIR)
  --compress            (no value; means "yes")
  --config FILE         (or --config=FILE)
and prints the final value of each of the three settings with the layer it
came from, one per line, in exactly this format:
  retention: <value> (<source>)
  dest: <value> (<source>)
  compress: <value> (<source>)
<source> is `flag`, `env`, `file` or `default`; the first one that provides a
value wins, in that order:
  flag      the options above
  env       TIDE_RETENTION, TIDE_DEST, TIDE_COMPRESS (empty counts as unset)
  file      `name=value` lines in the --config file, names retention, dest
            and compress (ignore comments, blank lines, unknown names, and
            blanks around names and values); without --config there is no file
  default   retention 7, dest /var/backups, compress no
Errors go to stderr with exit status 2: `unknown option: OPT` for any other
option starting with `-`, `unexpected argument: ARG` for anything else, and
`missing value for OPT` when an option that needs a value is last on the line.
An unreadable --config file prints `cannot read FILE` and exits 1.
concepts: precedence: flag, environment, file, default
while (( $# )); case $1 in ...; shift
associative arrays to track value and source

required_patterns.message: Walk through the arguments with a while loop, a case, and shift.

Last Tuesday a deploy for Harbour Bakery went out without `DB_HOST`. The app
started, failed to connect, and Theo fixed it, redeployed, and discovered
that `API_TOKEN` was missing too. Two deploys, two apologies. Priya adds a
gate to the pipeline: before anything is deployed, check the config and tell
the engineer everything that is wrong, all at once.

Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh CONFIG_FILE KEY [KEY...]`. The
KEY arguments are the required keys. CONFIG_FILE holds `NAME=VALUE` lines;
ignore blank lines and lines starting with `#`, and ignore blanks around the
name and around the value. A value may contain `=`. If a name appears more
than once, the last line counts.
A required key is missing when it does not appear, or when its value is
empty.
  - If nothing is missing, print `config ok: N required keys present` to
    stdout (N = number of KEY arguments) and exit 0.
  - Otherwise print one line `missing: KEY` to stderr for every missing key,

to stderr and exit 2. An unreadable CONFIG_FILE prints `cannot read FILE`
to stderr and exits 2.

declare -A to remember which keys have a value
counting failures instead of exiting on the first

title: XDG Config Paths
story:
Lanternfish's little CLI `pelican` keeps its settings in `~/.pelicanrc`, and
the home directories of the support desk are starting to look like attics.
Ollie suggests `~/.config/pelican/`. "That is the right idea," says Mara,
"but the standard says the base folder is `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` when the user
has set it, and only then `~/.config`. And the old file must keep working
for people who have not moved."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh APP`. Find the config file of the
application APP and print its location as one line:
  config: <path>
The candidates, in order, are:
  1. <BASE>/APP/config.ini, where BASE is `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` if that
     variable is set, not empty and an absolute path (starts with `/`),
     otherwise `$HOME/.config`. Only that one base is consulted, never both.
  2. the legacy file `$HOME/.APPrc` (for APP=pelican: `.pelicanrc`)
Print the first candidate that exists as a regular file. When the path
starts with `$HOME`, print `~` instead of the home directory, for example
`config: ~/.config/pelican/config.ini`.

title: Find the Project Config
story:
Theo keeps all of Lanternfish's web projects in one monorepo, and each project
can carry a `.lanternrc` with its own settings. Engineers run the `lantern`
tool from wherever they happen to be, often six folders deep inside `src/`.
"Same trick as git," Mara says. "Look here. Not here? Look in the parent. Keep
climbing, but stop at the repository root; we never want to read some stranger's
file from above it."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh START_DIR ROOT_DIR`. Starting in
START_DIR and going up one parent folder at a time, find the nearest folder that
contains a regular file named `.lanternrc`. Never look above ROOT_DIR (ROOT_DIR
itself is searched; START_DIR is inside ROOT_DIR or equal to it).
On success print two lines:
  config: ./<folder relative to ROOT_DIR>/.lanternrc
  project: <value of the project key>
Example: a file in ROOT_DIR/apps/web gives `config: ./apps/web/.lanternrc`;
one directly in ROOT_DIR gives `config: ./.lanternrc`.
The file holds `name=value` lines; ignore comments (`#`) and blank lines and
blanks around names and values. If there is no `project` key, print
`project: (none)`.
Errors, all on stderr:
  - an argument that is not a directory: `not a directory: ARG`, exit 2
  - START_DIR not inside ROOT_DIR: `START_DIR is not inside ROOT_DIR` (with the
    arguments as given), exit 2
  - nothing found: `no .lanternrc between START_DIR and ROOT_DIR` (with the
    arguments as given), exit 1
Compare real paths: resolve both arguments with `cd ... && pwd -P` first, so
that `..` and relative spellings work.
concepts: walk up with dirname until a boundary
canonical paths with cd + pwd -P
stop conditions so a loop cannot run forever

title: Type-Check Values
story:
A customer set `workers=lots` in the web tier's config, and the service
cheerfully started with no workers at all. Another typed `debug=Yes`, which
the app read as "no" because it only knew lowercase `true`. Everything in a
config file is text; somebody has to decide what the text means before the
rest of the program trusts it. Mara hands you that job.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh CONFIG_FILE`. The file holds
`name=value` lines (ignore blank lines, `#` comments and blanks around names
and values; a name that is not one of the three below is ignored). Check
these settings, using the default when the name does not appear:
  workers    integer from 1 to 64, default 2. Digits only (no sign, no
             decimals, no arithmetic). Leading zeros are allowed and are
             read as decimal: `08` means 8.
  debug      boolean, default false. Case-insensitive `true`, `yes`, `on`,
             `1` mean true; `false`, `no`, `off`, `0` mean false.
  log_level  one of `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` (case-insensitive),
             default `info`.
If every setting is valid, print the normalised values, nothing else:
  workers=<number without leading zeros>
  debug=<true or false>
  log_level=<lowercase level>
Otherwise print nothing on stdout and, for each invalid setting, in the order
workers, debug, log_level, one line on stderr (the value shown in double
quotes, exactly as written after trimming):
  invalid workers: "VALUE" (expected an integer from 1 to 64)
  invalid debug: "VALUE" (expected true/false, yes/no, on/off or 1/0)
  invalid log_level: "VALUE" (expected debug, info, warn or error)
and exit with status 1. If CONFIG_FILE is unreadable print
`cannot read CONFIG_FILE` to stderr and exit 2. If a name appears twice the
last line counts. An empty value is invalid.
concepts: validate before use: integers, booleans, enums
10#$value forces base ten so 08 is not octal
${var,,} normalises case; case patterns match word lists

title: Mask Secrets
story:
Noor pasted the output of `show-config` into a public support ticket, and with
it the pub's database password. Priya has rotated every key since, and now
makes one rule: the config printer may show everything a human needs to debug
a problem and nothing an attacker needs to break in. "Show that a secret
exists," she says, "and maybe its last four characters. That is enough to
tell two keys apart."
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh CONFIG_FILE`. The file holds
`NAME=VALUE` lines; skip blank lines and `#` comments, and ignore blanks around
the name and the value. A value may contain `=`. Print one line per setting,
in file order, as `NAME=VALUE` (name and value trimmed), with these masks:
  - If the name, compared case-insensitively, ends in `_KEY`, `_TOKEN`,
    `_SECRET` or `_PASSWORD`, the value is a secret. A secret with 12 or more
    characters prints as `****` followed by its last 4 characters; a shorter
    non-empty secret prints as `****`; an empty one stays empty.
  - Any other value that contains a URL with a password, that is
    `://USER:PASSWORD@` (USER may be empty, PASSWORD contains no `@` or `/`),
    keeps everything except the password, which becomes `****`.
  - Everything else is printed unchanged.
Names such as `MONKEY` or `KEYBOARD` do not end in `_KEY`, so they are not
secrets. An unreadable file prints `cannot read CONFIG_FILE` to stderr, exit 1.
concepts: redact secrets in output
suffix match on ${name^^} with a glob
BASH_REMATCH to rebuild a URL around a masked password

title: Secrets from Files
story:
Theo moves the storefront into containers, and the platform mounts each secret
as a file under `/run/secrets/` rather than putting it in the environment,
where every child process and every crash dump can see it. The convention is
simple: if `DB_PASSWORD_FILE` is set, the secret is in that file; otherwise
`DB_PASSWORD` may hold it directly. Priya wants the startup script to follow it
without ever echoing a secret.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh NAME [NAME...]`. For each NAME, find
the secret like this:
  - If the variable `NAME_FILE` is set and not empty, the secret is the content
    of the file it names, without its trailing newline(s).
  - Otherwise, if the variable `NAME` is set and not empty, that is the secret.
Never print a secret. Print one line per resolved NAME on stdout:
  NAME: <N> chars from file      (or: from env)
where N is the length of the secret. The problems below are reported on stderr
(one line each) and make the script exit with status 1 once all NAMEs have been
handled; the other names are still processed:
  NAME: set NAME or NAME_FILE, not both     (both variables are non-empty)
  NAME: cannot read FILE                    (FILE is not a readable file)
  NAME: secret file is empty                (the file has no content)
  NAME: missing                             (neither variable is set)
Process the names in the order given. Without any argument print
`usage: solution.sh NAME...` to stderr and exit 2. Do not use `eval`.
concepts: *_FILE convention for secrets
indirect expansion ${!var}
$(<file) reads a file without cat and drops trailing newlines

title: INI Sections
story:
The flat `key=value` files are not enough any more. Noor's new control panel
writes one INI file per customer with a `[web]` part, a `[mail]` part and a
`[backup]` part, and both the web and the mail part have a `port`. Asking
"what is the port?" now has two answers, and the old grep one-liners return
the wrong one about half of the time. You need a lookup that knows which
section it is in.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh FILE SECTION KEY`. It prints the
value of KEY inside the section named SECTION, followed by a newline.
INI rules:
  - a line `[name]` starts the section `name` (blanks around the line are
    ignored; names are case-sensitive and may contain dots or spaces)
  - lines starting with `#` or `;` (after optional blanks) and blank lines are
    comments; there are no inline comments, so `#` or `;` later in a value is
    part of the value
  - a setting is `key=value`; blanks around the key and around the value are
    removed; the value is everything after the first `=`
  - settings that appear before any section header belong to no section
  - a section may appear more than once, and a key may repeat: the last
    definition wins
If the key is not defined in that section (or the section does not exist),
print `missing key KEY in [SECTION]` to stderr and exit 1. An unreadable FILE
prints `cannot read FILE` and exits 2. Anything other than exactly three
arguments prints `usage: solution.sh FILE SECTION KEY` to stderr and exits 2.
concepts: parse [section] headers with a state variable
regex ^\[(.*)\]$ and BASH_REMATCH
the same key name in different sections

title: Reload on Signal
story:
The log shipper on `halibut` runs for weeks, and changing its log level used to
mean restarting it and losing the buffered lines. Mara's rule for daemons:
"Edit the file, send `kill -HUP`, and the process re-reads its config without
dropping anything. And if the new file is garbage, it keeps running on the old
settings and says so." You will build the skeleton of that behaviour and, to keep
the exercise deterministic, let the script play the administrator itself.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh CONFIG NEWLEVEL`. CONFIG holds
`name=value` lines (ignore blank lines, `#` comments, unknown names, and
blanks around names and values). The setting `level` must be one of `debug`,
`info`, `warn`, `error`; if it appears more than once, the last line counts.
Do these steps in order:
  1. Read the level from CONFIG and print `loaded: level=<level>`.
     If there is no valid level, print `no valid level in CONFIG` to stderr
     and exit 1.
  2. Install a handler for the HUP signal (use `trap`). On HUP the handler
     re-reads CONFIG. If the level is valid, it becomes the active level and the
     handler prints `reloaded: level=<level>`. If it is not valid, the active
     level is unchanged and the handler prints
     `reload rejected: keeping level=<active level>` to stderr.
  3. Pretend to be the administrator: append the line `level=NEWLEVEL` to
     CONFIG, then send HUP to yourself with `kill -HUP $$`.
  4. Print `done: level=<active level>` and exit 0.
Both the initial load and the reload must use the same function for reading
the level. Without exactly two arguments print `usage: solution.sh CONFIG
NEWLEVEL` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: trap handler HUP: re-read configuration on signal
kill -HUP $$ sends a signal to the script itself
keep the old config when the new one is invalid

Send the signal to yourself with `kill -HUP $$`.

title: Show Effective Config
story:
"It works on my machine" has a configuration cousin: "it says port 8080 in the
file". The support desk spends hours finding out which layer actually decided a
value, and Gus has started asking why that costs money. Ollie's request is the
one every configurable tool eventually gets: a `config show` command that prints
what the program will really use, and where each value came from.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh [CONFIG_FILE]`. It prints the
effective configuration, one line per setting, sorted by name:
  <name> = <value> [<source>]
The names are padded with spaces on the right to the width of the longest
name, so that the `=` signs line up. <source> is `env`, `file` or `default`.
Where values come from, strongest first:
  env      every environment variable called `LF_<NAME>` (NAME made of capital
           letters, digits and underscores, at least one character) defines
           the setting `<name>`: the part after `LF_`, in lowercase. Other
           variables are ignored. Variables that are set but empty are ignored.
  file     `name=value` lines in CONFIG_FILE, if one is given. Ignore blank
           lines, `#` comments and blanks around names and values; a name must
           be lowercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter
           or underscore, anything else is ignored. A value may contain `=`.
           Empty values are ignored; for a repeated name the last line counts.
  default  bind=127.0.0.1, log=info, port=8080, workers=2
A setting that is not a default can still appear: it comes from the file or the
environment. Sort with `sort` in the C locale (the tests run that way). An
unreadable CONFIG_FILE prints `cannot read CONFIG_FILE` to stderr, exit 1.
concepts: the final merged configuration with provenance
compgen -v LF_ lists variable names by prefix
printf '%-*s' pads to a computed width

title: Migrate an Old Format
story:
Version 2 of the Lanternfish proxy changes its config format: `key=value`
instead of `Key: value`, new setting names, and a log level in place of the old
debug switch. Two hundred customers still have version 1 files, and Gus does not
want two hundred support calls. Mara's brief for the migration tool: never touch
the old file, never overwrite an existing new one, and never convert a file twice.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh OLD_FILE NEW_FILE`. OLD_FILE is a
version 1 config, NEW_FILE is the version 2 file to create.
A v1 file has `Name: value` lines (split at the FIRST colon; blanks around the
name and the value are dropped), blank lines, and `#` comment lines. Convert
each setting:
  Listen: V      ->  port=V
  Hostname: V    ->  host=V
  Debug: V       ->  log_level=debug when V is `on` (any letter case),
                     otherwise log_level=info
  Timeout: V     ->  timeout_seconds=V with one trailing `s` removed, if any
  any other Name: V -> the name in lowercase, `=V`; also print
                     `unknown key: Name (copied as lowercase)` to stderr
A non-blank, non-comment line without a colon is not converted; print
`skipped line N` to stderr (N counts from 1 in the old file).
NEW_FILE starts with the line `version=2`, followed by the old comment lines
(unchanged) and the converted settings, in their original order. Blank lines
are dropped. After writing, print `migrated N settings` to stdout, where N
counts converted settings (unknown keys included, skipped lines not).
Checks, in this order:
  - not exactly two arguments: `usage: solution.sh OLD_FILE NEW_FILE`, exit 2
  - OLD_FILE unreadable: `cannot read OLD_FILE`, exit 1
  - the first line of OLD_FILE that is neither blank nor a comment is exactly
    `version=2`: print `already v2: nothing to do` and exit 0 without creating
    NEW_FILE
  - NEW_FILE already exists: `refusing to overwrite NEW_FILE`, exit 1
OLD_FILE is never modified.
concepts: config migration: map old keys and values to the new schema
idempotence: refuse to convert twice, refuse to overwrite
build the output first, write the file last
