title: Diff Two Configs
story:
A customer swears nothing changed on the pier-side proxy, yet it started
rejecting logins on Thursday. Support has Wednesday's backup of the config and
today's file, and plain `diff` shows forty lines of noise: someone re-ordered
the settings, re-indented them and added comments. Mara wants the opposite of
noise: a short report of what really changed, setting by setting, that she can
read at a glance during the incident call.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh OLD_FILE NEW_FILE`. Both files hold
`name=value` lines. Ignore blank lines, `#` comments and blanks around names and
values; a value may contain `=`; for a repeated name the last line counts. A
setting may have an empty value, which is still a value.
Compare the two files as sets of settings and print one line for every
difference, sorted by name (plain `sort`, the tests run in the C locale), mixed
together regardless of kind:
  + name=value          the name exists only in NEW_FILE
  - name=value          the name exists only in OLD_FILE
  ~ name: old -> new    the name exists in both with different values
An empty value is shown as '' (two single quotes) in all three forms.
If there is at least one difference, finish with a line
  summary: A added, R removed, C changed
and exit with status 1 (like `diff`). If the files hold the same settings,
print `no differences` and exit 0. The order of lines in the files, comments
and spacing never count as differences.
Anything other than exactly two arguments prints `usage: solution.sh OLD_FILE
NEW_FILE` to stderr and exits 2; an unreadable file prints `cannot read FILE`
and exits 2.
concepts: compare configs as key/value sets, not as text
union of keys with sort -u; added, removed, changed
exit status that reports whether differences exist

title: Quote to Stop Injection
story:
Priya has started her security review with the smallest script in the repo:
Theo's ticket filer, which Noor's desk uses to open one text file per customer.
Last week someone typed a customer name that contained a space, and another
typed a lone `*`. The filer overwrote a ticket that belonged to somebody else.
Priya's note on the pull request: "Input is data until you let the shell
re-read it. Show me where you stop it."
objective:
Write solution.sh that opens a ticket for the customer named in the first
argument. The folder `tickets` already exists, and the template is
`fixtures/ticket-template.txt`.

1. With no argument, print `usage: solution.sh CUSTOMER` to stderr, exit 2.
2. Otherwise copy the template to `tickets/CUSTOMER.txt` (CUSTOMER exactly as
   typed, even if it contains spaces, `*`, `;`, `$(...)` or a leading dash)
   and print `filed: tickets/CUSTOMER.txt`.

The customer name is data. It must never be split into several words, never
expand into a list of existing files, and never be run as a command.

data never becomes code

title: Replace eval
story:
Theo built `logsearch` for the support desk. Noor types a word and some
options, and the script assembles a grep command line in a string and runs it
with `eval`. Priya read it in under a minute, typed `$(touch pwned)` as the
search word, and a file called pwned appeared on the log server. "eval is
not a feature," she says, "it is a second front door."
objective:
Write solution.sh that searches the file `logs/app.log`.

Usage: solution.sh PATTERN [OPTION...]

PATTERN is searched for as a fixed-text word, even if it starts with a dash.
Each OPTION is one of these words, which you map to a grep flag:

    ignore-case  ->  -i
    count        ->  -c
    invert       ->  -v

Run grep once with the chosen flags and let its output and exit status be
the script's own (grep exits 1 when nothing matches, that is fine).

- With no argument: print `usage: solution.sh PATTERN [OPTION...]` to
  stderr, exit 2.
- Any other option word: print `unknown option: WORD` to stderr, exit 2,
  and run nothing.

Do not use eval. Collect the flags in an array and expand it as
"${flags[@]}". Use `case` to translate option words.
concepts: eval re-parses text as code
flags=(); flags+=(-i) builds a command safely
case maps words to known-good flags

Expand your flag array as "${flags[@]}".

title: Allow-List Input
story:
Ollie wrote a tiny "please restart this service" form handler for the support
desk. To stay safe he blocks the characters `;` and `&`. Priya pastes
`web$(touch pwned)` into the form and nothing stops it. "You cannot list every
bad thing," she says. "You can list every good thing, because there are four."
objective:
Write solution.sh that queues a restart request. The argument is SERVICE.

The services that may be restarted are listed one per line in
`fixtures/allowed-services.txt`.

1. No argument: print `usage: solution.sh SERVICE` to stderr, exit 2.
2. If SERVICE is exactly one of the lines in the allow-list file (whole
   line, same letters, no pattern matching): append SERVICE as a line to
   `queue.txt` and print `queued: SERVICE`.
3. Otherwise print `denied: SERVICE` to stderr, exit 1, and do not create or
   change `queue.txt`.

Decide by looking SERVICE up in the allow-list. Do not try to detect bad
characters. Names such as `we`, `.*` or `-v` must be denied too.
concepts: allow-list beats block-list
grep -Fxq -- "$value" file: exact whole-line lookup
-- ends options so a value cannot be read as a flag

required_patterns.message: Look the value up with grep -Fxq (fixed text, whole line, quiet).

test_cases.name: names with a dash and digits work when listed
a prefix of a good name is not good
a regex that would match everything
command substitution glued to a good name

title: Safe Temp Files
story:
Gus wants the three biggest invoices every Monday, and Theo's script sorts
them through a scratch file called `report.tmp` in the shared temp folder.
Priya shows how an attacker on the same machine waits for that name: they
create `report.tmp` first, as a symlink to a file they want destroyed, and
Theo's script obediently overwrites it. "A predictable name is an invitation.
Let the system pick the name."
objective:
Write solution.sh that reads invoice amounts from stdin, one whole number
per line, and prints the three largest, biggest first. If fewer than three
numbers arrive, print as many as there are.

The work must go through a scratch file in the folder named by `$TMPDIR`:

- create it with mktemp, using a template that ends in X characters
  inside "$TMPDIR" (for example "$TMPDIR/invoices.XXXXXX"). Never pick the
  name yourself, and do not use `$$` or the date as the "random" part;
- write the input into it, then `sort -rn` it and keep the first three lines;
- remove the scratch file when the script ends, however it ends (use a
  `trap ... EXIT`).

The tests plant a file called `report.tmp` and `invoices.tmp` in the temp
folder as traps, and check that nothing is left behind.
concepts: mktemp creates the file atomically with an unpredictable name
trap 'rm -f "$work"' EXIT
predictable names in shared folders can be hijacked

required_patterns.message: Create the scratch file with mktemp "$TMPDIR/something.XXXXXX".
Clean up with trap '...' EXIT so the file never lingers.

forbidden_patterns.message: $$, the date and $RANDOM are guessable. Let mktemp choose the name.

test_cases.name: a planted symlink must not be followed

title: umask for Secrets
story:
The deploy script stores each customer's API key in `secrets/NAME.key`. Theo
writes the file and then runs `chmod 600` on it, and he is proud of that.
Priya asks him how long the key sits readable by everyone between those two
commands. Theo goes quiet. "The file should be born private," she says,
"not tidied up afterwards."
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes NAME and KEY (a customer name and an API key).

1. With fewer than two arguments print `usage: solution.sh NAME KEY` to
   stderr and exit 2.
2. Create the folder `secrets` if needed and write KEY (one line) to
   `secrets/NAME.key`. The key file must have mode 600 and the folder mode 700
   (when the script created it), from the very first moment, so do not use
   chmod at all. Set a umask for this.
3. Append NAME as a line to `index.txt` in the current folder. The index is
   not secret: it must keep the normal, default permissions, so the umask
   must apply only to the secret part (use a subshell).
4. Print `stored: secrets/NAME.key`.
concepts: umask 077 makes new files 600 and new folders 700
( umask 077; ... ) limits the umask to a subshell
chmod after writing leaves a window

required_patterns.message: Use umask 077 so new files are created private.

forbidden_patterns.message: No chmod: a file fixed afterwards was readable for a moment. Use umask before creating it.

title: Find World-Writable Files
story:
After a customer's site got defaced, Priya wants a weekly sweep of the web
roots for files that anybody on the machine can rewrite. Ollie's first attempt
parses `ls -l` output and chokes on file names with spaces. Priya hands him a
better idea: "Ask the filesystem a question, don't read its handwriting."
objective:
Write solution.sh that audits one folder, given as the first argument.

1. With no argument print `usage: solution.sh DIR` to stderr, exit 2.
2. If DIR is not a folder print `no such folder: DIR` to stderr, exit 1.
3. Otherwise list every regular file anywhere below DIR that other users can
   write to (the "others write" permission bit is set, whatever the rest of
   the mode is). Print one path per line, in `sort` order, each starting with
   DIR exactly as given. Folders and symbolic links are not listed.
4. Finish with a line `world-writable: N` where N is how many files were
   listed (0 is fine).

Use `find` with a permission test. Do not parse `ls` output.
concepts: find -type f -perm -002
-perm -MODE: all of these bits set; -perm MODE: exactly this mode
ask the filesystem instead of parsing ls

required_patterns.message: Use find with -perm -002 (all of these bits set: others can write).

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not parse ls output; let find test the permission.
Use find -perm; stat has different flags on macOS and Linux.

test_cases.name: folders and links are not files

title: Refuse to Run as Root
story:
Mara found a log-rotation script that someone ran with root's powers "just to
make the permission errors go away". It now owns half of /var/log, and the web
server cannot write there any more. Priya's rule is short: a script that does
not need root must refuse to run with it, and say so before touching anything.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a log rotator for the `logs` folder.

1. If the effective user id is 0 (root), print
   `refusing to run as root: use a normal account` to stderr, exit 1, and do
   not touch any file.
2. Otherwise move `logs/app.log` to `logs/app.log.1` (replacing an older
   `app.log.1`), create a fresh empty `logs/app.log`, and print
   `rotated as uid UID`, where UID is the number you checked.

Find the user id with `id -u`, and compare it as a number.
(Here `id` is a practice stand-in so the tests can pretend to be root.)
concepts: id -u prints the numeric user id; 0 is root
(( $(id -u) == 0 )) numeric comparison
check privileges first, act second

required_patterns.message: Ask for the numeric user id with id -u.

forbidden_patterns.message: Use id -u here: the practice id can be switched per test, EUID cannot be faked.

files.logs/app.log:
line one
line two

test_cases.name: another normal id, old backup replaced

files.logs/app.log: fresh

test_cases.name: root is refused and nothing moves

files.logs/app.log: keep me where I am

test_cases.expected_stderr: refusing to run as root: use a normal account

test_cases.name: a uid that merely contains a zero is not root

files.logs/app.log: x

title: Path Traversal Guard
story:
North Pier Dental downloads its appointment sheets from a little "fetch" script
that prints a file from the `public` folder. Priya asks it for
`../private/keys.txt` and the keys come straight back. "Everything the user
types after `public/` is part of the path," she says. "Including the dots."
Theo's quick fix, refusing any name containing two dots, blocked a legitimate
file called `summary..final.txt` and the dentists complained.
objective:
Write solution.sh that prints a file from the folder `public`. The argument
is NAME, a path relative to `public`.

1. No argument: `usage: solution.sh NAME` to stderr, exit 2.
2. Refuse with `denied: NAME` on stderr and exit 1 when NAME is empty, starts
   with `/`, or contains a path component that is exactly `..` (that is
   `..` alone, `../x`, `x/../y` or `x/..`). Do this check *before* looking
   at any file. A name such as `summary..final.txt` has no `..` component
   and is allowed.
3. If the file `public/NAME` does not exist as a regular file, print
   `not found: NAME` on stderr and exit 1.
4. Otherwise print the file's contents.

Use a `case` pattern for the refusal rules. Do not call realpath or readlink.
concepts: a user path is untrusted: reject .. components and absolute paths
check by path component, not by substring

required_patterns.message: Express the refusal rules as a case statement.

forbidden_patterns.message: Not here: reject the dangerous names by their shape, before touching the disk.

test_cases.name: two dots inside a file name are fine
climbing out from a sub-folder is denied
a folder is not a file

title: Lock Down PATH
story:
The nightly spool report runs from cron with whatever PATH the caller happened
to have. Priya shows the team how little it takes: she drops a program named
`ls` into a folder that comes first on the PATH, and the next run executes her
program instead of the real one. "Your script trusts the word `ls`," she says.
"Tell it exactly where words are allowed to come from."
objective:
Write solution.sh that reports on a folder. The argument is DIR.

1. No argument: `usage: solution.sh DIR` to stderr, exit 2.
2. Otherwise print two things, using the commands `ls -1`, `wc -l`, `tr` and
   `cat` (as external commands):
     entries: N        (how many names `ls -1 DIR` lists)
   followed by the content of `DIR/motd.txt`.

Before running any external command, replace PATH with exactly
`/usr/bin:/bin`. Do not add the caller's PATH to it. The tests start your
script with hostile folders first on PATH, and a fake `ls` or `cat` in them
must never run.
concepts: PATH=/usr/bin:/bin at the top of the script
an empty PATH entry means the current directory
never append the caller's PATH to a trusted one

required_patterns.message: Set PATH=/usr/bin:/bin exactly, on a line of its own, before any command runs.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not append the old PATH; that keeps the attacker's folders.

test_cases.name: empty PATH entry means the current folder

title: Globs Not ls
story:
Noor asks for a one-glance "what does each customer log start with?" report.
Theo's version loops over `$(ls dir/*.log)`. It works until a customer uploads
a file called `Harbour Bakery.log`, and it prints an error when nobody has
uploaded anything yet. Priya adds a cruel test file named `-n.log` and a
folder named `old.log`, then asks for a version that survives all of it.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes a folder DIR and summarises its `.log` files.

1. No argument: `usage: solution.sh DIR` to stderr, exit 2.
2. DIR is not a folder: `no such folder: DIR` to stderr, exit 1.
3. For every regular file in DIR whose name ends in `.log`, in glob order,
   print `NAME: FIRST_LINE`, where NAME is the file name without the folder
   and FIRST_LINE is the first line of the file (an empty file gives an
   empty text after the colon and space).
   Folders that happen to end in `.log` are skipped.
4. Then print `logs: N`, N being how many files were summarised. With no
   matching files print only `logs: 0`.

Loop over a glob (`"$dir"/*.log`). Do not use ls or find, and do not loop
over command substitution.
concepts: for f in "$dir"/*.log: names stay whole
shopt -s nullglob: no match means an empty list
[[ -f $f ]] skips folders
never parse ls

required_patterns.message: Loop with: for f in "$dir"/*.log (quoted variable, unquoted star).
Use shopt -s nullglob so an unmatched glob gives an empty list.

forbidden_patterns.message: No ls or find here: a glob hands you each name as one safe word.
Do not loop over $( ... ): command output is split on spaces.

files.logs/app.log:
booted at six
second line

test_cases.expected_stdout:
app.log: booted at six
db.log: ready
logs: 2

test_cases.name: spaces in a name
test_cases.expected_stdout:
Harbour Bakery.log: orders: 14
Tidewater Books.log: orders: 3
logs: 2

title: Symlink Checks
story:
The support desk has a shared `notes` folder, and Noor's helper script appends
a line to a customer's note file. A customer with shell access on the same box
replaced `notes/halibut.txt` with a symbolic link to the billing price list.
The next note Noor saved went straight into the price list. Priya wants the
helper to look at what it is about to write to before it writes.
objective:
Write solution.sh that appends a note. Arguments: FILE and TEXT.

1. Fewer than two arguments: `usage: solution.sh FILE TEXT` to stderr,
   exit 2.
2. If FILE is a symbolic link (even one pointing nowhere), print
   `refusing: FILE is a symlink` to stderr and exit 1.
3. If the folder that holds FILE is a symbolic link, print
   `refusing: FOLDER is a symlink` to stderr (FOLDER is the folder part of
   FILE as written) and exit 1.
4. Otherwise append TEXT and a newline to FILE (creating it if needed) and
   print `noted: FILE`.

Nothing may be written anywhere when a check fails. Test with `-L`; plain
`-e` or `-f` tests follow links and are not enough.
concepts: [[ -L path ]] is true for a symlink, even a dangling one
-e and -f follow the link; -L does not
check the file and its folder before writing

required_patterns.message: Test for symbolic links with [[ -L path ]].

test_cases.name: plain file gets a new line
symlink to an existing file is refused
folder that is a symlink is refused
text with options and percent signs is just text

title: Create Exclusively
story:
The on-call desk has a job board: whoever grabs `claims/JOB.owner` first owns
the job. Theo's script checks that the file does not exist and then writes it.
Last night two engineers ran it in the same second, both saw "free", and both
worked on the same incident. Priya adds a worse twist: an attacker pre-created
claim files as symlinks. "Checking and then acting is two steps," she says.
"Make it one."
objective:
Write solution.sh that claims a job. Arguments: JOB and OWNER. The folder
`claims` exists.

1. Fewer than two arguments: `usage: solution.sh JOB OWNER` to stderr,
   exit 2.
2. Try to create `claims/JOB.owner` containing OWNER (one line) in a single
   step that fails when the path already exists, whatever it is (a file, a
   symlink to a file, or a dangling symlink). On success print
   `claimed: JOB`.
3. If creation fails, print `claim failed: JOB is already taken` to stderr
   and exit 1. Leave the existing path exactly as it was.

Use noclobber (`set -o noclobber` or `set -C`) so the shell itself refuses to
overwrite. Do not test with `[[ -e ... ]]`, `[[ -f ... ]]` or `[[ -L ... ]]`
before writing: that check-then-write gap is the bug being fixed.
concepts: set -o noclobber: > fails on an existing path
check-then-create is a race (TOCTOU); create-or-fail is atomic
a failed redirection is an ordinary failing command

required_patterns.message: Turn on noclobber: set -o noclobber (or set -C).

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not test the path first; let the noclobber redirection be the test.
>| overrides noclobber, which defeats the point.

test_cases.name: already taken job keeps its owner
a pre-planted symlink to a real file is not followed
a dangling symlink does not let the attacker create files

title: Forget Secrets
story:
Theo's nightly job reads the API token from the environment, signs one request
and then calls `support-bundle`, which snapshots its own environment for the
vendor's support team. Last month a bundle containing a live token went out by
email. Priya does not want the token rotated again; she wants the script to
forget it the moment it is finished with it.
objective:
Write solution.sh. The secret arrives in the environment variable API_TOKEN.

1. If API_TOKEN is unset or empty: print `API_TOKEN is not set` to stderr,
   exit 1, and do nothing else.
2. Write the file `request.txt` containing exactly one line,
   `Authorization: Bearer <the token>`.
3. As soon as the request file is written, discard the secret: `unset`
   the variable (and any copy of it you made).
4. Then run `support-bundle --out bundle.txt` (it records the environment
   it sees) and print `request signed, bundle sent`.

The tests read bundle.txt: it must still list the other variables (such as
REGION) but must not contain the token anywhere. Do not wipe the whole
environment with `env -i`.
concepts: unset VAR removes a variable (and its export)
child processes inherit exported variables
keep a secret's lifetime as short as its use

required_patterns.message: Discard the secret with unset API_TOKEN as soon as you are done with it.

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not wipe the whole environment; forget only the secret.

test_cases.name: a different token with odd characters

title: Redact Logs
story:
Priya's security review ends where most leaks begin: in the logs. A customer
sent Noor a "please look at this log" attachment, and in it were a password in
a query string, a bearer token in a header and a git password inside a URL.
Before any log leaves the building, it must go through a filter. Theo wrote
the filter's name on the whiteboard; you write its contents.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a filter. It reads a log from stdin and writes it to
stdout, line for line, with secrets replaced by `[REDACTED]`:

1. `password=VALUE` and `token=VALUE` become `password=[REDACTED]` and
   `token=[REDACTED]`. VALUE is everything up to the next whitespace or `&`.
   This also applies inside longer names such as `api_token=...`.
   A key with an empty value (`password=`) is left alone.
2. `Bearer VALUE` becomes `Bearer [REDACTED]` (VALUE runs to the next
   whitespace).
3. A URL with a password, `scheme://USER:PASSWORD@host`, becomes
   `scheme://USER:[REDACTED]@host`. The user name stays.
4. Every other character of every line is unchanged, and a line may contain
   several secrets. Key names are lowercase.

Use sed with -E. Do not touch the lines that contain no secret.
concepts: sed -E 's/(key)=[^[:space:]&]+/\1=[REDACTED]/g'
capture groups keep the safe part, replace the secret part
scrub before a log leaves the building, and test the scrubber with real shapes

required_patterns.message: Use sed -E so groups and + work without backslashes.

password= left blank
the word token is not a secret, nor is passwords=list
Bearer

password= left blank
the word token is not a secret, nor is passwords=list
Bearer

title: Fetch a Page
story:
Customers keep asking Noor whether "the internet at Lanternfish is broken".
Mara has put a tiny status page online: one text file per component. Noor
wants a script she can run in one line, so she stops opening a browser
for every ticket. It is your first script that speaks HTTP.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one argument, a component name such as `web`.
Fetch the page
  https://status.lanternfish.example/components/NAME.txt
with curl and print one line:
  NAME: <the page text>
If the page is empty, print `NAME: no data` instead.

Run curl in silent mode so no progress meter reaches stderr. If curl itself
fails (the host cannot be reached), print `status page unreachable` to
stderr and exit with status 1. With no argument (or more than one), print
`usage: solution.sh NAME` to stderr and exit with status 2.
concepts: curl URL prints the response body on stdout
curl -s switches the progress meter off
curl's own exit status tells you the request could not be made

required_patterns.message: Run curl with -s so the progress meter stays quiet.

test_cases.expected_stdout: mail: degraded: outgoing queue delayed 12 min

title: HTTP Status Codes
story:
Noor has a pile of "your website is down" tickets and no idea which ones
are real. A page can answer with a lot of text and still be an error, so
the body is the wrong thing to look at. Mara points at the three digits
every web server sends back first: the status code.
objective:
Write solution.sh. Every argument is a URL. For each one, in order, ask
curl for its HTTP status code only (throw the body away) and print
  <code> <url>
for example `200 https://www.gullandanchor.example/`.

A URL counts as a problem if the code is 400 or higher, or if curl could not
connect at all (curl then reports the code `000`). After the last line print
  problems: N
and exit with status 1 if N is above zero, otherwise 0.
With no arguments, print `usage: solution.sh URL...` to stderr and exit 2.

Use `-o /dev/null` to discard the body and `-w '%{http_code}'` to print the
code. Remember that a failed connection makes curl exit non-zero.
concepts: -w '%{http_code}' prints the status code after the transfer
-o /dev/null throws the body away
3xx redirects and 000 (no connection) need their own thought

required_patterns.message: Ask curl for the status code with -w '%{http_code}'.
Discard the body with -o /dev/null, or it ends up mixed into your output.

test_cases.name: two healthy URLs, one is a redirect
two server-side errors among the good
a host that cannot be reached

title: POST Form Data
story:
Ollie has been signing new customers up by clicking through the billing
web form, forty times a morning. "It is just a form," he says, "can't a
script fill it in?" It can. A form submission is only an HTTP request that
carries data, and curl knows how to send one.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes two arguments, an EMAIL and a PLAN.

Submit the signup form with a POST request to
  https://billing.lanternfish.example/signup
sending the form fields `email=EMAIL` and `plan=PLAN`, in that order
(the form encoding is `email=EMAIL&plan=PLAN`). Use curl's `-d` option;
do not write -X POST yourself, because -d already means POST.

Print the server's reply as a single line
  reply: <body of the response>
With any other number of arguments print
`usage: solution.sh EMAIL PLAN` to stderr and exit with status 2.
concepts: -d sends form data in the request body and switches curl to POST
fields are joined as name=value&name=value

required_patterns.message: Send the form fields with curl's -d option.

forbidden_patterns.message: -d already makes the request a POST; -X POST is redundant here.

POST https://billing.lanternfish.example/signup

title: JSON with Headers
story:
Gus wants invoices raised from a spreadsheet instead of by hand, and Theo
has finally put up a JSON endpoint for it. Theo's message was short:
"Send JSON, and tell it that it is JSON. It is picky." The first attempt,
a plain `-d`, came back with "unsupported media type".
objective:
Write solution.sh with two arguments: a CUSTOMER name (it may contain
spaces) and an AMOUNT.

Create an invoice with a POST to
  https://billing.lanternfish.example/api/v1/invoices
whose body is exactly this JSON, on one line:
  {"customer":"CUSTOMER","amount":AMOUNT}
(the amount is a bare number, the customer is a string in double quotes).
Send the one header `Content-Type: application/json` with -H.

Print the server's reply as `reply: <body>`.

Validate first and never contact the server on bad input:
- not exactly two arguments: print `usage: solution.sh CUSTOMER AMOUNT`
  to stderr, exit 2
- AMOUNT not a number like 120 or 49.90: print `amount must be a number`
  to stderr, exit 2
- CUSTOMER containing a double quote: print
  `customer must not contain double quotes` to stderr, exit 2
concepts: -H 'Name: value' adds a request header
Content-Type: application/json tells the server how to read the body
build JSON text carefully: quotes around strings, none around numbers

required_patterns.message: Add the header with curl's -H option.
Send the JSON body with -d.

test_cases.name: a customer with a space in the name
a quote in the name would break the JSON
test_cases.expected_stderr: customer must not contain double quotes

title: Bearer Tokens
story:
Priya found a billing script in the team wiki with the API token pasted
right into it, and in the shell history, and in a chat log. She did not
shout, which was worse. The new rule: the token lives in the environment
variable LF_TOKEN, the script reads it, and nobody ever sees it in output.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It asks the billing API for the current balance:
  GET https://billing.lanternfish.example/api/v1/balance
The request must carry the header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, where
the token comes from the environment variable `LF_TOKEN`.

- LF_TOKEN unset or empty: print `LF_TOKEN is not set` to stderr and exit 2,
  without contacting the server.
- HTTP 200: print the body as `balance: <body>` and exit 0.
- HTTP 401: print `billing rejected the token` to stderr and exit 1.
- any other code: print `unexpected HTTP <code>` to stderr and exit 1.

Find out the code with `-w '%{http_code}'` and keep the body in a temporary
file (`mktemp`) that you remove again. The token must never appear on
stdout or stderr, must not be written to any file, and must not be typed
into the script. Do not turn on `set -x`: it would print the token.
concepts: Authorization: Bearer TOKEN header
secrets come from the environment, never from the script
never echo, log or trace a secret

required_patterns.message: Send the header as -H "Authorization: Bearer $LF_TOKEN".

forbidden_patterns.message: set -x prints every command, token included. Leave tracing off.
Do not type a token into the script; read it from LF_TOKEN.

expected_files..calls.log:
GET https://billing.lanternfish.example/api/v1/balance
header: Authorization: Bearer ********

title: Fail on HTTP Errors
story:
Last Tuesday a nightly script "looked up" a customer plan, got a 500 error
page back, and happily copied the words "internal error: database is busy"
into the invoice run. Gus found out when a bakery was billed for a plan
called "internal". Mara's verdict: curl must be taught to fail when the
server says no.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one argument, a customer ID such as `c-204`,
and looks up the plan with
  https://billing.lanternfish.example/api/v1/customers/ID/plan
On success print `plan: <body>` and exit 0.

Make curl treat HTTP errors (status 400 and above) as failures with
`--fail`, and keep error messages visible with `-S` (so use `-sS`
together with `--fail`). Then tell the two kinds of failure apart by
curl's exit status:
- exit 22 (the server answered with an error): print
  `plan lookup failed: the API refused the request` to stderr, exit with 3
- any other curl failure (no DNS, connection refused, ...): print
  `plan lookup failed: network error (curl exit N)` to stderr, where N is
  curl's exit status, and exit with 4

title: Respect Retry-After
story:
The reports API at Lanternfish allows only a few calls per minute. When
you go over, it does not break; it answers "429 Too Many Requests" and
tells you exactly how long to wait in a header. Theo's cron job ignored
the header and retried instantly, 900 times. The API now blocks Theo's
server, and Theo is buying everyone coffee.
objective:
Write solution.sh, which takes no arguments and fetches
  https://reports.lanternfish.example/api/v1/monthly
Make up to 4 attempts in total.

- HTTP 200: print the body and exit 0.
- HTTP 429: read the number of seconds from the response header
  `Retry-After`, run `sleep N`, and try again. Header names are
  case-insensitive and the header line ends in a carriage return, which
  you must strip. If the header is missing or is not a whole number, wait
  1 second. Do not sleep after the last attempt.
- after 4 attempts that all got 429: print
  `still rate limited after 4 attempts` to stderr and exit 1.
- any other HTTP code: print `unexpected HTTP <code>` to stderr, exit 1
  (no retry).

Save the response headers with `-D FILE` and the status code with
`-w '%{http_code}'`; keep the body with `-o`. Use mktemp files and remove
them on exit. (The workspace `sleep` only records the request, so tests
are quick.)
concepts: -D saves the response headers
headers are case-insensitive and end in \r\n
Retry-After says how long to wait

required_patterns.message: Save the response headers with curl -D FILE.
Wait with sleep before you try again.
Header names are case-insensitive: match Retry-After without caring about case (grep -i).

title: Extract a JSON Field
story:
The customer API answers in JSON, and Noor only ever needs one value out
of it: the plan, or the balance, or whether the account is active. Mara
does not want to install a JSON tool on every server just for that. "The
replies are small and flat," she says. "Text tools will do. Just be
careful which text you grab."

Fetch

(use `-sS --fail`) and print the value of FIELD, without quotes around
strings. Numbers and booleans are printed as they are.

commas, quotes or braces; there may be a space after each colon and after
each comma. Use `sed` or `grep` (jq is not available). Match the whole

title: Follow Pagination
story:
Gus wants every invoice a customer has ever received, and the API hands
them out two at a time. Each reply ends with a little pointer: "next:
page 2", "next: page 3", and finally "next: null". The first version of
the export only fetched page one, and Gus noticed when Tidewater Books
had exactly two invoices in total.

  https://billing.lanternfish.example/api/v1/customers/ID/invoices

JSON such as
  {"items":["inv-2001","inv-2002"],"next":"?page=2"}
where `next` is either a query string to append to the same URL or the
word `null` (no quotes) on the last page.

its own line as soon as its page arrives. At the end print `total: N`.
A customer without invoices gives `total: 0`.

title: Is the Port Open?
story:
"The mail server is up," says Theo. "Then why does nothing arrive?" asks
Noor. A server can be alive and still have a door bolted: the service
listening on a port may have crashed. Mara wants a script that knocks on
doors, just checks whether anything answers, and reports back.

title: DNS Lookups
story:
Harbour Bakery moved their website to a new server and now half of their
customers see the old one. That smells like DNS. Noor has a list of names
and wants to know, for each, which IPv4 addresses the world currently
gets. Typing `dig` forty times is not how anyone wants to spend a

spaces.

title: Download and Verify
story:
Priya has one rule about software that arrives over the network: "Trust
it when you have checked it, not when it has arrived." Last month a
half-downloaded monitoring agent was installed on `marlin` and nobody
noticed until it crashed. The release server publishes a checksum file
next to every release, and Priya wants it used, every time.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes one argument, a release NAME such as
`lfagent-2.4.tar`, and downloads
  https://downloads.lanternfish.example/releases/NAME
into the current directory, but only keeps it if it is intact.

The server also publishes the expected values at
  https://downloads.lanternfish.example/releases/NAME.cksum
as one line `CRC SIZE NAME` (the output format of `cksum FILE`).

1. Download the release into a temporary file (use `mktemp`, not the
   final name) with `curl -sS --fail -o`.
2. Download the checksum line.
3. Compute `cksum` of the downloaded file and compare its CRC and SIZE
   (the first two fields) with the published ones.
4. Match: move the temporary file to NAME in the current directory, print
   `verified: NAME`, exit 0.
5. Mismatch: print `checksum mismatch for NAME` to stderr, exit 1.
Downloading the release fails: print `download failed: NAME`, exit 1.
Downloading the checksum fails: print `no checksum published for NAME`,
exit 1. After any failure, nothing may be left in the directory (remove
your temporary files, for example with a `trap`). With no argument print
`usage: solution.sh NAME` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: download to a temporary name, publish only after verification
cksum prints CRC and size; compare both
curl --fail -o FILE for downloads

title: Uptime Probe Report
story:
Lanternfish has outgrown "somebody refreshes the status page". Mara has
written down everything that should answer, websites and raw TCP services
alike, in one small text file, and wants a single script that probes the
whole list and reports. If anything is down, the script's own exit status
must say so, because tomorrow a cron job will read it instead of you.

Write solution.sh. Its one argument is a probe list file. Each line is one
of
  http NAME URL
  tcp NAME HOST PORT
Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored.

- `http`: status code via `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3`.

  code 000 (curl could not connect) prints `DOWN NAME (no connection)`.
- `tcp`: `nc -z -w 2 HOST PORT`. Success is up; failure prints
  `DOWN NAME (port closed)`.
- any other first word: `DOWN NAME (unknown type WORD)`.

zero, otherwise 0. No argument: print `usage: solution.sh PROBE_FILE` to
stderr, exit 2. A file that cannot be read: print `cannot read FILE` to
stderr, exit 2.

reading a config file line by line, skipping comments
the exit status as the machine-readable result

title: Timestamped Log Lines
story:
Welcome to the on-call rotation. Mara has pinned the first rule of the
rota above your desk: "A log line without a time is gossip." The nightly
backup script at Lanternfish currently prints bare sentences, so nobody can
tell whether "snapshot finished" happened at supper time or at 3 a.m.

Write solution.sh that turns its arguments into one timestamped log line.

Usage: solution.sh WHEN MESSAGE...

- WHEN is either a Unix epoch (digits only) or the word `now`.
- MESSAGE is every remaining argument, joined with single spaces.

Print exactly one line on stdout:

    2026-03-01T10:00:00Z snapshot finished

that is, the time as `YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ` (UTC), a space, then the message.
For `now` use the current time; for an epoch use that moment.
With fewer than two arguments, or a WHEN that is neither `now` nor all
digits, print `usage: solution.sh WHEN MESSAGE...` to stderr and exit 2.

Format the time with Bash's own `printf '%(...)T'`; do not start `date`.

-1 means now
ISO 8601 UTC timestamps sort as text

minute, and last night the one ERROR that mattered scrolled past unseen.

title: Rotate by Size

The Gull & Anchor Pub's web shop has a single `shop.log` that has grown to

At 02:40 last Tuesday the Tidewater Books backup server filled its disk and
stopped taking backups for two days before anyone noticed. Gus has asked for

of your rota: read `df`, compare with a limit, shout.

Barracuda hosts the pub's online ordering, and on Friday evenings it creaks.
Theo swears "it's not my code", Mara wants evidence. The kernel already keeps
the evidence: three load averages (1, 5 and 15 minutes) printed at the end of

heading.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh LIMIT`, where LIMIT is a number such as `2`
or `1.5` (anything else: print `usage: solution.sh LIMIT` to stderr,
exit 2).

`HIGH: 1m load 4.10 is above 2` (the load and LIMIT exactly as written). In
the HIGH case exit 1, otherwise exit 0.

third line `trend: rising`; when it is smaller add `trend: falling`; when

title: Memory from meminfo
story:
A customer's PHP shop on dory keeps getting its processes killed at random.
Noor suspects memory, and Ollie runs `free`, but Mara wants the script to read
the kernel's own ledger: `/proc/meminfo`, a plain-text file of `Name: number kB`
lines. Your workspace has copies from three machines, so you can practise
safely.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh MEMINFO LIMIT`. MEMINFO is a file in
`/proc/meminfo` format (all values in kB), LIMIT a whole percentage.

Print these lines:

    memory: 2048 MiB used of 8192 MiB (25%)
    swap: 0 MiB used of 2048 MiB

- used = MemTotal minus MemAvailable. If the file has no MemAvailable
  line (old kernels), use MemFree + Buffers + Cached as the available amount.
- MiB values are kB divided by 1024, the percentage is used * 100 / MemTotal;
  both use integer division (rounded down).
- Swap used = SwapTotal - SwapFree. If SwapTotal is 0, print `swap: none`.
- If the memory percentage is at or above LIMIT, add a third line
  `WARN: memory at 95% (limit 90%)` and exit 1.

Errors: unreadable file -> `cannot read MEMINFO` on stderr, exit 1; no
MemTotal line -> `no MemTotal in MEMINFO`, exit 3; missing or non-numeric
arguments -> `usage: solution.sh MEMINFO LIMIT`, exit 2.
concepts: /proc/meminfo is Name: value kB, one per line
IFS=': ' read splits key and value
fall back when a field is missing

title: PID File Health
story:
After a power cut on eel, the web server refuses to start because its PID file
says it is "already running". The number in the file belongs to a different
program now: the machine rebooted and the kernel handed the old number to cron.
Ollie asks how you can tell a live PID file from a leftover one. You decide
to write the checker, and to make it not fall for recycled numbers.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh PIDFILE NAME`. NAME is the program name
the PID file should belong to (for example `nginx`).

Look at PIDFILE and print exactly one line:

- the file does not exist: `stopped`, exit 3
- the file does not contain a single whole number: `bad pid file`, exit 2
- the process with that PID exists and its command name is NAME:
  `running pid=4242`, exit 0
- there is no such process: `stale: pid 4242 is not running`; delete the
  PID file, exit 1
- the process exists but has another name, for example cron:
  `stale: pid 977 belongs to cron, not nginx`; delete the PID file, exit 1

Ask `ps -p PID -o comm=` for the name of process PID (it prints nothing and
exits non-zero when the process does not exist). Wrong number of arguments:
`usage: solution.sh PIDFILE NAME` on stderr, exit 2.

ps -p PID -o comm= asks for one process's name
stale means the file lies; clean it up

title: Heartbeat Freshness

Lanternfish's batch jobs each `touch` a heartbeat file when they finish a
cycle: billing, mail-relay, report-builder. A job that hangs does not crash,
it just goes quiet, and Gus found out about the silent billing job when a
customer called. Mara's trick: a cron entry refreshes a stamp file so its
modification time is "five minutes ago", and any heartbeat older than the
stamp is dead.

and each BEAT is a heartbeat file path.

name (the part after the last `/`) with `.beat` removed:

- `fresh NAME` when BEAT exists and is not older than STAMP (the same
  modification time counts as fresh)
- `STALE NAME` when BEAT exists but is older than STAMP
- `MISSING NAME` when BEAT does not exist

A single error in the web log is weather; forty errors in one minute is a

title: Metrics File
story:
Lanternfish is finally getting a proper monitoring server, and it speaks
Prometheus: it reads a text file of metrics that every machine exposes. Mara
hands you the web server's access log and a promise: "turn it into numbers
the dashboard can chart, and never let the dashboard see a half-written file."
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh ACCESSLOG OUTFILE`.

Each access-log line has five fields:
`2026-03-01T10:00:01Z GET /menu 200 5123` (time, method, path, HTTP status,
bytes sent). A line is *valid* when it has exactly five fields and both
the status and the bytes are whole numbers; every other line is malformed.

Write OUTFILE in the Prometheus text format, exactly in this layout (codes
in ascending numeric order; the `{...}` sample lines appear only for codes
that occur):

    # HELP lanternfish_http_requests_total Requests served, by status code.
    # TYPE lanternfish_http_requests_total counter
    lanternfish_http_requests_total{code="200"} 3
    lanternfish_http_requests_total{code="404"} 1
    # HELP lanternfish_http_response_bytes_total Bytes sent to clients.
    # TYPE lanternfish_http_response_bytes_total counter
    lanternfish_http_response_bytes_total 7000
    # HELP lanternfish_http_largest_response_bytes Largest single response.
    # TYPE lanternfish_http_largest_response_bytes gauge
    lanternfish_http_largest_response_bytes 5123
    # HELP lanternfish_http_malformed_lines_total Log lines that could not be parsed.
    # TYPE lanternfish_http_malformed_lines_total counter
    lanternfish_http_malformed_lines_total 0

reader never sees a partial file. When done print `wrote OUTFILE (N requests)`
where N is the number of valid lines. If ACCESSLOG cannot be read print
`cannot read ACCESSLOG` to stderr, exit 1, and do not create OUTFILE. Wrong
argument count: `usage: solution.sh ACCESSLOG OUTFILE` to stderr, exit 2.
concepts: Prometheus text format: # HELP, # TYPE, name{label="v"} value
counters only grow, gauges go up and down
write to a temporary file and mv for an atomic update

story:
The on-call desk at Lanternfish has a spare monitor, and Gus wants it to show
"the fleet at a glance". Your checks already produce one line per server.

whether the server is called `eel` or `humpback-staging`.

Write solution.sh. It reads lines from stdin of the form `HOST STATE LOAD DISK`
(for example `eel up 0.42 31%`) and prints a status board.

Twice this month the mail relay on octopus died at night and nobody woke up
for it. Theo's reaction: "just restart it, it always comes back." Mara's

`usage: solution.sh SERVICE...` to stderr and exit 2.

keep going and report at the end

title: Alert Webhook
story:
The on-call team lives in a chat room, and the chat room has a webhook: POST
a little JSON document at its URL and the message appears, with a siren
emoji if the severity is critical. Priya insists on one rule: "An alert that
cannot be delivered must say so, loudly, or it did not happen." Your script
will be the last step of every check you wrote so far.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh HOST SEVERITY MESSAGE`.

- The webhook address comes from the environment variable WEBHOOK_URL. If it
  is unset or empty print `WEBHOOK_URL is not set` to stderr, exit 2.
- SEVERITY must be info, warning or critical; otherwise print
  `bad severity: SEVERITY` to stderr, exit 2. Wrong argument count:
  `usage: solution.sh HOST SEVERITY MESSAGE`, exit 2.
- Build this JSON document (one line, no spaces outside the strings; any
  `\` or `"` inside MESSAGE must be escaped with a backslash):

      {"host":"eel","severity":"critical","text":"disk is 97% full"}

- POST it with curl: method POST, header `Content-Type: application/json`,
  the JSON as the body (`-d`), silent but showing errors (`-sS`), the
  response body discarded, a 5 second limit (`--max-time 5`) and the HTTP
  status code printed with `-w '%{http_code}'`.
- A status from 200 to 299: print `alert sent (200)` (the real code) on
  stdout, exit 0. Anything else, including `000` when curl could not
  connect: print `alert failed (CODE)` on stderr, exit 1.

curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' returns only the status
build JSON text safely: escape before you wrap

title: Tamper-Evident Audit Trail
story:
After an incident, Priya found that someone had quietly edited the admin
activity log to remove their own tracks. She cannot stop a person with root
from editing a file, but she can make sure the edit *shows*. Her design
fits on a napkin: every entry carries a sequence number and a checksum that
also covers the previous entry's checksum, so changing, deleting or reordering
one line breaks every line after it.
objective:
Write solution.sh with two modes.

Entry format, one per line: `SEQ|SUM|MESSAGE`
- SEQ is 1 for the first entry, then 2, 3, ...
- SUM is the first number printed by `cksum` when it reads the text
  `PREV|SEQ|MESSAGE` (exactly that text, no trailing newline), where PREV is
  the previous entry's SUM, or `0` for the first entry.
- MESSAGE is the rest of the line; it may contain `|`.

`solution.sh append LOG MESSAGE` first verifies the log. If it is
intact (or does not exist yet) it appends the next entry and prints
`appended #N`. If it is tampered it prints
`refusing to append: log is tampered` to stderr and exits 1, changing nothing.

`solution.sh verify LOG` checks every line in order: the sequence number must
equal the line number and SUM must match the recomputed value (using the SUM
*stored* on the previous line as PREV). On success print `OK: N entries`
(N = number of lines; an empty log is fine). At the first bad line print
`TAMPERED: line N` and exit 1.

`verify` on a missing file: `cannot read LOG` to stderr, exit 2. Any other
mode or wrong argument count: `usage: solution.sh append LOG MESSAGE | verify LOG`
to stderr, exit 2.
concepts: a hash chain: each entry's checksum covers the previous one
cksum reads a stream; no trailing newline when you want the exact text
IFS='|' read splits fields, the last one keeps the rest

required_patterns.message: Use cksum to compute each entry's checksum.

When the card gateway went down on Tuesday, Tidewater Books' checkout wrote
the same line, `cannot reach gateway`, eleven thousand times in nine

`HH:MM:SS message words...`, and prints them with runs of repeats folded.

- A line is *kept as is* and ends the current run even if it has no message

title: Daily Summary
story:
Gus reads exactly one thing from operations every morning, and it is not the
logs. He wants a short report: how many lines, how many warnings and errors,
which servers were the noisiest, and when trouble began and ended. The
servers each write their own log, and each file also holds the tail of the
day before. Time to put the whole rota together in one script.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh DATE LOGFILE...` where DATE looks like
`2026-03-01` and there is at least one LOGFILE.

Log lines look like `2026-03-01 08:14:03 ERROR eel upstream timed out`
(date, time, level, host, message). Only lines that start with DATE followed
by a space count; lines from other days and malformed lines are ignored.
Combine all files and print exactly this report:

    Daily summary for 2026-03-01
    lines: 9
    INFO: 5
    WARN: 1
    ERROR: 3
    errors by host:
      eel 2
      dory 1
    first error: 08:14:03 (eel)
    last error: 17:45:10 (dory)

- `lines:` counts every line of that day (any level, including DEBUG).
- The INFO, WARN and ERROR counts are always printed, even when 0.
- Hosts are listed with their ERROR counts, most first, ties by host name,
  at most three hosts, each indented with two spaces.
- First and last error are the earliest and latest ERROR times of that day
  (files are not sorted against each other). With no errors print `  none`
  under `errors by host:` and `first error: none` / `last error: none`.
- A LOGFILE that cannot be read: print `cannot read LOGFILE` to stderr,
  exit 1, and print no report. Bad DATE or no LOGFILE:
  `usage: solution.sh DATE LOGFILE...` to stderr, exit 2.
concepts: awk aggregates counts and extremes in one pass
combining several files in one run
sort + head for a top-N list

title: Step Runner
story:
Lanternfish ships every day, and Theo's release "pipeline" is a text file of
commands pasted into a terminal. Last Friday the tests failed, nobody noticed,
and the deploy step ran anyway. Mara wants a tiny step runner that treats a
failing step as a full stop, the way every real CI system does.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called with a list of step scripts: `solution.sh STEP...`.
Run the steps in the order given, each with `bash STEP`. Before each step
print (to stdout):
  step N/TOTAL: <step file name>
where N counts from 1 and TOTAL is the number of arguments.
If a step exits non-zero, stop at once: do not run the remaining steps,
print `FAILED at step N: <step file name> (exit CODE)` to stderr, and exit
with that same CODE.
If every step succeeds, print `pipeline passed: TOTAL step(s)` and exit 0.
With no arguments print `usage: solution.sh STEP...` to stderr and exit 2.
Your script must keep `set -e` on and still handle the failing step itself,
so no step after a failure ever runs.
concepts: stop on the first failing step
if ! cmd; then rc=$?; ... fi  and  cmd || rc=$?  under set -e
pass a child's exit status on as your own

required_patterns.message: Keep `set -e` (or -euo pipefail) on; handle each step's status explicitly.

step 2/3: test.sh

pipeline passed: 3 step(s)

title: Run All Linters
story:
Ollie pushed a branch, waited eight minutes for the pipeline, and got a red
cross: the shell linter failed. He fixed it, pushed again, waited again, and
the YAML linter failed. "Why didn't it just tell me about both?" he asks,
and nobody has a good answer. Make the lint stage report everything at once.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh FILE...`. Run these three linters,
in this order, each as `LINTER -q FILE...` with all the files:
  shellcheck, yamllint, markdownlint
A linter failing must NOT stop the others. After each linter print
  <linter>: ok
or
  <linter>: FAILED (exit CODE)
to stdout. When all three have run: if none failed print
`all linters passed` and exit 0; otherwise print
`lint failed: <failed linters separated by spaces, in run order>` to stderr
and exit 1. With no FILE arguments print `usage: solution.sh FILE...` to
stderr and exit 2 without running anything.

cmd || rc=$? to survive set -e
accumulate results in an array

title: Parse Test Results
story:
The storefront tests now print TAP, the Test Anything Protocol, and Gus
wants one line on the dashboard: how many passed, how many failed. Theo's
first attempt was `grep -c ok`, which counted the line "not ok" as a pass
and a comment that said "ok to ignore". Time for a real parser.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh TAP_FILE`. Read the TAP stream
line by line. Only lines that START with `ok ` or `not ok ` are results
(`ok N description` / `not ok N - description`; the dash is optional).
Everything else (the `TAP version` line, `#` comments, indented diagnostics)
is ignored, except the plan line `1..N`.
Classify each result:
  - `ok` with a `# SKIP` directive           -> skipped
  - `not ok` with a `# TODO` directive       -> todo (not a failure)
  - any other `ok`                           -> passed
  - any other `not ok`                       -> failed
For every failed result print `FAIL N: <description>` (in file order). The
description has the optional `- ` removed; for SKIP/TODO results the
directive is removed too, other `# text` stays.
Then print `passed=P failed=F skipped=S todo=T`.
Exit codes: if the plan line is missing, or N differs from the number of
results, print `plan mismatch: planned N, ran R` (use N=0 when there is no
plan) to stderr and exit 3. Otherwise exit 1 if anything failed, else 0.
If TAP_FILE cannot be read print `cannot read TAP_FILE` to stderr, exit 2.
concepts: parsing a line protocol with [[ =~ ]] and BASH_REMATCH
counters and exit codes that summarise a run
a plan line detects a runner that crashed halfway

required_patterns.message: Capture the pieces of each result line with a regex and BASH_REMATCH.

title: Coverage Gate
story:
North Pier Dental's booking widget went live with a test suite that covered
almost nothing, and a Saturday bug cost them forty appointments. Priya
proposes a rule: a build may not ship below an agreed coverage percentage.
The coverage tool already writes a plain report; someone must read it and say
yes or no. Bash has no decimals, so the trick is to avoid needing them.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh THRESHOLD REPORT`. THRESHOLD is a
whole number from 0 to 100. REPORT has one line per source file:
  <path> <covered lines> <total lines>
Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored. Use integer arithmetic
only (no awk, bc or floating point).
Output, in this order:
  coverage=<overall>% (threshold <THRESHOLD>%)
  low: <path> <percent>%          one line per file below the threshold
  gate: PASS    or    gate: FAIL
Overall coverage is total covered / total lines over all files, shown with
one decimal, rounded half up (82.5, 100.0, 0.5). A file percentage is shown
the same way; a file is "low" when its exact ratio is below THRESHOLD
(files with 0 total lines are skipped). The gate decides on the EXACT
overall ratio, not the rounded text: PASS when covered*100 >= THRESHOLD*total.
Exit 0 on PASS, 1 on FAIL.
Errors go to stderr with exit 2: a THRESHOLD that is not a whole number 0-100
or a missing argument prints `usage: solution.sh THRESHOLD REPORT`; an
unreadable REPORT prints `cannot read REPORT`; a line that is not
`<path> <number> <number>` or has covered > total prints `bad report line N`
(N counts every line, including comments); a report with no files prints
`no measurable lines`.
concepts: integer arithmetic for percentages (scale by 10 or 100)
compare exact ratios by cross-multiplying
validate numeric input with a regex before $(( ))

required_patterns.message: Do the percentage math with Bash arithmetic: $(( ... )).

forbidden_patterns.message: Keep it in Bash: scale the numbers instead of using floating point.

title: Semver Bump
story:
Lanternfish's version numbers are edited by hand, and last month somebody
released 1.9.10 as 1.10.0 and 1.10.0 as 1.1.0, which sorted below it. Theo
has been promising a bump tool for weeks. Mara hands you the rules of
semantic versioning and asks for a script that cannot get them wrong.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh VERSION PART`. PART is one of
`major`, `minor`, `patch`. Print the bumped version and nothing else.
VERSION is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, optionally with a leading `v` (which the
output keeps). Each number is `0` or a number without leading zeros.
Bumping rules: major adds 1 to MAJOR and resets MINOR and PATCH to 0;
minor adds 1 to MINOR and resets PATCH; patch adds 1 to PATCH.
Numbers are real numbers, not digits: 1.9.9 minor gives 1.10.0.
Errors go to stderr with exit 2:
  - wrong number of arguments or an unknown PART:
      usage: solution.sh VERSION major|minor|patch
  - a VERSION that does not match the format above (`1.2`, `1.2.3.4`,
    `v1.2.3-rc1`, `01.2.3`, ` 1.2.3`):
      invalid version: <VERSION as given>
Do the splitting with Bash only: no awk, cut, sed or tr.
concepts: validate a version with a regex, then split it with BASH_REMATCH
case statement to select the bump
arithmetic on numbers that must not be treated as octal

required_patterns.message: Use a case statement to choose between major, minor and patch.

forbidden_patterns.message: Split the version with a regex and BASH_REMATCH, not an external tool.

title: Changelog from Commits
story:
Noor keeps asking the same question from customers: "what changed in this
release?" Theo answers by scrolling through `git log` and typing from
memory. Mara points out that the team already writes commit subjects in the
conventional style, `feat(cart): ...` and `fix: ...`, so the changelog can
write itself. The release job pipes the subjects into your script.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh VERSION`. It reads commit subjects
from stdin, one per line (the output of `git log --format=%s`), and prints a
Markdown changelog. Ignore blank lines and subjects starting with `Merge `.
A conventional subject looks like `type: text`, `type(scope): text`, or the
same with a `!` before the colon (`feat!: text`, `fix(api)!: text`), where
type is lowercase letters. Sort each subject into ONE section:
  - has a `!`                     -> Breaking changes
  - type `feat`                   -> Features
  - type `fix`                    -> Fixes
  - anything else, including subjects that are not conventional -> Other
A bullet is `- scope: text` when there is a scope and `- text` when there
is not (for Breaking, Features and Fixes). Bullets in Other are the subject
exactly as written. Keep input order inside each section.
Output: first `## VERSION`; then for every section that has bullets, in
the order Breaking changes, Features, Fixes, Other: an empty line,
`### <section name>`, and its bullets. If there is nothing to list print
`## VERSION`, an empty line, and `No changes.`
Without VERSION print `usage: solution.sh VERSION` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: group lines into buckets (arrays) while reading stdin
regex captures for type, scope, bang and text
emit sections in a fixed order, skipping empty ones

required_patterns.message: Split each subject into type, scope and text with a regex and BASH_REMATCH.

title: Tag a Release
story:
Release day at Lanternfish used to mean Theo typing `git tag v1.5.0` from
memory. Twice he tagged with uncommitted changes, and once he re-used a tag
that was already out, so two different builds both claimed to be 1.5.0. The
tag is the contract with customers. It should only be created when the tree
is clean and the name is new.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh VERSION`. VERSION is
`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, with or without a leading `v`; the tag is always
`v` + the numbers (`1.5.0` and `v1.5.0` both give `v1.5.0`). Anything else
prints `invalid version: <VERSION>` to stderr and exits 2, before git is
called at all.
Then, using `git`, in exactly this order:
  1. `git status --porcelain` - if it prints anything, print
     `working tree is not clean` to stderr and exit 1.
  2. `git rev-parse -q --verify refs/tags/<tag>` - if it succeeds, the tag
     exists: print `tag <tag> already exists` to stderr and exit 1.
     (Its output is not wanted; send it to /dev/null.)
  3. `git tag -a <tag> -m "Release <tag>"`
  4. `git push origin <tag>` - if it fails, print
     `push failed: tag <tag> exists locally, remove it with: git tag -d <tag>`
     to stderr and exit 1.
On success print `released <tag>`. Steps after a refusal must not run.
concepts: driving git (status --porcelain, rev-parse --verify, tag -a, push)
guard clauses before a state-changing command
cleaning up after a half-finished release

required_patterns.message: Create an annotated tag: git tag -a TAG -m MESSAGE.
Use `git status --porcelain`: empty output means a clean tree.

title: Version from git describe
story:
Every Lanternfish build prints a version into its footer, and Noor can never
tell from a support ticket which code a customer is running: the footer
says "1.4.0" for builds made on the tag and for builds made twelve commits
later. Mara wants the build to ask git where it is, and to derive the
version from the answer instead of from a file somebody forgot to edit.
objective:
Write solution.sh (no arguments). Run exactly
  git describe --tags --long --dirty --match 'v[0-9]*'
Its output looks like `v1.4.0-12-g3f2a1bc` (last tag, commits since the tag,
`g` + abbreviated hash) with `-dirty` appended when the tree has uncommitted
changes. The tag itself may contain hyphens (`v1.5.0-rc1`). Print one line,
`version=<V>`, built like this:
  - tag only, 0 commits since, clean tree   -> the tag without its `v`:
                                               version=1.4.0
  - anything else                           -> <tag without v>-dev.<N>+g<hash>
                                               and `.dirty` after the hash
                                               when dirty:
                                               version=1.4.0-dev.12+g3f2a1bc
                                               version=1.4.0-dev.0+g3f2a1bc.dirty
If `git describe` fails (there is no tag yet) use the short hash from
`git rev-parse --short HEAD`: version=0.0.0-dev+g<hash>
If describe succeeds but its output does not parse, print
`cannot parse describe output: <text>` to stderr and exit 1.
concepts: git describe --tags --long: tag, distance and hash in one string
parse from the right: the tag may contain hyphens
fall back when a command fails: if out=$(cmd); then ... else ... fi

required_patterns.message: Take the tag, distance and hash out of the describe text with a regex and BASH_REMATCH.

title: Build Matrix
story:
The Lanternfish agent now has to run on Linux and macOS, against two or three
runtime versions each. Priya counts six combinations and refuses to
hand-write six pipeline lines that someone will forget to update. A matrix
is how every CI system solves this: list the operating systems, list the
versions, and build every pair.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh OSES RUNTIMES [EXCLUDE...]`.
OSES and RUNTIMES are comma-separated lists (`linux,macos` and `3.11,3.12`).
Each EXCLUDE is a combination written `OS/VERSION` that must not be built.
For every OS (in list order) and, inside it, every runtime (in list order)
run the build job as
  build-job --os OS --runtime VERSION
and print one line per combination:
  [OS/VERSION] ok          the job exited 0
  [OS/VERSION] FAILED      the job exited non-zero
  [OS/VERSION] skipped     the combination is excluded (job not run)
A failing job must not stop the rest. Finish with
  matrix: P/T passed
where T is the number of jobs actually run (skipped ones do not count) and P
how many of them passed. Exit 1 if any job failed, otherwise 0.
If either list is missing, empty, or has an empty item (`linux,,macos`,
`3.11,`), print `usage: solution.sh OSES RUNTIMES [OS/VERSION...]` to
stderr and exit 2 without running anything.
concepts: nested for loops: every pair from two lists
IFS=, read -ra to split a list into an array
skip with continue; count jobs run and passed

required_patterns.message: Use two nested for loops: one over the operating systems, one over the runtimes.
Split the comma lists with IFS=, read -ra name <<< "$list".

title: Artifact Names and Checksums
story:
The build matrix drops its results into `dist/` with names like
`linux-amd64.tar`. Harbour Bakery downloaded one last week, could not tell
which release it belonged to, and could not tell whether the download had
been cut short. Gus would like the files to carry the product name and
version, and a manifest beside them so anyone can verify a download.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh NAME VERSION`. NAME is lowercase
letters, digits and hyphens; VERSION is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. Otherwise print
`usage: solution.sh NAME VERSION` to stderr and exit 2.
Work on the files `dist/*.tar`:
  1. Rename each one `<os>-<arch>.tar` to `NAME-VERSION-<os>-<arch>.tar`
     (`dist/linux-amd64.tar` -> `dist/lanternfish-agent-2.3.1-linux-amd64.tar`).
     A file whose name already starts with `NAME-VERSION-` is left alone, so
     the script is safe to run twice.
  2. Write `dist/MANIFEST.txt`: one line per tar, sorted by file name:
       <checksum> <size in bytes> <file name>
     with the checksum and size exactly as printed by `cksum` (file name
     only, no directory).
  3. Print `wrote dist/MANIFEST.txt (N artifact(s))`.
Other files in dist/ are not touched and not listed. If there is no
`dist/*.tar` at all print `no artifacts in dist/` to stderr and exit 1
(nothing is created).
concepts: derive file names with parameter expansion and mv
cksum for portable checksums (CRC and size)
write a manifest atomically; keep reruns idempotent

required_patterns.message: Use cksum: it prints the checksum, the size and the name, on every platform.

title: Build and Tag an Image
story:
Lanternfish moves its apps into containers, and the first thing Ollie learns
is that `latest` is a trap: Theo pushed a release candidate as `latest` on
Friday and half the staging fleet pulled it. Mara's rule is that every image
carries its exact version, stable releases also move the short `MAJOR.MINOR`
tag and `latest`, and pre-releases never touch either.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh IMAGE VERSION [CONTEXT]`.
IMAGE is a repository such as `registry.lanternfish.example/shop`, VERSION is
`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with an optional pre-release suffix (`2.0.0-rc1`), and
CONTEXT is the build directory (default `.`). A malformed VERSION or a
missing IMAGE prints `usage: solution.sh IMAGE VERSION [CONTEXT]` to stderr
and exits 2 before docker is called.
Run, in this order:
  docker build --build-arg VERSION=<version> -t IMAGE:<version> CONTEXT
  docker tag IMAGE:<version> IMAGE:<major>.<minor>     (stable versions only)
  docker tag IMAGE:<version> IMAGE:latest              (stable versions only)
  docker push IMAGE:<tag>                              (once per tag, in the
                                                        order created)
A version is stable when it has no `-suffix`. After each successful push print
`pushed IMAGE:<tag>`.
If the build fails print `build failed` to stderr, exit 1 and do not tag or
push anything. If a push fails print `push failed: IMAGE:<tag>` to stderr
and exit 1; later pushes do not happen.
concepts: docker build -t NAME:TAG, docker tag, docker push
build once, then tag and push the same image
tag policy: exact version always, moving tags only for stable releases

Build once, then add extra tags with docker tag instead of building again.

title: Deploy with a Health Gate
story:
Theo's deploy script prints "Done!" the moment the files are copied. The new
version of the booking service then spends forty seconds starting, serves 503s
to Harbour Bakery's customers, and the script is long gone. Mara wants a gate:
a deploy is finished only when the service answers its health endpoint, and
if it never does, the pipeline must fail loudly instead of waiting forever.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh VERSION URL [MAX_ATTEMPTS]`.
MAX_ATTEMPTS defaults to 5 and must be a whole number of at least 1;
otherwise print `usage: solution.sh VERSION URL [MAX_ATTEMPTS]` to stderr and
exit 2 before doing anything.
1. Run `deployctl push VERSION`. If it fails print `deploy failed` to stderr
   and exit 1, without polling.
2. Poll the health endpoint with exactly
     curl -fs --max-time 2 URL
   (its output is not wanted; send stdout and stderr to /dev/null). The
   endpoint is healthy when curl exits 0.
   For each attempt N that is not healthy print `attempt N/MAX: not healthy`.
   Between two attempts run `sleep 2`; never sleep after the last attempt
   and never after a success.
3. On the first healthy answer print `healthy after N attempt(s)` and exit 0.
4. If all attempts fail print `gave up after MAX attempts` to stderr and
   exit 1.
concepts: retry loop with a maximum number of attempts
using a command's exit status as the loop test
no sleep after the final attempt; fail loudly on timeout

required_patterns.message: Wait with `sleep 2` between attempts.

title: Roll Back on Failure
story:
Lanternfish servers keep every release in its own folder, and a symlink
called `current` says which one is live. On Tuesday Theo switched `current`
to a release that crashed on start, then spent six minutes remembering what
it had pointed at before. A deploy script should remember that for him: if
the new release fails its smoke test, put the old one back before anyone
notices.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh VERSION`, run inside the server's
deploy directory. Releases are the directories `releases/<name>`; `current`
is a symlink such as `releases/v1`. (It may not exist on a first deploy.)
1. If `releases/VERSION` is not a directory print `no such release: VERSION`
   to stderr and exit 2. Nothing is changed.
2. Remember where `current` pointed before (use `readlink current`; the
   target text is e.g. `releases/v1`).
3. If `current` already points at `releases/VERSION`, print
   `already on VERSION` and exit 0 without running anything else.
4. Point `current` at `releases/VERSION` (a symlink with the relative
   target `releases/VERSION`; use `ln -sfn`).
5. Run `smoke-test`. If it passes, print `deployed VERSION`, then
   `current -> releases/VERSION`, and exit 0.
6. If the smoke test fails: print `smoke test failed for VERSION` to stderr.
     - With a previous target, point `current` back at exactly that text,
       print `rolled back to <previous target without the releases/ part>`
       and `current -> <previous target>`, and exit 1.
     - With no previous target, remove `current`, print
       `no previous release to roll back to` to stderr, and exit 1.
concepts: symlink switch: ln -sfn TARGET LINK, readlink LINK
remember the old state before changing it, restore on failure
failure handling around a verification step

required_patterns.message: Switch the link with `ln -sfn TARGET current` (-n so an existing directory link is replaced, not entered).
Read the old target with readlink before you replace the link.

test_cases.expected_stdout:

current -> releases/v2

test_cases.expected_stderr: no previous release to roll back to

title: Render a Template
story:
Every Lanternfish customer site needs an nginx config that differs in three
places: the hostname, the port and the log folder. Theo keeps one template
and fills it in with `sed`, which worked until Gull & Anchor Pub chose a
site title with an ampersand in it and the config turned into gibberish.
Time for a renderer that treats values as data and tells you when a
variable is missing instead of printing an empty hole.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh TEMPLATE`. Read the template and
write the rendered text to stdout, replacing placeholders with environment
variables:
  ${NAME}            the value of NAME
  ${NAME:-fallback}  the value of NAME, or `fallback` when NAME is unset OR empty
NAME is letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit. The
fallback is any text up to the first `}` (it may be empty).
Everything else is copied exactly: `$NAME` without braces, `$5`, and a `${`
that is not a valid placeholder (`${1x}`, `${open`) stay as they are.
A replaced value is never scanned again: if a value contains `${OTHER}`
that text stays literal. Values may contain `&`, `/`, `\` or spaces.
A variable that is unset and has no fallback is an error. A variable set to
the empty string is fine (it renders as nothing). Report every missing name
once, in the order first seen, as `missing variable: NAME` on stderr; then
print nothing at all to stdout and exit 1.
If TEMPLATE cannot be read print `cannot read TEMPLATE` to stderr, exit 2.
Only exported environment variables count. The script's own internal
variables (for example a template asking for ${line} or ${template}) must
never leak into the output: treat them like any other unset name.
Do not use eval, envsubst, sed or awk.
concepts: placeholder substitution by scanning with parameter expansion and a regex
[[ -v name ]] and ${!name}: set/unset and indirect expansion
values are data: no re-scanning, no eval

forbidden_patterns.message: Render with a Bash loop (regex plus ${!name}); eval, envsubst, sed and awk are not allowed.

required_patterns.message: Read a variable whose name is stored in another variable with ${!name}.

title: Promote Between Environments
story:
Lanternfish has three environments, dev, staging and prod, and a single rule
about them: a version reaches prod only by living in staging first, and only
after Priya has approved it. Last quarter Theo deployed straight from his
laptop to prod and, by accident, an older build over a newer one. Each
environment keeps a file naming what it runs. A promotion script should read
those files and enforce the rules, so the rules stop depending on people.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh FROM TO`. The environments, in
order, are `dev staging prod`. The file `versions/ENV` contains the version
(`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`) that ENV currently runs.
Checks, in this order; each failure prints its message to stderr, exits and
changes nothing:
  1. FROM or TO is not one of the three names, or an argument is missing:
       usage: solution.sh FROM TO   (environments: dev staging prod)    exit 2
  2. TO is not exactly the next environment after FROM:
       cannot promote FROM to TO                                        exit 2
  3. `versions/FROM` is missing, empty, or not a version:
       nothing deployable in FROM                                       exit 1
  4. TO already runs that version: print `TO already runs VERSION` to
     stdout and exit 0 (no deploy).
  5. `versions/TO` exists and is a NEWER version than the one being
     promoted: refusing to downgrade TO from CURRENT to VERSION        exit 1
     (compare the numbers part by part: 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.0).
  6. TO is `prod` and the file `approvals/VERSION` does not exist:
       VERSION is not approved for prod                                 exit 1
Then run `deployctl deploy --env TO --version VERSION`. If it fails print
`deploy to TO failed` to stderr and exit 1, leaving `versions/TO` as it was.
If it succeeds write VERSION to `versions/TO` (one line) and print
`promoted VERSION: FROM -> TO`.
concepts: an ordered pipeline of stages as an array and its indexes
compare version numbers part by part (no sort -V)
update state only after the action succeeded

title: Cron Wrapper
story:
The nightly backup of Tidewater Books started at 02:00, was still running at
02:00 the next night because the disk was slow, and two copies fought over the
same files until the dory server fell over. Cron does not care. It starts
jobs on time, whether or not the last one has finished, and it throws away
output nobody redirected. Mara wants one wrapper that every cron entry goes
through: only one copy at a time, a log you can read in the morning, and the
real exit status preserved.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh NAME COMMAND [ARG...]`. NAME is
letters, digits, `_` and `-` only; otherwise, or without a COMMAND, print
`usage: solution.sh NAME COMMAND [ARG...]` to stderr and exit 2.
Use the files `locks/NAME.lock` (a directory) and `logs/NAME.log`; create
`locks` and `logs` if they do not exist.
1. Take the lock with `mkdir locks/NAME.lock` (mkdir is atomic: exactly one
   caller can create it). If that fails, another run is active: append
     [NAME] skipped: previous run still active
   to the log, run nothing, and exit 0. Do NOT remove that other run's lock.
2. Otherwise make sure the lock is removed when the script ends, however it
   ends (normal exit, failure, SIGINT or SIGTERM), then append
     [NAME] start: COMMAND ARG...
   (command and arguments joined by single spaces) to the log.
3. Run COMMAND with its arguments. Its stdout AND stderr are appended to the
   log; the wrapper itself prints nothing.
4. Append `[NAME] finish: exit CODE` to the log and exit with CODE, the
   command's own exit status.
concepts: mkdir as an atomic lock
trap ... EXIT to always release the lock (only a lock you took)
append output to a log; pass the command's exit status through

required_patterns.message: Release the lock with a trap, so it is removed even if the job fails or is interrupted.
Take the lock with mkdir: it either creates the directory or fails, atomically.
