title: Idempotent Setup
story:
Setting up a new Lanternfish app server takes eight commands, and the
runbook says "run setup.sh". Ollie ran it twice by mistake, and the second
run overwrote the customer's edited config and added the same `umask` line
to the profile again. A setup script should be like a good light switch:
pressing it twice leaves the room as it is after pressing it once.
objective:
Write solution.sh (no arguments) that brings the current directory to this
state, touching only what is not already right, and prints one line per item
(`created ...` when it had to make it, `ok ...` when it was already in place),
in this order:
  1. group `deploy`: check with `getent group deploy` (exit 0 = exists); if
     missing run `groupadd deploy`.            created group deploy | ok group deploy
  2. directories `app/releases`, `app/shared`, `app/logs`, one line each
                                               created dir PATH | ok dir PATH
  3. file `app/shared/config.env` holding the single line `PORT=8080`. An
     existing file is NEVER changed, even if its content is different.
                                               created file PATH | ok file PATH
  4. the exact line `umask 027` in `app/profile` (create the file if needed).
     "Exact" means a whole line: `# umask 027` or `umask 0277` do not count.
     Append to the end, on a line of its own, even if the file lacks a final
     newline.
                                               created line umask 027 in app/profile
                                               | ok line umask 027 in app/profile
  5. a symbolic link `app/current-logs` pointing at `logs` (relative to
     app/, i.e. `ln -s logs app/current-logs`). If something that is not a
     link already has that name print `conflict: app/current-logs exists and is not a link`
     to stderr and exit 1.                     created link PATH | ok link PATH
Finish with `setup complete: N created, M already in place`.
Running the script twice must change nothing the second time.
concepts: idempotence: check, then create
test before you act: -d, -e, -L, grep -qxF, getent
never overwrite what the operator already edited

required_patterns.message: Test for the whole line with `grep -qxF`: -x whole line, -F literal text.

title: Prune Old Artifacts
story:
The artifact store behind Lanternfish's pipeline now holds four hundred
tarballs, one per build, and Gus has noticed the storage bill. Theo's cleanup
one-liner, `ls -t | tail -n +6 | xargs rm`, deleted a file called
`release notes.tar` as two non-existent files and left the real thing behind.
Mara asks for a cleanup that keeps the newest few builds, whatever their
names look like, and can be trusted to run unattended.
objective:
Write solution.sh, called as `solution.sh DIR KEEP`. KEEP is a whole number
(0 or more); anything else prints `usage: solution.sh DIR KEEP` to stderr
and exits 2. If DIR is not a directory print `no such directory: DIR` to
stderr and exit 1.
Consider the regular files directly inside DIR whose names do not start with
a dot (not directories, not symbolic links, nothing deeper). The KEEP newest
by modification time stay; all others are deleted. If two files have the
same modification time, the name that sorts LATER counts as newer.
Print one line per file in name order (the order a `DIR/*` glob gives):
  keep <file name>
  remove <file name>
then `kept K file(s), removed R file(s)`.
File names can contain spaces or start with `-`. Do not parse `ls` output;
compare modification times with the `-nt` test of `[[ ]]`.
concepts: rank files by mtime without ls: [[ a -nt b ]]
globs and arrays are safe with spaces; ls output is not
rm -- for names that start with a dash; deleting only what you decided to

forbidden_patterns.message: Do not parse ls output; it breaks on spaces and newlines. Compare files with [[ a -nt b ]].
No xargs: loop over an array of names and call rm yourself, so spaces cannot split a name.

required_patterns.message: Use [[ $a -nt $b ]] to ask which of two files is newer.

title: Parse CSV Rows
story:
Gus has a spreadsheet export of every invoice, and a habit of printing it and
circling things in red. This morning he wants only the unpaid ones, in a
layout he can read across the table without his glasses. The export comes from
three different tools, so some files end without a final newline and some
were saved by a Windows laptop.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, an invoice export in CSV. The
first line is a header:
  invoice,customer,amount,status
Customer names may contain spaces but never commas. Skip the header and any
blank lines. For every row whose status is exactly `open`, print:
  <invoice> | <customer> | <amount>
After the last row print a summary line:
  open invoices: <count>
The last line of the file may have no newline, and lines may end in `\r\n`
(Windows); neither may change the result. Read the file with a Bash
`while IFS=, read` loop, not with awk or cut.
concepts: IFS=, read -r splits a line into variables
the last variable of read receives the rest of the line
a final line without newline: || [[ -n $var ]]
stripping a trailing carriage return: ${var%$'\r'}

required_patterns.message: Split each row with IFS=, read -r invoice customer amount status.
Loop over the rows with while ... read ... done < file.

title: Validate CSV Schema
story:
Noor's support desk exports tickets every night, and last Tuesday somebody
pasted a subject with an extra comma into the tool. The importer swallowed
the row, shifted every column by one, and Gus received a report saying that
"urgent" tickets were opened in the year "Harbour Bakery". From now on the
export is checked before anything reads it.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a ticket export in CSV. The
expected header is exactly:
  id,opened,priority,subject
Lines may end in `\r\n`; ignore the `\r`. Blank lines are skipped and are not
counted as rows. Check the file in this order:
  * No lines at all: print `error: empty file` and exit 1.
  * Header differs: print `error: unexpected header: <header line>` and exit 1.
  * Then check every data row. A row with a field count other than 4 prints
      line <N>: expected 4 fields, found <M>
    (N is the physical line number in the file, header = line 1). Otherwise,
    an empty id prints `line <N>: empty id`, and a priority that is not one
    of low, normal, high, urgent prints `line <N>: bad priority "<value>"`.
    Each bad row is reported once, with the first problem found.
At the end: if there were bad rows, print `invalid: <bad> of <rows> rows` and
exit 1; otherwise print `valid: <rows> rows` and exit 0. All messages go to
standard output.
concepts: NF is the number of fields in the current record
NR is the physical line number, so it survives skipped lines
exit inside awk, and exit status from END
validating before processing

title: Filter Rows
story:
Gus is deciding which data centre rack to rent a second shelf in, and he only
cares about servers that really move data: more than a threshold of traffic,
in one region, and not already on their way to the scrap heap. The monthly
bandwidth export is a mess: some hosts report "n/a", some report nothing,
and the traffic figures have decimals.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes three arguments: a CSV file, a region name and
a minimum traffic in GB. The file has a header:
  host,region,gb,tier
Print the header line, then every data row that satisfies ALL of:
  * the region column equals the region argument exactly (it may contain
    spaces, for example `north pier`),
  * gb is a number (digits with an optional decimal part) that is greater
    than or equal to the minimum, compared as numbers (9 is less than 10),
  * tier is not `retired`.
Rows are printed unchanged and in file order. Lines may end in `\r\n`; the
output must not contain `\r`. The header is printed even if nothing matches.
If fewer than three arguments are given, print
`usage: solution.sh FILE REGION MIN_GB` to stderr and exit 2.

numeric versus string comparison: $3 + 0
combining conditions with && in a pattern
a pattern with no action prints the line

title: Reorder Columns
story:
The newsletter tool wants "email,name" and nothing else. The billing tool
wants "id,plan,email". The customer export that feeds both has five columns
in an order nobody chose, and Theo has already said, twice, that he will not
hard-code column numbers because the export team keeps adding columns.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes two arguments: a CSV file with a header line
(for example `id,name,email,plan,signup`) and a comma-separated list of
column names, for example `email,name`. Print the CSV again with only those
columns, in the order requested, header included. The columns are found by
looking their names up in the file's own header, never by fixed numbers, so
the same script works if the export gains or loses columns. A column may be
requested more than once. Lines may end in `\r\n`; do not print the `\r`.
Values contain spaces but never commas.
If a requested name is not in the header, print `unknown column: <name>` to
stderr, print nothing to stdout, and exit 1. A row shorter than the header
yields empty values for the missing columns.
concepts: map header names to positions: pos[$i] = i
$(expr) selects a field by computed number

it in a form she can feed to her own tools: one tidy line per request, no

title: Time Window Filter
story:
The deploy log of the whole fleet is one big file, and Theo needs to show that
nothing was released between the 14:00 snapshot and the 15:30 backup. Gus
needs a different slice: everything on the fourth of March, "whatever the
clock said". You could convert every timestamp to seconds, but Mara has a
better trick: nothing needs converting, because of the way the timestamps
were written.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes three arguments: a log file, a FROM and a TO.

free-text message:
  2026-03-04T14:05:10Z halibut deployed web-3.4.1

FROM and strictly before TO (a half-open window, so two adjacent windows
never both contain the same line). FROM and TO are compared as plain text,
so they may be full timestamps, a date (`2026-03-04`), or an hour
(`2026-03-04T14`); no date conversion tools are allowed.

line endings are stripped. If FROM sorts after TO, print
`error: FROM is after TO` to stderr and exit 1. With fewer than three
arguments print `usage: solution.sh LOG FROM TO` to stderr and exit 2.

string comparison in awk: $1 >= from && $1 < to
half-open intervals [from, to)
partial timestamps as prefixes (a date is a valid bound)

title: Latest Record Wins
story:
The signup form, the support desk and the billing system all append to the
same subscriber log every time somebody changes their plan, so every customer
appears once per change, in whatever order the three systems happened to
flush. Noor needs the current state, one line per customer, to mail the
right people. Some customers typed their address in capitals, and one row has
no timestamp at all.
objective:
Write solution.sh that takes one argument, a CSV file with header
`email,updated,plan` (more columns after `plan` are possible and must be
kept). `updated` is an ISO timestamp like `2026-10-01T09:30:00Z`. Print the
header, then exactly one row per customer: the one with the greatest
`updated`. Rules:
  * Customers are identified by email compared in lowercase, and the printed
    email is lowercase too.
  * If two rows have the same email and the same `updated`, the one that
    comes later in the file wins.
  * A row whose email is empty or whose `updated` is not a full timestamp
    of the form `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` prints `skipped line <N>` to stderr
    (N is the file line number) and is ignored.
  * Rows come out sorted by email (character order, by the email alone).
  * Skip blank lines; ignore `\r`. A completely empty file prints nothing.
Timestamps are compared as text.
concepts: keep the best record per key while streaming: if (ts > best[key])
tie-break with >= so the later line wins
normalising the key with tolower()
sort -t, -k1,1 and reading the remaining lines after a read

title: Streaming Transform
story:
The payment processor streams every transaction to `octopus` as it happens,
and Gus wants a running balance appended to each line as it goes by, so a
dashboard can show "money in today" live. The stream never ends, so the
script cannot wait for the end of the input, cannot collect lines in an
array, and the disk on `octopus` is full, so it cannot write temporary files
either. Mara's rule for the final exam of this module: the script's memory
use must be the same after a million lines as after ten.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a filter: it reads standard input and writes standard
output, no arguments. The input starts with the header line `ts,cents` and
continues with rows such as `2026-11-01T09:00:00Z,1250`, where cents is a
whole number that may be negative (refunds). Process the lines one at a time
and print each result as soon as it is known:
  * for the header: `ts,amount,running`
  * for each good row: `<ts>,<amount in dollars>,<running total in dollars>`
    where dollars are written with exactly two decimals and a leading `-`
    for negative values (`-3.05`, `0.07`, `1250.00`). Use integer arithmetic
    only; do not compute with floating point.
  * a row with an empty ts, or a cents value that is not a whole number
    (optional leading `-`, then digits) prints `bad line <N>: <the line>`
    to stderr (N is the input line number) and is skipped.
  * blank lines are skipped silently (they still count as lines).
When the input ends, print one last line:
  # rows=<good rows> total=<final running total in dollars>
If there was no input at all, print nothing. Ignore `\r` at line ends.
The script must not create temporary files (no `mktemp`, no `/tmp`, no
`> something.tmp`) and must not store the whole input (no `mapfile`,
`readarray`, `$(cat ...)` or `sort`); keep only the running total and two
counters.
concepts: a filter reads stdin and writes stdout, so it composes in pipelines
constant memory: state is a few numbers, never a list of lines
integer money: cents in, dollars out, with sign handling
no temp files: the pipe is the buffer

title: Timestamped Backup
story:
Gus asked a simple question over lunch: "If someone deletes the Harbour
Bakery website folder, how long until we get it back?" Nobody liked the
silence that followed. Mara hands you the first job of your new fleet-wide
role: a backup script that every other tool will build on, one archive per
run, never overwriting yesterday's.
objective:
Write solution.sh. It takes three arguments: SRC (a directory), DEST (a
directory for archives) and STAMP (a label such as `20260301`; the
caller supplies it so the script never guesses the date).

- If there are not exactly three arguments, print
  `usage: solution.sh SRC DEST STAMP` to stderr and exit 2.
- If SRC is not a directory, print `no such directory: SRC` to stderr and
  exit 1.
- Create DEST if it does not exist.
- The archive is `DEST/NAME-STAMP.tar.gz`, where NAME is the last component
  of SRC (a trailing slash on SRC must not matter). Inside the archive the
  paths must start with NAME/ (not with the full path of SRC), so a restore
  recreates one tidy folder.
- If that archive already exists, print `archive already exists: PATH` to
  stderr, exit 1, and leave the old archive untouched.
- On success print two lines on stdout:
    created DEST/NAME-STAMP.tar.gz
    files: N
  where N is the number of regular files in the archive (list it back with
  `tar -tzf`; directory entries end in `/` and do not count).

tar -tzf lists an archive without extracting it
refuse to overwrite an existing backup

delete the old ones", which is how you end up with no old ones when a
customer asks for last month's invoice database. Mara wants a policy

title: Verify a Backup
story:
Last quarter Noor restored a customer database from the backup disk and
found the dump was half a megabyte of zeros. The disk had been failing
for weeks and every nightly job reported "success". Priya's rule since
then: a backup folder carries a manifest of checksums, and a verifier
runs before anyone trusts a single file in it.
objective:
Write solution.sh DIR. DIR holds backup files and a manifest called
MANIFEST, one line per file in the format `cksum` prints:
  CRC SIZE NAME
(for example `3650393976 6 orders.sql`).

For each manifest line, in manifest order, recompute the checksum of
DIR/NAME with `cksum` and print exactly one of:
  OK NAME          (CRC and SIZE both match)
  FAILED NAME      (the file exists but CRC or SIZE differs)
  MISSING NAME     (the file does not exist)
Then print `UNLISTED NAME` for every file in DIR (other than MANIFEST
itself) that the manifest does not mention, in file-name order, and a
summary line:
  verified: A ok, B failed, C missing, D unlisted
Exit with status 0 only when there are no FAILED and no MISSING files
(unlisted files are only a warning); otherwise exit 1.

If DIR has no MANIFEST print `no manifest in DIR` to stderr and exit 1.
With no argument print `usage: solution.sh DIR` to stderr and exit 2.
Use `cksum` (it is the same on every platform), not sha256sum or md5.

read -r a b c splits a manifest line into fields
compare what the manifest says with what the disk says

Dana from the billing team left on Friday and Priya has one question:

forgets something, so the order is now fixed: shut the door first, then

title: Fleet Command Runner
story:
A kernel advisory landed at 08:55 and Priya wants to know, before the
stand-up, which hosts are still on the vulnerable version. There are
thirty-odd machines, and the old way is a terminal tab per host. Mara
shows you the pattern every fleet tool starts from: a loop that runs one
command everywhere and keeps going when one host is down.
objective:
Write solution.sh HOSTFILE COMMAND [ARGS...]. HOSTFILE lists one host per
line; blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored.

For each host, in file order, run the command with
  ssh -n -o BatchMode=yes HOST COMMAND...
(give ssh all the command words as one string with "$*") and capture its
output (standard output and error together, `2>&1`) and exit status. Then print:
- every line of the output, prefixed with `HOST: `
- if ssh exited with 255 (host unreachable), print `HOST: UNREACHABLE`
  instead (ignore any output)
- if the command exited with another non-zero status N, print the output
  lines and then `HOST: FAILED (exit N)`

Never stop at a failing host. At the end print
  hosts: T, ok: O, failed: F
and exit 1 if F is greater than 0, else 0. A host counts as failed when it
was unreachable or the command exited non-zero.

on it. With no host file readable print `cannot read FILE` to stderr and
exit 1. With fewer than two arguments print
`usage: solution.sh HOSTFILE COMMAND [ARGS...]` to stderr and exit 2.

ssh exit status 255 means the connection failed, anything else is the remote command's status
ssh swallows stdin inside a while-read loop

title: Certificate Expiry Report
story:
On a Sunday morning the Gull & Anchor Pub's booking site started showing
a browser warning that frightens customers: its certificate had expired
at midnight. Nobody was watching the date. Priya wants a report that runs
every morning and turns "expires on Mar 15" into "14 days left", sorted so
the scary ones are on top.
objective:
Write solution.sh TODAY CERTDIR. TODAY is a date like `2026-03-01` (passed
in, so the report is repeatable). CERTDIR holds files named `NAME.pem`.

For each certificate get its end date with
  openssl x509 -enddate -noout -in FILE
which prints one line such as `notAfter=Mar  4 12:00:00 2026 GMT` (note:
single-digit days are padded with a space, so split on whitespace, not on
single spaces). Work out the number of whole days from TODAY to that date
(negative if already past), without using `date -d`: turn each date into a
day number with integer arithmetic (the days-since-year-0 formula in hint 3
works) and subtract.

Print one line per certificate, sorted by days remaining (smallest first,
ties by name), with exactly this layout:
  printf '%-10s %5d  %s\n' NAME DAYS STATUS
where STATUS is EXPIRED (days < 0), WARN (0 to 30 days) or OK (more than
30). NAME is the file name without `.pem`. After the table print
  checked N certificates, B need attention
where B counts EXPIRED and WARN. Exit 1 if B is greater than 0, else 0.

If openssl cannot read a certificate, print `cannot read certificate: NAME`
to stderr, leave it out of the table (it still counts toward N and B) and
carry on. TODAY not in the form YYYY-MM-DD: `bad date: TODAY` on stderr,
exit 2. No `.pem` files in CERTDIR: `no certificates in CERTDIR` on stderr,
exit 1. Wrong argument count: `usage: solution.sh TODAY CERTDIR`, exit 2.
concepts: openssl x509 -enddate prints notAfter=...
date arithmetic with integers: convert to a day number, subtract
month name to number lookup
sort a report by a numeric key

title: Log Archiver
story:
Barracuda's /var/log filled up overnight. Not with anything exciting: just
eighteen months of access logs nobody had touched. Theo says "compress
them", Noor says "do not touch today's, the support tools are still
writing to it", and Mara adds the rule that matters most in practice:
never delete the original until you have checked the compressed copy.
objective:
Write solution.sh LOGDIR DAYS. DAYS is a whole number. Look only at regular
files named `*.log` directly inside LOGDIR (not in sub-folders) that were
last modified MORE than DAYS days ago (`find -mtime +DAYS`). Handle them in
file-name order.

For each such file NAME.log:
- If `LOGDIR/archive/NAME.log.gz` already exists, print
  `skipped NAME.log (already archived)` and leave the log alone.
- Otherwise create `LOGDIR/archive/` if needed and compress with
  `gzip -c` into `LOGDIR/archive/NAME.log.gz.partial`. Check that file with
  `gzip -t`, rename it to `NAME.log.gz`, and only then delete the original.
  Print `archived NAME.log`.

End with `archived A, skipped S` (always printed, even when both are 0).

DAYS that is not a whole number: `bad day count: DAYS` on stderr, exit 2.
LOGDIR not a directory: `no such directory: LOGDIR` on stderr, exit 1.
Wrong argument count: `usage: solution.sh LOGDIR DAYS` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: find -type f -name -mtime +N selects files by age
gzip -c writes to stdout and keeps the original
gzip -t verifies, then rename into place before deleting

Verify the compressed copy with gzip -t before deleting the original.

title: Disk Cleanup Policy
story:
Cuttlefish is the build server, and builds leave rubbish: temp files,
crash dumps, enormous debug dumps nobody reads. A cron job that runs
"rm *.tmp" would have been fine, if only the rules were that simple.
Ollie suggests a policy file so the rules are written down where
Priya can review them, and a dry run so nobody has to trust the script.
objective:
Write solution.sh [-n] POLICY DIR. POLICY has one rule per line, three
whitespace-separated fields:
  PATTERN MIN_AGE_DAYS MIN_BYTES
Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored. A rule selects regular
files anywhere under DIR whose NAME matches PATTERN (a shell wildcard such
as `*.tmp`, matched with `find -name`), and that are older than
MIN_AGE_DAYS days (`-mtime +N`, skipped when N is 0) and larger than
MIN_BYTES bytes (`-size +Nc`, skipped when N is 0).

Validate the whole policy first: a rule needs exactly three fields and the
last two must be whole numbers; otherwise print
`policy line N: invalid rule: TEXT` to stderr (N counts every line of the
file, TEXT is the line as written), exit 1 and delete nothing.

Apply the rules in file order. Within a rule go in sorted path order. A
file removed by an earlier rule is not touched again. For each file print
  delete PATH (rule R)
(R counts rules only, starting at 1, PATH is as printed by find) and remove
it. Finish with `removed N files, freed B bytes` (B is the sum of the sizes
of the removed files).

With -n delete nothing, print `would delete PATH (rule R)` lines and
finish with `would remove N files, B bytes`.
POLICY unreadable: `cannot read POLICY` (stderr, exit 1). DIR not a
directory: `no such directory: DIR` (stderr, exit 1). Wrong arguments:
`usage: solution.sh [-n] POLICY DIR` (stderr, exit 2).
concepts: policy as data: rules in a file, one engine
find -name -mtime +N -size +Nc
validate everything before deleting anything

Use find -mtime +N for the age rule.

title: Package Audit
story:
Priya's quarterly audit asks the same three questions about every server:
is the software we depend on there, is the software we banned absent, and
is the security-critical software new enough? Until now the answer came
from someone scrolling through `dpkg -l`. Gus would like it in a form he
can attach to a spreadsheet.
objective:
Write solution.sh POLICY. POLICY has one rule per line (blank lines and
`#` comments ignored):
  require NAME             the package must be installed
  forbid NAME              the package must not be installed
  minver NAME VERSION      installed and at least VERSION
Get the installed packages by running
  dpkg-query -W -f='${Package} ${Version}\n'
which prints one `name version` pair per line.

Check the rules in policy order and print one line per problem:
  MISSING NAME                              (require or minver, not installed)
  FORBIDDEN NAME (installed VERSION)        (forbid, but installed)
  OUTDATED NAME INSTALLED < REQUIRED        (minver, too old)
For the comparison use only the numeric part of a version: its leading
digits and dots (`1.9.5p2-3` becomes `1.9.5`, `3.0.2-0ubuntu1` becomes
`3.0.2`). Compare component by component as numbers (3.0.9 is older than
3.0.13), treating missing components as 0. OUTDATED shows both versions in
their numeric form.

Finish with `audit: clean` (exit 0) or `audit: N problem(s)` (exit 1).
An unknown rule word: `policy line N: unknown rule 'WORD'` on stderr,
exit 1 (before printing anything). Unreadable policy: `cannot read POLICY`
on stderr, exit 1. No argument: `usage: solution.sh POLICY` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: dpkg-query -W -f lists installed packages
an associative array as a lookup table
numeric version comparison component by component

required_patterns.message: Read the package list with dpkg-query -W -f=...
Keep the installed packages in an associative array (declare -A) for quick lookups.

title: Rolling Restart
story:
Theo shipped a config change for nginx and, in a moment of enthusiasm,
asked for "restart it everywhere". Everywhere at once is also known as an
outage. The load balancer can lose one web host without anyone noticing,
but not all four. Mara's rule for restarts: one host at a time, wait until
it is healthy again, and if one does not come back, stop and leave the rest
of the fleet exactly as it was.
objective:
Write solution.sh HOSTFILE SERVICE. HOSTFILE lists one host per line
(blank lines and `#` comments ignored). SERVICE is a systemd unit name such
as `nginx` (letters, digits and `@._-` only; anything else prints
`bad service name: SERVICE` to stderr and exits 2).

Process the hosts strictly one after another. For each host HOST:
1. Print `restarting HOST`.
2. Run `ssh -n -o BatchMode=yes HOST systemctl restart SERVICE`. If that
   fails (any non-zero status), abort as described below with reason
   `restart failed`.
3. Ask for the state with `ssh -n -o BatchMode=yes HOST systemctl is-active SERVICE`
   (it prints the state, `active` when healthy; its exit status is non-zero
   when not active). Check at most 3 times in total, immediately one after
   the other (a real script would sleep between checks; this simulated
   fleet answers at once). As soon as the state is `active`, print
   `HOST healthy after N check(s)` (N = checks used) and go on to the next host.
4. If it is still not active after 3 checks, abort with reason
   `did not recover (last state: STATE)`.

Abort means: print `ABORT: HOST REASON; K hosts left untouched` to stderr
(K = hosts after this one in the file), do not touch any further host, and
exit 1 (ssh's own error text may also appear on stderr before it). When every host went well print `rolling restart complete: N hosts`.
Unreadable host file: `cannot read FILE` (stderr, exit 1). Wrong argument
count: `usage: solution.sh HOSTFILE SERVICE` (stderr, exit 2).
concepts: serial rollout: one host at a time, health gate before the next
bounded retry loop
stop the line on the first failure; report what was left untouched

title: Database Dump Rotation
story:
The Tidewater Books order database lives on one Postgres server, and the
only copy of last month's orders is a dump somebody made "that one time".
Gus wants a nightly dump, Theo wants it compressed, and Mara wants the one
property that makes it trustworthy: a failed dump must never push out a good
old one. The classic disaster is a script that prunes first and dumps
second, and finds out at 3 a.m. which half failed.
objective:
Write solution.sh DB OUTDIR STAMP KEEP.
- DB is a database name matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$`
  (else `bad database name: DB` on stderr, exit 2).
- OUTDIR receives the dumps (create it if needed); STAMP is a label such as
  `20260301`; KEEP is how many dumps of this database to retain, a whole
  number of at least 1 (else `bad keep count: KEEP`, exit 2).

1. Dump with `pg_dump --no-owner DB`, compress the stream with gzip and
   write it to `OUTDIR/DB-STAMP.sql.gz.partial`. If either pg_dump or gzip
   fails, delete the partial file, print `dump failed for DB` to stderr, exit
   1, and do NOT prune anything (pg_dump's own error text may also appear).
2. Check the partial file with `gzip -t`, rename it to `DB-STAMP.sql.gz`
   (replacing a dump with the same stamp, if any) and print
   `dumped OUTDIR/DB-STAMP.sql.gz`.
3. Prune: the dumps of this database are the files named
   `OUTDIR/DB-<digits>.sql.gz` (so dumps of a database called `app-staging`
   are never mistaken for `app`). Sorted by name, keep the newest KEEP and
   delete the rest, printing `pruned NAME` for each.
4. Print `kept K dumps` (K = how many dumps of DB remain).

Wrong argument count: `usage: solution.sh DB OUTDIR STAMP KEEP` on stderr,
exit 2.
concepts: pipefail makes a failing pg_dump visible through a pipe
write to .partial, verify, rename; prune only after success
glob precisely so one database's dumps are not confused with another's

Compress the dump with gzip.

title: Port Inventory
story:
Last month a contractor left a MySQL port open to the internet on
barracuda, and the only reason anyone knew was a stray scan from a
stranger. Priya now wants a weekly inventory: which of the interesting
ports answer on each host, and where that differs from what the host is
supposed to offer. Noor asks for something she can read without knowing
what 5432 means.
objective:
Write solution.sh HOSTFILE EXPECTED. HOSTFILE lists one host per line
(blank lines and `#` comments ignored). EXPECTED has lines of the form
  HOST PORT [PORT...]
naming the ports each host is supposed to listen on; a line starting with
the word `default` applies to every host that has no line of its own, and
if there is no default either, nothing is expected. Comments and blank
lines are ignored there too.

Probe exactly these ports, in this order: 22 25 80 443 3306 5432. Test one
port with `nc -z -w 1 HOST PORT` (exit status 0 means open; hide nc's
error text). For each host print
  HOST: open=P1,P2,...        (comma-separated, scan order; `-` if none)
and then one indented line per deviation, in scan order:
  "  UNEXPECTED P"       the port is open but not expected
  "  NOT-LISTENING P"    the port is expected but closed
(two leading spaces). Expected ports outside the six scanned ones are
ignored. Finish with
  scanned N hosts, D deviations
and exit 1 if D is greater than 0, else 0.

Unreadable file: `cannot read FILE` on stderr, exit 1. Wrong argument
count: `usage: solution.sh HOSTFILE EXPECTED` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: nc -z probes a port without sending data
scan loop with an expected-state table
a lookup table loaded from a file (associative array)

title: Firewall Rule Audit
story:
Priya exports every host's firewall each night with iptables-save and
files the text away. Nobody reads it, which is how a "temporary" rule
opening the database port to the whole internet survived for eleven
weeks. She hands you a sample export and a short list of things that must
never appear in the INPUT chain, and asks for a checker that points at the
offending line numbers.
objective:
Write solution.sh FILE. FILE is the output of `iptables-save` (see
`fixtures/sample-rules.txt` for the shape). Report problems in the INPUT
chain, in file order, one line each, using the line number inside FILE
(counting every line, comments included).

Rules to check:
- A chain policy line `:INPUT ACCEPT [0:0]` (default-allow) gives
  `line N: INPUT policy is ACCEPT`
- A rule `-A INPUT ... -j ACCEPT` that is open to the world, meaning it has
  no `-s` option or `-s 0.0.0.0/0`, and whose port selection
  (`--dport X` or `-m multiport --dports X,Y,...`) contains
    * a sensitive port (22, 3306, 5432 or 6379): `line N: port P open to the world`
      (one line per sensitive port in that rule, in the order written)
    * a range such as `8000:9000`: `line N: port range A:B open to the world`
  If such a world-open ACCEPT rule has no port selection and no `-i`, no
  `-p` and no `-m` option at all (it simply accepts everything), report
  `line N: accepts all traffic`.
Rules in other chains (FORWARD, OUTPUT, ...) and rules that are not
ACCEPT rules are ignored.

Finally print `audited R rules, F findings` where R counts every `-A` line
of any chain. Exit 1 if F is greater than 0, else 0.
If FILE has no `*filter` line print `not an iptables-save export: FILE` to
stderr and exit 1. Unreadable FILE: `cannot read FILE` (stderr, exit 1).
No argument: `usage: solution.sh FILE` (stderr, exit 2).
concepts: parsing a structured text export field by field (awk)
iptables-save format: -A CHAIN options -j TARGET
audit rules as small predicates over parsed fields

required_patterns.message: awk is the natural tool for walking the fields of each rule line.

title: SSH Hardening Check
story:
Priya's checklist for a new server starts with five lines of sshd_config.
The trouble is that people do read the file and still get it wrong:
somebody adds "PermitRootLogin no" at the bottom, never noticing that
"PermitRootLogin yes" sits higher up, and sshd obeys the first one.
She wants a checker that reads the file the way sshd does, not the way a
tired human does.
objective:
Write solution.sh FILE, which audits an sshd_config the way sshd reads it:
- Blank lines and lines starting with `#` (after optional blanks) are ignored.
- A line is `Keyword value` (blanks) or `Keyword=value` or `Keyword = value`.
  Keywords and values are case-insensitive; compare and print values in
  lowercase.
- For each keyword the FIRST occurrence wins.
- Reading stops at the first line whose keyword is `Match`: everything below
  belongs to conditional blocks and is not part of the global settings.
- A keyword that never appears has its built-in default value.

Check these five settings, in this order (default in brackets):
  PermitRootLogin           must be `no`            [prohibit-password]
  PasswordAuthentication    must be `no`            [yes]
  PermitEmptyPasswords      must be `no`            [no]
  X11Forwarding             must be `no`            [no]
  MaxAuthTries              must be a number <= 4   [6]
Print one line per setting:
  PASS Keyword=value
  FAIL Keyword=value (want no)                 (explicit value; MaxAuthTries: want <=4)
and when the value came from the built-in default, add the word `default`:
  PASS Keyword=value (default)
  FAIL Keyword=value (default, want no)        (MaxAuthTries: want <=4)
A MaxAuthTries value that is not a whole number fails. Keyword spelling in
the output is exactly as listed above.

Finish with `hardening: all 5 checks passed` (exit 0) or
`hardening: F of 5 checks failed` (exit 1). Unreadable FILE:
`cannot read FILE` (stderr, exit 1). No argument:
`usage: solution.sh FILE` (stderr, exit 2).
concepts: first match wins, then stop (awk exit / flags)
case-insensitive keyword matching with tolower()
defaults for unset values

required_patterns.message: sshd keywords and values are case-insensitive; normalise case before comparing.

title: Cron Inventory
story:
At 03:00 every night something on grouper makes the whole host crawl, and
nobody knows what, because scheduled jobs live in a different file for each
user and half of them were added by people who left. Ollie asks the
obvious question: "Is there a way to see them all in one place?" Mara
smiles, because there is, and it is a script you are about to write.
objective:
Write solution.sh DIR. DIR contains one crontab file per user (the file name
is the user name, like the contents of /var/spool/cron/crontabs). Print one
table of every scheduled job, using this layout for every line
  printf '%-10s %-17s %s\n' USER SCHEDULE COMMAND
starting with the header line USER / SCHEDULE / COMMAND.

Rules:
- Users in file-name order (plain files only, names starting with `.` are
  skipped); within a user, jobs in file order.
- Ignore blank lines, comment lines (first non-blank character is `#`) and
  environment settings such as `MAILTO=ops@example` or `PATH=/usr/bin`.
- A job line has five schedule fields and then the command, or a single
  `@name` schedule (`@reboot`, `@daily`, ...) and then the command. The
  SCHEDULE column shows the schedule fields joined by single spaces,
  whatever mix of blanks and tabs the file used. The command is the rest of
  the line.
- A user whose file has no jobs still gets a row: schedule `-`, command
  `(no jobs)`.
- A line with too few fields to contain a command is skipped and reported on
  stderr as `USER line N: malformed entry` (N counts lines in that file).

Finish with `J jobs across U users` (U counts only users that have at least
one job). DIR not a directory: `no such directory: DIR` on stderr, exit 1.
No argument: `usage: solution.sh DIR` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: read -r splits a crontab line into fields; the last variable keeps the rest
classify lines: comment, environment, @special, five-field job
report tables with printf column widths

title: Account Audit
story:
Priya's yearly audit always finds the same four things: a second account
with UID 0, service accounts that quietly got a real shell, two people
sharing a UID, and a password field that is simply empty. She has copies of
/etc/passwd and /etc/shadow from every host. Reading them by eye is how the
last "backdoor" account went unnoticed for a year. Your job: let the script
do the squinting.
objective:
Write solution.sh PASSWD SHADOW. PASSWD is in /etc/passwd format
(`name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`, 7 fields), SHADOW in /etc/shadow
format (`name:hash:...`, the hash is field 2).

Ignore blank lines and lines starting with `#`. Then report, grouped by
check in exactly this order, and inside a check in file order:
1. `MALFORMED line N`  a passwd line that does not have exactly 7 fields
   (N = line number in PASSWD). Malformed lines are not accounts and take
   no part in the other checks.
2. `EXTRA-ROOT NAME`  UID 0 but the name is not `root`.
3. `DUP-UID UID NAME1 NAME2 ...`  a UID used by more than one account, names
   in file order; one line per UID, ordered by first appearance.
4. `SERVICE-SHELL NAME SHELL`  UID from 1 to 999 whose shell's file name
   (last path component) is one of sh, bash, dash, zsh, ksh.
5. `EMPTY-PASSWORD NAME`  the account's SHADOW entry has an empty hash field.
6. `NO-SHADOW NAME`  an account with no entry in SHADOW at all.

Finish with `audited N accounts, F findings` (N counts well-formed accounts,
F counts reported lines) and exit 1 if F is greater than 0, else 0.
An unreadable file: `cannot read FILE` on stderr, exit 1. Wrong argument
count: `usage: solution.sh PASSWD SHADOW` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: awk -F: or IFS=: for colon-separated system files
grouping with associative arrays (UID -> names)
one pass to collect, several passes to report in a fixed order

required_patterns.message: These files are colon-separated: use IFS=: read, or awk -F:.

title: Incident Snapshot
story:
At 09:30 anchovy is at 97% disk, load average 8, and the customer-facing
nginx is eating a whole CPU. Mara's first instruction is not "fix it": it
is "collect evidence before you touch anything". Once somebody restarts
the service, the clues are gone. She wants a one-command snapshot of the
host, saved in a private folder, with checksums so nobody can later
claim the files were edited.
objective:
Write solution.sh HOST STAMP (STAMP is a label such as `20260301-0930`).
Create the evidence folder `incident-STAMP-HOST` (mode 700, so only you can
read it) and fill it with the output of four remote commands, each run as
  ssh -n -o BatchMode=yes HOST COMMAND
with standard output and error both saved to the file:
  uptime.txt   <- uptime
  df.txt       <- df -P
  ps.txt       <- ps -ef
  ss.txt       <- ss -tan
Collect in that order. If a command exits non-zero (other than 255), keep
what it printed, append one more line `ERROR: exit N` to that file, count it
as failed and carry on: partial evidence is better than none.

If ssh exits with 255 (host unreachable) at any point, remove the folder
again, print `cannot reach HOST` to stderr and exit 1.

Then write `meta.txt` into the folder with exactly three lines
  host=HOST
  stamp=STAMP
  collected_by=USER
(USER is the value of the \$USER environment variable). Finally write
`MANIFEST`: the output of \`cksum\` for the five files meta.txt, df.txt,
ps.txt, ss.txt and uptime.txt, sorted by file name, with bare file names
(run cksum from inside the folder). MANIFEST does not list itself.

Print three lines on stdout:
  snapshot: incident-STAMP-HOST
  collected: N files, F failed          (N counts the four command files)
  manifest: incident-STAMP-HOST/MANIFEST
Evidence is never overwritten: if the folder already exists print
`evidence folder already exists: DIR` to stderr and exit 1 before doing
anything else. Wrong argument count: `usage: solution.sh HOST STAMP` on
stderr, exit 2.
concepts: mkdir -m 700 for private output
collect first, tolerate failures, record them in the evidence
cksum manifest taken after the files are final

Write the manifest with cksum.

title: Compliance Report
story:
The Harbour Savings Co-op, Lanternfish's biggest customer, will renew its
contract only if Lanternfish can show a compliance report for the hosts that
carry its data. Gus has promised it for Friday. Priya has the four
controls she cares about, and the evidence collected from each host sits in
a folder per machine. You have everything you need: it just has to become
one honest, readable pass/fail report.
objective:
Write solution.sh [-f] [-m PCT] HOSTSDIR. Each sub-folder of HOSTSDIR is a
host (plain files are ignored; hosts in name order) holding the evidence
files described below. Apply four checks to every host, in this order:
1. `root-login-disabled`: file `sshd_config` exists and its first
   `PermitRootLogin` line (keyword case-insensitive, blanks allowed before
   it, comments ignored) has the value `no` (case-insensitive).
2. `disk-under-90`: file `df.txt` (output of `df -P`, header on the first
   line, Capacity such as `97%` in column 5) exists and every filesystem is
   below 90%.
3. `time-sync`: file `services.txt` (lines `NAME STATE`) has a line
   `chronyd active`.
4. `no-pending-reboot`: there is NO file called `reboot-required`.
A check whose evidence file is missing fails (except check 4, which passes
when the file is absent).

Print for each host a header `HOST: P/4` (P = checks passed) followed by one
line per check, indented by two spaces: `  [PASS] NAME` or `  [FAIL] NAME`.
With `-f` print only the failing check lines (headers always appear).
Then print
  fleet: P/T checks passed (X%)
where X = P*100/T rounded down (integer arithmetic), and a verdict line
  result: PASS
or `result: FAIL (need M%)`. The fleet passes when X is at least M, where
M comes from `-m PCT` (a whole number from 0 to 100; default 100). Exit 0
on PASS, 1 on FAIL.

A bad PCT: `bad minimum: PCT` on stderr, exit 2. A HOSTSDIR with no host
folders: `no hosts in HOSTSDIR` on stderr, exit 1. HOSTSDIR not a
directory: `no such directory: HOSTSDIR` on stderr, exit 1. Without a
HOSTSDIR argument: `usage: solution.sh [-f] [-m PCT] HOSTSDIR` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: getopts with a flag and an option argument
several independent checks combined into one scorecard
integer percentage with $(( )) and a pass threshold

required_patterns.message: Parse -f and -m PCT with getopts.

title: The Deployment Pipeline
story:
The first named storm of the season, Hurricane Hilda, is two days out, and Theo
wants the new `shrimp-api` release live before the harbour loses its uplink.
Last year a "quick manual deploy" went out untested and took the ferry booking
site down for six hours. Mara's rule for storm season: nobody deploys by hand.
Tonight you write the pipeline that builds, tests, ships, checks, and undoes its
own work when the check fails.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a deployment pipeline: `solution.sh APP VERSION`.

The company tools are on PATH (they print nothing useful, only their exit
status matters; exit 0 means success):
  harbor-build  APP VERSION     build the release
  harbor-test   APP             run the test suite
  harbor-deploy APP VERSION     put a version live
  harbor-health APP             0 = healthy

Rules:
- Exactly two arguments, otherwise print `usage: solution.sh APP VERSION` to
  stderr and exit 2. VERSION must look like `1.2.3` (three numbers with dots);
  otherwise print `error: bad version 'X'` to stderr and exit 2.
- State lives in `state/`. `state/APP.version` holds the version currently live
  (the file may not exist yet; then the previous version is `none`).
- Lock: if `state/APP.lock` exists, print `error: pipeline already running for APP`
  to stderr and exit 7 without touching the lock. Otherwise create it and
  guarantee it is removed when the script ends, however it ends (use a trap).
- Run the stages in order build, test, deploy, verify. After each stage print
  `stage NAME: ok` or `stage NAME: FAILED` on stdout, and append the line
  `APP VERSION NAME ok` (or `fail`) to `state/pipeline.log`.
  The verify stage calls `harbor-health APP` up to 3 times; between failed
  attempts it runs `sleep 5`. Its success line is `stage verify: ok (attempt N)`.
- A failed build stops everything: stderr `pipeline failed at build: nothing was deployed`,
  exit 3. A failed test stage: same message with `test`, exit 4.
- If deploy or verify fails, roll back: if there is a previous version, run
  `harbor-deploy APP PREVIOUS`, print `rolled back to PREVIOUS` on stdout, then
  print `pipeline failed: APP VERSION was rolled back` to stderr and exit 5.
  With no previous version print `error: no previous version to roll back to`
  to stderr and exit 6.
- On success write the new version to `state/APP.version` and print
  `deployed APP VERSION (previous: PREVIOUS)`.
concepts: stages as functions with one failure policy
trap EXIT for a lock file
retry loop with a pause
rollback to the recorded previous state
exit codes that name the failure

required_patterns.message: Remove the lock with a trap so every exit path cleans up.

title: The Log Investigator
story:
At 03:14 the storm knocked a ferry-booking backend over, and by morning three
teams have three different stories. The web tier logs one way, the database
another, and the haproxy box writes plain syslog with no year in sight. Gus
wants one page that says what broke first and how it spread, before the
insurance call at nine. You are the investigator: merge every log into a single
timeline.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh FROM TO LOGFILE...`

FROM and TO are the window, each as one argument in the form
`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` (both ends included). At least one log file is required.
Three log formats may appear, even inside one file:
  A  `[2026-11-12 03:14:07] web ERROR upstream timed out`      (service, level, message)
  B  `2026-11-12T03:14:09Z|db|WARN|connection pool at 95%`     (message may contain `|`)
  C  `Nov 12 03:14:11 marlin haproxy[221]: [ERROR] backend is DOWN`
In C the service is the process name without `[pid]` or the trailing colon, the
day may be space padded (`Nov  9`), the year is the year of FROM, and a line
without a `[LEVEL]` right after the colon counts as INFO.
Level names WARNING, CRITICAL and ERR are normalised to WARN, CRIT and ERROR.
Ranking: INFO < WARN < ERROR < CRIT. Only events inside the window with level
WARN or worse are kept. Blank lines are ignored; any other line that matches
none of the formats is counted as unparseable.

Output (stdout):
  == Incident timeline FROM .. TO ==
  one line per kept event, sorted by time (ties: file order on the command
  line, then line order), formatted with printf '%s %-8s %-5s %s\n'
  on: timestamp (`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`), service, level, message
  (or the single line `(no WARN-or-worse events in window)`)
  == Summary ==
  files: N | lines: R | in window: W | kept: K | unparseable: U
  first error: TIMESTAMP SERVICE        (first ERROR or CRIT, or `first error: none`)
  by service: svc=count svc=count ...   (kept events, services in alphabetical order, or `by service: none`)

R counts non-blank lines read, W the parseable lines inside the window.
Exit status: 0 normally, 1 if the timeline contains at least one CRIT event.
Errors go to stderr with exit 2: wrong argument count `usage: solution.sh FROM TO LOGFILE...`,
a bad timestamp `error: bad timestamp 'X'`, FROM not before TO `error: window is empty`,
an unreadable file `error: cannot read FILE` (checked before any output).
Use only POSIX awk (no interval expressions like {4}).
concepts: one awk pass per log format, normalised into one record shape
ISO timestamps sort as plain strings
sort with several keys for a stable merge
mktemp -d plus trap cleanup
exit status as an alert signal

required_patterns.message: Use awk to parse the three formats.
Merge the events with sort.

title: The Secret Rotator
story:
At 2 a.m., mid-storm, Theo pasted the bakery database password into a public
support ticket "just so Noor could see the error". Priya noticed at 6 a.m. and has
been awake ever since. Every credential that ever touched that ticket must change
today, without taking a single site down. A secret that is rotated badly is worse
than one that is leaked: a half-changed password locks everybody out. You are
writing the rotator that changes it everywhere, proves it works, and puts
everything back if it does not.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--dry-run] [NAME...]`

`rotation.map` lists what can be rotated, one per line, fields separated by `|`:
  NAME|CONFIG_FILE|KEY|DBUSER
(blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored). Each secret's current
value is the single line in `secrets/NAME.secret`. If `rotation.map` cannot be
read: `error: cannot read rotation.map` on stderr, exit 2.

With no NAME, rotate every entry in map order, otherwise the names given, in the
order given. An unknown name prints `error: unknown secret NAME` to stderr and
exits 2 before anything is changed.

Tools on PATH:
  vault-gen NAME                    prints a fresh secret
  dbctl set-password USER SECRET    change the database password (exit 0 = done)
  dbctl check USER SECRET           exit 0 if SECRET is the current password

Rotating one NAME, in this order:
  1. `secrets/NAME.secret` must be readable, else FAILED (no current secret on disk).
  2. CONFIG_FILE must contain a line starting with `KEY=`, else FAILED (config has no KEY).
  3. new=$(vault-gen NAME); `dbctl set-password DBUSER new`; on error FAILED
     (database refused the new password), nothing else has changed.
  4. Rewrite the `KEY=` line of CONFIG_FILE with the new value, keeping every other
     line and the file's permissions. Never leave a half-written config: build the new
     file next to the old one and `mv` it over. Keep the old config as
     `CONFIG_FILE.rotate-bak` until step 5 has finished.
  5. `dbctl check DBUSER new`. If it fails: restore the old config from the backup,
     set the old password back with `dbctl set-password`, FAILED (verification failed,
     old secret restored).
  6. On success delete the backup and write the new secret to `secrets/NAME.secret`
     with mode 600.
The new secret must never appear on stdout, stderr or in the log, and must not be
passed to awk as a command-line argument (it would show up in `ps`): hand it over
through the environment (ENVIRON) instead.

Output: per name `rotate NAME: ok` or `rotate NAME: FAILED (reason)` and one line
appended to `rotation.log`: `NAME ok` or `NAME failed: reason`. A failure does not
stop the other names. At the end print `rotated: a b` and `failed: c` (names
separated by spaces, `none` when empty). Exit 1 if anything failed, else 0.

`--dry-run` changes nothing, writes no log, and prints per name
`would rotate NAME: CONFIG_FILE KEY (db user DBUSER)`, then exits 0.
concepts: associative arrays loaded from a map file
write-new-then-mv: atomic config updates
verify, and roll back to the saved copy
secrets via environment, not argv, and never in logs
file permissions preserved and enforced

required_patterns.message: Pass the secret to awk through ENVIRON, not on the command line.
Replace the config atomically with mv.

title: The Capacity Planner
story:
Storm season means webcams, weather feeds and a flood of customers re-uploading
boat photos, and the disks are filling faster than anyone expected. Gus does not
want a graph, he wants one sentence per disk: "this one is full on the 6th of
December". The monitoring export only has weekly samples of used space, so the
forecast is yours to build. Mara's one hard rule: no `date -d`, the build machines
are a mix of macOS and Linux and the script must give the same answer on both.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--warn DAYS] [--crit DAYS] FILE`

FILE is a CSV of disk samples, one per line: `DATE,HOST,MOUNT,USED_GB,TOTAL_GB`
(DATE is `YYYY-MM-DD`; numbers may have decimals; rows are in any order). A first
line starting with `date,` is a header and is skipped, blank lines are ignored.
Any other line that is not five fields with a valid date and positive numbers
is skipped and counted. If there were any, print
`warning: skipped N malformed line(s)` to stderr (N is the count).

Group samples by HOST and MOUNT. For a group with at least 3 samples:
- fit a straight line through (day, used GB) by least squares; the slope is the
  growth in GB per day. Day numbers must come from your own calendar arithmetic
  (days since 1970-01-01), not from the `date` command.
- USED% = last sample's used / total * 100. The last sample is the one with the
  latest date and also provides USED and TOTAL.
- if slope > 0: DAYS_LEFT = whole days (rounded down) until the disk is full,
  counted from the last sample, = (total - used) / slope (0 if already full), and
  FULL_ON is the last sample's date plus DAYS_LEFT days as `YYYY-MM-DD`
  (leap years count). Otherwise DAYS_LEFT and FULL_ON are `-`.
- STATUS: `CRIT` if DAYS_LEFT <= crit (default 14), `WARN` if DAYS_LEFT <= warn
  (default 45), else `OK`; any disk at 95.0% or more is `CRIT` regardless of growth.
A group with fewer than 3 samples gets `-` in every numeric column and STATUS `NODATA`.

Print a header and one row per group using
  printf '%-8s %-8s %6s %8s %9s  %-10s  %s\n'
with the columns HOST MOUNT USED% GB/DAY DAYS_LEFT FULL_ON STATUS (USED% with one
decimal, GB/DAY with two). Row order: CRIT disks that are not growing first, then
growing disks by fewest days left, then non-growing ones, then NODATA; ties by
host then mount. After the table print
  summary: C crit, W warn, O ok, N nodata
Exit status (like a monitoring plugin): 0 if nothing is WARN or CRIT, 1 if the
worst is WARN, 2 if any CRIT. Usage errors exit 3:
`usage: solution.sh [--warn DAYS] [--crit DAYS] FILE`; a threshold that is not a whole
number `error: --warn needs a whole number of days` (same for --crit);
`error: --crit must not exceed --warn`; `error: cannot read FILE`; and a file
with no usable samples `error: no usable samples in FILE`.
concepts: least-squares regression in awk
calendar arithmetic without date(1): days since the epoch and back
grouping with composite awk keys
plugin-style exit codes 0/1/2/3
sorting by a computed key, then dropping it

required_patterns.message: Use awk for the regression and the calendar maths.

forbidden_patterns.message: No date command here: compute day numbers yourself so macOS and Linux agree.

title: The User Auditor
story:
During the storm emergency Lanternfish handed out accounts like lifejackets:
contractors to rewire the dock network, a volunteer to watch the webcams, a
"temporary" developer who was never removed. Now the insurer's auditor is coming,
and Priya has one sentence for you: "Tell me everything on these servers that
should not be there, before they do." She wants orphans, stale accounts, sloppy
key permissions and any account that quietly shares root's powers, in one report.
objective:
Write solution.sh:
  `solution.sh [--stale-days N] [--ignore USER]... PASSWD SHADOW LASTLOG`

Inputs (all must be readable, else `error: cannot read FILE` on stderr, exit 2):
- PASSWD: standard `user:x:uid:gid:comment:home:shell` lines.
- SHADOW: `user:hash:...`; only the first two fields matter. An empty hash means
  no password; `!` or `*` means locked.
- LASTLOG: `user|days` where days is the number of days since the last login, or
  the word `never`. A user missing from LASTLOG counts as `never`.
- Home directories are looked up relative to the current directory: a passwd home
  of `/home/anna` is `home/anna`. Homes outside `/home/` are never inspected.
Blank lines and `#` lines in the three files are ignored. `--ignore USER` (repeatable)
silences every finding about that user, but its home directory still counts as owned.
`--stale-days N` (whole number, default 90; otherwise `error: --stale-days needs a
whole number`, exit 2). Other usage mistakes: `usage: solution.sh [--stale-days N]
[--ignore USER]... PASSWD SHADOW LASTLOG`, exit 2.

Findings (severity, kind, user, detail):
- CRIT UID0: uid 0 but the name is not `root` -> `uid 0 but not root`
- CRIT NOPASS: uid >= 1000, login shell, SHADOW hash empty -> `no password set`
- WARN DUPUID: any account whose uid is already used by an earlier PASSWD line
  -> `uid N shared with FIRSTUSER`
- For uid >= 1000 with a login shell (a shell not ending in `nologin` or `false`):
  WARN STALE `never logged in`, or `last login N days ago` when N > stale-days
- For uid >= 1000 with a home under /home/: WARN NOHOME `home /home/x missing`
  when the directory does not exist; otherwise inspect, inside the home:
  CRIT BADPERM `.ssh/id_rsa is MODE` and `.netrc is MODE` if the file exists and
  group or others have any permission (MODE is the first 10 characters of `ls -l`);
  WARN BADPERM `.ssh/authorized_keys is MODE` if group or others can write it.
- INFO ORPHAN: a directory directly inside `home/` that no PASSWD line points to
  -> user column is the directory name, detail `home directory has no account`

Output: a header `printf '%-5s %-8s %-10s %s\n' SEV KIND USER DETAIL`, then one row per
finding in the same format, ordered CRIT, WARN, INFO, then by kind, then by user.
Last line: `findings: C crit, W warn, I info`. Exit 0 when there are no findings, 1
when there is at least one.
concepts: associative arrays as lookup tables for several files
IFS-split loops over passwd-style files
reading permissions from ls -l without stat
an allow-list option that can repeat
ranked findings sorted at the end

required_patterns.message: Use associative arrays to look users up across the three files.
Read permissions from `ls -l` (stat differs between macOS and Linux).

title: The API Poller
story:
The harbour's ferry, webcam and tide services all expose a tiny status API, and the
town's emergency channel wants a ping the moment one of them changes state. Last
week the old script paged people forty times in one night because a single flaky
response flipped `ok` to `down` and back. Noor received every page. She would like
the new poller to be calm: confirm a change before shouting about it, never alert
for the same thing twice, and never lose an alert just because the webhook was
itself down for a minute.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a poller that is run once per minute by cron:
  `solution.sh --webhook URL [--confirm N] ENDPOINTS`

ENDPOINTS has lines `NAME|URL` (blank lines and `#` lines ignored). `--confirm N`
(positive whole number, default 2; otherwise `error: --confirm needs a positive
whole number`, exit 2). Missing --webhook or wrong argument count:
`usage: solution.sh --webhook URL [--confirm N] ENDPOINTS`; unreadable ENDPOINTS:
`error: cannot read ENDPOINTS`; all exit 2. State lives in `state/`.

`curl` is on PATH. Fetch a status with `curl -sS --fail --max-time 5 URL`. The body
contains a JSON field such as `"status": "down"` (maybe pretty printed over several
lines; extract it with sed, there is no jq). The reading is that value if it is
`ok`, `degraded` or `down`; `unreachable` if curl failed; `invalid` for anything else.

Per endpoint keep `state/NAME.state` with one line `CONFIRMED CANDIDATE COUNT`
(`-` for no candidate). Start with CONFIRMED `unknown`.
- First reading (confirmed `unknown`): accepted at once. Print
  `NAME: R (first reading)`; if R is not `ok` also send a webhook (from `unknown`)
  and print `NAME: R (first reading, webhook sent)` (or `webhook queued`) instead.
- Reading equals confirmed: print `NAME: R`, clear the candidate.
- Reading differs: if it equals the candidate, COUNT+1, else it becomes the new
  candidate with COUNT 1. When COUNT reaches N the change is confirmed: send the
  webhook, print `NAME: OLD -> NEW (webhook sent)` (or `queued`), set the confirmed
  status and clear the candidate. Otherwise print
  `NAME: CONFIRMED (saw R, pending COUNT/N)`.
The webhook is `curl -sS --fail --max-time 5 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
-d BODY WEBHOOK_URL` with BODY exactly
  {"service":"NAME","from":"OLD","to":"NEW"}
If the POST fails the body is appended to `state/outbox` (one per line) instead.
At the start of every run, before polling, retry every queued body; keep the ones that
fail again, and if the outbox was not empty print `outbox: sent S, K still queued`.
Exit 1 if any endpoint's confirmed status is not `ok` after this run, otherwise 0.
concepts: state machine per endpoint stored in a file
debouncing: confirm a change before reporting it
extracting JSON fields with sed when jq is unavailable
an outbox for at-least-once webhook delivery
read the old state, write it back, every run

required_patterns.message: Use curl to poll and to post the webhook.
Pull the status field out of the JSON body with sed.

title: The Backup Verifier
story:
Before the storm reaches the harbour, Gus wants one question answered: "If the
server room floods tonight, can we actually get our data back?" Everyone says the
nightly backups run. Nobody has restored one since March. Mara's creed is that a
backup you have not restored is a rumour, so you are building the verifier that
restores the newest backups of every set into a scratch directory, compares every
file with its recorded checksum, and refuses archives that try to write outside it.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--keep-last N] [--set NAME] BACKUP_DIR`

BACKUP_DIR holds backups named `SET-YYYY-MM-DD.tar.gz` (SET may itself contain
dashes) with a manifest `SET-YYYY-MM-DD.sums` next to each one. A manifest line is
`CRC SIZE PATH`: the two numbers `cksum` prints for the file, and its path inside
the archive (no spaces). Other files in the directory are ignored.

Options: `--keep-last N` (positive whole number, default 2): verify only the N newest
backups of each set (newest = latest date in the name). `--set NAME`: only that set.
Errors go to stderr with exit 3: `usage: solution.sh [--keep-last N] [--set NAME] BACKUP_DIR`;
`error: --keep-last needs a positive whole number`; `error: cannot read BACKUP_DIR`
(not a directory); `error: no backups found` (nothing matched, including a --set with no
backups).

Verify each selected backup in this order, stopping at the first problem type:
1. no manifest: `no sums file`
2. `tar -tzf` must succeed, else `corrupt archive`
3. any listed entry that is absolute or contains a `..` path component:
   `unsafe path in archive: ENTRY` (first one) - nothing is extracted
4. extract into a scratch directory (`mktemp -d`, always deleted by a trap, even on
   errors); if extraction fails, `corrupt archive`
5. compare with the manifest. Collect, in this order, `missing: P...` (listed but not
   restored), `mismatch: P...` (restored but cksum CRC or size differ) and
   `unlisted: P...` (restored files not in the manifest, sorted), paths separated by single
   spaces, groups joined with `; `. Any group means failure. An empty manifest is
   `empty manifest`.
A good backup has the detail `N files restored, checksums match`.

concepts: restore into a scratch directory and always clean it up
cksum on stdin gives name-free CRC and size
list the archive before extracting it: refuse path traversal
group by a name prefix and keep the newest N
layered failure reasons and an exit status for the whole run

title: The Cron Analyzer
story:
Hurricane prep added eleven new cron jobs to the shared server in three days:
tide-sync every half hour, webcam archiving, a nightly database dump, a report for
the insurer. At 02:15 on Thursday the dump, the log rotation and the sync all fought
for the same disk and the ferry site crawled. Nobody can tell from `crontab -l`
which jobs collide, because nobody wants to expand `*/30` and `1-5` by hand at two
in the morning. Mara asks you for the tool that does it for them.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--min-shared N] MONTH DOM DOW CRONTAB`

MONTH (1-12), DOM (1-31) and DOW (0-6, Sunday is 0) name the day to analyse and
must be whole numbers in range. `--min-shared N` (default 1, whole number >= 1)
hides overlaps shorter than N minutes. Errors, exit 2, on stderr:
`usage: solution.sh [--min-shared N] MONTH DOM DOW CRONTAB`, `error: bad day 'X'`
for an out-of-range or non-numeric day part, `error: cannot read CRONTAB`.

CRONTAB lines: blank lines, `#` comments and environment lines (`NAME=value`)
are ignored; `@reboot` lines are ignored; `@hourly` (0 * * * *), `@daily` and
`@midnight` (0 0 * * *), `@weekly` (0 0 * * 0), `@monthly` (0 0 1 * *), `@yearly`
and `@annually` (0 0 1 1 *) are shortcuts. Otherwise a job is five fields
`minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week` followed by the command. Each field is
a comma-separated list of `*`, `N`, `A-B`, `*/S` or `A-B/S` (numbers only). Day of
week 7 also means Sunday. A job may end with a comment `# runs 25m` or `# runs 2h`
giving its run time (default 1 minute); strip it from the command.
A job whose line cannot be parsed prints `warning: line N skipped: bad FIELDNAME field`
to stderr (FIELDNAME: minute, hour, day-of-month, month or day-of-week; a line with fewer than 6
words: `warning: line N skipped: too few fields`) and is otherwise ignored.

A job runs on the chosen day when MONTH is in its month field and the day matches.
Cron's day rule: if neither day-of-month nor day-of-week field starts with `*`, the job
runs when EITHER matches; otherwise when BOTH match.
The job name is the basename of the command's first word; a repeated name gets `#2`,
`#3` ... Jobs are numbered 1, 2, ... in file order (parsed jobs only).
A start at minute S occupies minutes S .. S+run-1; ignore anything past 23:59.

Output:
  == Jobs on MONTH-DOM (weekday DOW) ==
  printf '%-3s %-12s %6s %-5s %-5s %4s\n' with columns ID NAME STARTS FIRST LAST RUN
  one row per parsed job (FIRST/LAST are HH:MM of the first and last start, `-` when
  STARTS is 0; RUN is like `25m`)
  == Overlaps ==
  For every pair of jobs A < B (by id) that are running at the same minute at least
  MIN times: `A x B: N shared minutes, first at HH:MM`; for a job that overlaps with
  itself (two of its own runs at once): `A x A: N minutes running twice, first at HH:MM`.
  Names, not ids. Sort by the number of minutes, largest first, then by ids.
  With no overlaps print `(none)`.
Exit status 0 when there are no overlaps to report, 1 otherwise.
concepts: expanding cron fields (lists, ranges, steps) into sets
cron's day-of-month OR day-of-week rule
a minute-by-minute occupancy table
tagged awk output split and sorted by the shell
warnings to stderr that do not stop the run

required_patterns.message: Use awk to expand the fields and build the occupancy table.

title: The Config Drift Detector
story:
Three engineers touched the production proxy at 4 a.m. during the power flicker,
each one sure they were "just restoring" the old settings. By dawn the live config
no longer matches the golden copy in the repository, and nobody can say how. A
plain `diff -r` is useless: it shouts about comments, spacing and a timestamp that
changes every reload. Priya wants a drift report that only mentions differences that
matter, hides secrets, and can print the commands to put things back.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--plan] GOLDEN_DIR LIVE_DIR`

Errors on stderr, exit 2: wrong arguments `usage: solution.sh [--plan] GOLDEN_DIR LIVE_DIR`;
a directory that does not exist `error: DIR is not a directory` (with the name given).

The managed files are all regular files under GOLDEN_DIR except the two control files
`.modes` and `.ignore` (at its top level). Compare them with the same relative path under
LIVE_DIR. Files under LIVE_DIR that are not in the golden tree are `UNMANAGED`.
- `.ignore`: key names, one per line; those keys are ignored in `.conf` comparisons.
- `.modes`: lines `RELATIVE_PATH OCTAL` (for example `ssl/site.key 600`). For listed files
  the live permissions must match; read them from `ls -l` (no stat) and convert to octal.

Comparing a pair of files:
- `.conf` files are compared by settings. Ignore blank lines, lines whose first
  non-space character is `#` or `;`, and lines without `=`. A setting is `KEY=VALUE`:
  trim spaces around both parts, strip one pair of double quotes around the value, last
  duplicate wins. Report each difference, sorted by key:
    `  ~ KEY: GOLDEN -> LIVE`    value differs
    `  + KEY: LIVE`              only in live
    `  - KEY: GOLDEN`            only in golden
  Keys that contain `pass`, `secret`, `token` or `key` (any case) show `***` instead of
  values. Ignored keys never appear. Differences in comments, spacing, quoting or order
  are not drift.
- every other file is compared with cksum; if it differs: `  ~ content differs`.
- mode mismatch: `  ~ mode: expected 640, found 644`.
Report format (paths sorted, golden and live paths merged):
  `DRIFT path` followed by its detail lines, for files present on both sides with a
  difference; `MISSING path` for golden files absent live; `UNMANAGED path`.
Finish with `files: N checked, D drifted, M missing, U unmanaged` (N = golden files).
Exit 0 when nothing drifted, is missing or is unmanaged, otherwise 1.

With `--plan`, print instead (and no report) a remediation plan, then exit as above:
first the line `# remediation plan (review before running)`, then in path order:
for MISSING files `mkdir -p 'LIVE/dir'` (only when the file is in a subdirectory) and
`cp 'GOLDEN/path' 'LIVE/path'`; for DRIFT files with a content difference the `cp`; for
any file with a golden mode listed whose live mode is wrong, or which was just copied,
`chmod OCTAL 'LIVE/path'`; for UNMANAGED files `# unmanaged: LIVE/path (decide by hand)`.
A plan with nothing to do prints only the header. (Use the directory names exactly as given.)
concepts: normalising before comparing, so only meaningful differences remain
merging two sorted file lists
ls -l permission string to octal
masking secrets in output
a dry-run plan instead of a risky auto-fix

required_patterns.message: Use awk to normalise and compare the settings.
Read permissions with ls -l; stat is not portable.

title: The Release Manager
story:
Theo has been cutting releases by hand: guess a version number, write the changelog
from memory, tar something up, tag it, and remember to tell the channel. During last
night's storm he shipped `v1.5.0` containing a breaking change, and a customer's
integration broke at breakfast. Mara wants versioning to stop being a matter of mood.
The commit messages already say what changed, so a script can decide the version,
write the changelog, package the artifacts, tag the release and announce it, all
or nothing.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--dry-run] [--notify URL] APP`
Usage error (exit 2): `usage: solution.sh [--dry-run] [--notify URL] APP`.

Tools on PATH: `git` and `curl`. Use exactly these git commands:
  git status --porcelain                       (any output means a dirty tree)
  git describe --tags --abbrev=0               (latest tag; fails when there is none)
  git log --pretty=format:%s RANGE             (one commit subject per line)
  git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "APP X.Y.Z"
Steps, in this order (any failure stops the release; exit codes below):
1. A dirty tree: `error: working tree is not clean` on stderr, exit 3.
2. Last tag: if there is one it must be `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, else
   `error: last tag 'T' is not vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, exit 3. With no tag the base is
   v0.0.0 and RANGE is `HEAD`; otherwise RANGE is `TAG..HEAD`.
3. No commits in RANGE: `nothing to release since TAG` on stderr (with no tag: `nothing to release`),
   exit 4.
4. Classify every subject. A conventional subject looks like `type(scope)!: text`
   (scope and `!` optional, type lowercase letters). `!` means breaking; type `feat` is a
   feature; `fix` a fix; every other type, and any subject that is not conventional,
   is `other`. Breaking commits are listed only under Breaking.
5. Next version: any breaking commit raises MAJOR (MINOR and PATCH reset to 0), else any feature
   raises MINOR (PATCH reset), else PATCH is raised.
6. `dist/` must contain at least one file, else `error: dist/ is empty - build first`, exit 3.
7. In `--dry-run` mode print `would release APP vNEXT (was vOLD)` and then the changelog
   section (below) to stdout, change nothing, and exit 0. Check steps 1 to 6 first.
8. Write `releases/APP-NEXT.tar.gz` (`tar -czf ... -C dist .`) and
   `releases/APP-NEXT.sums`: one line `CRC SIZE PATH` per file of dist (sorted by path, relative
   path, the two numbers `cksum` prints for the file).
9. Build the new CHANGELOG.md (do not touch the real one yet): its first two lines are
   `# Changelog` and an empty line (created if the file does not exist), then the new section,
   an empty line, then the rest of the old file after its first two lines. The section is
     ## vNEXT - DATE
     (empty line)
     ### Breaking changes | ### Features | ### Fixes | ### Other   (only non-empty ones,
     in that order, each followed by `- ITEM` lines in commit order and an empty line)
   DATE is `date +%Y-%m-%d`, or the value of RELEASE_DATE when that variable is set. ITEM is the
   text after the colon, prefixed with `(scope) ` when there was a scope; `other` items from
   non-conventional or other-type subjects are the full subject.
10. Create the tag. If `git tag` fails: delete the two files from step 8 and the new changelog,
    print `error: could not create tag vNEXT` on stderr and exit 5. Otherwise move the new
    changelog into place.
11. With `--notify URL`: `curl -sS --fail --max-time 5 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
    -d BODY URL` where BODY is {"text":"APP vNEXT released: B breaking, F features, X fixes, O other"}.
    If it fails print `warning: notification failed` on stderr but the release stands.
Final stdout (real release): `released APP vNEXT (was vOLD): B breaking, F features, X fixes, O other`
then `artifact: releases/APP-NEXT.tar.gz`; with --notify also `notified: URL`. For a first release
OLD is `v0.0.0`.
concepts: conventional commit subjects decide the semantic version
regex capture groups with BASH_REMATCH
build everything first, commit the irreversible step last, undo on failure
prepending to a file without sed -i
release notes grouped by category

required_patterns.message: Parse the commit subjects with =~ and BASH_REMATCH.
Create the tag with git tag.
