title: The Certificate Watchdog
story:
The ferry booking site went dark for four hours last spring because a TLS certificate
expired on a Sunday and nobody's calendar reminder fired. With a hurricane warning
driving ten times the usual traffic to the harbour status pages, Priya refuses to
gamble again. She wants a watchdog that looks at every certificate, tells the truth
about each one, renews the ones that are close to the edge (but never hammers the
certificate authority), and reloads the web server exactly once if anything changed.
objective:
Write solution.sh:
  `solution.sh [--warn DAYS] [--crit DAYS] [--renew] [--max-renewals N] CERTDIR`

Options: `--warn` (default 30) and `--crit` (default 7) are whole numbers of days with
crit <= warn; `--max-renewals` (default 3) is a whole number >= 1. Errors go to stderr
with exit status 64: `usage: solution.sh [--warn DAYS] [--crit DAYS] [--renew] [--max-renewals N] CERTDIR`,
`error: --warn needs a whole number of days` (same for --crit and, with
"a positive whole number", --max-renewals), `error: --crit must not exceed --warn`,
`error: CERTDIR is not a directory` (with the directory as given),
`error: no certificates in CERTDIR`.

Certificates are the files `CERTDIR/*.pem`, handled in name order; the name is the file
name without `.pem`. Inspect them with openssl only:
  openssl x509 -noout -enddate -in FILE       prints `notAfter=Nov 20 12:00:00 2026 GMT`, fails
                                              for a file that is not a certificate
  openssl x509 -noout -checkend SECONDS -in FILE   exit 0 if the certificate is still valid
                                              SECONDS from now, 1 if not (it also exits 1 for
                                              an unreadable certificate, so ask for -enddate first)
Status of a certificate:
  INVALID  `-enddate` failed
  EXPIRED  not valid now (-checkend 0 fails)
  CRIT     not valid in crit days (crit*86400 seconds)
  WARN     not valid in warn days
  OK       otherwise
EXPIRES is the text after `notAfter=` (`-` for INVALID).

With `--renew`, every WARN, CRIT or EXPIRED certificate (not INVALID) is renewed, in order,
with `certbot renew --cert-name NAME --config-dir CERTDIR` (exit 0 = renewed). At most
N renewal attempts are made per run, successful or not; further candidates keep their status and
get the note `renew skipped`. After a successful renewal inspect the file again, the new status and
expiry replace the old ones, and the note is `renewed`; after a failed attempt the note is
`renew failed`. If at least one renewal succeeded, run `systemctl reload nginx` once at the end
(after the table); print `reload: nginx reloaded`, or on failure
`reload: nginx reload FAILED` (stdout) and `warning: nginx reload failed` (stderr).

Output: a header and one row per certificate with
  printf '%-14s %-8s %-30s %s\n' NAME STATUS EXPIRES NOTE
(NOTE is the note, possibly empty; the format is applied even then, so such rows end
with a space.)
Then the reload line if any, then
  summary: O ok, W warn, C crit, E expired, I invalid
Exit status: 2 if any certificate is CRIT, EXPIRED or INVALID, else 1 if any is WARN, else 0.
concepts: openssl x509 -checkend instead of date arithmetic
an exit status that is ambiguous: check the cheap, specific thing first
rate limiting your own automation (max renewals)
do the side effect once: reload after the loop
re-inspect after changing something

required_patterns.message: Use openssl x509 -checkend to ask whether a certificate expires within a number of seconds.

title: The Service Health Dashboard
story:
The storm command post has one wall monitor and a dozen people staring at it. The
harbour master wants to see, in one glance, whether the ferry site, the tide API,
the buoy link and the back-office disks are fine, without opening six dashboards.
Ollie volunteered to "just ping everything in a loop", and the first version took
forty seconds because every check waited for the one before it. The new board has
to run all checks at once, group them sensibly, and be honest about which failures
are cosmetic and which are an emergency.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--color] [--problems-only] CONFIG`
Errors on stderr, exit 2: `usage: solution.sh [--color] [--problems-only] CONFIG`
and `error: cannot read CONFIG`.

CONFIG lines (blank lines and `#` lines ignored): `GROUP|NAME|TYPE|TARGET|ARG`, all five
fields non-empty (use `-` when ARG is unused). A NAME ending in `!` marks a critical
service. A malformed config stops the run before any check, exit 3, on stderr:
`error: CONFIG line N: need GROUP|NAME|TYPE|TARGET|ARG` or
`error: CONFIG line N: unknown type 'T'` (N counts every line, including comments).
Types and their states (each check yields a state UP, DEGRADED or DOWN and a detail):
- `http`: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 3 TARGET` (a curl failure counts
  as code 000). ARG is the expected status. Equal: UP `HTTP 200`. 000: DOWN `no response`.
  500 or more: DOWN `HTTP 503`. Anything else: DEGRADED `HTTP 301 (want 200)`.
- `tcp`: TARGET is `HOST:PORT`; `nc -z -w 2 HOST PORT` succeeds: UP `port open`,
  else DOWN `connection refused`.
- `file`: a heartbeat file TARGET that must have been modified within ARG minutes
  (`find TARGET -mmin -ARG`): UP `fresh (<= ARG min)`; DOWN `stale (> ARG min)`;
  a file that does not exist: DOWN `missing`.
- `disk`: `df -P TARGET` shows the Capacity column (field 5 of the second line, e.g. `85%`);
  with P the percent used and ARG the limit: P >= ARG is DOWN, P >= ARG-10 is DEGRADED,
  else UP; the detail is `P% used`.
All checks run concurrently (background jobs and `wait`); their results are collected
in a scratch directory made with `mktemp -d` and removed by a trap. Output order must
not depend on which check finishes first.

Output:
  == Lanternfish Status Board ==
  then for each group in order of first appearance:
  `== GROUP == [U/N up]`   (U services UP out of N in the group)
  and one row per service in config order: printf '  %-8s %-14s %s\n' STATE NAME DETAIL
With `--problems-only` only the groups that contain at least one non-UP service are shown
(and only their non-UP rows); the group header still shows the full count.
With `--color` the STATE word (after padding to 8) is wrapped in ANSI codes:
UP `\033[32m`, DEGRADED `\033[33m`, DOWN `\033[31m`, followed by `\033[0m`.
Last line: `overall: STATE (D down, G degraded, U up)` where STATE is DOWN if any critical
service is DOWN, else DEGRADED if any service is not UP, else UP. Exit status: 0 UP,
1 DEGRADED, 2 DOWN.
concepts: parallel checks with background jobs, wait and per-job result files
one function per check type with a uniform STATE|detail result
deterministic output from nondeterministic work
ANSI colour only on request
validate the whole config before running anything

required_patterns.message: Run the checks in the background and use wait.
Collect results in a directory made with mktemp -d.

title: The Incident Responder
story:
Last night the tide-sync server hit a load of 40 for six minutes, then calmed down on
its own. By morning nobody could say what had been running, because the one person who
looked had already restarted things. Theo's verdict: "It fixed itself." Priya's verdict:
"That is the scariest sentence in operations." From now on the machine must keep its own
evidence. When a metric crosses a line, a script freezes a snapshot of the processes, disks,
connections and recent logs, but without flooding the disk when the alarm keeps ringing.
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--cooldown SECONDS] [--keep N] RULES SAMPLE`, run
every minute by cron. `--cooldown` (whole number, default 300) and `--keep` (positive
whole number, default 5). Errors on stderr: exit 2 for `usage: solution.sh [--cooldown SECONDS] [--keep N] RULES SAMPLE`,
`error: --cooldown needs a whole number`, `error: --keep needs a positive whole number`,
`error: cannot read FILE`; exit 3 for a bad rules file (below).

SAMPLE has `key=value` lines (the current metrics; values may be missing or non-numeric).
RULES lines (blank and `#` lines ignored): `NAME|KEY|OP|THRESHOLD|COLLECTORS`
- OP is one of `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `==` (numeric comparison, decimals allowed; use awk);
- COLLECTORS is a comma-separated list of: `procs` (`ps aux`), `disk` (`df -P`),
  `net` (`ss -tn`), `logs:PATH:N` (`tail -n N PATH`; PATH contains no colon).
A rule with fewer than 5 fields, a bad OP or a non-numeric THRESHOLD gives
`error: RULES line N: need NAME|KEY|OP|THRESHOLD|COLLECTORS` or `error: RULES line N: bad operator 'X'` or
`error: RULES line N: bad threshold 'X'`; an unknown collector gives
`error: RULES line N: unknown collector 'X'`. Everything is validated before anything is evaluated.

Time: `NOW` is the current epoch second: `date +%s`, unless the environment variable NOW is
set, in which case that value is used.

For each rule, in order:
- the KEY is missing from SAMPLE or its value is not a number: print `rule NAME: no data for KEY`;
- the comparison `VALUE OP THRESHOLD` is false: `rule NAME: ok (KEY=VALUE)`;
- true (a breach) and `incidents/.last/NAME` exists with a number L and NOW - L < cooldown:
  `rule NAME: BREACH KEY=VALUE (OP THRESHOLD) - cooling down (R s left)` where R = cooldown - (NOW - L);
- otherwise take a snapshot and print
  `rule NAME: BREACH KEY=VALUE (OP THRESHOLD) - snapshot INC-SEQ-NAME (C collectors)`.
Snapshot: SEQ is the contents of `incidents/.seq` plus one (0 when missing), written back and shown
with `%04d`. Build the snapshot in a temporary directory inside `incidents/` (removed by a trap if
anything goes wrong) and `mv` it to `incidents/INC-SEQ-NAME` when complete. It holds
`trigger.txt` (lines `rule=NAME`, `key=KEY`, `value=VALUE`, `op=OP`, `threshold=THRESHOLD`, `at=NOW`)
and one file per collector: `procs.txt`, `disk.txt`, `net.txt`, `log-BASENAME.txt` with the command's
output. A collector whose command fails does not stop the snapshot: its file contains the single line
`collector failed` and an indented line `  ! collector COLLECTORNAME failed` is printed after the
rule line. Then write NOW into `incidents/.last/NAME`, append `INC-SEQ-NAME|NOW|VALUE` to
`incidents/INDEX`, and prune: keep only the N newest `incidents/INC-*` directories (names sort
by SEQ), deleting older ones.
Finally print `breaches: B, snapshots: S, pruned: P` (a cooling breach counts as a breach, not a
snapshot). Exit 0 if there were no breaches, else 1.
concepts: evidence collection triggered by a threshold rule
cooldown state so a flapping alarm does not flood the disk
build in a temp directory then mv: atomic publication
numeric comparison with an operator held in a variable
retention: prune the oldest beyond N

title: The Multi-Env Deployer
story:
With the storm closing in, everybody wants their fix in production "right now". Last
week a change that had never been near staging went straight to prod because the
deploy command accepted any environment, and a typo took the booking page down. Mara
draws a line on the whiteboard: dev, staging, prod, and a gate between each step.
The code must have soaked, the smoke tests must pass, a second person must have signed
off, and nothing ships during a change freeze. You are building the promotion tool that
enforces the line and also tells people exactly which gate stopped them.
objective:
Write solution.sh with two commands:
  `solution.sh status APP`
  `solution.sh [--dry-run] promote APP FROM TO`
Anything else: `usage: solution.sh status APP | [--dry-run] promote APP FROM TO` on stderr, exit 2.
Time: NOW = `date +%s` unless the environment variable NOW is set. The person doing the
deploy is `$DEPLOYER` if set, else `$USER`.

Configuration is `pipeline.conf` (fields separated by `|`; blank and `#` lines ignored):
  order|dev staging prod                    the environments, in promotion order (must come first)
  gate|ENV|GATE|ARG                         a gate that must pass to promote INTO ENV
Gates: `soak` (ARG minutes, a whole number), `tests`, `approval`, `freeze` (ARG is `-`).
Problems exit 3 with a message on stderr: `error: pipeline.conf is missing`,
`error: pipeline.conf line N: unknown gate 'G'`, `error: pipeline.conf line N: bad soak minutes 'X'`,
`error: pipeline.conf line N: unknown environment 'E'`, `error: pipeline.conf has no order line`
(N counts every line).

State: `state/APP/ENV.version` (current version) and `state/APP/ENV.since` (epoch when it
arrived), `state/APP/history.log`.

`status APP` prints `printf '%-8s %-10s %s\n' ENV VERSION AGE` and one row per environment in
order; AGE is `M min` (whole minutes since `.since`); an environment with no version shows `-` and `-`.

`promote APP FROM TO`: FROM and TO must be environments and TO must be the one right after FROM,
else `error: TO does not follow FROM in the pipeline`; FROM must have a version, else
`error: FROM has no version of APP` (both exit 3, checked in that order). VERSION is what FROM
runs now. If TO already runs it, print `TO already runs VERSION` and exit 0.
Print `promote APP VERSION: FROM -> TO` and then evaluate EVERY gate of TO, in config order,
without stopping at the first failure, one line each:
  `gate LABEL: PASS` or `gate LABEL: PASS (detail)` / `gate LABEL: FAIL (reason)`
LABEL is `soak(N)` for soak and the gate name otherwise.
- soak: minutes in FROM = (NOW - FROM's .since) / 60 (a missing .since fails with `no arrival time`):
  PASS `(M min in FROM)`, else FAIL `(M min in FROM, need N)`.
- tests: run `smoke-test FROM APP VERSION`; exit 0 passes, else FAIL `(smoke-test failed)`.
- approval: file `approvals/APP-VERSION-TO` with a line `approver=NAME`. Missing file: FAIL
  `(no approval file approvals/APP-VERSION-TO)`; NAME equal to the deployer: FAIL
  `(self-approval is not allowed)`; a file without an `approver=` line (or an empty name): FAIL
  `(approval file names no approver)`; otherwise PASS `(approved by NAME)`.
- freeze: if the file `FREEZE` exists FAIL `(change freeze: FIRST LINE OF THE FILE)`, else PASS.
If any gate failed print `gates failed: N - not promoting` and exit 1. With `--dry-run` and all
gates passing print `dry run: gates passed, would deploy VERSION to TO` and exit 0.
Otherwise deploy with the tool `deployctl`:
  `deployctl push APP VERSION ENV`, then `deployctl health ENV APP`
Print `push: ok` (a failed push: `push: FAILED` and, on stderr, `error: push to TO failed`, exit 4,
nothing recorded), then `health: ok`. After a healthy deploy write TO's .version and .since (= NOW),
append `NOW promote VERSION FROM->TO by DEPLOYER` to history.log and print
`promoted APP VERSION to TO (previous: PREV)` (PREV is `none` if TO had no version).
If health fails: print `health: FAILED`; with a previous version run `deployctl push APP PREV TO`,
print `rolled back TO to PREV`, `error: health check failed after promotion` on stderr, exit 5;
without a previous version print `error: health check failed and TO has no previous version`
on stderr, exit 6. State files stay untouched in both cases.
concepts: gates as data: evaluate all, report all
separation of duties: approver differs from deployer
state files per app and environment
promote what the previous environment runs, never a free-typed version
rollback to the recorded previous version

required_patterns.message: Deploy with deployctl push and verify with deployctl health.

title: The Data Pipeline
story:
The storm sent thousands of customers to the harbour shop at once, and the partner
chandleries now drop order files into an inbox all night: some from Linux, some from
a Windows machine that adds carriage returns, one that sends the same file twice
whenever its upload hiccups. Gus wants tomorrow's revenue figure to be right, which
means every row must be checked, nothing may be loaded twice, and bad rows must be set
aside with a reason instead of silently dropped. Mara calls it "a small ETL, and a
chance to be proud of your Bash".
objective:
Write solution.sh: `solution.sh [--dry-run] INBOX`
Errors on stderr, exit 2: `usage: solution.sh [--dry-run] INBOX` and
`error: cannot read INBOX` (not a directory). Work happens in the current directory.

Stages for every `INBOX/*.csv`, in name order (an INBOX without any prints `inbox is empty`
and exits 0):
1. ingest: strip a trailing carriage return from every line. The file must start with exactly
   `order_id,customer,sku,qty,unit_price,date`, else it is quarantined: print
   `NAME: quarantined (bad header)` and move it to `quarantine/`. A file whose `cksum` (CRC and
   size) is already listed in `state/processed.list` (lines `CRC SIZE NAME`) is skipped: print
   `NAME: skipped (already processed as OLDNAME)` and move it to `archive/NAME.dup`.
2. validate each data row (blank lines ignored). Checked in this order, the first failure is the
   reason: wrong number of fields (not 6) -> `wrong field count`; empty order id -> `empty order id`;
   empty customer after trimming spaces -> `empty customer`; qty not a positive whole number ->
   `bad quantity`; unit_price not a non-negative number with optional decimals -> `bad price`; date not
   `YYYY-MM-DD` with month 01-12 and day 01-31 -> `bad date`. Rejected rows are appended to
   `rejects/NAME.rej` as `LINENO|REASON|ORIGINAL ROW` (line numbers count the header as line 1).
3. deduplicate: an order id already in `db/orders.psv` (first field) or loaded earlier in this run
   is a duplicate: counted, not loaded, not rejected.
4. transform: `order_id|customer|SKU|qty|total|date` with the customer trimmed, SKU in upper case
   and total = qty * unit_price with two decimals.
5. load: append the transformed rows of the file to `db/orders.psv` in one go (build them
   in a scratch directory made with `mktemp -d` and removed by a trap), then add the file's
   `CRC SIZE NAME` to `state/processed.list` and move the file to `archive/`.
Per file print `NAME: R rows, L loaded, X rejected, D duplicate` (R = data rows, blank lines not counted).
Finish with
  `total: F files, R rows, L loaded, X rejected, D duplicates, revenue V`   (V = sum of loaded totals, 2 decimals)
  `quarantined: Q, already processed: S`
and, only when X > 0, `rejected by reason:` followed by one line `  REASON: COUNT` per reason, most
frequent first, ties alphabetical. F counts files that were read (not quarantined or skipped).
Exit status 1 if any row was rejected or any file quarantined, else 0.
With `--dry-run` all stages run and the same text is printed, but nothing is written, moved
or created in the working directory, and the very last line is `dry run: nothing was written`
(printed after the others, no effect on the exit status).
concepts: extract, validate, transform, load as separate stages
idempotent loading: content checksums and unique keys
reject files with reasons instead of dropping rows
normalising CRLF input
dry run that shares the real code path

required_patterns.message: Use awk for the row validation and transformation.
Use cksum to recognise a file that was already processed.
Stage the new rows in a scratch directory made with mktemp -d.

title: The Test Harness Builder
story:
Ollie wrote forty small helper scripts for the storm rota and trusts every one of them,
until one silently deleted the wrong file on Tuesday. "Where are the tests?" asked Mara.
There are none, because the team has no way to run shell tests without installing a
framework on a locked-down server. Her answer is typically Mara: "We have Bash. Build
the harness." It must discover tests, isolate them from each other, give them
assertions, survive crashes, and report in a way that makes failures obvious at 3 a.m.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a test runner:
  `solution.sh [--filter TEXT] [--fail-fast] [--verbose] PATH...`
Each PATH is a test file or a directory (then its `*.test.sh` files, in name order). Errors on
stderr, exit 2: `usage: solution.sh [--filter TEXT] [--fail-fast] [--verbose] PATH...`,
`error: cannot read PATH`, and, when no test function was found in any file,
`error: no tests found`.

Discovery: a test is a function declared in the file as a line starting with
`test_NAME()` or `function test_NAME` (NAME is letters, digits and underscores; the line may
continue after the parentheses). Tests run in the order of appearance. `--filter TEXT` keeps only
tests whose full name contains TEXT.
Before running a file check it with `bash -n`; a file with a syntax error is not run, its report is
the single line `  ERROR syntax error` and it counts as a file error.

Running a test: in its own subshell, in its own fresh empty working directory (removed afterwards),
with `set -e` in force and the environment variable TEST_DIR set to the absolute path of the directory
that holds the test file. The test file is sourced in that subshell; then, if the file defined
`setup`, it runs; then the test; if it defined `teardown`, that always runs at the end, whether the test
passed or failed. The subshell's stdout and stderr are captured. Beware: errexit is switched off for any
command that is part of an `||` or `if` condition, which includes a subshell run that way; run the
subshell as a plain command.
The harness provides these functions to tests:
  `fail MESSAGE`                         fail with that message
  `skip REASON`                          skip the test (exit status 77 inside the subshell)
  `assert_eq EXPECTED ACTUAL`            message `expected 'E' but got 'A'`
  `assert_contains HAYSTACK NEEDLE`      message `'H' does not contain 'N'`
  `assert_success COMMAND...`            runs it quietly; message `command failed (status N): COMMAND...`
  `assert_status CODE COMMAND...`        message `expected status C but got N from: COMMAND...`
A message is passed from the subshell to the harness through a file. Outcome: status 0 is PASS; 77
is SKIP; anything else is FAIL, with the message if there is one, else `exited with status N`.

Report, on stdout: for each file its path as given, then for each test one line
  `  PASS NAME`   `  FAIL NAME: MESSAGE` (first line of the message)   `  SKIP NAME (REASON)`
With `--verbose`, after a FAIL line print the test's captured output, each line prefixed by
`    | `. With `--fail-fast` stop running tests after the first failure (still print the summary).
Finish with `summary: T tests, P passed, F failed, S skipped`; when there were file errors also
`file errors: E`. Exit status 1 if anything failed or any file had an error, else 0.
concepts: discovering functions by reading the file
subshell isolation: fresh directory and clean state per test
the set -e / || gotcha with subshells
assertion helpers that report through a file and an exit status
setup and teardown with trap EXIT

required_patterns.message: Give each test its own fresh directory made with mktemp -d.

title: The Plugin System
story:
Every team at Lanternfish now wants to hook into the storm deploy: the weather desk
wants a tide sync, Noor wants a customer notice, Priya wants an audit step, Ollie wants
"something with the webcams". Theo's answer so far was one 600-line script that nobody
dares to edit. Mara proposes the grown-up fix: a tiny host that discovers plugin files, works
out the order from their declared dependencies, runs each plugin in isolation so that one
bad plugin cannot take down the rest, and says exactly why anything was skipped.
objective:
Write solution.sh, the plugin host:
  `solution.sh [--plugins DIR] [--disable NAME]... list`
  `solution.sh [--plugins DIR] [--disable NAME]... run HOOK [ARG...]`
DIR defaults to `plugins`. Errors on stderr: exit 2 for
`usage: solution.sh [--plugins DIR] [--disable NAME]... list | run HOOK [ARG...]` and for a HOOK that is not
lowercase letters and underscores (`error: bad hook name 'X'`); exit 3 for
`error: cannot read DIR` (not a directory).

A plugin is a file `DIR/*.plugin`. Only its header is read for discovery (the first 15 lines;
nothing is executed): `# name: NAME` (required; lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with
a letter), `# requires: NAME NAME...` (optional) and `# priority: N` (optional whole number, default 50).
A file without a valid name is `bad header (no name)`; a name already taken by an earlier file (files in
name order) is `bad header (duplicate name)`. Plugins named by `--disable` or listed one per line in
`DIR/disabled.list` are disabled.

Order: dependencies first (a plugin comes after everything it requires); among plugins that are ready at
the same time the lowest priority number comes first, ties by name. Requirements that name a missing
plugin do not influence the order. Plugins that can never become ready (they are in a dependency cycle, or
depend on one) are `cyclic dependency` and have no position.
Status of each ordered plugin, decided in that order: `disabled`; else for its requirements in the
order written: `missing dependency: X` (no such plugin), `dependency disabled: X`, `dependency not usable: X`
(X has any other non-ok status); else `ok`.

`list` prints `printf '%-5s %-10s %4s  %s\n' ORDER NAME PRIO STATUS` as a header, then one row per plugin:
ordered plugins with ORDER 1, 2, ..., then cyclic ones (ORDER `-`, name order), then bad headers with
NAME = the file name and PRIO `-`. Exit 0 when every plugin is ok, else 1.

`run HOOK ARG...` prints `== hook HOOK ==`, then walks the ordered plugins. A plugin that is not ok prints
`NAME: skipped (STATUS)`. A plugin that requires a plugin that FAILED during this run prints
`NAME: skipped (needs X which failed)`. Otherwise it is run in an isolated subshell: the plugin file is
sourced, and if it defines the function `NAME__HOOK` (dashes in NAME become underscores) that function is called
with the ARGs; if not, the plugin prints `NAME: no hook`. The plugin's output (stdout and stderr) is shown
line by line before its result line. A plugin can call the host function `host_log MESSAGE...`, which prints
`[NAME] MESSAGE...`. Status 0 prints `NAME: ok`; any other status `NAME: FAILED (status N)`. A plugin that calls
`exit`, crashes or changes variables must not affect the host or the other plugins. Finish with
`ran: R, failed: F, skipped: S, no hook: H` (R counts ok plugins) and exit 1 if F > 0, else 0.
concepts: discovering plugins by reading headers, never by executing them
topological ordering with a priority tie-break (Kahn's algorithm)
isolation: one subshell per plugin, status as the only channel back
dependency failure propagation
host API functions inherited by the subshell

title: The CLI Framework
story:
The storm rota lives in a spreadsheet that three people edit at once, and on Thursday it
told two pilots to fly the same shift. Theo offers to "knock up a tiny CLI" and shows a
600-line `case` statement with hand-written usage text that already disagrees with itself.
Mara asks for something better: a small command-line *framework*. Commands are declared as
data, and the parser, the help screens, the version flag and the "did you mean" hints are
generated from that data, so adding a command never means copying a parser. The roster tool
`lantern` is the first customer.
objective:
Write solution.sh: the `lantern` roster tool, built around a command registry.
  `lantern [--db FILE] [-h|--help] [-V|--version] [--] COMMAND [OPTIONS] [ARGS]`
The script is called solution.sh but must always call itself `lantern` in messages.
The roster file is, in order of precedence, `--db FILE`, the environment variable LANTERN_DB, or
`crew.db`. Each line is `NAME|ROLE|SHIFT`.

Commands, in this order, with their descriptions, argument words and options (the framework must
produce every help text from this data):
  add     "Add a crew member"        arg NAME     -r --role ROLE "Role: pilot, engineer or cook (default: engineer)"
                                                    -s --shift SHIFT "Shift: day or night (default: day)"
  list    "List crew members"        no args      -r --role ROLE "Only this role"
                                                    -f --format FORMAT "table or csv (default: table)"
  remove  "Remove a crew member"     arg NAME     -f --force "Remove without asking"
  show    "Show one crew member"     arg NAME
  help    "Show help for a command"  arg [COMMAND]
  version "Print the version"
Allowed values: role = pilot engineer cook; shift = day night; format = table csv.
Version string: `lantern 1.4.0`.

Help screens (stdout, exit 0). Overall (`lantern`, `--help`, `-h`, `help`; with no COMMAND at all the
overall help goes to stderr and the exit status is 64):
  lantern 1.4.0 - crew roster for the storm shift
  (blank)
  Usage: lantern [--db FILE] COMMAND [OPTIONS] [ARGS]
  (blank)
  Commands:
    NAME<padding>DESCRIPTION             (printf '  %-8s %s\n')
  (blank)
  Run 'lantern help COMMAND' for details.
Per command (`lantern help CMD`, `lantern CMD --help`, `lantern CMD -h`):
  Usage: lantern CMD [OPTIONS] ARGWORDS    (`[OPTIONS]` only if the command has options; ARGWORDS only if it has
  (blank)                                   an argument word)
  DESCRIPTION
  (blank)
  Options:                                 (only if it has options)
    LABEL<padding>TEXT                     (printf '  %-20s %s\n'; LABEL is `-r, --role ROLE`, or `-f, --force`
                                            for an option without a value)
Option syntax: `--role pilot`, `--role=pilot`, `-r pilot`; options may appear before or after the arguments;
`--` ends option parsing. `lantern -V` / `--version` and `lantern version` print the version.

Usage errors exit 64, print `lantern: MESSAGE` (or `lantern CMD: MESSAGE` inside a command) on stderr and then
`Run 'lantern help' for usage.` (or `Run 'lantern help CMD' for usage.`). Messages:
  unknown command 'X'                       (global: also for `help X`)
  unknown option 'X'                        (global, before the command)
  unknown option 'X'                        (inside a command)
  option 'X' needs a value                  (X as typed, e.g. --role)
  invalid value 'V' for --role (expected pilot, engineer or cook)   (allowed values joined with ', ' and ' or ')
  missing NAME                              (the command's argument word; `help` needs none)
  unexpected argument 'X'                   (the first extra positional)
An unknown command or option adds ` (did you mean 'Y'?)` when the typed word (without leading dashes, at least
two letters) is a subsequence of a known command / option name of that scope (first match in registry order)
and is not equal to it; for options use the long names.

Behaviour (runtime errors are `lantern: MESSAGE` on stderr, exit 1, no usage hint):
- add: NAME must match letters and dashes starting with a letter (else `lantern: 'NAME' is not a valid name`); a name
  already on the roster, compared case-insensitively: `lantern: 'NAME' is already on the roster`.
  Appends `NAME|ROLE|SHIFT`, prints `added NAME (ROLE, SHIFT)`.
- list: rows sorted by name. `table` prints `printf '%-12s %-10s %s\n' NAME ROLE SHIFT` header and rows, or the single
  line `(no crew)` when there are no rows (after filtering); `csv` prints `name,role,shift` and the rows with commas.
- remove: without --force `lantern: refusing to remove 'NAME' without --force`; an unknown (case-insensitive)
  name `lantern: no such crew member 'NAME'`; else rewrites the roster without that line and prints `removed NAME`
  (NAME as stored).
- show: prints three lines `Name:  NAME`, `Role:  ROLE`, `Shift: SHIFT` or the no-such-member error.
concepts: a command registry: commands and options as data, parsers and help generated
generic option parsing: --opt value, --opt=value, short aliases, --
did-you-mean via a subsequence test
exit codes: 64 for usage, 1 for runtime errors
precedence: flag, environment variable, default

title: The Config Manager
story:
During the storm the booking service was started with a "temporary" port from a shell
alias, a log level from an old environment variable, and a database host from a file
nobody remembered. It ran for three days before anyone could say which setting came from
where. Priya wants every setting to have a type, a default and a *source*, secrets that never
print themselves, and errors that are all reported at once rather than one per attempt.
You are writing the config manager that sits between the files, the environment, the
command line and the program that finally reads them.
objective:
Write solution.sh:
  `solution.sh [--layer FILE]... [--set KEY=VALUE]... [--prefix P] [--reveal] SCHEMA COMMAND [ARG]`
Commands: `validate`, `show`, `get KEY`, `export env|json|shell`. Anything else, a missing command or
a missing/extra argument: `usage: solution.sh [--layer FILE]... [--set KEY=VALUE]... [--prefix P] [--reveal] SCHEMA COMMAND [ARG]`
on stderr, exit 2. An unreadable SCHEMA or layer file: `error: cannot read FILE`, exit 2. `--prefix`
defaults to `APP`.

SCHEMA lines (blank and `#` lines ignored): `KEY|TYPE|DEFAULT|FLAGS|DESCRIPTION`. TYPE is `string`, `int`,
`bool`, `port` or `enum:a,b,c`. FLAGS is `-` or a comma list of `required` and `secret`. DEFAULT may be empty.
Key order in the schema is the order of every output.

Layers, lowest to highest priority: the DEFAULT of the schema (source `default`); each `--layer FILE` in the order
given (source: the file's base name); environment variables (source `env`): for key `db.port` and prefix `APP`
the variable `APP_DB_PORT` (upper case, dots become underscores), only when it is set; then each `--set KEY=VALUE` in
order (source `--set`). The highest layer that provides a key wins.
Layer files have lines `key = value` (blank and `#` lines ignored; spaces around key and value trimmed; one pair
of surrounding single or double quotes removed from the value).

Problems are collected and ALL printed to stderr, then exit 1, before any normal output; one line each,
starting with `config error: `, in this order: problems while reading layers (layer order, then line order:
`unknown key 'K' in FILE:LINE` for a key not in the schema, `bad line in FILE:LINE: expected key = value`; a --set with an
unknown key is `unknown key 'K' in --set`, one without `=` is `bad --set 'X': expected KEY=VALUE`), then validation in
schema order:
  `KEY: required but not set`            (a required key whose final value is empty)
  `KEY: 'V' is not an integer`           (int: optional minus sign and digits)
  `KEY: 'V' is not a valid port (1-65535)`
  `KEY: 'V' is not a boolean`            (bool accepts true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0 in any case, normalised to true/false)
  `KEY: 'V' is not one of a, b, c`
Empty values of non-required keys are accepted (and not validated).

`validate` prints `config ok (N keys)` (N = number of schema keys). `show` prints
`printf '%-14s %-20s %s\n' KEY VALUE SOURCE` as a header and one row per key; a non-empty secret value shows as
`********` unless --reveal is given. `get KEY` prints the value (masked like show; unknown key:
`error: unknown key 'KEY'` on stderr, exit 2).
`export env` prints `PREFIX_KEY=value` lines, `export shell` prints `export PREFIX_KEY='value'` (a single quote in a
value becomes `'\''`), `export json` a JSON object, one key per line, 2-space indent, keys as written in the schema,
int and port values as numbers, bool as true/false, everything else as a string with backslash and double quote escaped.
Secrets are left out of all three exports unless --reveal is given. Use only Bash and standard tools (no jq).
concepts: layered configuration with explicit precedence and provenance
schema-driven validation that reports every problem at once
indirect expansion for reading environment variables by computed name
output encodings: env, shell quoting, JSON escaping
secrets masked by default

title: The Job Queue
story:
Storm season means a flood of small chores: regenerate the tide tables, resend the
ferry notices, re-index the photo uploads. Theo launches them all with `&` from a terminal
and loses track of which ones finished; last Wednesday two copies of the same invoice
job ran side by side and customers were billed twice. Mara wants a real queue: jobs
go in as files, a small pool of workers takes them in order, a job is never run twice,
failures are retried and then parked where someone can look at them, and a crashed
run does not strand work.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a file-based FIFO job queue rooted in `queue/` (pending/, done/, failed/, claims/):
  `solution.sh submit [--name NAME] COMMAND...`
  `solution.sh work [--workers N] [--max-tries T] [--limit K]`
  `solution.sh status`
  `solution.sh retry ID`
  `solution.sh log ID`
Anything else, bad numbers (`--workers`, `--max-tries`, `--limit` must be positive whole numbers) or a
missing COMMAND: `usage: solution.sh submit [--name NAME] COMMAND... | work [--workers N] [--max-tries T] [--limit K] | status | retry ID | log ID`
on stderr, exit 2.

Jobs: `queue/pending/ID.job` with exactly two lines, `name=NAME` and `cmd=COMMAND` (COMMAND is the
arguments joined by single spaces). IDs are four digits, `0001`, `0002`, ..., taken from the counter
file `queue/.next` (missing means 1; it is updated after each submit). NAME defaults to the base name of
the first word of COMMAND. The job file must appear in pending/ atomically (write it elsewhere, then `mv`).
`submit` prints `submitted ID (NAME)`.

`work`: first take the lock by creating the directory `queue/work.lock` (if it exists:
`error: another work run is active` on stderr, exit 4); a trap removes it however the run ends. Then recover
orphans: every `queue/claims/ID` directory whose job is still in pending/ is a leftover of a crashed run; remove
the claim and print `recovered job ID` (ascending). Select the pending jobs in ascending ID order, only the
first K with --limit. If none: print `queue is empty` and exit 0.
Run the selected jobs with W workers (default 2) running at the same time as background jobs. A worker
walks the selected IDs in order and claims a job by creating `queue/claims/ID` with `mkdir`; if mkdir fails another
worker has it, so skip it. Right after claiming, check that the job file is still in pending/ (a slow worker may
win mkdir for a job somebody else has just finished and released); if it is gone, remove the claim and skip it.
A claimed job is run with `bash -c COMMAND` with stdout and stderr captured; up to
T attempts (default 2) are made, running `sleep 1` between attempts. Success: the job file and its output (as
`ID.out`) move to done/; after the last failed attempt they move to failed/. Then the claim is removed.
After `wait`, print one line per job in ID order: `ID STATE NAME (attempts: A, exit: E)` with STATE `done` or
`failed` and E the exit status of the last attempt; then `worked: D done, F failed`. Exit 1 if any job failed, else 0.

`status` prints `pending: N`, `running: N`, `done: N`, `failed: N` (running = a pending job that has a claim) and then
`printf '%-6s %-8s %s\n' ID STATE NAME` with one row per job in ID order (states pending, running, done, failed).
`retry ID` moves a failed job back to pending (dropping its output) and prints `requeued ID`; if ID is not in failed/:
`error: no failed job ID` on stderr, exit 3. `log ID` prints the captured output of a done or failed job, or
`error: no output for job ID` on stderr, exit 3.
concepts: directories as queues: state is where the file lives
mkdir as an atomic claim between concurrent workers
background worker pool with wait
retry with a pause, then park the failure
crash recovery and a run lock released by trap

required_patterns.message: Claim a job with mkdir: it either creates the directory or fails, atomically.
Start the workers in the background and wait for them.

title: The Audit Logger
story:
After the storm, the insurer's auditor asks one question: "Can you prove nobody touched
the admin log after the incident?" Priya has been waiting for it. The old trick, a chained
checksum per line, catches an edited line but not a clever one: delete the *last* entries
and the chain still verifies, rewrite the tail with fresh checksums and it still verifies.
So the log needs the whole kit: a chain across rotated files, a checkpoint kept somewhere
else (the anchor), a lock so two writers cannot fork the chain, and search that refuses to
answer from a log it cannot trust.
objective:
Write solution.sh, an audit-log tool working in the directory `audit/`:
  `solution.sh append ACTOR ACTION DETAIL...`
  `solution.sh verify [--anchor]`
  `solution.sh checkpoint`
  `solution.sh rotate [--max N]`
  `solution.sh search [--actor A] [--action X] [--from SEQ] [--to SEQ] [--force]`
A wrong command or option, a missing argument, an ACTOR not matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*$`, an ACTION not
matching `^[A-Z_]+$` or an empty DETAIL: `usage: solution.sh append ACTOR ACTION DETAIL... | verify [--anchor] | checkpoint | rotate [--max N] | search [--actor A] [--action X] [--from SEQ] [--to SEQ] [--force]`
on stderr, exit 2.

Storage: finished segments `audit/seg-0001.log`, `audit/seg-0002.log`, ... and the live file `audit/current.log`
(read in that order; missing files are fine). One entry per line: `SEQ|SUM|TS|ACTOR|ACTION|DETAIL` (DETAIL is the rest of
the line and may contain `|`). SEQ counts 1, 2, 3, ... continuously across all segments. SUM is the first number
`cksum` prints for the text `PREV|SEQ|TS|ACTOR|ACTION|DETAIL` (exactly that, no trailing newline), PREV being the
previous entry's SUM across segment boundaries, `0` for the very first entry. TS is `AUDIT_NOW` when that environment
variable is set, otherwise `date +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S`; it must look like `2026-11-12T03:14:07`.

Checking the chain (used by every command except usage errors): walk all segments in order and stop at the first bad
line; a line is `bad format` if SEQ or SUM is not a number, TS/ACTOR/ACTION do not match the patterns above, or DETAIL is
empty; `sequence gap` if SEQ is not the expected number; `checksum mismatch` otherwise. The failure is described as
`FILE line N (REASON)` with FILE the base name (`seg-0001.log`).
- `verify` prints `OK: N entries in S segments` (S = number of files read) and exits 0, or `TAMPERED: FILE line N (REASON)`
  and exits 1. `verify --anchor` additionally compares with `audit/anchor` (one line `SEQ SUM`): when the chain is
  intact and the anchor matches print the OK line and then `anchor OK (#SEQ)`; with no anchor file print only
  `NO ANCHOR: run checkpoint first` (exit 1); if the anchored SEQ is beyond the last entry print only
  `TRUNCATED: anchor expects #A, log ends at #L` (exit 1); if the log's entry with that SEQ has another SUM print only
  `TAMPERED: anchor mismatch at #A` (exit 1). An anchor older than the log's end is fine.
- `append`, `checkpoint` and `rotate` first take a lock by creating the directory `audit/lock` (creating `audit/` if needed); if
  it exists they print `error: audit log is locked by another process` on stderr and exit 4; a trap removes the lock when
  they end. `append` checks the chain first: if broken, `refusing to append: log is tampered` on stderr, exit 1, nothing
  written. Otherwise it appends the next entry to current.log and prints `logged #SEQ`.
- `checkpoint` checks the chain (`refusing to checkpoint: log is tampered`, exit 1; an empty log: `error: nothing to anchor`,
  exit 1), writes `SEQ SUM` of the last entry to `audit/anchor` (written to a temporary file and moved into place) and prints
  `anchored #SEQ`.
- `rotate [--max N]` (N default 1000, positive whole number): after checking the chain (`refusing to rotate: log is tampered`,
  exit 1), if current.log has fewer than N entries print `no rotation needed (K entries)`; otherwise move it to the next free
  segment name and print `rotated to seg-NNNN.log (K entries)`.
- `search` filters by exact actor, exact action and an inclusive SEQ range. A broken chain prints
  `refusing to search: log is tampered` (stderr, exit 1) unless `--force`. Output: one line `#SEQ TS ACTOR ACTION DETAIL` per match, then
  `N matches`.
concepts: a hash chain that continues across rotated files
an external anchor detects truncation and consistent rewrites
mkdir lock with trap, taken only by writers
tail-field parsing: the last field keeps the separator
refuse to answer from data you cannot trust, unless forced

required_patterns.message: Compute each entry's SUM with cksum.
Release the lock with a trap.

title: The Self-Updating Script
story:
The `lantern` rota tool is now installed on thirty laptops, and half of them run a
version that still has the Thursday double-booking bug. Theo suggests the obvious fix:
"Let it update itself." Priya goes pale. A script that downloads code from the network
and replaces itself is exactly what an attacker would love, so the update must
distrust the server: check the checksum, check the syntax, check what the new script says
about itself, never downgrade, and swap the file in one atomic step so a power cut during
the storm cannot leave half a script behind.
objective:
Write solution.sh, the `lantern` tool whose own version is the constant `1.0.0`:
  `solution.sh version`
  `solution.sh update [--check] [--force] [--channel NAME]`
  `solution.sh rollback`
Anything else (including a channel that does not match `^[a-z]+$`): `usage: solution.sh version | update [--check] [--force] [--channel NAME] | rollback`
on stderr, exit 2. `version` prints `lantern 1.0.0`. The tool refers to itself as `$0`.

The update server is reached with `curl` (on PATH): files live under
`https://updates.lanternfish.example/lantern/CHANNEL/` (CHANNEL defaults to `stable`). Download with
`curl -sS --fail --max-time 10 -o OUTFILE URL`. The server publishes `VERSION` (one line, the latest version),
and for that version `lantern-X.Y.Z.sh` (the new script) and `lantern-X.Y.Z.cksum` (one line `CRC SIZE`).

`update` does, in order:
1. Fetch VERSION. A download failure: `update check failed: cannot reach server` on stderr, exit 3. A value that is not
   `X.Y.Z` (three whole numbers): `update check failed: server sent a bad version 'V'`, exit 3.
2. Compare numerically with 1.0.0 (component by component, not as text: 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.0).
   - Same version: `lantern 1.0.0 is up to date` and exit 0, unless `--force` (continue and reinstall).
   - Older: `refusing to downgrade from 1.0.0 to V` on stderr, exit 4 (even with --force).
   - Newer with `--check`: print `update available: 1.0.0 -> V` and exit 10, changing nothing.
   - Newer without --check: go on. (`--check` with the same version behaves like the first case.)
3. Download the script and the checksum file into a scratch directory made with `mktemp -d` (removed by a trap, always);
   a failed download is `update aborted: download failed` (stderr, exit 5).
4. Verify, in this order, each failure printing `update aborted: REASON` on stderr and exiting 5, with nothing changed:
   `checksum mismatch` (the `cksum` of the downloaded file, CRC and size, differs from the checksum file),
   `downloaded script has a syntax error` (`bash -n`), `downloaded script reports version R, expected V`
   (its output of `bash NEWSCRIPT version` must be exactly `lantern V`; R is what it printed after removing `lantern `, or `nothing`).
5. Install: copy the current script to `$0.old` (keeping its permissions), prepare the new script next to the old one as
   `$0.new` (same permissions as the current script: start from `cp -p` of it), and move it over `$0`
   with `mv` (never write into the running file). Then print `updated lantern 1.0.0 -> V (previous kept as $0.old)` and
   exit 0 immediately: the file that was running is gone.
`rollback`: without `$0.old`: `error: no previous version to roll back to` on stderr, exit 3. Otherwise ask it
(`bash $0.old version`), move it over `$0` and print `rolled back to <what it printed>`.
concepts: never trust the server: verify before you install
numeric version comparison, no downgrades
atomic replacement with mv; never overwrite a running script
validating a download in a scratch directory
keeping the previous version for rollback

required_patterns.message: Check the downloaded script with bash -n before installing it.
Verify the download with cksum.
Replace the script with mv, which swaps the file atomically.
Download into a scratch directory made with mktemp -d.

title: The Distributed Lock
story:
The first storm of the season knocked out the Lanternfish primary link for
forty seconds, and when it came back two deploy scripts woke up at the same
moment and both started rewriting the same config. Theo's version of "locking"
was a file called `deploy.lock` that nobody ever deleted. Mara wants a real
one: a lock that only one process can take, that says who holds it, and that
gives itself up when its owner crashes in the dark and never comes back.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a small lock manager built on the fact that `mkdir` is
atomic: of two processes creating the same directory, exactly one succeeds.
The lock IS a directory LOCK. Inside it two files record the holder:
`owner` (the owner name) and `expires` (epoch seconds, a plain integer).
There is no real clock: the current time is always passed in as NOW.

  solution.sh acquire LOCK OWNER TTL NOW
  solution.sh release LOCK OWNER
  solution.sh status  LOCK NOW

acquire (TTL and NOW must be positive integers):
  - Try `mkdir LOCK`. If it works, write `owner` and `expires` (NOW+TTL) and
    print `acquired LOCK by OWNER until EXPIRES`.
  - If LOCK already exists and its owner is the same OWNER and it has not
    expired, extend it: set `expires` to NOW+TTL and print
    `renewed LOCK by OWNER until EXPIRES`.
  - If it exists, is held by someone else, and EXPIRES is greater than NOW,
    print `busy: LOCK held by HOLDER for another N s` to stderr (N =
    EXPIRES-NOW) and exit 1. Change nothing.
  - If it exists and EXPIRES is less than or equal to NOW, the holder is
    presumed dead: print `reclaimed stale lock of HOLDER` to stdout, remove the
    old lock and take it with the normal steps (so a second line,
    `acquired ...`, follows).
  - If the `owner` or `expires` file is missing, or `expires` is not a
    number, someone is probably mid-acquire. Never steal it: treat it as busy
    with holder `unknown` and print `busy: LOCK held by unknown` to stderr,
    exit 1.
  - If `mkdir` fails and LOCK does not exist (for example the parent folder is
    missing), print `cannot create LOCK` to stderr and exit 2.
  - Do not use `mkdir -p`: it succeeds when the directory exists, which
    defeats the whole idea.

release LOCK OWNER:
  - No LOCK: `not locked: LOCK` to stderr, exit 1.
  - Held by another owner: `refused: LOCK belongs to HOLDER, not OWNER` to
    stderr, exit 3. Nothing is removed.
  - Otherwise remove the two files and the directory, print `released LOCK`.
    (An expired lock may still be released by its owner.)

status LOCK NOW prints exactly one line and exits 0:
  `free` when there is no LOCK;
  `held by HOLDER, N s left` while EXPIRES is greater than NOW;
  `expired, was held by HOLDER` otherwise.

Any other command or the wrong number of arguments, or a TTL/NOW that is
not a positive integer: print
`usage: solution.sh acquire LOCK OWNER TTL NOW | release LOCK OWNER | status LOCK NOW`
to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: mkdir as an atomic test-and-set
lock metadata: owner and expiry
stale lock detection with an injected clock
validating input before acting

required_patterns.message: Take the lock with mkdir: it either creates the directory or fails, atomically.

forbidden_patterns.message: flock is not available everywhere; build the lock from mkdir.
mkdir -p succeeds on an existing directory, so it cannot tell you who got there first.

title: The Rate Limiter
story:
When the storm closed the road to the data centre, every customer dashboard
in town started refreshing itself twice a second, and Harbour Bakery's
"just checking" script took the status API down for everyone else. Gus does
not want to ban anyone. He wants fairness: each client gets a bucket of
tokens that refills slowly, a request spends a token, and an empty bucket
means "come back in a moment". Priya adds one condition: no wall clock, so
she can replay last night's traffic and get the same answers.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a token-bucket rate limiter that replays requests.

  solution.sh LIMITS STATE < requests

LIMITS is a text file, one rule per line: `CLIENT CAPACITY SECONDS_PER_TOKEN`
(all integers, at least 1). `CLIENT` may be `*`, the default rule for
clients without their own. Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are
ignored.

STATE is the saved buckets, one per line: `CLIENT TOKENS LAST`. It may not
exist yet (no buckets). It is rewritten at the end, sorted by client name
(plain `sort`), and it keeps the buckets of clients that made no request.

Requests arrive on stdin, one per line: `TS CLIENT [COST]`. TS is the
request time in whole seconds (your fake clock), COST defaults to 1.
Blank and `#` lines are ignored but still count in line numbers.

Bucket rules:
  - A client seen for the first time starts with a full bucket and LAST=TS.
  - Refill before every request: ELAPSED = TS - LAST. Add ELAPSED /
    SECONDS_PER_TOKEN whole tokens (integer division) and move LAST forward by
    exactly (tokens added x SECONDS_PER_TOKEN), so partial progress is not
    lost. Never exceed CAPACITY; whenever the bucket is full, set LAST to TS.
  - If TOKENS >= COST: subtract COST and print
      `TS CLIENT allow tokens=N`   (N = tokens left)
  - Otherwise print `TS CLIENT deny retry=S`, where S is the number of
    seconds from TS until the bucket would hold COST tokens (the bucket is
    left unchanged).
  - If COST is larger than CAPACITY it can never succeed: print
    `TS CLIENT reject cost=COST capacity=CAPACITY`.

After all requests print `summary: allowed=A denied=D` (rejects count as
denied).

Errors (print to stderr, skip that line, keep going, and exit 1 at the end):
  `line N: no limit for CLIENT`    no rule and no `*` rule
  `line N: bad request`            wrong field count, TS or COST not a
                                   non-negative integer (COST must be >= 1)
  `line N: time goes backwards`    TS smaller than the previous accepted TS
N is the physical line number on stdin.

If LIMITS cannot be read print `cannot read LIMITS` to stderr and exit 2.
Wrong number of arguments: `usage: solution.sh LIMITS STATE < requests` to
stderr, exit 2. Use associative arrays (`declare -A`) for the buckets.
concepts: token bucket: capacity, refill, spend
integer-only refill that keeps the remainder
state persisted between runs
an injected clock makes traffic replayable

required_patterns.message: Keep the buckets in associative arrays (declare -A).

title: The Circuit Breaker
story:
During the storm the card gateway started timing out, and the shop checkout
kept calling it anyway: every customer waited thirty seconds to be told no,
and the retry pile-up kept the gateway down after it had recovered. Theo
wants what electricians have had for a century: after a few failures, stop
calling, let the other side rest, then send one careful probe. Because each
checkout is a separate process, the breaker's memory has to live in a file.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a circuit breaker that guards any command.

  solution.sh STATE run NOW CMD [ARGS...]
  solution.sh STATE status NOW
  solution.sh STATE reset

STATE is the breaker's file. NOW is the current time in whole seconds (no
real clock). The file holds exactly three lines, in this order:
  state=closed|open|half-open
  failures=N
  opened_at=TS          (0 while closed)
A missing file means `closed`, 0 failures. Any other content (unknown
state, a missing key, a non-numeric number) is corrupt: print
`corrupt state file STATE` to stderr and exit 2.

Settings come from environment variables: THRESHOLD (default 3, consecutive
failures that open the circuit) and COOLDOWN (default 30 seconds). If one is
not a positive integer print `invalid THRESHOLD` or `invalid COOLDOWN` to
stderr and exit 2.

`run` behaviour. The guarded command's own stdout and stderr pass through
untouched; the breaker reports on stderr with a `breaker: ` prefix.
  closed:    run CMD. Success: failures=0, print `breaker: ok`, exit 0.
             Failure: failures+1 and print `breaker: failure K/T`. When K
             reaches T the state becomes open with opened_at=NOW and the
             message is `breaker: failure K/T, circuit OPEN`. Exit with the
             command's own exit status.
  open:      if NOW - opened_at is less than COOLDOWN do NOT run CMD: print
             `breaker: circuit open, call skipped (retry in S s)` where S is
             the seconds still to wait, and exit 75. Otherwise treat it as
             half-open.
  half-open: (also what an elapsed `open` becomes, and what a crashed earlier
             probe leaves behind) run CMD once as a probe. Success: closed,
             failures=0, `breaker: probe succeeded, circuit CLOSED`, exit 0.
             Failure: open again with opened_at=NOW and failures unchanged,
             `breaker: probe failed, circuit OPEN again`, exit with the
             command's status.
Write the new state through a temporary file in the same folder and `mv` it
into place, so a crash can never leave a half-written state file.

`status` prints one line to stdout, never runs anything:
  `closed (failures K/T)` | `open (probe in S s)` | `open (probe due)` |
  `half-open (probe due)`
`reset` deletes STATE and prints `breaker reset`.

Wrong arguments: print `usage: solution.sh STATE run NOW CMD [ARGS...] | status NOW | reset`
to stderr, exit 2. NOW must be a non-negative integer.
concepts: closed / open / half-open state machine
state persisted in a file across separate runs
atomic write: temp file then mv
passing a command through and keeping its exit status

required_patterns.message: Write the state to a temp file and mv it into place.
Run the guarded command with "$@" (or an array) so its arguments stay intact.

title: The Feature Flag System
story:
Theo shipped the new checkout on the Friday before the worst storm of the
year, and it did exactly what Theo's code always does: worked on his laptop.
Half the shop's customers could not pay. Rolling back meant a full deploy
in the middle of a gale. Never again, says Mara: from now on risky features
ship dark, switch on for a slice of users, and switch off with one line in a
config file, no deploy required. She wants the flag tool by tonight.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a feature-flag evaluator.

  solution.sh FLAGS check FLAG USER [ENV]
  solution.sh FLAGS list USER [ENV]
  solution.sh FLAGS validate

FLAGS is a config file, one flag per line:

  NAME = STATE [rollout=N] [allow=u1,u2] [deny=u1,u2] [env=e1,e2]

Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are ignored; spaces around `=` and
between options are free. NAME matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`. STATE is `on`
or `off`. rollout is an integer 0..100 (default 100).
ENV defaults to `prod` when not given on the command line.

Parse problems are reported as `FILE:LINE: MESSAGE` on stderr, in file order,
one per bad line (the first problem on a line only), using FILE exactly as it
was given:
  `expected NAME = STATE`      (no `=` on the line)
  `bad flag name 'NAME'`
  `state must be on or off`
  `rollout must be 0-100`      (also for a non-number)
  `unknown option 'KEY'`
  `duplicate flag 'NAME'`      (second and later definitions)
`validate` prints these and exits 1, or prints `OK: N flags` (N = number of
flags) and exits 0. `check` and `list` print them too, but exit 3 and do
nothing else, so a typo can never half-enable a feature.

`check` decides for one user. The rules apply in this order, the first match
wins:
  1. STATE is off              -> off, reason `kill switch`
  2. USER is in deny           -> off, reason `denied`
  3. env= is present and ENV is not in it -> off, reason `not enabled in ENV`
  4. USER is in allow          -> on,  reason `allow list`
  5. rollout is 100            -> on,  reason `fully on`
  6. otherwise take BUCKET = (first number printed by `cksum` for the text
     `FLAG:USER`, with no newline) modulo 100. On when BUCKET < rollout.
     Reason: `rollout N%, bucket B`.
Print `FLAG for USER: on (REASON)` or `FLAG for USER: off (REASON)`. Exit 0
when on, 1 when off. An unknown FLAG prints `unknown flag FLAG` to stderr and
exits 2.

`list` prints one line per flag, in file order, formatted with
`printf '%-14s %s\n'`: the name padded to 14 columns, then `on` or `off`
(the same decision as `check`). Exit 0.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh FLAGS check FLAG USER [ENV] | list USER [ENV] | validate`
on stderr, exit 2. An unreadable FLAGS file: `cannot read FLAGS`, exit 2.
concepts: config-driven behaviour with ordered rules
deterministic percentage rollout from a hash
parse once, report every problem with its line number
kill switch beats everything

required_patterns.message: Derive the rollout bucket from cksum of FLAG:USER so a user always gets the same answer.
Keep the parsed flags in associative arrays.

forbidden_patterns.message: A random roll would flip a user on and off between page loads. Hash the user instead.

title: The Blue-Green Switcher
story:
Deploying in place means the shop is half old code and half new code for a
few seconds, and during a storm those seconds are when the customers arrive.
Mara's answer is two identical release folders, `blue` and `green`. One is
live, the other is idle and gets the new version at leisure. When it passes a
smoke test, a single symlink flips and every request sees the new release at
once. If it is wrong, one more flip puts the old one back. She has been
drawing the picture for a week; now she wants the tool.
objective:
Write solution.sh, the release switcher.

  solution.sh ROOT status
  solution.sh ROOT switch
  solution.sh ROOT rollback

Layout under ROOT:
  releases/blue/VERSION      releases/green/VERSION   (one line, e.g. v1.4.2)
  current                    a symlink with the relative target
                             `releases/blue` or `releases/green`
  previous                   (written by you) the slot name that was live
                             before the last switch/rollback
  switch.log                 (written by you) one line appended per change

`current` must be a symlink that resolves to an existing slot. Otherwise
every command prints `current is not a valid release link` to stderr and
exits 1. Read where it points with `ls -ld` (there is no `readlink`).
The LIVE slot is the one `current` points at, the IDLE slot is the other one.

status prints two lines and exits 0:
  live: SLOT (VERSION)
  idle: SLOT (VERSION)
A slot with a missing or empty VERSION shows `(none)` instead of a version.

switch:
  1. If the idle slot has no VERSION, print `idle slot SLOT has no VERSION`
     to stderr, exit 1.
  2. If both slots have the same VERSION print
     `nothing to switch: both slots run VERSION` to stderr, exit 1.
  3. Run `smoke-test ROOT/releases/IDLE` (a stub). Hide its output. If it
     fails print `smoke test failed for IDLE, staying on LIVE` to stderr and
     exit 1, changing nothing.
  4. Otherwise flip the symlink ATOMICALLY: create the new link under a
     temporary name inside ROOT (`.current.tmp`) with `ln -sfn`, then rename
     it over `current`. Never delete `current` first: there must be no
     moment when it does not exist.
  5. Write LIVE (the slot you just left) to ROOT/previous, append
     `switch LIVE->IDLE VERSION` to ROOT/switch.log, and print
     `switched: LIVE -> IDLE (VERSION)`.

rollback:
  If ROOT/previous is missing, or names the slot that is already live, print
  `nothing to roll back to` to stderr and exit 1. Otherwise flip back (same
  atomic method, no smoke test), set previous to the slot you just left,
  append `rollback LEFT->BACK VERSION` to switch.log, and print
  `rolled back: LEFT -> BACK (VERSION)`.

Careful: `mv -f .current.tmp current` does not do what it seems when
`current` is a symlink to a directory; the hints explain. No temporary
files may remain afterwards.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh ROOT status | switch | rollback` to
stderr, exit 2.
concepts: atomic symlink replacement: ln -sfn then rename
mv onto a symlink-to-directory moves INTO it (mv -T / -h)
reading a symlink target with ls -ld
pre-flight check before the switch, instant rollback after

title: The Canary Releaser
story:
Blue-green moves everyone at once, which is lovely until the new release has
a bug that only shows up under real traffic. Priya has seen it twice: the
smoke test is green, the flip happens, and ten minutes later the support
desk is on fire. A canary sends the new version 5% of the traffic, then 10%,
then 50%, and watches the error rate each time. Mara does not want a human
staring at graphs during a gale: the script must notice, pull the traffic
back to zero, and say exactly why.
objective:
Write solution.sh, the canary controller.

  solution.sh PLAN METRICS RELEASE

PLAN lists traffic steps in percent, one integer per line (blank lines and
`#` comments ignored). The steps must be strictly increasing, each between
1 and 100, and the last one must be 100. Otherwise print
`bad plan: steps must increase and end at 100` to stderr and exit 2.

METRICS records what was observed at each step, one line per step:
`STEP CANARY_REQS CANARY_ERRS BASE_REQS BASE_ERRS` (integers; blank and `#`
lines ignored). Lines are looked up by STEP; if a step appears twice the later
line wins. An unreadable PLAN or METRICS file: `cannot read FILE` on stderr,
exit 2.

Settings from the environment (positive integers, defaults in brackets):
SOAK [60] seconds to wait at each step, MIN_REQS [100] fewest canary requests
needed to trust a step, TOLERANCE_PM [20] how many permille (tenths of a
percent) the canary's error rate may exceed the baseline's.

Run the steps in order. For every step below 100:
  1. `lbctl weight STEP`
  2. `sleep SOAK`
  3. Look up the metrics for STEP. Rates are integer permille:
     RATE = ERRS * 1000 / REQS (integer division, 0 when REQS is 0). Show a
     rate as tenths: 25 -> `2.5%`, 5 -> `0.5%`, 0 -> `0.0%`.
  4. Judge the step:
     - no metrics line  -> abort, reason `no metrics recorded`
     - CANARY_REQS < MIN_REQS -> abort, reason
       `only N canary requests (need MIN_REQS)`
     - canary rate > baseline rate + TOLERANCE_PM -> abort, reason
       `canary C% vs baseline B% (limit L%)` where L = baseline + tolerance
     - otherwise print `step STEP%: canary C% baseline B% ok` and continue.
For step 100 (never judged: nothing is left to compare with) run
`lbctl weight 100` then `lbctl promote`, print `step 100%: all traffic on the
canary` and finally `RELEASE promoted`.

Abort means: run `lbctl weight 0`, print `RELEASE aborted at STEP%: REASON`
to stdout, exit 1. Nothing runs after an abort.

If any `lbctl` call fails (non-zero) print `cannot set weight N%` (N is the
weight you were setting) to stderr, make one attempt at `lbctl weight 0`
(ignoring its result) and exit 3. A failing `promote` prints
`cannot promote RELEASE` to stderr, exit 3 (no rollback attempt: at that point
all traffic is already on the canary).

Wrong argument count: `usage: solution.sh PLAN METRICS RELEASE` to stderr,
exit 2. A SOAK, MIN_REQS or TOLERANCE_PM that is not a positive integer:
`invalid NAME` (the variable's name) on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: progressive delivery with an automatic abort
integer permille instead of floating point
judging evidence: rates, minimum sample size, tolerance
always roll back on any failure

title: The Chaos Monkey
story:
The storm took out `dory` for twenty minutes and the failover that "had been
tested" turned out to have been tested once, in 2023, by someone who has
since left. Priya's rule is blunt: if you have never broken it on purpose,
you do not know that it works. Mara agrees, with one condition. A chaos
tool that breaks things randomly is a menace; one that breaks things from a
seed, so that last Tuesday's disaster can be replayed to the exact fault, is
engineering.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a seeded chaos monkey.

  solution.sh [--dry-run] SEED ROUNDS FLEET

SEED is a non-negative integer (up to 18 digits), ROUNDS a positive integer.
FLEET lists services, one per line: `SERVICE` or `SERVICE protected`. Blank
and `#` lines are ignored. Protected services are never touched. The eligible
targets are the unprotected services in file order. If there are none print
`no eligible services in FLEET` to stderr and exit 1.

Do NOT use $RANDOM: its sequence differs between Bash versions. Implement a
tiny linear congruential generator with Bash arithmetic:
  state starts as SEED & 2147483647
  next(): state = (state * 1103515245 + 12345) & 2147483647
          and the value returned is  state >> 16
Every draw calls next() once, in exactly this order, for each round:
  1. ROLL = next() % 100. If ROLL >= CHANCE (environment variable, an integer
     0..100, default 50) the round is calm and there are no more draws.
  2. TARGET = targets[next() % number_of_targets]
  3. FAULT  = next() % 3: 0 kill, 1 delay, 2 drop
  4. P = next() % 9 + 1 (always drawn, only used by delay and drop)
     delay uses P*100 milliseconds, drop uses P*10 percent.
The fault description is `kill SVC`, `delay SVC 600ms` or `drop SVC 60%`.

Output, one line per round, rounds numbered from 1:
  calm round:      `round N: calm`
  dry run:         `round N: would DESCRIPTION`
  live run:        `round N: DESCRIPTION -> S1 -> S2`
A live run injects with `chaosctl kill SVC`, `chaosctl delay SVC MS` or
`chaosctl drop SVC PERCENT`, reads S1 with `chaosctl status SVC`, repairs with
`chaosctl heal SVC`, then reads S2 with `chaosctl status SVC`. A round is
unhealed when S2 is not `healthy`. A dry run calls nothing.

Finally print
  live:    `summary: rounds=R faults=F unhealed=U`
  dry run: `summary: rounds=R faults=F (dry run)`
and exit 1 if any round was unhealed (live only), otherwise 0.

Errors, all on stderr with exit 2: a bad SEED, ROUNDS or CHANCE prints
`usage: solution.sh [--dry-run] SEED ROUNDS FLEET` (for CHANCE print
`invalid CHANCE`); an unreadable FLEET prints `cannot read FLEET`.
concepts: a seeded pseudo-random generator written in shell arithmetic
determinism: same seed, same disaster
bit masking & and shifts >> to keep numbers in range
inject, observe, repair, verify

title: The SLA Monitor
story:
Gus has read the hosting contracts again, and this time he found the clause
about "99.9% monthly availability". Storm season is chewing through that
number, and he wants to know, per service, how much downtime is left before
Lanternfish owes customers money. The probe robot already writes one line a
minute per service; nobody has ever turned that pile into a verdict. Mara
asks for a tool that is blunt about the budget, and honest about the minutes
when the probe robot itself was blind.
objective:
Write solution.sh, an uptime and error-budget calculator.

  solution.sh [--strict] SLO PROBES

SLO lists the promise per service, one per line: `SERVICE TARGET`, where
TARGET is a percentage with at most 3 decimals (`99.9`, `99.95`, `99`,
`100`), between 0 and 100. Blank lines and `#` comments are ignored. A
malformed line prints `bad SLO line N` to stderr and exits 2.

PROBES holds one probe per line: `EPOCH SERVICE STATE`, STATE being `up`,
`degraded` or `down`. EPOCH is in seconds; the MINUTE of a probe is
EPOCH / 60 (integer division). The robot probes every minute. For each
service the window runs from its first probe's minute to its last probe's
minute, inclusive, so
  TOTAL = last_minute - first_minute + 1
Every minute of the window without a probe is a blind minute and counts as
DOWN. `down` probes are down; `degraded` probes count as up, unless
`--strict` is given, then they count as down too.
  BAD = down minutes (probed or blind),  UP = TOTAL - BAD

Per service compute:
  UPTIME  = UP * 100 / TOTAL as a percentage with 3 decimals, rounded DOWN
            (use integer maths on thousandths of a percent: UP*100000/TOTAL
            and print it as `99.500`)
  ALLOWED = TOTAL * (100 - TARGET) / 100 minutes, integer part only. Do the
            maths in thousandths of a percent: TOTAL * (100000 - T1000) / 100000
            where T1000 is the target in thousandths (99.9 -> 99900)
  OUTAGES = number of runs of consecutive bad minutes; LONGEST = the length
            of the longest run, in minutes
The service MEETS its target when BAD * 100000 <= TOTAL * (100000 - T1000)
(compare exactly; do not use the rounded ALLOWED for this).

Print one line per service, in SLO file order:
  `NAME: uptime U% (target T%) used BAD of ALLOWED min, outages=O longest=L min -> STATUS`
with T printed with 3 decimals like U, and STATUS one of
  `BREACHED`  does not meet the target
  `AT RISK`   meets it, BAD > 0, and BAD * 100 >= ALLOWED * 80
  `OK`        otherwise
A service in SLO without any probe prints `NAME: no data -> NO DATA`.

Probe lines that are damaged are skipped with a message on stderr and do not
stop the run: `line N: bad probe` (wrong field count, EPOCH not an integer,
unknown STATE), `line N: no SLO for NAME`, `line N: out of order` (the
minute is not greater than the previous accepted minute of that service).
N is the physical line number in PROBES. A skipped probe is simply a
missing probe, so its minute becomes a blind minute (if it lies between two
accepted probes).

Exit 1 if any service is BREACHED, otherwise 0. Unreadable files:
`cannot read FILE` on stderr, exit 2. Wrong arguments:
`usage: solution.sh [--strict] SLO PROBES` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: uptime from probes, and blind minutes as downtime
error budget: how much failure the promise allows
decimal percentages with integer arithmetic
run-length counting of outages

title: The Cost Analyzer
story:
The storm month is over and Gus is staring at a spreadsheet that is wrong in
three different ways: it forgets that the first 50 GB of bandwidth are free,
it charges the big storage customer the small-customer price, and it rounds
every line in the customer's favour. He asked the question out loud in the
office, "can't a script just do this?", and Ollie, the intern, was the only
one who answered. You can do better than a spreadsheet: read the price list
with its tiers, read the month's usage, and print real invoices, to the cent,
with the same rounding every single time.
objective:
Write solution.sh, an invoice generator.

  solution.sh PRICES USAGE [DISCOUNTS]

PRICES, one item per line: `ITEM UNIT TIER [TIER ...]`. Blank lines and `#`
comments are ignored. A TIER is `UPTO:PRICE`: UPTO is the cumulative top of
the tier in units (or `*` for "everything beyond"), PRICE is dollars per unit
with up to 4 decimals (`0.0125`, `0.09`, `0`). Tiers are graduated: each
unit is charged at the price of the tier it falls in. Example:
`storage GB 100:0.08 1000:0.05 *:0.03` charges the first 100 GB at 0.08, the
next 900 at 0.05 and the rest at 0.03. UPTO values must strictly increase and
the last tier must be `*`; otherwise print `bad price line N` to stderr and
exit 2. Do the maths in integers: PRICE in ten-thousandths of a dollar.

USAGE is CSV: `CUSTOMER,ITEM,QUANTITY` (QUANTITY is a non-negative integer).
A first line equal to `customer,item,quantity` is a header and is skipped.
Rows for the same customer and item add up.

DISCOUNTS (optional): lines `CUSTOMER PERCENT`, PERCENT an integer 0..100,
`#` comments and blanks ignored; a bad line prints `bad discount line N` and
exits 2.

Environment (integers >= 0, default 0, else `invalid NAME` on stderr and
exit 2): TAX_PCT, the sales tax percentage, and MIN_CHARGE, the smallest
invoice in CENTS.

Rounding: the cost of one item line is rounded to whole cents, half up:
(tenthousandths + 50) / 100. Discount and tax are also rounded half up:
(cents * PERCENT + 50) / 100. Work in cents from there on.

For each customer (sorted by name, only customers with at least one valid
row) print an invoice. Item lines follow the PRICES order, only for items
the customer used, formatted with
  printf '%-10s %6d %-5s %10s\n'   (item, quantity, unit, money)
and the summary lines with
  printf '%-23s %10s\n'            (label, money)
Money is `$D.CC`, a negative amount `-$D.CC`. The invoice is:
  `== CUSTOMER ==`
  item lines
  `subtotal`                       the sum of the item lines
  `discount P%`      (negative)    only when P > 0
  `minimum charge`   (positive)    only when the discounted subtotal is below
                                   MIN_CHARGE: the difference that tops it up
  `tax T%`                         only when TAX_PCT > 0, on the amount after
                                   discount and minimum
  `total`
After all invoices print `customers: N, grand total: $X.XX`.

Bad usage rows are skipped with a message on stderr, the rest is still
invoiced, and the exit status is 1 (otherwise 0):
  `line N: expected CUSTOMER,ITEM,QUANTITY`  (not exactly three fields)
  `line N: unknown item NAME`
  `line N: bad quantity`
N is the physical line number of USAGE. Unreadable files: `cannot read FILE`
on stderr, exit 2. Wrong arguments:
`usage: solution.sh PRICES USAGE [DISCOUNTS]` on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: graduated pricing tiers
money as integers: ten-thousandths, then cents
round half up, always the same way
aggregating CSV rows with associative arrays
