title: The Security Scanner
story:
Priya found an SSH key readable by every user on `halibut`, which was
Theo's, which has been there since spring, and which nobody noticed because
nobody looks. In storm season the team is working from kitchens and train
stations and the usual shortcuts multiply. She wants a scanner she can run
against any server's file tree every night: it should find the classic
mistakes, rank them by how fast an attacker would use them, and fail the
nightly job when something truly dangerous is lying around.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a configuration and permission scanner.

  solution.sh [--fail-on LEVEL] ROOT [ALLOWLIST]

ROOT is the directory tree to scan (all paths are reported relative to it,
without a leading `./` or `/`). ALLOWLIST is an optional file listing, one
per line, the setuid/setgid files that are expected (paths relative to ROOT;
blank lines and `#` comments ignored). LEVEL is `critical`, `high` or
`medium` (default `high`).

Checks (use `find` for the permission checks):
  1. `world-writable file`  HIGH. Any regular file where "others" have the
     write bit. Symlinks are not followed or reported.
  2. `private key accessible by group or others`  CRITICAL. Regular files
     named `*.key`, `id_rsa`, `id_ed25519` or `id_ecdsa` where group or
     others have ANY permission bit (read, write or execute). Public keys
     (`.pub`) are fine. Beware: `find -perm -MODE` means "all of these bits",
     so test the six bits separately.
  3. `setuid/setgid binary not on allowlist`  HIGH. Regular files with the
     setuid or setgid bit whose relative path is not in ALLOWLIST.
  4. If ROOT/etc/ssh/sshd_config exists, read it like sshd does: `#` starts a
     comment, keys are case-insensitive, and the FIRST occurrence of a key
     wins. Report, using the first value (compared case-insensitively):
       PermitEmptyPasswords yes   CRITICAL `ssh accepts empty passwords`
       PermitRootLogin yes        HIGH     `ssh root login enabled`
       PasswordAuthentication yes MEDIUM   `ssh password login enabled`
  5. `plaintext credential on line N`  MEDIUM. In files named `*.conf`,
     `*.env`, `*.ini` or `*.yml`: a line (not a comment) of the form
     `KEY = VALUE` or `KEY: VALUE` where KEY (case-insensitive) contains
     `password`, `passwd`, `secret`, `token` or `api_key`, and VALUE is not
     empty, not quoted-empty (`""` or `''`), and does not start with `$` or
     `<` (placeholders). Never print the value itself.

Print one line per finding, `SEVERITY path: message` (path relative to
ROOT), ordered CRITICAL first, then HIGH, then MEDIUM, and inside a severity
alphabetically by the rest of the line (use `LC_ALL=C sort`). Then print
  `scan complete: C critical, H high, M medium`
Exit 1 if there is at least one finding at LEVEL or above (critical > high >
medium), otherwise 0.

A ROOT that is not a directory: `not a directory: ROOT` to stderr, exit 2.
An unreadable ALLOWLIST: `cannot read ALLOWLIST`, exit 2. A bad LEVEL or other
wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh [--fail-on LEVEL] ROOT [ALLOWLIST]` on
stderr, exit 2.
concepts: find -perm: all-bits vs any-bit tests
first-match-wins config parsing (sshd style)
severity ranking and a configurable exit threshold
reporting a secret's location, never its value

Test permission bits with find -perm.

title: The Forensics Collector
story:
At 22:15 on the worst night of the storm, someone logged into `halibut` as
Theo and read the shadow file. Theo was asleep, and a power cut had just
rebooted half the fleet. Priya has one rule for nights like this: before you
look at anything, preserve it. Copy the evidence somewhere safe, fingerprint
it, lock it, and write down who touched it and when, so that a week from now
nobody, including a lawyer, can say it was altered. Mara hands you the
keyboard: build the collector and the verifier.
objective:
Write solution.sh, an evidence collector with a chain of custody.

  solution.sh collect CASE ANALYST NOW SRC...
  solution.sh verify  CASE ANALYST NOW

NOW is the time as epoch seconds (a non-negative integer; no real clock).

collect:
  - If CASE already exists (as anything) print `case CASE already exists` to
    stderr and exit 1; never overwrite evidence.
  - Sources that are not regular files (missing, folders, symlinks) print
    `skipped SRC: not a regular file` to stderr and are left out. If no
    source is left print `nothing to collect` to stderr, exit 1, and do not
    create CASE at all.
  - Otherwise create CASE/ and CASE/evidence/. Copy the valid sources in the
    order given with `cp -p`, to the names `NNN-BASENAME` (NNN counts from
    001 over the copied files only). Compute `cksum` of the source and of the
    copy; if they differ print `copy of SRC does not match the source` and
    exit 3. Make each copy read-only (mode 0444); the originals are never
    modified or moved.
  - Write CASE/manifest.txt, one line per file in order:
    `NAME SUM SIZE SRC` (SUM and SIZE are the two numbers `cksum` prints,
    SRC exactly as given on the command line, and it may contain spaces).
  - Write CASE/manifest.seal: the first number of `cksum` over the whole
    manifest.txt, on one line.
  - Append `NOW ANALYST collect N items` to CASE/custody.log.
  - Print `collected N items into CASE (seal SEAL)`.

verify:
  - A missing CASE: `no such case: CASE`; missing manifest.txt:
    `no manifest in CASE`; both to stderr, exit 2.
  - Print `seal OK`, or `SEAL MISMATCH` if manifest.seal is missing or does
    not equal the cksum of manifest.txt.
  - For each manifest line, in order, print exactly one of (first match):
      `MISSING NAME`   the evidence file is gone
      `MODIFIED NAME`  its `cksum` output differs from `SUM SIZE`
      `WRITABLE NAME`  intact but anyone has write permission (the owner
                       write bit, mode bit 0200, is set; test with find -perm)
      `OK NAME`
  - Then, sorted with `LC_ALL=C sort`, every regular file in CASE/evidence
    that is not in the manifest: `EXTRA NAME`.
  - Print `verify: N ok, M problems` (a SEAL MISMATCH counts as one problem,
    as does each MISSING, MODIFIED, WRITABLE and EXTRA line).
  - Append `NOW ANALYST verify OK` or `NOW ANALYST verify FAILED` to
    CASE/custody.log, and exit 1 if there were problems, else 0.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh collect CASE ANALYST NOW SRC... | verify CASE ANALYST NOW`
on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: preserve before you analyse: copy, hash, lock
cksum fingerprints and a sealed manifest
read-only evidence and an append-only custody log
verifying: missing, modified, extra and writable files

required_patterns.message: Fingerprint every file with cksum.
Copy with cp -p so the evidence keeps the original timestamps.
Lock the evidence copies with chmod 0444.

title: The Self-Healing Script
story:
At 03:10 the storm killed `web`, the on-call phone rang, Theo typed
`restart web`, went back to bed, and at 03:40 it rang again. And at 04:10.
Mara has seen enough. Most outages have a boring fix that a script can
apply faster and more calmly than a half-asleep human: try the gentlest
remedy, wait, check again, try the next. But a script that restarts a sick
service forever is a menace, so it must also know when to stop, when a
service keeps coming back sick every run, and when to wake a person up.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a self-healing watchdog.

  solution.sh PLAYBOOK STATE

PLAYBOOK, one service per line: `SERVICE ACTION[,ACTION...]`, the actions
being tried in the order given. Valid actions: `restart`, `clear-cache`,
`rotate-logs`, `failover`. Blank lines and `#` comments are ignored. An
unknown action prints `playbook line N: unknown action NAME` to stderr and
exits 2 before anything is touched.

STATE remembers, per service, how many runs in a row needed a heal. Lines are
`SERVICE COUNT`; the file may not exist yet. It is rewritten at the end,
sorted by service name, with every service in the playbook. (Services
that are in STATE but no longer in the playbook are dropped.)

Settings (environment, positive integers): GRACE seconds to wait after each
action [5], MAX_ACTIONS the most actions one run may take in total [6],
FLAP_LIMIT [3]. A bad value prints `invalid NAME` and exits 2.

Only one healer may run at a time. Take a lock by creating the directory
`STATE.lock` with `mkdir`; if it exists print `another healer is running` to
stderr and exit 1. Remove the lock on every exit path (use a trap).

For each service, in playbook order, using the stubs `svcctl` and `pagerctl`:
  1. DETECT: `svcctl status SERVICE`. Exit status 0 means healthy: print
     `SERVICE: healthy` and reset its count to 0. Exit status 3 means
     svcctl does not know it: print `SERVICE: unknown service`, count it as a
     failure, and leave its count unchanged. Any other non-zero status means
     it is sick.
  2. FLAPPING: if the stored count is >= FLAP_LIMIT, do not touch it. Print
     `SERVICE: flapping (N heals), paging instead`, run
     `pagerctl notify SERVICE "flapping after N heals"`, count a failure.
  3. REMEDIATE: for each action in order: if MAX_ACTIONS actions have
     already been run in this run, print `SERVICE: skipped (action budget
     exhausted)`, count a failure and move on without paging. Otherwise run
     `svcctl ACTION SERVICE`, then `sleep GRACE`, then check status again.
     When it is healthy: print `SERVICE: healed by ACTION (attempt K)` (K =
     1 for the first action tried on that service), add 1 to its count
     and continue with the next service.
  4. If every action failed: print `SERVICE: UNHEALED after K actions`, run
     `pagerctl notify SERVICE "unhealed after K actions"`, count a failure.
Finish with `summary: healthy=A healed=B failed=C` and exit 1 when C > 0,
else 0. `svcctl status` output is for you to ignore (discard it).

Wrong arguments or an unreadable PLAYBOOK: print
`usage: solution.sh PLAYBOOK STATE` to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: detect, remediate, verify as a loop
escalation ladder and a global action budget
flap detection from state saved between runs
mkdir lock and trap cleanup

required_patterns.message: Release the lock with a trap, so every exit path cleans up.
Take the single-instance lock with mkdir.

title: The Dependency Graph
story:
After the storm the whole fleet cold-started at once and ended up in a heap:
`web` came up before `api`, `api` before `db`, and `db` before its disk was
mounted, so everything crashed three times and had to be restarted by hand
in an order that only Theo remembered. Mara wants that order written down
where a machine can use it, as a graph of "needs" lines, plus a tool that
turns the graph into a start order, a stop order and a list of what can start
in parallel. It must also complain, loudly and usefully, when somebody adds a
line that makes two services wait for each other forever.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a dependency resolver.

  solution.sh levels GRAPH [TARGET...]
  solution.sh order  GRAPH [TARGET...]
  solution.sh stop   GRAPH [TARGET...]
  solution.sh check  GRAPH

GRAPH: one service per line, `NAME: DEP DEP ...` (dependencies are started
FIRST; the list may be empty, `cache:`). Names match `[a-z0-9-]+`. Blank lines
and `#` comments are ignored. Problems are reported on stderr as
`GRAPH:LINE: MESSAGE` (GRAPH exactly as given), all of them in file order,
then exit 2:
  `expected NAME: DEPENDENCIES`    no colon on the line
  `bad name 'X'`
  `duplicate service 'X'`          the second and later definitions
  `unknown dependency 'X' of 'Y'`  X is never defined as a service (reported at
                                   Y's line)
Repeated names inside one dependency list count once.

Resolution uses Kahn's algorithm in layers: LEVEL 1 is every service without
unmet dependencies; LEVEL 2 is every service whose dependencies are all in
level 1; and so on. Inside a level, names are sorted alphabetically
(`LC_ALL=C sort`).

levels: print one line per level, `N: name name ...`.
order:  print the services one per line, level by level (the start order).
stop:   the same list in exactly reverse order (the stop order).
check:  print `OK: N services in M levels`.
With TARGET arguments, `levels`, `order` and `stop` consider only the targets
and everything they depend on, directly or indirectly. A TARGET that is not a
service prints `unknown service 'X'` to stderr and exits 2.

Cycles: if some services can never be placed in a level, print to stdout
`cycle detected: a -> b -> c -> a` and exit 1, with this exact search: take
the alphabetically first unplaced service, repeatedly follow its alphabetically
first dependency that is also unplaced, until a service repeats; print the path
from the first occurrence of that repeated service to its second occurrence.
A service that depends on itself is a cycle: `cycle detected: x -> x`. Only
the part of the graph being resolved is examined (so asking for targets that
do not lead into a cycle succeeds).

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh levels|order|stop GRAPH [TARGET...] | check GRAPH`
on stderr, exit 2. An unreadable GRAPH: `cannot read GRAPH`, exit 2.
concepts: topological sort with Kahn's algorithm, layer by layer
cycle detection and printing an actual cycle
reverse edges (dependents) to release waiting nodes
transitive closure of the targets

required_patterns.message: Keep the graph in associative arrays (declare -A).

title: The Template Engine
story:
During the storm migration Theo hand-edited forty nginx configs, and the one
he forgot to edit was the one for Tidewater Books, which now sends customers
to a server that is underwater. Mara is done with copy-and-paste. Configs
should be generated from one template plus a small file of variables:
a placeholder here, an optional TLS block there, a repeated line per backend.
Every tool she has found for this wants a language runtime the harbour
servers do not have, so you will write a tiny template engine in Bash.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a template renderer.

  solution.sh [-D NAME=VALUE]... TEMPLATE VARS

VARS: lines `NAME=VALUE` (VALUE is everything after the first `=`, and may be
empty or contain `=`). Blank lines and `#` lines are ignored. NAME matches
`[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`; anything else prints `bad vars line N` to stderr
and exits 2. Each `-D NAME=VALUE` option sets or overrides a variable (same
rules; a bad one prints `bad -D option` and exits 2). A list is a value
with items separated by commas.

TEMPLATE is text with two kinds of markup.

1. Placeholders `{{NAME}}`, `{{ NAME }}` or `{{NAME:-FALLBACK}}`. They are
   replaced by the variable's value, or by FALLBACK when the variable is unset
   or empty. A variable named like `loop.index` is allowed inside loops
   (see below). Any number of placeholders may appear on one line.
2. Block directives, each alone on its own line (leading and trailing
   spaces allowed); the directive line itself produces no output:
     {% if COND %} ... {% else %} ... {% endif %}        (else is optional)
     {% for ITEM in LISTVAR %} ... {% endfor %}
   COND is one of `VAR`, `not VAR`, `VAR == WORD`, `VAR != WORD`. `VAR` is
   true when it is set and its value, in lower case, is not empty, `0`,
   `false`, `no` or `off`. An unset variable is false in a condition and
   never an error. WORD is compared literally with the value.
   A `for` runs its body once per comma-separated item (an empty list runs it
   zero times). Inside the body `{{ITEM}}` is the current item and
   `{{loop.index}}` is its 1-based position. Blocks nest. After a loop ends,
   ITEM and loop.index have the values they had before it (nested loops
   must not leak into the outer one).

Plain lines are copied as they are (after placeholder replacement).

Errors go to stderr as `line N: MESSAGE` (N is the template's physical line),
produce no stdout at all, and exit 1:
  `unclosed 'if'`  /  `unclosed 'for'`      (reported at the opening line)
  `'else' without 'if'`, `'endif' without 'if'`, `'endfor' without 'for'`
  `bad directive 'TEXT'`    (anything else inside {% %}, TEXT trimmed)
  `unclosed '{{'`           a placeholder that never ends
  `undefined variable 'NAME'`  a placeholder without fallback whose variable
                               is unset (an EMPTY variable is fine), or a
                               `for` over an unset list
Structural errors are all listed, in line order. Undefined-variable and
unclosed-placeholder errors are found while rendering: report only the first
one of those, and only when there are no structural errors.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh [-D NAME=VALUE]... TEMPLATE VARS` on
stderr, exit 2. Unreadable files: `cannot read FILE`, exit 2.
concepts: parsing a small markup language into a block structure
recursive rendering of nested blocks
scoped variables: save and restore around a loop
no output until you know the whole template is valid

required_patterns.message: Keep the variables in an associative array.

forbidden_patterns.message: eval would run template text as code; the whole point is that templates are data.
envsubst is not available everywhere, and it cannot do blocks.

title: The State Machine
story:
Noor's ticket board turned into a free-for-all during the storm. Tickets went
from "open" straight to "closed" without anyone fixing anything, a resolved
ticket was resolved again with no summary, and an intern "reopened" a ticket
that had been closed by the CFO on purpose. Mara wants the life of a ticket
written down as a state machine: which states exist, which events move a
ticket between them, who may fire each event, and what must be filled in
first. The rules should live in a file Noor can read, and the script should
enforce them without exception.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a ticket state machine.

  solution.sh MACHINE validate
  solution.sh MACHINE show TICKET
  solution.sh MACHINE fire TICKET EVENT ROLE [FIELD=VALUE...]

MACHINE is the definition file. Blank lines and `#` comments are ignored.
  `initial STATE`
  `final STATE[,STATE...]`
  `FROM EVENT TO [role=R1,R2] [require=FIELD]`   a transition
State, event, role and field names match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*`. `role=` limits
who may fire the transition (without it anyone may), `require=` names a
field that must be non-empty before the transition. States are all names
that appear in `initial`, `final` or as FROM/TO. A line that does not fit
(transition with fewer than 3 fields, unknown option, bad name, `initial`
or `final` without a value) is reported on stderr as
`MACHINE:LINE: bad line` and makes every command exit 2 (all bad lines are
listed first, in order). A machine without an `initial` line prints
`MACHINE: no initial state` and exits 2. If two transitions share FROM and
EVENT the first one is used.

validate prints problems on stdout, then exits 1 if there were any:
  `duplicate transition: FROM EVENT`          (file order)
  `unreachable state: S`                      (not reachable from initial; sorted)
  `dead end: S`                               (not final, no outgoing transition; sorted)
  `final state has outgoing transitions: S`   (sorted)
and as the last line `N problems found`. Without problems print
`OK: S states, T transitions` and exit 0 (T counts the transitions in use,
without duplicates).

A TICKET file holds lines (any order is accepted when reading):
  `state=NAME`   `history=FROM EVENT TO ROLE` (several)   `FIELD=VALUE`
A ticket file that does not exist is a new ticket in the initial state. A
state that the machine does not know prints
`corrupt ticket TICKET: unknown state 'X'` to stderr and exits 2.

show prints `state: S`, `allowed: e1, e2` (sorted events that leave S, or
`none`), `steps: N` (number of history lines) and one `field NAME=VALUE` line
per field, sorted by name.

fire applies EVENT as ROLE; each FIELD=VALUE argument sets a field first
(a bad argument without `=` or with a bad name is a usage error). Checks,
in this order:
  1. EVENT not allowed in the current state:
     `illegal: event 'E' not allowed in state 'S' (allowed: a, b)` (or
     `allowed: none`), exit 1.
  2. ROLE not in the transition's role list:
     `denied: role 'R' may not 'E' (needs: r1, r2)`, exit 3, the roles in the
     order written in the machine.
  3. A required field missing or empty (after applying the arguments):
     `blocked: field 'F' is required`, exit 4.
A failed check changes nothing. On success rewrite TICKET (write a
temporary file next to it, then `mv` it over): first `state=NEW`, then the
fields sorted by name as `NAME=VALUE`, then every `history=` line in order,
with `history=FROM EVENT TO ROLE` appended. Print
`FROM -> TO (EVENT by ROLE)`.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh MACHINE validate | show TICKET | fire TICKET EVENT ROLE [FIELD=VALUE...]`
on stderr, exit 2. An unreadable MACHINE: `cannot read MACHINE`, exit 2.
concepts: states, events and a transition table
guards: who may fire, what must be filled in
static validation: reachability, dead ends, duplicates
a failed transition changes nothing; a good one is written atomically

title: The Event Bus
story:
Every system at Lanternfish learned about a failed deploy in a different
way: Theo's script emailed Priya, the status board polled a file, the audit
log was updated by hand on Fridays. When the storm hit, three of the four
never heard the news. Mara's fix is the oldest pattern in messaging: whoever
has news publishes it to a named topic, whoever cares subscribes, and a
dispatcher delivers each message to each subscriber, in order, once, and
without letting one broken listener stop the rest. No network, no daemon:
a folder on disk is the bus.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a file-based publish/subscribe bus.

  solution.sh BUS subscribe PATTERN NAME HANDLER
  solution.sh BUS unsubscribe NAME
  solution.sh BUS publish TOPIC MESSAGE...
  solution.sh BUS dispatch
  solution.sh BUS status

BUS is a directory that must already exist (`no such bus: BUS` on stderr,
exit 2). Layout (create sub-folders as needed):
  BUS/spool/NNNNNN      one file per message, 6-digit number, content:
                        line 1 the topic, line 2 the message
  BUS/subs/NAME         two lines: the pattern, the handler
  BUS/cursor/NAME       the highest message number this subscriber is done with
  BUS/tries/NAME        `SEQ COUNT`: failed attempts so far for message SEQ
  BUS/dead/NAME.NNNNNN  a dead-lettered message (same format as spool)

Names: a TOPIC matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*`; a PATTERN is a topic where
`*` may also appear (glob matching: `deploy.*`, `*`); NAME matches
`[a-z][a-z0-9-]*`; HANDLER matches `[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+` (one command word).
A violation prints `bad topic 'X'`, `bad pattern 'X'`, `bad name 'X'` or
`bad handler 'X'` to stderr and exits 2.

subscribe: a name may be used once (`subscriber NAME already exists`, exit
1). The new subscriber starts at the current last message number: cursor =
that number (0 on an empty spool), so it only sees future messages. Print
`NAME subscribed to PATTERN (cursor C)`.
unsubscribe: remove the subscription, its cursor and tries file. Print
`NAME unsubscribed`, or `no such subscriber: NAME` (exit 1).
publish: the message text is all remaining arguments joined with single
spaces. Its number is the highest number in the spool plus 1. Claim the file
atomically: turn on `noclobber` (`set -C`) in a subshell so that `>` refuses
to overwrite an existing file, and if it does refuse, try the next number.
Print `published #N to TOPIC (S subscribers)`, S being how many subscribers'
patterns match the topic.
dispatch: handle subscribers in alphabetical order of NAME. For each, look at
every message with number greater than its cursor, in order:
  - a topic that does not match the pattern is skipped: cursor moves on
    silently;
  - otherwise run `HANDLER TOPIC SEQ MESSAGE` (three arguments) and:
      success -> print `deliver #SEQ TOPIC -> NAME ok`, cursor = SEQ, and
                 forget any tries record for that message;
      failure -> the failed attempt count for this message becomes (stored
                 count + 1), saved in BUS/tries/NAME as `SEQ COUNT`. If it
                 reached MAX_TRIES (environment, default 3) move the
                 message to BUS/dead/NAME.NNNNNN, print
                 `dead-letter #SEQ TOPIC -> NAME after K attempts`, move the
                 cursor to SEQ, delete the tries file and carry on with the next
                 message. Otherwise print
                 `deliver #SEQ TOPIC -> NAME failed (attempt K/MAX)` and
                 stop this subscriber for this run (its later messages wait,
                 so order is kept). Other subscribers are unaffected.
Write each cursor as soon as it moves. At the end print
`dispatch: delivered=D failed=F dead=X` and exit 1 if F or X is not zero.
status: print `messages: N` (the last number) and then one line per
subscriber, alphabetical: `NAME topic=PATTERN handler=H cursor=C pending=P dead=D`
(pending = messages above the cursor that match the pattern, dead = files in
BUS/dead for that name), or `no subscribers`.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh BUS subscribe PATTERN NAME HANDLER | unsubscribe NAME | publish TOPIC MESSAGE... | dispatch | status`
on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: publish / subscribe through a spool directory
per-subscriber cursors give each listener its own pace
retry counting and a dead-letter folder
noclobber: atomic file creation to claim a sequence number

title: The Retry Framework
story:
The storm made everything flaky at once: the DNS resolver, the backup
uploader, the payment gateway. Theo's fix was `until command; do sleep 1;
done`, and at 04:00 four hundred of those loops hit a recovering gateway
every second and knocked it flat again. Mara has a better idea: one wrapper
every script in the company uses, with a policy you can choose (wait the
same time, wait a little longer each time, or double it), a ceiling, a total
budget, and the good sense not to retry a command that does not exist.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a retry wrapper with three back-off strategies.

  solution.sh plan STRATEGY ATTEMPTS DELAY [MAX]
  solution.sh run [OPTIONS] -- COMMAND [ARGS...]

STRATEGY is `fixed`, `linear` or `exponential`. After the failed attempt
number N (1, 2, 3, ...) the wait is
  fixed:        DELAY
  linear:       DELAY * N
  exponential:  DELAY * 2^(N-1)
in whole seconds, and never more than MAX when MAX is given and above 0
(a cap of 0 means "no cap"). Nothing may exceed 86400 seconds, whatever the
settings. ATTEMPTS is the total number of tries, so there are ATTEMPTS-1
waits.

plan prints the waits without running anything, one line per wait,
  `after attempt N: wait Ds`
and finally `total wait: Ts`. ATTEMPTS must be 1..30, DELAY a non-negative
integer, MAX a non-negative integer.

run options (all optional, any order, before the `--`):
  --strategy S      default exponential
  --attempts N      default 4 (1..30)
  --delay D         default 1 (non-negative integer, seconds)
  --max-delay M     default 0 (no cap)
  --budget B        default 0 (unlimited): the most total waiting allowed
  --retry-on C,C    exit codes worth retrying, e.g. 7,28. Default: every
                    non-zero code except 126 and 127.
Run COMMAND (its stdout and stderr pass through untouched). All messages of
the wrapper itself go to STDERR:
  - exit 0: print `succeeded on attempt K`, exit 0.
  - the exit code is not retryable (not in --retry-on, or 126/127 with the
    default): print `not retrying: exit E is not retryable`, exit E at once.
  - a retryable failure on the last attempt: print
    `gave up after N attempts (last exit E)` and exit E.
  - otherwise compute the wait W (as in `plan`). If --budget is set and the
    total already waited plus W would exceed it, print
    `retry budget of Bs exhausted after K attempts` and exit E. Else print
    `attempt K/N failed (exit E), retrying in Ws`, call `sleep W` (only when
    W is above 0; `sleep` is a stub in the tests), and try again.
In every failure case the wrapper exits with the command's own last exit
status.

Wrong arguments, an unknown option or strategy, a value that is out of range,
or a missing command after `--`: print
`usage: solution.sh plan STRATEGY ATTEMPTS DELAY [MAX] | run [--strategy S] [--attempts N] [--delay D] [--max-delay M] [--budget B] [--retry-on C,C] -- COMMAND...`
to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: fixed, linear and exponential back-off
caps and budgets so waiting stays bounded
deciding what is retryable from the exit status
wrapping a command while keeping its output and exit status

title: The Observability Kit
story:
The nightly backup took four hours on Tuesday and nobody knows why. The
logs say "done", the graph shows a flat line, and the one person who
understood the script is on a boat. Priya's verdict: the company has logs, it
has numbers, and it has nothing that says where the time went. Build the
three pillars into one small kit that any script can use: metrics (counters),
structured logs, and spans, timed records of each step that know which
step they belong to. Then a report that puts all three on one screen.
objective:
Write solution.sh, an observability kit.

  solution.sh OUT metric inc NAME [N]
  solution.sh OUT metric set NAME VALUE
  solution.sh OUT log LEVEL MESSAGE...
  solution.sh OUT span NAME -- COMMAND [ARGS...]
  solution.sh OUT report [--slow N]

OUT is a directory that must exist (`no such directory: OUT` on stderr, exit
2). It holds metrics.txt, logs.txt, spans.txt and ids. Time always comes from
`date +%s` (a stub in the tests that returns the number in `.clock`).

metric: NAME matches `[a-z][a-z0-9_.]*`, N and VALUE are non-negative
integers (N defaults to 1). metrics.txt has one `NAME VALUE` line per metric,
sorted with `LC_ALL=C sort`; rewrite it through a temporary file and `mv`.
`inc` adds N (a new metric starts at 0), `set` replaces the value. Print
`NAME=VALUE`.

log: LEVEL is debug, info, warn or error in any letter case; store it in
lower case. Append `TS LEVEL trace=TRACE MESSAGE` to logs.txt, where TS is
`date +%s`, TRACE is the environment variable OBS_TRACE or `-`, and MESSAGE is
the remaining arguments joined with single spaces. Also increase the metric
`log.LEVEL` by 1 (same rules as `metric inc`). Print nothing.

span: run COMMAND and record how long it took.
  - TRACE is OBS_TRACE if set, otherwise a new trace id `tN`. The span id is a
    new `sN`. Counters live in OUT/ids as one line `trace=N span=M` (missing
    file means 0 and 0); allocate by increasing and rewriting the file
    (temporary file + `mv`) BEFORE running the command.
  - PARENT is OBS_PARENT if set, otherwise `-`.
  - START = `date +%s` before the command, DUR = `date +%s` after minus START.
  - Run COMMAND with OBS_TRACE=TRACE and OBS_PARENT=SPANID in its environment,
    so a nested `solution.sh ... span` becomes its child. Its stdout and
    stderr pass through. Remember its exit status.
  - Append `TRACE SPANID PARENT START DUR STATUS NAME` to spans.txt, STATUS
    being `ok` or `exit=E`. NAME matches `[a-z0-9._-]+`.
  - Increase the metrics `span.total`, and `span.errors` if the command
    failed. Exit with COMMAND's status.

report [--slow N] prints (N defaults to 5, a non-negative integer):
  `== metrics ==` then the lines of metrics.txt, or `(none)`
  `== logs ==`, `levels: debug=D info=I warn=W error=E` (counted from
      logs.txt) and then one line `error trace=TRACE: MESSAGE` per error log,
      in file order
  `== traces ==` then, for each trace in numeric order of its id (tN; ids
      are compared by the number), `trace TID` and its spans as a tree:
      roots are spans whose parent is `-` or unknown; children follow their
      parent, ordered by span number; each line is indented by 2 spaces
      times (depth + 1) and reads `SPANID NAME DURs STATUS`, followed by
      ` SLOW` when DUR is greater than N. `(none)` if there are no spans.
  `summary: traces=T spans=S errors=E slow=L` (errors = spans whose status
      is not ok, slow = spans flagged SLOW).
Missing files count as empty.

Wrong arguments, a bad level, name or number: print
`usage: solution.sh OUT metric inc NAME [N] | metric set NAME VALUE | log LEVEL MESSAGE... | span NAME -- COMMAND... | report [--slow N]`
to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: three signals: metrics, logs, spans
trace and parent ids passed through the environment
atomic counters and sorted state files
building a tree from flat records

title: The Compliance Enforcer
story:
The auditors arrive Monday. Priya's compliance spreadsheet says "mostly
green", which in her experience means "mostly unchecked". She wants the
policy as a file of rules that a machine can read, a mode that only reports,
a mode that fixes what it can and proves the fix, and a way for a human to
say "this one is waived until the migration is done" without the waiver
living forever. And whatever it changes, it must keep a backup of the
original, because the auditors will ask what it looked like before.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a policy checker and enforcer.

  solution.sh [--dry-run] check   ROOT RULES NOW [WAIVERS]
  solution.sh [--dry-run] enforce ROOT RULES NOW [WAIVERS]

`--dry-run` is only allowed with `enforce`. ROOT is the directory the rules
apply to; every PATH in a rule is relative to it. NOW is epoch seconds (a
non-negative integer).

RULES: one rule per line, `ID SEVERITY TYPE PATH [ARGUMENTS...]`. Blank lines
and `#` comments are ignored. ID is unique. SEVERITY is `high`, `medium` or
`low`. PATH must not start with `/` or contain `..` (else
`rules line N: path escapes ROOT`). Types and their arguments (the arguments
are the rest of the line, internal spaces included):
  mode PATH MODE         the rwx permission bits of PATH must be MODE (3 or 4
                         octal digits; only the last three digits are
                         compared, so 0600 equals 600). Read the current mode
                         from `ls -ld`.
  line PATH TEXT         PATH must contain a line exactly equal to TEXT.
  noline PATH REGEX      no line of PATH may match the extended regex REGEX
                         (a missing file passes).
  setting PATH KEY VALUE a line `KEY VALUE` (whitespace separated, KEY compared
                         case-insensitively, lines starting with # ignored)
                         must exist; the first such line decides and its
                         value (the rest of the line, trimmed) must equal
                         VALUE exactly.
  absent PATH            PATH must not exist.
Any other problem prints `rules line N: MESSAGE` on stderr, exit 2:
`unknown type 'X'`, `bad severity 'X'`, `duplicate id 'X'`, `wrong arguments`
(a rule needs its arguments: mode 1, line 1+ words, noline 1+, setting 2+,
absent none), `bad mode 'X'`. All such lines are listed before exiting.

Evaluation of one rule, with MSG describing a failure:
  mode:    PATH missing -> `PATH does not exist`; else `PATH has mode MMMM,
           wants WWWW` (4-digit octal, e.g. 0644 and 0600)
  line:    PATH missing or without the line -> `PATH is missing the required line`
  noline:  `PATH has N forbidden line(s)`
  setting: no such key -> `KEY is not set`; else `KEY is 'ACTUAL', wants 'VALUE'`
  absent:  `PATH exists`

WAIVERS (optional): lines `ID until=EPOCH [REASON...]`, `#` and blank lines
ignored; a bad line prints `waivers line N: bad waiver` and exits 2. A rule
with a waiver whose EPOCH is >= NOW is waived: print
`WAIVED ID (SEV) until EPOCH: REASON` (REASON defaults to `no reason`) and do
nothing else for that rule. A waiver with EPOCH < NOW has expired: print
`waiver for ID expired` to stderr and treat the rule normally.

check prints per rule, in file order:
  `PASS ID`   or   `FAIL ID (SEV): MSG`
enforce handles a failing rule like this:
  1. Can it be fixed? Not when the target of a `mode` rule is missing, when
     an `absent` target is a directory, or when the parent folder of a
     `line`/`setting` target does not exist. Then print
     `CANNOT FIX ID (SEV): MSG`.
  2. With --dry-run print `WOULD FIX ID (SEV): FIXTEXT` and change nothing.
  3. Otherwise, before the first change to an existing file in this run, copy
     it with `cp -p` to ROOT/.compliance-backup/PATH (create the folders,
     never overwrite an existing backup), then apply the fix:
       mode    `chmod MMMM PATH` with the wanted mode as 4 digits
       line    append TEXT as a line (add a missing final newline first;
               create the file if needed)
       noline  keep only non-matching lines (note: `mktemp` files are 0600,
               write the result back over the original so its mode survives)
       setting replace the first `KEY` line by `KEY VALUE`, or append
               `KEY VALUE` if there was none
       absent  remove the file
     and evaluate the rule again. If it passes print `FIXED ID (SEV): FIXTEXT`
     where FIXTEXT is `chmod MMMM PATH`, `appended line to PATH`,
     `removed N line(s) from PATH`, `set KEY=VALUE in PATH` (literally
     `set KEY=VALUE in PATH`) or `removed PATH`; if not print
     `STILL FAILING ID (SEV): MSG`.
The last line is `summary: pass=P fixed=F waived=W failed=X`. P counts PASS,
F counts FIXED (or WOULD FIX in a dry run), W counts waived, X counts FAIL in
check and CANNOT FIX / STILL FAILING in enforce. The exit status is 1 when
X is above 0, or, in a dry run or in `check`, when any rule failed; otherwise 0.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh [--dry-run] check|enforce ROOT RULES NOW [WAIVERS]`
on stderr, exit 2. Unreadable files: `cannot read FILE`, exit 2.
concepts: policy as data: rules, severities, waivers with an expiry
check, enforce and dry-run on the same rule engine
reading permissions with ls -ld and comparing octal modes
back up before changing, verify after changing

title: The Migration Runner
story:
The storm-week schema change was applied by hand on three of the four
database servers, in a different order on each, and one of them ran the
`add-email` step twice. Theo swears he only edited the file "a little" after
it was deployed. Mara's rule from now on: schema changes are numbered files,
applied in order, recorded in a ledger with a fingerprint, never applied
twice, never silently edited afterwards, and always paired with a way back.
She needs the tool that enforces all of it.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a migration runner.

  solution.sh DIR LEDGER status
  solution.sh DIR LEDGER up [--dry-run] [--allow-out-of-order] [TARGET]
  solution.sh DIR LEDGER down [N]
  solution.sh DIR LEDGER verify

DIR holds migration files named `NNN-NAME.up` and `NNN-NAME.down`: NNN is
exactly three digits (the id), NAME matches `[a-z0-9-]+`. Other files are
ignored. Two `.up` files with the same id print
`duplicate migration id NNN` to stderr and exit 2. A `.down` file is
optional.

LEDGER records what has been applied, one line per migration: `ID SUM NAME`,
where SUM is the first number printed by `cksum` for the `.up` file (read as
`cksum < FILE`). A missing ledger means nothing is applied. Migrations are
executed with the command `dbexec FILE` (a stub): exit status 0 is success.

Definitions: a migration is APPLIED when its id is in the ledger and its
`.up` file still has the recorded SUM; MODIFIED when the id is in the ledger
but the SUM differs; MISSING when the ledger has the id and DIR has no `.up`
file for it; PENDING when only the file exists.

status: one line per id found in DIR or in the ledger, in ascending id order:
  printf '%s %-14s %s\n' ID NAME STATE
with STATE one of `applied`, `MODIFIED`, `MISSING`, `pending` (for a MISSING
migration the NAME comes from the ledger). Exit 0.

up: first check the history, and refuse with exit 3 before running anything:
  `refusing to migrate: ID was modified after it was applied`
  `refusing to migrate: ID is missing from DIR`
  `refusing to migrate: ID is older than the newest applied migration (NEWEST)`
    (a pending id lower than the highest id in the ledger; the check is
     skipped with --allow-out-of-order)
Report the first problem found, checking ledger entries in id order first,
then the pending ones in id order. Then run the pending migrations in
ascending id order, up to and including TARGET (a three-digit id that must
exist in DIR as a `.up` file, otherwise `unknown migration TARGET`, exit 2):
  run `dbexec DIR/NNN-NAME.up`; on success append `ID SUM NAME` to the ledger
  at once and print `applied ID NAME`; on failure print
  `FAILED ID NAME (exit E)` to stderr and stop with exit 1: what already
  succeeded stays recorded and nothing after it runs.
Finish with `up complete: N applied`, or `nothing to do` when nothing was
pending (up to TARGET). With --dry-run run nothing, write nothing, print
`would apply ID NAME` for each pending migration and finish with
`up complete: N pending (dry run)` (or `nothing to do`).

down [N] (N defaults to 1, positive integer) reverts the N most recently
applied migrations, highest id first. For each: the `.down` file must exist
(else `no down migration for ID` to stderr and stop with exit 1); run
`dbexec DIR/NNN-NAME.down`; on success remove its line from the ledger
(rewrite the ledger through a temporary file and `mv`) and print
`reverted ID NAME`; on failure print `FAILED ID NAME (exit E)` to stderr, stop,
exit 1. If fewer than N are applied revert all of them; with nothing applied
print `nothing to revert`.

verify: print one line `MODIFIED ID NAME` or `MISSING ID NAME` per problem
in ascending id order and exit 3, or `OK: N migrations verified` (N = ledger
entries) and exit 0.

Wrong arguments: `usage: solution.sh DIR LEDGER status | up [--dry-run] [--allow-out-of-order] [TARGET] | down [N] | verify`
on stderr, exit 2. A DIR that is not a directory: `not a directory: DIR`, exit 2.
concepts: numbered migrations applied in order, once
a ledger with fingerprints: detect edited history
record each success immediately; stop at the first failure
up and down, dry run, and refusing unsafe states

required_patterns.message: Fingerprint each .up file with cksum and compare with the ledger.
Run migrations through dbexec.

title: The Ultimate Deployer
story:
The storm is over, and Mara has one thing left on her list: nobody should
ever have to type a deploy command again. From now on the truth lives in the
git repository, one small manifest per application, and a reconciler makes
the live fleet match it: create what is missing, update what differs,
check that every change is healthy, and put back whatever is not. It must
refuse to run during a freeze, refuse a deploy that changes too much at
once, never run twice at the same time, and leave an audit trail with the
commit it deployed. This is the biggest script you have written so far; it
uses almost everything.
objective:
Write solution.sh, a pull-based deployer.

  solution.sh [--dry-run] [--prune] REPO LIVE NOW

REPO is a git working copy with the desired state: one file per application,
`REPO/apps/NAME.app`. LIVE is a directory with what is deployed: one
`NAME.state` file per application, plus the audit log. NOW is epoch seconds
(a non-negative integer). Both directories must exist
(`not a directory: X`, exit 2).

A manifest and a state file have lines `KEY=VALUE`:
  version=1.5.0     required, `N.N.N` digits
  replicas=3        1..20, default 1
  port=8080         1..65535, default 8080
  order=30          0..99, default 50 (manifests only; lower goes first)
Blank lines and `#` lines are ignored. NAME matches `[a-z0-9-]+`.

Do these steps in this order:
  1. FREEZE: if REPO/FREEZE exists and is not empty print
     `deploy freeze active: FIRST LINE` to stderr, exit 1.
  2. LOCK: create the directory LIVE/.lock with `mkdir`. If that fails print
     `another deploy is running` to stderr, exit 1. Remove it on every exit
     path (trap).
  3. PULL: run `git -C REPO pull --ff-only` (output discarded). On failure
     print `git pull failed, nothing deployed` to stderr, exit 1. Then
     SHA=`git -C REPO rev-parse --short HEAD`.
  4. VALIDATE every manifest before any change. All problems are printed to
     stderr as `invalid manifest apps/NAME.app: MESSAGE` (files in glob
     order, messages in line order, `missing version` last for that file),
     then exit 2: `bad name` (the file name), `bad version 'X'`,
     `bad replicas 'X'`, `bad port 'X'`, `bad order 'X'`, `unknown key 'X'`,
     `missing version`. No applications at all: `no applications in
     REPO/apps` on stderr, exit 2.
  5. PLAN: apps sorted by (order, name). An app is `create` when there is no
     state file, `unchanged` when version, replicas and port all match its
     state file, otherwise `update`. State files without a manifest are
     orphans. Let CHANGES be creates + updates (+ orphans when --prune).
     MAX_CHANGES (environment, default 5, positive integer, else
     `invalid MAX_CHANGES`, exit 2): if CHANGES is larger, print
     `too many changes (N > MAX), refusing` to stderr, exit 1. (With
     --dry-run print `warning: N changes exceed MAX_CHANGES=MAX` to stderr
     instead and carry on.)
  6. APPLY each app in plan order:
     unchanged -> print `unchanged NAME VERSION`.
     Otherwise `deployctl apply NAME VERSION REPLICAS PORT`. If that exits
     non-zero print `FAILED NAME (deployctl exit E)` and move on (failed).
     Otherwise run `healthctl NAME`. Healthy: write NAME.state (three lines,
     `version=`, `replicas=`, `port=`), print `created NAME VERSION` or
     `updated NAME OLD -> NEW`. Unhealthy: for a create run
     `deployctl remove NAME` and print `removed NAME (health check failed on
     create)`; for an update re-apply the OLD version with its old replicas
     and port (`deployctl apply NAME OLDVERSION OLDREPLICAS OLDPORT`), leave
     the state file as it was and print `rolled back NAME NEW -> OLD
     (health check failed)`. Both count as rolled back.
     Every create/update outcome is appended to LIVE/audit.log as
     `NOW SHA ACTION NAME DETAIL RESULT` (ACTION create or update; DETAIL is
     the version for a create and `OLD->NEW` for an update; RESULT ok, failed
     or rolled-back).
  7. ORPHANS (after all apps, alphabetical): without --prune print `orphan
     NAME (not in repo, use --prune to remove)`. With --prune run
     `deployctl remove NAME`, delete its state file, audit it as
     `NOW SHA delete NAME OLDVERSION ok` and print `deleted NAME`.
  8. REPORT: print
     `deploy SHA: created=C updated=U deleted=D rolled-back=R failed=F unchanged=K`.
     If R + F is above 0 also run `notifyctl send "deploy SHA: R rolled back,
     F failed"` and exit 1; else exit 0.
With --dry-run steps 1-5 run as usual (the pull included), nothing is
applied, written or audited, and the output is `unchanged NAME VERSION`,
`would create NAME VERSION`, `would update NAME OLD -> NEW`, `orphan ...`
or `would delete NAME` per app, then
`plan for SHA: create=C update=U delete=D unchanged=K`, exit 0.

Wrong arguments or unknown options: `usage: solution.sh [--dry-run] [--prune] REPO LIVE NOW`
on stderr, exit 2.
concepts: GitOps: desired state in git, a reconciler makes live match
plan, validate, apply, verify, roll back
guards: freeze, lock, change budget
audit trail tied to the deployed commit

Take the deploy lock with mkdir.
Talk to git with git -C REPO so the script does not depend on the current directory.

title: The Grand Finale
story:
The last storm of the season is over. The shop is up, the backups are
fresh, the fleet is quiet, and Mara has been unusually silent for ten
minutes, which for Mara means she is about to say something nice. She slides
her pager across the desk. "Before you take it, one tool. Everything you
built this season, behind one command, so the person on call needs
nothing else: `lantern health`, `lantern backups`, `lantern report`. And
`lantern handover`, which only works when everything is green, because you
never hand someone a pager on a bad night." You pick up your keyboard. This
is the last mission.
objective:
Write solution.sh, the `lantern` operations CLI. Work in the current
directory; all dates are written YYYYMMDD and passed in as TODAY (a valid
calendar date, leap years included) so that nothing depends on the clock.

  solution.sh version
  solution.sh health [SERVICES]
  solution.sh backups TODAY [DIR]
  solution.sh report TODAY
  solution.sh handover TODAY PERSON

version: print `lantern 1.0.0`.

health: SERVICES defaults to `services.conf`: lines `NAME URL` (`#` and blank
lines ignored). For each service run
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' URL
(it prints a three-digit code; a failed connection gives `000`, and curl may
also exit non-zero, which must not stop you). Print for each
  printf '%-8s %s %s\n' NAME CODE LABEL
where LABEL is `ok` for 2xx, `WARN` for 3xx and 4xx, `DOWN` for everything
else (5xx, 000). Then `health: A ok, B warn, C down`. Exit 1 if C > 0, else 0.
An unreadable SERVICES file prints `cannot read SERVICES` to stderr, exit 2.

backups: DIR defaults to `backups`. It holds `NAME-YYYYMMDD.bak` files, each
with a companion `NAME-YYYYMMDD.bak.sum` holding the two numbers that
`cksum < FILE` printed when the backup was made (`SUM SIZE`). Files that do
not match the name pattern, or whose date is not a real date, are ignored.
Only the NEWEST backup of each NAME is examined. MAX_AGE (environment, whole
days, default 7) is the oldest acceptable age. AGE is the number of days from
the backup's date to TODAY. For each NAME in alphabetical order print
  printf '%-10s %s age %dd %s\n' NAME YYYY-MM-DD AGE STATUS
STATUS is the first that applies: `CORRUPT` (a sum file exists but differs
from the current `cksum < FILE` output), `NOSUM` (no sum file), `STALE`
(AGE greater than MAX_AGE), else `ok`. Finally
`backups: N ok, M problems`. Exit 1 if there is any problem. If DIR holds no
valid backup print `no backups found in DIR` to stderr and exit 1.
Date arithmetic: compute day numbers yourself (days_from_civil: shift
January and February to the end of the previous year, then
`era*146097 + yoe*365 + yoe/4 - yoe/100 + doy`), because `date -d` does not
exist everywhere.

report: print
  `LANTERN STATUS YYYY-MM-DD`, `-- services --`, the lines of `health`
  (no summary line), `-- backups --`, the lines of `backups` (no summary
  line), `-- verdict --`, and the verdict word.
The verdict is RED if any service is DOWN, any newest backup is CORRUPT or
STALE, or there are no backups; otherwise AMBER if any service is WARN or any
backup is NOSUM; otherwise GREEN. Exit status 0 for GREEN, 1 for AMBER, 3 for
RED. In the report an unreadable `services.conf` is a RED verdict with the
line `cannot read services.conf` in the services section, and a missing
backups folder is RED with `no backups found in backups`.

handover: PERSON matches `[a-z]+`. `oncall.txt` holds `PERSON since YYYYMMDD`
(missing means nobody). Run the report silently first: if the verdict is not
GREEN print `refusing handover: status is VERDICT` to stderr and exit 3,
changing nothing. If PERSON already has the pager print `PERSON is already on
call` to stderr and exit 1. Otherwise write `PERSON since TODAY` to
oncall.txt, append `TODAY OLD -> PERSON` to handover.log (OLD is `nobody` when
there was none), and print two lines:
  pager handed over: OLD -> PERSON
  Good luck, PERSON. The lantern is yours.

A bad TODAY (not YYYYMMDD or not a real date) or a bad PERSON, an unknown
subcommand, or the wrong number of arguments: print
`usage: solution.sh version | health [SERVICES] | backups TODAY [DIR] | report TODAY | handover TODAY PERSON`
to stderr and exit 2.
concepts: one CLI, many subcommands, shared functions
calendar arithmetic with integers (days from civil)
checksums to verify backups; status codes to classify health
a verdict that gates a risky action

api      404 WARN
health: 0 ok, 1 warn, 0 down

test_cases.name: backups, newest per name, with a boundary age
test_cases.expected_stdout:
dns        2026-11-01 age 11d STALE
mail       2026-11-05 age 7d ok
shop       2026-11-10 age 2d ok
backups: 2 ok, 1 problems

test_cases.name: corrupt and unsummed backups, MAX_AGE from the environment
test_cases.expected_stdout:
dns        2026-11-01 age 11d ok
mail       2026-11-05 age 7d NOSUM
shop       2026-11-10 age 2d CORRUPT
backups: 1 ok, 2 problems

test_cases.name: leap years and new years are counted correctly
test_cases.expected_stdout:
century    1900-03-01 age 45291d STALE
leap       2024-02-28 age 2d ok
newyear    2023-12-31 age 61d ok
backups: 2 ok, 1 problems

test_cases.expected_stdout:
LANTERN STATUS 2026-11-12
-- services --
shop     200 ok
mail     204 ok
-- backups --
mail       2026-11-05 age 7d ok
shop       2026-11-10 age 2d ok

GREEN
